A0.r: For a general bibliography of creation myths, see Alexander N. Am. 278 n. 15. For bibliographies of North American Indian mythologies arranged by areas, see Thompson Tales 272 n. 1; **Feilberg Skabelses og Syndflodssagn; Jewish: Neuman.—Mexican Indian: (Tarascan) Alexander Lat. Am. 85, (Zapotecan) ibid. 87; Guarayú: Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147; Polynesia: Dixon 21 n. 47; Hawaiian: Beckwith Myth 42; Mono-Alu: Wheeler 28, 66f., 70; Easter Is.: Métraux BMB CLX 313; Marshall Is.: Davenport Folk Tales 221f.; Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti 335ff.; New Hebrides: Codrington II 365.—Armenian: Ananikian 20; African: Werner African 127ff., **Frobenius and Fox, (Loango): Pechuël-Loesche 267; Hindu: Penzer I 10; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 338; Icel.: Boberg, MacCulloch Eddic 326; Irish myth: Cross.
A0.p: A general heading for stories in which someone or something creates the world or its beings.

A1.p: Stories that name who the creator of the world is.

A1.1.p: The creator of the world is the sun-god.

A1.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359, (Guarayú): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147.
A1.2.p: The creator of the world is a grandfather figure.

A1.3.p: The creator of the world is a woman made of stone.

A1.4.p: The creator of the world is the god Brahma.

A2.p: Stories in which the world is made by more than one creator.

A2.1.r: Icel.: Boberg, MacCulloch Eddic 327.—Oceanic: Dixon 24; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 42.
A2.1.p: The world is made by three creators working together.

A2.2.r: (Cf. A1270.) Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 115 No. 70.
A2.2.p: The first human couple are regarded as creators of the world.

A3.p: A creative mother is the source of everything that exists.

A5.p: Stories giving the reason why the creator made the world.

A5.1.p: The gods make the earth so that they have a place to rest their feet.

A7.p: Stories about the descendants of the creator.

A10.p: A general heading for stories describing what the creator is like.

A11.p: The creator is invisible and cannot be seen.

A11.1.p: The creator's invisibility is known because no one can stare at the sun, which is his servant.

A12.r: *Lang Myth I 200f., 299; Güntert 324.—Greek: Eisler 396; Egyptian: Maspéro Histoire ancienne des peuples de l’Orient classique 141; Indian (Hindu): Keith 75.—Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 88.
A12.p: The creator is both male and female, either half man and half woman or thought of as both sexes.

A12.1.r: Japanese: Anesaki 222; Hawaii: Henry Ancient Tahiti 345.
A12.1.p: The creators are a male and a female pair.

A13.p: An animal is the creator of the world.

A13.1.p: The creator of the world is an animal, one of the beasts of the field or forest, who shapes the world or its creatures.

A13.1.1.p: The creator of the world is a cow, who makes the earth or its creatures.

A13.2.p: The creator of the world is a bird, who makes the earth, the sky, or living things.

A13.2.1.r: Eskimo: Nelson RBAE XVIII 454; Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 218.
A13.2.1.p: The creator of the world is a raven, who makes the earth or its creatures.

A13.2.2.p: The creator of humankind is an eagle, which makes the first people.

A13.2.3.p: The creator of the world is a black-winged bird, who makes the earth or its creatures.

A13.3.p: The creator of the world is an insect, which makes the earth or living things.

A13.3.1.p: The creator of the world is a spider, which spins or weaves the earth or its creatures.

A13.3.2.r: So. Am. Indian (Lengua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A13.3.2.p: The creator of the world is a beetle, which makes the earth or its creatures.

A13.4.p: The creator of the world is a reptile, which makes the earth or living things.

A13.4.1.p: The creator of the world is a snake, which makes the earth or its creatures.

A13.4.2.p: The creator of the world is a worm, which makes the earth or living things.

A15.p: The creator of the world is a human being rather than a god or animal.

A15.1.p: The creator of the world is a woman.

A15.1.1.p: The creator of the world is an old woman, who makes the earth or people.

A15.2.r: So. Am. Indian (Guaporé River): Levi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 379.
A15.2.p: The creator of the world is a pair of brothers, who together make the earth or people.

A15.3.p: The creator of the world is an old man, who makes the earth or people.

A15.3.1.p: The creator of the world is an old man carrying a staff, who makes the earth or people.

A15.4.p: The creator of the world is a skilled craftsman, who makes the earth or people by working as an artisan.

A15.4.1.p: The creator of the world is a potter, who shapes the earth or people out of clay.

A17.p: The creator of the world is depicted as an angel.

A18.p: Pictures or images showing what the creator looks like.

A18.1.p: The creator is pictured with a dragon's head.

A18.2.p: The creator is pictured with two horns on his head.

A18.3.p: The creator is pictured as a dwarf or very small figure.

A18.4.p: The creator is pictured wearing bear-skin or leaves as clothing.

A18.5.p: The creator is pictured holding a hammer and chisel.

A18.6.p: The creator is pictured holding the sun and moon in his hands.

A19.p: Miscellaneous other features or traits describing the nature of the creator.

A19.1.r: So. Am. Indian: (Cashibo) Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 594.
A19.1.p: The sun and the moon, as a married couple, are the creators of the world.

A19.2.p: The creator is described as having the appearance of a Black person.

A20.p: Where or how the creator himself came into being.

A21.p: The creator comes down from the sky or heavens.

A21.1.r: Daughter of the sky-chief falls from the sky, is caught by birds, and lowered to the surface of the water. She becomes the creator.—*Iroquois: Thompson Tales n. 27.—Cf. Finnish: Kalevala rune 1.
A21.1.p: A woman falls from the sky and becomes the creator or mother of creation.

A21.2.r: Old man with his wife comes from the sky. Are the first couple on earth. Have seven sons and seven daughters. Each son marries a daughter.—Ekoi: Talbot 366.
A21.2.p: An old man who comes from the sky creates the world.

A22.p: The creator emerges out of chaos, a formless or disordered state.

A23.p: The creator arises from the joining of two opposite natural forces, male and female.

A25.p: The creator rises up from beneath, from the center of the spiritual world, and then creates the world.

A25.1.r: So. Am. Indian (Chibcha): Kroeber BBAE CXLIII (2) 908, (Aymara): Tschopik BBAE CXLIII (2) 570.
A25.1.p: The creator comes up out of a lake.

A26.p: The creator comes from a particular direction.

A26.1.p: The creator of the world is said to come from the east.

A27.p: The creator is born from an egg.

A30.r: Inca: Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 315; Tahiti: Henry 342; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 45.
A30.p: The creator has companions who accompany or help him.

A31.p: The creator's grandmother appears, mentioned only in passing during the creation story.

A32.p: The creator has a family, such as children or a wife.

A32.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—So. Am. Indian: (Chibcha): Kroeber BBAE CXLIII (2) 908.

A32.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—So. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 281.

A32.3.1.r: So. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 281.
A32.3.1.p: The creator's son seduces the creator's wife.

A32.3.2.r: So. Am. Indian (Guarayú): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147.
A32.3.2.p: The creator, drunk on a drink he has invented, beats his wife.

A33.p: An animal is the creator's companion.

A33.1.p: A beast, a four-legged wild animal, is the creator's companion.

A33.1.1.r: A63.4.).—*Dh I 98—111 passim, especially 108.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 347.—Kato: Goddard UCal V 183ff.
A33.1.1.p: The creator is accompanied by a dog.

A33.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Sumatra: Dixon 160; Samoa, Tonga: ibid. *164 n. 33, 34.
A33.2.p: A bird is the creator's companion.

A33.3.p: An insect is the creator's companion.

A33.3.1.p: God sends a bee to secretly overhear the devil's plans.

A33.4.p: The creator has other animal companions not listed in the more specific categories.

A33.4.1.r: So. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 281.
A33.4.1.p: An armadillo is the creator's companion.

A36.p: The creator's companions are a unicorn, a phoenix, a tortoise, and a dragon.

A37.p: Two or more beings together create the world.

A37.1.p: The falcon and the crow are named together as the two beings who jointly created the world.

A38.p: Heavenly bodies serve as companions who help the creator in making the world.

A38.1.p: The sun and the moon are named as the creator's companions who help make the world.

A40.p: The creator consults advisers before or during the work of creation.

A41.p: Human beings are said to have advised God on the creation.

A42.p: Angels are said to have advised God on the creation.

A42.1.p: The seraphim, a high order of angels, are named as the creator's advisers.

A42.1.1.p: God takes counsel with two angels about how to create the world.

A42.2.p: God consults Mercy, who sits at his right hand, and Justice, who sits at his left, about creating.

A43.p: The devil is said to have advised God on the creation.

A44.p: The Torah, the Jewish sacred law, is named as God's adviser in creating the world.

A45.p: The souls of pious people are said to advise the creator.

A50.r: *Dh I 1—89 passim, 172ff.—Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Persian: Carnoy 261f., 275.—Banks Island: Dixon 106.
A50.p: Two opposing creators, one good and one evil, each make part of the world and fight over it.

A50.1.p: The good and the evil creator each make angels and devils, respectively.

A51.p: The devil or devils are created, often by an evil creator or as part of a rivalry in creation.

A52.p: Angels are created, in some accounts by the creator and in others by other beings.

A52.0.1.p: Angels are created specifically to carry out God's will.

A52.0.2.p: Gods that have fallen from high status become angels.

A52.0.3.p: Angels existed before the world was created.

A52.0.4.p: Angels are the transformed souls of pious people who have died.

A52.0.5.p: God makes angels out of three elements, such as earth, water, and fire. This is one version of how the angels were created at the beginning of the world.

A52.0.6.p: God creates angels simply by speaking words, so the angels come into being from what he says.

A52.0.7.p: God shakes water drops off his finger, and the drops turn into angels. In the same story, Lucifer copies God and makes devils.

A52.0.8.p: God strikes one small stone against another to create angels. In the same story, Lucifer makes devils by imitating this.

A52.1.p: A heading for stories in which particular angels are each created separately, often from a specific material.

A52.1.1.p: God creates the angel of death as a separate being.

A52.1.2.p: The angel Michael is created out of fire.

A52.1.3.p: The angel Gabriel is created out of snow.

A52.1.4.p: The angel Raphael is created out of water.

A52.1.5.p: An angel of destruction is created out of hail and fire.

A52.2.p: A heading for stories about when during the creation week the angels were made.

A52.2.1.p: The angels are created on the first day of creation.

A52.2.2.p: The angels are created on the second day of creation.

A52.2.3.p: The angels are created on the third day of creation.

A52.2.4.p: The archangels are created on the first day of creation, and the ordinary angels on the third day.

A52.2.5.p: The angels are created on the fifth day, together with the other winged creatures.

A52.3.p: A heading for stories about the substances from which angels are made, such as fire, water, and snow.

A54.p: A heading for stories about angels who rebel against God or against the order of creation.

A54.1.p: The angel of the sea rebels when the world is being created, and God puts him to death.

A60.r: Jewish: Neuman; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 315f.—Borneo: Dixon 170; Melanesian: *Codrington JAI X 293; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 45.—So. Am. Indian (Toba, Mataco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 368f.—India: *Thompson-Balys.
A60.p: An evil opponent tries to spoil or undo the creator's work at the time of creation.

A61.p: Coyote, a trickster figure, interferes with or spoils the work of creation. He acts as a marplot, a meddler who undoes or complicates what the creator intends.

A63.r: *Dh I 6—89 passim, 127—205 passim; *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX (Nachträge) 276f.—Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 458f.
A63.p: The devil acts as a marplot, a meddler who disrupts God's work during the making of the world.

A63.1.p: While God is asleep, the devil secretly does work of his own during the creation of the world.

A63.2.r: *Dh I 184f.—Lithuanian: Balys Index 3005; Balys Legends No. 11.
A63.2.p: The devil plots to drown God while the world is being created.

A63.3.p: The devil and God wrestle with each other at the time of creation.

A63.4.r: BP III 199 (Gr. No. 148); Dh I 127—205 passim.
A63.4.p: The devil and God each create animals. God makes the wolf as his dog, and the devil makes goats to destroy things.

A63.4.1.r: devil is unable to find means of protecting himself.—Lithuanian: Balys Index 3082; Balys Legends No. 131ff.
A63.4.1.p: God and the devil torment each other with the creatures they made. The devil pesters God with gnats, and God defends himself with fire and plagues the devil with fleas.

A63.5.p: Lucifer is the cause of the fall of man, leading the first humans into sin.

A63.5.1.p: Satan tempts Adam into sin out of jealousy of him.

A63.6.p: The devil, in the form of a serpent, tempts the first woman to sin.

A63.7.p: A rebel god is said to have created all poisonous things.

A63.8.p: Satan tries to create a world of his own.

A67.p: God makes things and throws them into the air. Whatever his opponent catches becomes bad for humankind, and whatever God catches becomes good for people.

A70.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about the creator, not covered by more specific categories.

A71.r: Greek: cf. Roscher II 1540.—Tehuelche (Patagonia): Alexander Lat. Am. 335.
A71.p: The creator tries to eat his own son, who is a culture hero bringing benefits to people.

A72.r: See A900ff. for work of the transformers, with references.—Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 85; So. Am. Indian: *Métraux RMLP XXXIII 122, BBAE CXLIII (3) 437.
A72.p: An original creator is followed by transformers, demigods who change the first creation into the forms the world has now.

A73.r: Finnish: Kalevala rune 2.—So. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A73.p: The creator, lonely and tired of being alone, begins creation.

A74.p: The creator is reluctant to create at first and must be persuaded or forced to begin.

A74.1.p: God agrees to create the world only on condition that Israel accepts the Torah.

A74.2.p: A creator god regrets having made certain things and wishes he had not created them.

A75.p: A creator is told as the ancestor of the sky (heaven) and the earth, meaning the world's origin is traced back to him.

A77.p: The creator's works continue to exist after he is gone.

A78.p: The creator goes off to make the land of the dead (the afterworld).

A81.p: The creator goes up to the sky to live there.

A84.p: A creator god makes the animals.

A85.p: A goddess-wife and god-husband compete in creating the world, in a contest of making things.

A87.r: So. Am. Indian (Guarayú): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147.
A87.p: The creator becomes drunk from a drink that he himself invented.

A100.p: A deity, meaning a god or divine being in general.

A101.r: Durkheim 274, 409ff.; Leroy La raison primitive 125ff.; Holmberg Gudstron 61ff.; C. Koch Der römische Juppiter.—Semitic: Smith Semites@3 529; Jewish: Neuman; Greek: Fox 153, *Grote I 57f.; Assyrian: Spence 206ff.; Babylonian: ibid. 199ff.; Hindu: Keith 21f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 148, 309; Siberian: Karjalainen FFC XLIV 259, 268ff.; Armenian: Ananikian 11, 14, 37; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 61; Chinese: Ferguson 50, Eberhard FFC CXX 115 No. 70.—Indonesian: Kruyt Archipel 465ff.; Maori: Clark 32; Tahiti: Henry 121, 128; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 45.—African: Frobenius Atlantis X 82, Werner African 123ff.; N. A. Indian: Alexander N. Am. 80, 82, 187, 284 n. 28; So. Am. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93; Africa (Fang): Trilles 130, (Luba): Donohugh V 180.
A101.p: A supreme god who is the chief of all the other gods; often he is not worshipped the way the other gods are.

A101.1.r: (cf. A0). Lowie Primitive Religion 85; Goldenweiser Early Civilization 97; Oldenberg Die Religion des Veda 278.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 326; Armenian: Ananikian 20; India: Thompson-Balys; Tarascan: Alexander Lat. Am. 85.
A101.1.p: The supreme god is also the creator of the world.

A102.p: General qualities or attributes that belong to a deity.

A102.1.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 47 (Odin); Irish Myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.—So. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 173, (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93.

A102.2.r: Jewish: Neuman; Greek: Aeschylus Suppliants line 138.

A102.5.p: A god who is present everywhere at once.

A102.6.p: A god who has no beginning or end and lives forever.

A102.7.p: God is described as holy, set apart and free from sin or imperfection.

A102.8.p: God never sleeps; he remains awake and watchful at all times.

A102.9.p: God cannot be seen by ordinary eyes; he is invisible.

A102.10.p: God is one; there is only a single supreme deity.

A102.11.p: God is pure and without any stain or corruption.

A102.12.p: God is perfect and without any flaw or lack.

A102.13.p: God shows love and kindness toward people.

A102.14.p: God is good and does good to those who live rightly.

A102.15.p: God is modest and does not boast or display himself.

A102.16.p: God is just and punishes wrongdoing fairly.

A102.17.p: God becomes angry and may punish people for their sins.

A102.18.p: God is imperfect: he can die and then be born again.

A102.19.p: God is torn between being just and being merciful when deciding how to treat people.

A103.r: Greek: Grote I 3; Hindu: Keith 50ff., 73ff., 82ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
A103.p: A supreme god who is thought of as a father to gods or people.

A104.p: General heading for stories about how beings or things come to be gods.

A104.1.p: A living person is transformed into a god.

A104.2.p: A dead body is transformed into a god.

A104.3.p: Various ordinary objects are transformed into gods.

A106.r: Hindu: Keith 84; *Penzer I 197; India: Thompson-Balys.—Tarahumare (Mexican Indian): Alexander N. Am. 176; S. Am. Indians (Antioquians): Alexander Lat. Am. 197.—Jewish: Neuman.
A106.p: Good gods and evil gods are in conflict or opposed to one another.

A106.0.1.p: The gods and the demons quarrel with each other over who should rule.

A106.1.p: The wicked gods rise up in rebellion against the good gods.

A106.1.1.p: A goddess rebels against her father because he forbids her to marry.

A106.2.r: Jensen Dania II 180; Olrik ibid. II 67; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3002, Legends Nos. 5, 6; Jewish: *Neuman; Irish: Beal. XXI 323.
A106.2.p: Evil angels rise up in revolt against God.

A106.2.1.p: The rebel devil is thrown down into hell as punishment.

A106.2.1.1.p: The banished devil comes up to earth only on the night of the new moon, when the moon is dark.

A106.2.1.2.p: The demon opposed to God is allowed to visit earth four times a year, but he must reveal who he is and may not deceive people.

A106.2.2.p: Satan falls from heaven after his rebellion against God.

A106.3.p: Beings that God created turn against him and rebel.

A107.r: Babylonian: Spence 74; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
A107.p: There are gods of darkness and gods of light, with darkness regarded as evil and light as good.

A108.p: A god who rules both the living and the dead in the otherworld.

A108.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 60.
A108.1.p: A god who rules over the dead.

A109.p: Miscellaneous motifs about deities that do not fit other categories.

A109.1.p: A god who exists as three persons or aspects together.

A109.2.p: A goddess who is the mother of the Pacific Ocean.

A110.p: How the gods came into being.

A111.p: Who the parents of the gods were.

A111.1.r: (cf. A116.2). **Showerman; Smith Dragon viii; *Holmberg Baum 84ff.—Babylonian: Spence 123ff.; Hindu: Penzer I 270ff., 276, VII 231; India: Thompson-Balys; Hittite: Garstang The Hittite Empire 305ff.; Gaster Thespis 179.—Oceanic: Beckwith Myth 294; So. Am. Indian (Apapocuvú-Guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 122.

A111.3.p: An ancestor from whom the gods descended.

A111.3.0.1.p: A god who has both male and female sexual organs carries the seed from which other gods are born.

A111.3.1.p: A god lives together with his grandfathers, who are themselves divine ancestors.

A111.3.2.p: Sea creatures are the ancestors of a goddess.

A111.3.3.p: A great bird is the ancestor of the gods.

A112.p: Gods are born, told as a general account of how the gods come into being.

A112.1.r: Krappe The Review of Religion (1941); India: Thompson-Balys.
A112.1.p: A god is born from a union between close relatives.

A112.1.1.p: A god is born from a union between a father and his daughter.

A112.1.1.1.p: A goddess of music and dance is born from incest between the god Brahma and his daughter.

A112.2.p: A male creator and a female creator together produce the gods as their children.

A112.3.p: Gods are born from different parts of a creator's body.

A112.4.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 139 (Loki), 324 (Odin, Vili, and Ve), Boberg.
A112.4.p: A god is the son or daughter of a giant.

A112.4.1.p: A god is the son of a giantess.

A112.4.2.p: A goddess is the daughter of a giant.

A112.5.p: A god is born as the son of nine giantesses.

A112.6.p: Several gods are the sons of one supreme god.

A112.7.p: A god is born from a particular part of a parent's body rather than in the usual way.

A112.7.1.p: A god is born from his mother's ear.

A112.7.2.p: A god is born from his mother's armpit.

A112.7.3.p: A goddess is born from her mother's eyes.

A112.7.4.p: A god is born after a pregnancy that lasts much less than the usual time.

A112.8.p: A god is born from the union of an adulterous couple, meaning a relationship outside marriage.

A112.9.p: A god is born to a human woman, so the deity has a human mother.

A112.9.1.p: Lesser spirits, such as elementary nature spirits, are born to a human woman.

A112.10.p: A divine child is abandoned or thrown out right after being born.

A112.11.p: A child is born from a union between a god and a hen, a bird.

A113.r: Babylonian: Spence 93; India: *Thompson-Balys; Irish myth: Cross.
A113.p: Gods are linked with particular animals, which serve as their emblems or sacred creatures.

A114.p: A god comes into being out of some physical object rather than through ordinary birth.

A114.1.r: Aphrodite. Greek: Roscher I 402; *Frazer Pausanias III 544.
A114.1.p: A deity is born from sea-foam.

A114.1.1.p: A goddess is born from the sweat of a rock that is washed by the sea.

A114.1.1.1.p: A god is born from the sweat of another god.

A114.1.1.2.p: Lesser gods come into being from the spittle of a great god.

A114.2.r: Tahiti: Henry 337; Marquesas: Handy 104.—So. Am. Indian (Huamachuco): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 151.
A114.2.p: A god hatches or is born from an egg.

A114.2.1.p: A deity is born in the shape of an egg.

A114.3.p: A deity is born from a skull.

A114.4.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 279, 284.—So. Am. Indian (Tembé): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 122.
A114.4.p: A deity is born from a tree.

A115.p: A deity comes forth or emerges into existence from some source, rather than being born.

A115.1.p: The first deity grows out of primeval chaos, the formless void at the start of the world.

A115.2.p: A god comes forth out of the earth.

A115.3.p: A deity arises out of mist.

A115.4.p: A deity emerges out of the darkness of the underworld.

A115.5.p: Gods come into being by emerging from a place above and a place below, rising up into existence from both directions.

A115.6.p: A deity comes into existence by arising from a shell of darkness where it has lain for millions of ages.

A115.7.p: Gods come out of a hole in a tree.

A116.r: *Harris Twins, Boanerges, Picus who is also Zeus; Krappe Etudes de mythologie 137ff.; Güntert Weltkönig 253ff.; S. Eitrem Die göttlichen Zwillinge bei den Griechen (Christiania 1902); H. A116.p: Two gods who are twins appear in the myth, as a pair of divine brothers or siblings born together.

A116.1.p: Of a pair of divine twins, one is a mortal human and the other is an immortal god.

A116.2.p: Two or three goddesses who are twins or form a set of three sisters appear together as a divine group.

A116.2.1.p: A god has twin daughters, who are goddesses.

A117.p: Ordinary mortal humans become gods after death or through some transformation.

A117.1.p: The first humans were created with eternal life and, as a result, they became gods.

A117.2.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Maori: Clark Maori Folk Tales 167.
A117.2.p: A mortal is taken up to heaven and made into a god.

A117.3.p: Spirits become gods when they reach extreme old age.

A117.4.p: A mortal is transfigured into a god while on a mountaintop.

A117.5.p: Gods are the spirits of dead people who have been deified, that is, worshipped as gods after dying.

A118.p: A deity creates itself, arising without any parent or outside maker.

A119.p: Miscellaneous other ways gods come into being that do not fit the other categories in this section.

A119.1.r: Tahiti: Henry 341.—So. Am. Indian (Apapocuvá-Guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 122.
A119.1.p: A god is brought into being through magic.

A119.2.p: A goddess comes into being from the heat of the earth.

A119.3.p: The gods arrive in and settle a particular country or land.

A120.p: Describes what the gods are like in nature and how they look.

A120.1.p: A god can change its shape at will, taking different forms.

A120.2.p: A god who can change his size, growing very large or shrinking very small at will.

A120.3.p: A god who has no physical body and is not made of matter.

A120.4.p: Gods who have no fixed shape or form.

A121.r: H. Gressmann Die hellenistische Gestirn-religion (Leipzig 1925); Gaster Thespis 228f.—Zuñi: Alexander N. Am. 187.
A121.p: The stars are regarded as gods.

A121.1.p: The moon is regarded as a god.

A121.2.r: (cf. A220). Jewish: Neuman; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 217.
A121.2.p: The sun is regarded as a god.

A122.p: A god who is part mortal and part immortal: his hair, skin, flesh, bones and marrow can die, while his mind, voice, breath, eye and ear are immortal.

A123.p: Gods who are monstrous or grotesque in appearance.

A123.1.p: A god whose body is monstrous or unnatural in form.

A123.1.1.p: A goddess with three bodies that stand back to back and look in three directions. Hekate is the example given.

A123.1.2.p: A god whose two bodies are joined together.

A123.1.3.p: A god with one beautiful body and one ugly body.

A123.1.4.p: A god whose body is made of an earthquake, whirlwind, or similar natural force.

A123.1.5.p: A god whose body is made of caterpillars.

A123.1.6.p: A god whose body is a stream of blood.

A123.1.7.p: A goddess with three supernatural bodies made of fire, a cliff, and the sea.

A123.2.p: A god with an unusual or monstrous face.

A123.2.1.p: A god who has many faces.

A123.2.1.1.r: *Krappe Balor 7 n. 24; Usener IV 347ff.; *Frazer Ovid II 95ff; India: Thompson-Balys.
A123.2.1.1.p: A god who has two faces.

A123.2.1.2.p: A god who has three faces.

A123.2.1.3.r: Greek: Roscher “Ianus”; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A123.2.1.3.p: A god is described as having four faces, so it can look in several directions at once.

A123.2.1.4.p: A god is described as having five faces.

A123.2.1.5.p: A god is described as having six faces.

A123.2.2.p: A god has a mouth that is strange or unusual in some way.

A123.2.2.1.p: Maggots crawl out of the mouth of a god who eats people.

A123.2.2.2.p: A goddess is described as having eight mouths.

A123.3.p: A god has eyes that are strange or unusual in some way.

A123.3.1.r: *Krappe Balor 19ff. (Argos); Usener IV 223.—Hindu: Penzer II 46 n. 4, VIII 75, 116, IX 19; Keith 110, 134; Chinese: Werner 144.
A123.3.1.p: A god is described as having many eyes.

A123.3.1.1.r: *Usener IV 224 n. 1; *Frazer Pausanias III 209; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 32; India: Thompson-Balys.

A123.3.1.2.p: A god is described as having a hundred eyes.

A123.3.1.3.p: A god is described as having thirteen eyes.

A123.3.1.4.p: A god is described as having a thousand eyes.

A123.3.1.4.1.p: A goddess is described as having a thousand eyes.

A123.3.2.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 30; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 32.
A123.3.2.p: A god has eyes that flash or shine brightly.

A123.4.p: A god has a head that is monstrous or unusual in form.

A123.4.1.p: A god is described as having many heads.

A123.4.2.p: A god has a head made of stone.

A123.5.p: A god has unusual arms, such as an unusual number or form of arms.

A123.5.1.r: Siva has ten arms.—Hindu: Keith 110; Chinese: Werner 144, 324.—Cf. Greek: Roscher “Briareos”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Irish Myth: Cross.

A123.5.2.p: Wonders are told about a god's arm and fingers.

A123.6.p: A god has unusual legs or feet.

A123.7.p: A god has an unusual color.

A123.7.2.r: Icel.: *Boberg, MacCulloch Eddic 304; W. Golther Deutsche Myth. (1895) 473f. (Hell); Hindu: Keith 126 (Krsna).
A123.7.2.p: A god or goddess is black.

A123.8.p: A goddess has one and a half buttocks.

A123.9.p: Lotus plants grow out of the navel of the god Vishnu.

A123.10.p: A god is wrapped in snakes around the waist, and the moon shines on his forehead.

A123.11.r: Mangaia (Cook Is.): Clark 140; Fiji: Beckwith Myth 76; Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 113.

A124.p: A god is luminous, giving off light or glowing.

A124.0.1.p: A god has a face that shines with light.

A124.1.p: A god has an eye that blazes like fire.

A124.3.p: A goddess has a body full of fire.

A124.4.p: God's radiance shines on the face of Moses.

A124.5.p: God appears in the form of a comet.

A125.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Samoa: Henry 346.
A125.p: A god appears in human form. This form is assumed in most mythologies.

A125.1.p: A war goddess appears as an ugly old woman.

A125.1.1.p: A war goddess appears as a woman with red coloring.

A125.2.p: A god is described as having a red beard.

A125.3.p: A god is described as having teeth made of gold.

A125.4.r: So. Am. Indian (Huarochiri): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 169.
A125.4.p: A goddess is described as being extremely beautiful.

A128.r: Egyptian: Müller 92ff.; Jewish: Neuman; Greek: Argonautica IV line 984 (Chronos); India: Thompson-Balys.
A128.p: A god is described as having lost a body part or is otherwise physically maimed.

A128.1.r: Hödhr.—Icel.: Boberg, De la Saussaye 268.—India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 284.

A128.2.r: Odin.—Harrison (Jane E.) Prolegomena to the Study of Greek Religion 194; Holmberg Finno-Ugric 179.—Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: Boberg, De la Saussaye 226, MacCulloch Eddic 21; Jewish: Neuman.
A128.2.p: A god has only one eye.

A128.2.1.p: A one-eyed god has an eye that casts a harmful evil glare.

A128.2.2.p: A one-eyed god has a single eye covered by a lid that is lifted with a polished handle passing through it.

A128.3.p: A god has no legs or arms and is held up or carried by an animal.

A128.3.1.p: A god has only one leg or foot.

A128.4.r: *Krappe Études 11ff.—Icel.: Boberg, MacCulloch Eddic 21 (Tyr); Irish myth: Cross.
A128.4.p: A god has only one hand, the other having been cut or bitten off.

A128.5.p: A god is lame and walks with difficulty.

A128.5.1.p: A lame god wears a thick iron shoe or boot.

A131.r: *De Visser Die nicht menschengestaltigen Götter der Griechen (Leiden 1903).—Egyptian: Müller 15ff.—Mexican: Alexander Lat. Am. 57ff.—Irish myth: Cross.
A131.p: Gods are described as having animal characteristics in their appearance.

A131.1.r: Babylonian: Spence 151 (Dagon); Assyrian: ibid. 216; Jewish: Neuman.—Samoa: Beckwith Myth 76.
A131.1.p: A god is part man and part fish.

A131.2.r: Hindu: Penzer II 99ff., 125 n. 1, 147 n. 1, 170, III 155 n. 2, V 196, VII 131, IX 1.
A131.2.p: A god has an elephant's face.

A131.3.p: A deity has the head of an animal.

A131.3.1.p: A deity has a cat's head.

A131.3.2.p: A goddess who has the head of a pig.

A131.3.3.p: A god who has the head of a ram.

A131.4.p: A god who wears the skin of a tiger.

A131.5.p: A god who has the feet of a goat.

A131.8.p: A goddess who has the teeth of a pig, such as tusks.

A132.r: *De Visser Die nicht menschengestaltigen Götter der Griechen (Leiden, 1903).—Egyptian: Müller 15ff.; Chibcha: Alexander Lat. Am. 204 (fox, bear); Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: *Krappe “Far Eastern Fox Lore” CFQ III (1944) 124ff.; Jewish: Neuman.
A132.p: A god who appears or takes the form of an animal.

A132.0.1.p: A god who changes into a series of different animals one after another.

A132.0.1.1.p: A god who takes the shape, one after another, of ants, a scorpion, and a cobra.

A132.0.1.2.p: A god who takes three forms in turn: a gecko, a shark, or a priest.

A132.1.r: Smith Dragon 85.—Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Penzer X 240 s. v. “Nagas”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 139.—Fiji: Beckwith Myth 138, 316.
A132.1.p: A god who takes the form of a snake.

A132.1.1.p: A snake-god who has children that are snakes.

A132.2.r: Chinese: Werner 325ff.; Hindu: Penzer II 73, 197 n. 2, IV 126, VIII 44; India: Thompson-Balys.
A132.2.p: A monkey who is worshipped or regarded as a god.

A132.3.p: A god or goddess who takes the form of a horse or other equine animal.

A132.3.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A132.3.1.p: A god who takes the form of a horse.

A132.3.1.1.p: A god who takes the form of a mule.

A132.3.2.p: A goddess who takes the form of a horse.

A132.3.3.p: A god who takes the form of a donkey or ass.

A132.4.p: A god who takes the form of a stag or deer.

A132.5.p: A god or goddess who takes the form of a bear.

A132.6.p: A deity who takes the form of a bird.

A132.6.1.p: A god who takes the form of a bird.

A132.6.2.p: A goddess who takes the form of a bird.

A132.6.3.p: A god who takes the form of a rooster.

A132.6.4.p: Goddesses who catch flies, appearing as fly-catching figures.

A132.6.5.p: A god who takes the form of a pigeon or dove.

A132.7.p: A god who takes the form of a pig.

A132.8.p: A god who takes the form of a dog or wolf.

A132.9.p: A god who takes the form of a bull.

A132.9.1.p: A cow regarded as a god.

A132.10.p: A god who takes the form of a tiger.

A132.11.p: A god who takes the form of a seal.

A132.12.p: A god who takes the form of an eel.

A132.13.p: A god who takes the form of a fish.

A132.14.p: A god who takes the form of a ram.

A132.15.p: A god who takes the form of a tortoise or turtle.

A133.p: A god who is of enormous size, far larger than ordinary beings.

A133.1.p: A giant god who drinks so much that lakes are emptied.

A133.2.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 30; Irish myth: Cross.
A133.2.p: A giant goddess who straddles the whole land, with one foot in the north and the other in the south.

A133.2.1.r: Güntert Weltkönig 293ff.; Hopkins JAOS XVI Proc. cxlvii.
A133.2.1.p: A giant god is so vast that he crosses the whole world in just three strides.

A133.2.2.p: The sky is pictured as the throne of God, and the earth as the footstool under his feet.

A133.3.p: A giant serves as an attendant or servant among the gods.

A134.r: Japanese: Anesaki 229; Hindu: Penzer I 144 n. 2.
A134.p: A god who is very small in size, a dwarf deity.

A135.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 29f.; Maori: Beckwith Myth 243.
A135.p: A god or goddess who eats human beings.

A136.p: Gods who travel by unusual means of transport, such as strange animals or vehicles.

A136.1.p: A god rides on an unusual animal instead of an ordinary mount.

A136.1.1.p: A god rides on a wild boar.

A136.1.2.p: A god rides a horse that is unusual in some way.

A136.1.2.1.p: Sleipnir, the god Odin's horse, which has eight legs.

A136.1.3.p: A god rides on a bull.

A136.1.4.r: Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) 94ff. (Vishnu on Garuda); Penzer Ocean X 159 s. v. Garuda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A136.1.4.p: A god rides on a bird.

A136.1.4.1.p: A god rides on a swan.

A136.1.5.p: A god rides on a flying elephant.

A136.1.6.p: A god rides on a buffalo.

A136.1.7.p: A god rides on a lion.

A136.1.8.p: A goddess travels by flying in the form of a bird, wearing bird feathers.

A136.2.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 22 (Thor’s goats, Freya’s cats), 109 (Frey’s boars); Greek: *Frazer Pausanias IV 142 (dragons).
A136.2.p: A god's or goddess's wagon or chariot is pulled by unusual animals.

A136.2.1.p: A goddess's chariot is pulled by a team of sparrows.

A136.2.2.p: A goddess's chariot is pulled by a horse with only one foot.

A136.3.p: A god travels through the air in a chariot.

A136.3.1.p: The god's chariot is made of fire and pulled by four fiery horses.

A137.p: Descriptions or depictions of what gods look like in pictures or images.

A137.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: Boberg; Gaster Thespis 135, 363.
A137.1.p: A god is shown carrying a hammer.

A137.1.1.p: A god is shown carrying an axe, a variant of the hammer-bearing god.

A137.2.p: A god is shown carrying a club.

A137.3.p: A god is shown with a wheel.

A137.3.1.p: A wheel is used as a symbol for a god.

A137.3.1.1.p: The swastika, a cross with hooked arms, is used as a symbol of a god.

A137.4.p: A god or goddess is shown carrying a basket.

A137.4.1.p: A god carries his brothers and sisters on his back inside a basket.

A137.5.p: A god or goddess is shown holding a cornucopia, a horn overflowing with fruit and plenty.

A137.6.p: A god is shown sitting squatting down rather than standing or enthroned.

A137.7.p: A bull is shown with three cranes, as a depiction of a god.

A137.8.p: The smallpox deity is shown riding naked on a donkey, holding a broom and a swing, with half a winnowing fan as an umbrella.

A137.9.p: A goddess is shown riding a drake (male duck), attended by eight chief snakes and wearing snake jewels.

A137.10.p: A god is shown as a king, with the whole world as his kingdom.

A137.11.p: A god is shown appearing within a cloud.

A137.12.p: A god is shown as a bridegroom.

A137.13.p: A god is shown as a priest.

A137.14.p: A god is pictured carrying a weapon as his defining attribute.

A137.14.1.p: A god is pictured holding a bow made of fire.

A137.14.1.1.p: A god is pictured shooting an arrow made of flames from a fiery bow.

A137.14.2.p: A god is pictured with spears that burn like torches.

A137.14.3.p: A god is pictured using clouds as his shield.

A137.14.4.p: A god is pictured wielding a sword made of lightning flashes.

A137.15.p: God is pictured seated on a lofty throne with angels around him.

A137.16.p: God is pictured as a meteor or shooting star.

A137.17.p: God is pictured as existing behind or within seven layers of fire.

A137.18.p: God is pictured as an old man with a long white beard and white moustache.

A138.p: God has a secret name that may not be spoken or known.

A139.p: Miscellaneous traits of the appearance and nature of the gods that do not fit other categories.

A139.1.p: Gods, as supernatural beings, are known by many different names.

A139.2.p: A god uses a tortoise as his footstool.

A139.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 136.
A139.3.p: A god takes the form of a dragon.

A139.5.p: God's voice has notable physical power.

A139.5.1.p: God's voice is so powerful that it shatters a mountain.

A139.6.p: God's spoken words have notable effects or power.

A139.7.p: The gods are said to give off a distinctive, recognizable smell.

A139.8.p: A god takes the form of an ordinary object rather than a person.

A139.8.1.p: A god appears in the form of a tree trunk.

A139.8.2.p: A goddess appears in the form of a coral reef.

A139.8.3.p: A goddess's head is represented by the smoldering fire of a volcano.

A139.8.4.p: A wind god takes the form of a kite.

A139.8.5.p: A goddess takes the form of a tree.

A139.8.6.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 2, Chap. I passim.
A139.8.6.p: A god appears in the form of an image or statue.

A139.9.p: Gods have unusual bodily features that set them apart from humans.

A139.9.2.p: Gods bleed a fluid called ichor instead of blood, so they can be wounded but not killed.

A139.9.3.p: Gods are covered in red and yellow feathers.

A139.10.p: A god has countless different forms or natures.

A139.11.p: Gods are recognized by natural signs linked to their worship, such as a particular color or scent.

A139.12.p: A god endures a great deal of suffering patiently.

A139.13.p: A goddess has a quick, moody, changeable temper.

A139.14.p: A god is ugly in appearance.

A139.15.p: A god is greedy, always wanting more.

A140.p: Gods work as craftsmen or laborers, doing manual work like humans.

A141.p: A god works as a skilled craftsman, making things with his hands.

A141.1.r: Icel.: Boberg; Greek: Fox 207; Africa (Luba): Donohugh Africa V 180.
A141.1.p: God creates mechanical figures that move on their own, and brings them to life.

A141.2.p: God builds a temple in heaven and later brings it down to earth.

A141.3.p: God drills a hole into Hell, so that great heat rises up and warms the earth.

A141.4.p: God lays the foundations of the earth.

A142.r: Greek: Fox 206; Gaster Thespis 154ff.; *Krappe Archiv f. d. Studium d. neueren Sprachen CLVIII—CLXI passim.; Norse: Herrmann Nordische Mythologie 115ff.; Lithuanian: Gray 330; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
A142.p: A god who works as a smith, making metal goods for the gods.

A142.1.p: A god who works as a brazier, making bronze or copper vessels for the gods.

A143.p: A god who works as a carpenter or wright, building things out of wood.

A144.p: A god who acts as physician to the other gods, healing them.

A145.p: Gods who serve as champions, fighting on behalf of the gods.

A150.p: The everyday activities and routines of the gods.

A151.p: The dwelling place of the gods, a home where they live; such places are often imagined as paradises like Elysium, Avalon, or an earthly paradise.

A151.0.1.p: A god's home where he is the only living being.

A151.0.2.p: The dwelling place of a god is unknown to anyone.

A151.1.p: The gods live on a high mountain.

A151.1.1.r: Irish myth: Cross.—Cheyenne: Alexander N. Am. 123, 127; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 39.
A151.1.1.p: The gods live inside a hill.

A151.1.2.p: The gods live in a cave.

A151.1.3.p: The gods live in the crater of a volcano.

A151.1.4.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 64, 67; Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 31.
A151.1.4.p: The gods live up in the clouds.

A151.2.r: Hindu: Penzer I 66 n. 1, 68, 96, II 34, III 5, 24, 138, VI 82, VII 129, 148, VIII 73, 165, 170, IX 21, 87 n. 4; Irish myth: Cross; Babylonian: Ungnad Das Gilgamesch Epos IX 163, cf. 148, 163ff.; Jewish: Neuman; Gaster Thespis 171, Oldest Stories 48.
A151.2.p: The gods have a garden where they live or spend time.

A151.3.p: The gods make their home under the sea.

A151.3.1.p: The gods live in the spring season, or in a place of springtime.

A151.3.2.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 67f., 85; Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 178.
A151.3.2.p: The gods have their home on an island.

A151.4.1.p: A god's palace or temple is made of jewels.

A151.4.2.p: The gods' palace has a door at each end, so the sun can pass through it on its daily journey.

A151.4.3.p: The gods live in golden mansions.

A151.4.4.p: A god's house has pillars made of the bones of a dead chief.

A151.5.p: The gods live in a city of their own.

A151.6.p: A god lives on a heavenly body such as the sun, moon, or Milky Way.

A151.6.2.p: The sun and moon are the dwelling places of gods.

A151.7.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1059.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 36f.
A151.7.p: A deity lives in a forest.

A151.7.1.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1319.—India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 136.
A151.7.1.p: A deity lives inside a tree.

A151.7.1.1.p: A god's home is beneath the tree of life.

A151.8.p: A god lives in a sea of milk.

A151.9.p: A god once lived among humans before leaving to dwell elsewhere.

A151.10.p: A god stays fixed at one particular place on earth.

A151.12.p: A god's place of landing, namely an island where the god first comes down or settles.

A151.13.p: A god lives alone in complete darkness, apart from anyone else.

A151.14.p: Assorted other places where gods are said to live, not covered by the more specific motifs.

A152.p: God has a throne, a seat of power and majesty in the heavens.

A152.1.p: God has two thrones, one for showing mercy and one for judging justice.

A152.2.p: Flames burn all around God's throne.

A152.3.p: God's throne moves about because it stands on wheels.

A152.4.p: Attendants stand or serve around God's throne.

A152.5.p: A heavenly curtain hangs around God's throne, screening it.

A152.6.p: A footstool is placed in front of the divine throne.

A152.7.p: Certain beings are said to carry or bear God's throne on their shoulders.

A152.8.p: The heavenly throne has the face of Jacob engraved on it.

A152.9.p: God's throne grows hot because of what people do down on earth.

A153.r: Ambrosia.—Smith Dragon 188; Hindu: Keith 106, Tawney I 425, 478; India: Thompson-Balys; Greek: Roscher I 280.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 67; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 313; Irish myth: Cross.
A153.p: Gods have food, and this motif covers the food that the gods eat.

A153.1.p: Someone steals the food of the gods, the ambrosia that gives them their special qualities.

A153.2.p: A special food eaten by the gods makes them immortal and never-dying.

A153.2.1.r: Irish Myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Greek: Grote I 43.
A153.2.1.p: Eating the gods' food makes a person or creature grow supernaturally fast or large.

A153.3.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 23; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 137.—So. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 178.
A153.3.p: The gods hold feasts or banquets.

A153.3.1.p: The Moon steals food from the gods' banquet.

A153.3.2.p: The sun, moon, wind, thunder and lightning are gathered at a feast hosted by their uncle and aunt among the gods.

A153.4.p: A magical food restores youth or vitality to the gods, keeping them young.

A153.5.p: The gods' food is the meat of a magical cow that never runs out and provides plenty.

A153.6.p: An explanation for why the gods will accept only blood as an offering or food.

A153.7.p: The gods prefer their food cooked rather than raw, and an explanation is given for this taste.

A153.8.p: Some gods eat human flesh, so they are cannibals.

A153.9.p: The gods live on air alone and need no ordinary food.

A154.r: Greek: Grote I 43; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 54, 86, 172, 313; Hindu: Penzer X 243 s. v. “nectar”; Keith 46 and passim; India: *Thompson-Balys; Persian: Carnoy 265; Chinese: Ferguson 130.
A154.p: The drink that the gods consume or enjoy, as a general category.

A154.1.r: (cf. D1040). Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 31, 54; Hindu: Keith 46.
A154.1.p: A magical drink that makes the gods immortal, so they never die.

A154.2.p: The god Odin steals a magical mead that grants poetic inspiration or wisdom and carries it away.

A154.3.p: The gods are the first to discover how to make alcoholic drink.

A154.4.p: Milk is the drink of the gods, and the myth tells of it being theirs.

A155.p: The animals that belong to the gods, as a general category.

A155.1.p: The sun owns a herd of cattle that are kept as his own special animals.

A155.2.r: (cf. A171.1). Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 216; Snorra Edda Gylf. XV.
A155.2.p: The gods own horses, which are special or magnificent animals.

A155.3.p: The gods own birds, which are special or magical animals belonging to them.

A155.4.p: The gods keep mosquitoes as household pets.

A155.5.p: A god owns an elephant that is his special animal.

A155.5.1.p: A god has an unusually huge elephant.

A155.6.p: A goddess sleeps on a bed made of snakes.

A155.7.p: The gods keep dairy cattle and water buffaloes of their own, as ordinary herders do.

A156.p: The gods own valuable treasures and luxury items of the kind people prize.

A156.1.p: The gods wear or own jewels.

A156.3.p: A god possesses a scepter, the staff of rulership.

A156.4.p: A god owns a seal, used to stamp or authenticate documents.

A156.5.r: Virgil Aeneid X line 635; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 77, 916.
A156.5.p: The gods travel in a chariot.

A157.p: The gods own and use weapons.

A157.1.r: Blinkenberg The Thunder Weapon 1911; Hdwb. d. d. Aberglaubens II 325; Saintyves Corpus du Folklore Prehistorique en France et dans les Colonies Françaises (1934—36) I—III; J. Balys Tautosakos Darbai III 1937 223ff.; Jewish: *Neuman.
A157.1.p: A god's weapon is a thunderbolt, here a stone axe that the Thunder God hurls down from the sky.

A157.1.1.r: Greek: Fox 159; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 214, 309, II 1060.
A157.1.1.p: The thunderbolt itself is regarded as the weapon of the gods.

A157.2.p: A god owns and shoots arrows.

A157.4.p: A god carries a shield for protection in battle.

A157.6.p: A god owns and uses a bow.

A157.7.p: The thunder god wields a hammer as his weapon.

A158.p: The gods have clothing of their own.

A159.p: Miscellaneous details about how the gods live day to day that do not fit the other categories.

A159.1.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 965. C916.2. Animals produced when forbidden drum is beaten.
A159.1.p: A particular deity owns a special drum.

A160.p: The gods relate to one another in various ways, such as through kinship, rivalry, or alliance.

A161.r: Persian: Carnoy 260; Irish myth: Cross; Hindu: Müller 142f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Greek: Grote I 3, 9; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 729.
A161.p: The gods are arranged in a ranking, with some gods holding higher authority than others.

A161.1.p: Control of the universe is divided among the gods, each god ruling a share of it.

A161.2.r: See all references to A101 (Supreme god).
A161.2.p: One god is the king who rules over all the other gods.

A161.3.r: Greek: Grote I 10; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 13, chap. II passim.
A161.3.p: A goddess is the queen who holds the highest rank among the gods.

A161.4.p: One god is in charge of all the male spirits.

A161.5.p: Among the gods, the eldest is the one born first, with the younger gods placed behind him in birth order.

A162.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Grote I 1, 3, 8; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 26ff., 172; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 356, 411; Hindu: Penzer I 197ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 225; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 318, 1104.—Gaster Thespis 115ff., 125.
A162.p: The gods fight or quarrel with one another.

A162.1.r: Jünger (F. G.) Die Titanen (Frankfurt a. M. 1944); Mayer Die Giganten und Titanen in der antiken Sage (Berlin 1887).—Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 11, *42 n. 1, *43 n. 2; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 82, Herrmann Saxo II 97ff; Irish myth: Cross; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 356; Chinese: Werner 159; Hindu: Penzer X 77 s.v. “Asuras”, X 118 s.v. “Daityas”, X 119 s.v. “Danavas”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Samoa: Beckwith Myth 254.
A162.1.p: The gods battle against the giants in a fight between the two divine and giant peoples.

A162.1.0.1.p: The battle between the gods and giants never ends and is fought again and again without final victory.

A162.2.r: Jewish: Neuman; Babylonian and Egyptian: Müller 104; cf. Chinese: Werner 215.
A162.2.p: A god of light fights a dragon that lives in the ocean.

A162.3.r: (cf. A157.1, A189.1.1, A284, A285). *Balys “Donner und Teufel in den Volkserzählungen der baltischen und skandinavischen Völker” Tautosakos Darbai VI (1939) 1—220.
A162.3.p: The thunder god fights a devil in a battle.

A162.3.1.r: Icel.: Thrymskvida; Lappish, Finnish, Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian: *Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI (1939) 33—43.
A162.3.1.p: The devil or ogre steals the thunder god's tools or weapons.

A162.3.2.r: Norwegian, Danish, Swedish, Finnish, Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian: *Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI (1939) 111—128.

A162.4.p: The other gods curse Brahma so that he has no temples built in his honor.

A162.5.p: A god is born again from a human woman in order to take revenge on a giant.

A162.6.p: A battle takes place between a god's servant, a giant, and a plague.

A162.7.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 17, 206; Marquesas: Handy 109; Icel.: Boberg.
A162.7.p: Two gods fight each other one-on-one in single combat.

A162.8.p: The lesser gods rise up in revolt against their chief god.

A163.p: The gods compete against one another in contests.

A163.1.p: The gods play a game against one another.

A163.1.1.p: The gods are said to play a game of chess against one another.

A164.r: Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 964; India: Thompson-Balys.
A164.p: The gods marry one another or take lovers, forming unions among themselves.

A164.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 102; Greek: Grote I 58; Marquesas: Handy 122.
A164.1.p: A god and goddess who are brother and sister marry each other.

A164.1.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; So. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 281.
A164.1.1.p: A god marries his mother, so a mother and son are wed among the gods.

A164.2.p: A god or goddess commits adultery, being unfaithful to a divine spouse.

A164.3.r: Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 186.
A164.3.p: A god has more than one wife at the same time.

A164.3.1.p: The Hindu god Krishna is said to play cards with his three wives.

A164.4.p: Among the gods, women hold power and rule, with a female-led order.

A164.5.p: A goddess has several husbands at the same time.

A164.6.p: A god takes a giantess as his lover.

A164.7.p: A god's wife is jealous of him, often of his other lovers.

A165.r: Greek: Grote I 10, 67; Icel.: *Boberg (A165.3); Jewish: *Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 964f.; Hindu: *Penzer I 200, X 158 s. v. “Ganas”, “Gandharvas”.
A165.p: The gods have attendants and servants who serve them.

A165.1.p: Animals serve a god as attendants.

A165.1.1.r: Grimm Deutsche Mythologie I 122.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 65, Boberg.
A165.1.1.p: Ravens serve a god as attendants.

A165.1.2.p: The eagle is the bird belonging to a god.

A165.1.3.p: A red sea-bird is kept as a pet by a god.

A165.2.r: *Güntert Weltkönig 280; Gaster Thespis 139.—Greek: Fox 191 (Hermes, Iris), Grote I 43; Irish: Beal XXI 319, 336; India: *Thompson-Balys; Jewish: *Neuman; Huichol: Alexander Lat. Am. 122.—Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 31, Henry 164.
A165.2.p: The gods have a messenger who carries their orders to people and other beings.

A165.2.0.1.p: A god's messenger can take on whatever form or appearance he chooses.

A165.2.1.p: Animals act as messengers carrying the gods' messages.

A165.2.1.1.p: Wild beasts act as messengers carrying the gods' messages.

A165.2.1.1.1.p: Wolves are imagined as the dogs or hunting animals of a god, serving as his messengers among wild beasts.

A165.2.1.1.2.p: A tiger serves a god as his messenger or envoy.

A165.2.1.1.3.p: An elephant serves a god as his messenger or envoy.

A165.2.1.1.4.p: Bears serve God as his messengers.

A165.2.1.1.5.p: Leopards serve God as his messengers.

A165.2.1.1.6.p: Lions serve God as his messengers.

A165.2.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Pawnee: Alexander N. Am. 81; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 177.
A165.2.2.p: Birds serve the gods as their messengers.

A165.2.2.1.p: A rooster serves a god as his envoy or ambassador.

A165.2.3.p: Angels serve God as his messengers.

A165.2.4.p: Forces of nature, such as the sun and moon, serve God as his messengers.

A165.3.p: A god serves the other gods by pouring their drink, acting as their cupbearer.

A165.3.1.p: The god who serves as cupbearer to the gods is also the god of metalworking and smithing.

A165.3.2.p: The god who serves as cupbearer to the gods also has power over the waters.

A165.4.p: A being serves the gods as a guard who keeps watch for them.

A165.4.1.p: Demons serve the gods by keeping watch over the earth for them.

A165.5.p: A being serves the gods by guarding the door of their dwelling.

A165.6.r: Siberian, Babylonian, Egyptian: Holmberg Siberian 410; Armenian: Ananikian 30ff.
A165.6.p: A being serves the gods as their scribe, writing down their records.

A165.7.r: (cf. A162). Icel.: Herrmann Nordische Mythologie 279 (Einherjar), Neckel Walhall 68ff; India: Thompson-Balys.
A165.7.p: The gods have an army of beings who fight for them.

A165.8.p: A being serves the gods as their magician, performing magic for them.

A165.9.p: A being serves the gods as their fisherman, catching fish for them.

A166.r: Hindu: Keith 143; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 186.
A166.p: The gods perform dances, sometimes described as dancing with one another or for their own pleasure.

A167.p: The gods gather together in a meeting or assembly.

A167.1.p: The gods meet as a council to discuss matters and make decisions.

A168.r: (cf. A111, A164). Greek: Fox 151ff. passim.—Tahiti: Henry 231; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 311; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 964.
A168.p: The gods are described as a family, with relationships such as parents, children, and siblings among them.

A169.p: Miscellaneous relationships among the gods that do not fit a more specific heading in this group.

A169.1.p: The gods have a judge and a court that hear cases and pass judgment among them.

A170.p: A general heading for actions and deeds that the gods carry out.

A171.p: The gods travel through the air, moving across the sky.

A171.0.1.p: A god drives a chariot across the surface of the waves or sea.

A171.0.2.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 109; Maori: Beckwith Myth 83; So. Am. Indian (Huamachuco): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 151.
A171.0.2.p: A god rises up into heaven.

A171.0.3.p: A god comes down from heaven to the earth.

A171.0.3.1.p: A god comes down from heaven by way of a rainbow.

A171.0.3.2.p: A god comes down from heaven disguised as a shooting star.

A171.1.p: A god rides through the air on a horse that moves as swiftly as the wind.

A171.1.1.p: A god rides through the air in a chariot.

A171.1.2.p: The Valkyries, warrior maidens of Norse myth, ride through both the air and the water on their horses.

A171.2.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 83, Boberg; Greek: Iliad and Odyssey passim.
A171.2.p: A god flies by taking the form of a bird or by wearing bird feathers.

A171.3.p: A god flies inside a column of drifting clouds, accompanied by thunder and lightning.

A172.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Iliad passim; Norse: Herrmann Nordische Mythologie 291ff, Boberg; Gaster Thespis 349; Hindu: Tawney I 412, II 473—477; Jewish: *Neuman.
A172.p: The gods take sides and join in fighting during a battle, affecting its outcome.

A173.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: De Vries FFC XCIV 38ff., Herrmann Saxo II 109ff.; Hindu: Tawney II 581.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 11, 17, 177.
A173.p: The gods lose their power or position for a period of time and are set aside from their rule.

A173.1.p: When a god is absent or removed from power for a time, things such as death and reproduction stop working until the god returns.

A173.2.p: Gods are captured and locked up in prison.

A175.r: Greek: Fox 9; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 20ff.
A175.p: A god brings the chaotic elements of the world into an orderly arrangement.

A175.1.p: A god gives the power of reproduction and fertility to all living things.

A176.r: Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 40.
A176.p: A god establishes rituals, ceremonies, and rules that people must follow.

A177.p: A god steals something, acting as a thief.

A177.1.p: A god is tricked or fooled, or plays tricks himself as a trickster.

A178.p: A god acts as a prophet, foretelling future events.

A179.p: A miscellaneous group of other deeds performed by gods that do not fit the more specific categories.

A179.1.p: A god builds a rath, which is an earthen fort or ringwork.

A179.2.p: A god is given rule over a floating island.

A179.3.p: A god arranges for his enemies to kill him on purpose.

A179.4.p: A god's head is bitten off by a shark.

A179.5.p: A deity is reborn in a new body after dying.

A179.6.p: A god has the power to create human beings.

A179.7.p: A god takes off his earthly clothing and dresses himself in lightning.

A179.8.p: A god hides from the sun by standing in the shadow of a cloud.

A179.9.p: A god plays with a leviathan, a huge sea monster.

A180.r: Irish myth: Cross; Norse: Olrik Kilderne til Sakses Oldhistorie I (1892) 30ff., 32ff.
A180.p: A general heading for stories about how gods deal with, interact with, or relate to human beings.

A181.r: Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus II 20 n. 1, Grote I 36, 53, 108; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 142; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 962; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A181.p: A god takes on the role of a servant or menial worker while living on earth.

A181.1.p: God takes on a humble servant's job on earth and clears the plains (flat open land) of obstacles.

A181.2.p: God works on earth as a farmer, tilling and cultivating the land.

A182.p: God makes himself known or appears directly to human beings.

A182.0.1.p: God does not show himself to people, because humans could not survive the sight of his glory.

A182.0.2.p: Human reason is unable to grasp or understand the true nature of God.

A182.1.p: God discloses hidden secrets or mysteries to human beings.

A182.1.1.p: The household gods speak aloud to explain something that has happened in the house.

A182.2.p: God gives a name to a child.

A182.3.p: God, or an angel acting for him, speaks directly to a human being.

A182.3.0.1.p: God speaks to Moses out of a burning bush.

A182.3.0.1.1.p: An angel speaks to Saint Patrick from a bush that only appears to be burning, not actually on fire.

A182.3.0.2.p: God speaks to a saint while the saint is held in prison.

A182.3.0.3.p: A saint regularly converses with God every Thursday.

A182.3.0.3.1.p: A saint travels to heaven every Thursday, or every day, and talks there with angels.

A182.3.0.4.p: God does not speak to women directly but uses an intermediary to convey his words.

A182.3.1.p: God speaks to a human being to comfort them.

A182.3.2.p: God speaks to a human being to rebuke or scold them.

A182.3.3.p: God speaks to a human being and gives them a blessing.

A182.3.4.p: God speaks to a human being and makes them a promise.

A182.3.4.1.p: God, disguised as a wandering holy man (a fakir), visits a king and gives him advice.

A182.3.4.2.p: God promises a mortal that he and his descendants will prosper.

A182.3.5.p: God gives advice to a mortal speaking with him.

A182.3.6.p: A moon-god, having lost a contest with a mortal, threatens to hold back rain and game animals as revenge.

A183.r: Greek: Odyssey IX line 528, Iliad I 218, et passim; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 2, chap. 1 passim.
A183.p: A god is called upon or prayed to for help by a mortal.

A183.1.p: A male god is invoked from the east and a female goddess from the west.

A184.p: A god is the founder and guardian of certain peoples or nations.

A184.1.p: God watches over and protects the people of Israel.

A185.r: Greek: Fox 33, 170f., 197; Icelandic: Volsunga Saga chap. 13, Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 187f.
A185.p: A god takes special care of certain favored humans.

A185.1.p: A god comes to a mortal's aid in battle.

A185.2.p: A god shields a mortal from harm.

A185.2.1.p: God rescues a man who is asleep from an attacker.

A185.2.2.p: God makes a man's hand stiff so he can no longer torture his captive.

A185.2.3.p: God makes an attacker's sword fall from his hands.

A185.3.p: A god instructs a mortal in some skill or knowledge.

A185.4.p: A god buries a dead mortal.

A185.5.p: A god attends a mortal's wedding.

A185.6.p: A god is a close personal friend of one particular mortal.

A185.6.1.1.p: A god's kiss brings a mortal a painless death.

A185.7.p: God provides food for a human being, showing special care for a favored person.

A185.8.p: A god promises that a destroyed city will be rebuilt and restored.

A185.9.p: God makes a binding agreement or pact with a human being.

A185.10.r: Jewish: Neuman; Oahu (Hawaii): Beckwith Myth 328; Tahiti: ibid. 221; Africa (Fang): Einstein 94.
A185.10.p: A god travels with a human being on a journey and acts as guide.

A185.11.p: God gives a reward to a human being for a pious or devout deed.

A185.12.p: God gives a human being a soul.

A185.12.1.r: Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 188 No. 128.
A185.12.1.p: God brings a dead man back to life by restoring his soul.

A185.12.2.p: God takes away a human being's soul.

A185.13.p: God tests a human being to see how faithful or obedient he is.

A185.14.p: God controls whether or not human beings sin.

A185.14.1.p: God causes human beings to sin.

A185.14.2.p: God keeps a human being from sinning.

A185.15.p: God makes peace between human beings who were at odds.

A185.16.p: God feels pity or compassion for a human being.

A185.17.p: God visits a human being who is sick.

A187.p: Gods and human beings pass judgment on one another.

A187.1.r: Greek: Fox 227, Wienert FFC LVI 36; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 162 (Forseti); Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer I 198ff., II 249, IV 238, 275f., VIII 64, 108 n. 1, 163 n. 1, 184, 215.
A187.1.p: God acts as judge over human beings.

A187.2.r: Icel.: Boberg; Celtic-Norse: FFC LXXXIII, xxxviii-xli.—India: *Thompson-Balys.
A187.2.p: A human being is chosen to settle a quarrel between gods.

A188.r: Babylonian: Gilgamesch Epos VI (Ishtar).—Irish myth: Cross; Norse: Herrmann Saxo Gr. II 238ff., *Boberg; Greek: Fox 29, 157, 199, 211.—Tahiti: Henry 231, Beckwith Myth 37, Porapora (Society Is.): *Beckwith Myth 38; Maori: Clark 148; So. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 154, 165.
A188.p: Gods and goddesses fall in love with human beings.

A188.1.p: A god who is a habitual womanizer or philanderer, pursuing many human lovers.

A188.2.r: Irish myth: Cross (A188.1); Hawaii: Beckwith myth 2, 70, 294, 300; Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 37; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/1010); Easter Is.: Métraux 310; So. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 171; Inca: Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 315.
A188.2.p: The gods are said to be the ancestors of humankind, so people descend from divine beings.

A189.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about how gods interact with mortal humans.

A189.0.1.p: A category label for beings classed as either gods or not-gods, a distinction that marks divine from non-divine beings.

A189.1.p: A mortal person who becomes an assistant or ally to the gods.

A189.1.1.r: Lithuanian, Latvian, Livonian, Estonian, Ukrainian, Polish, and Rumanian: *Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI 53—83, 107f.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1147A; Prussian: Plenzat 60.
A189.1.1.p: A human who helps the thunder god in his work.

A189.2.p: A god is called to appear when a person weeps or cries.

A189.3.p: A man wins a game of dice against a god by cheating.

A189.4.p: A god becomes envious of a human being.

A189.5.p: A goddess's throne shakes when a loyal worshipper suffers some misfortune, signaling her concern for them.

A189.6.p: A deity appears in person to a human after that human has prayed.

A189.7.p: A god determines a newborn baby's destiny and writes it on the baby's forehead.

A189.8.p: A god has accountants who record the good and bad deeds of all people.

A189.9.p: An early age when gods and humans lived together, the gods ruled people, set rules for how they should live, and created many customs.

A189.10.p: Goddesses descend to earth on a silken thread, are offended by a raja (ruler), and cause a drought as a result.

A189.11.p: A god formally adopts a mortal person as a son.

A189.12.p: A goddess protects wild animals from being hunted.

A189.13.p: Humans force gods to hide underground to escape them.

A189.14.p: A god has enemies who oppose him.

A189.15.p: A god makes both humankind and the earth fertile and productive.

A189.16.p: Gods grant divinity to a mortal person, making them a god.

A189.17.p: The night belongs to the gods and the day belongs to humankind, so each has its own period of time.

A190.p: A miscellaneous motif about the gods in general that does not fit a more specific category.

A191.p: A goddess renews her youth and vigor when she grows old.

A191.1.p: The gods are said to have lived for a very long time, far longer than humans.

A192.p: A god dies or leaves the world for good.

A192.1.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 340ff. (at the Doom); Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 110; Tahiti: Henry 231; Chinese: Werner 99, Eberhard FFC CXX 141; Africa: Bouveignes 12.

A192.1.1.p: An older god is killed by a younger god who takes his place.

A192.1.2.p: A god is killed and then eaten.

A192.2.p: A god goes away from the world and leaves humans behind.

A192.2.1.r: Polynesia: Moriori (Chatham Is.), Pora Pora (Society Is.), Samoa: Beckwith Myth 38, 43, *241ff., 254; So. Am. Indian (Apapocuvá-Guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 122.
A192.2.1.p: A deity goes up to heaven or the sky and stays there.

A192.2.1.1.r: Polynesia: Hawaii, Beckwith Myth 220, *241; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/931).
A192.2.1.1.p: A deity goes to live on the moon.

A192.2.2.p: A deity sails away across the sea in a boat.

A192.2.3.p: A deity departs to a home under the sea.

A192.2.4.p: A deity leaves the world rising up in a column of fire.

A192.3.p: A god who has left is expected to come back someday.

A192.4.p: A divine being gives up its divinity and becomes a mortal human.

A193.p: A god dies and then comes back to life.

A515.1.2.p: Two sworn brothers, bound by an oath of friendship, together become culture heroes.

A515.2.r: Irish myth: Cross.—Amazon tribes: Alexander Lat. Am. 311.
A515.2.p: A father and his son together act as culture heroes who bring civilization to the world.

A515.3.p: A culture hero has a blood brother, a close companion sworn to him by a blood bond.

A515.4.p: A culture hero is accompanied by a loyal servant or helper who stays with him faithfully.

A515.5.p: A culture hero fights with or meets his own son without recognizing him.

A516.p: A culture hero is driven out of his community or goes away, and later comes back.

A520.p: General heading on what kind of being a culture hero (demigod) is.

A520.1.p: The culture hero is a god, not merely a human or demigod, who brings culture to people.

A522.p: General heading: an animal serves as the culture hero who brings benefits to people.

A522.1.p: A wild animal, a beast, serves as the culture hero.

A522.1.1.p: A dog serves as the culture hero.

A522.1.1.1.p: A dog acts as the culture hero's watchdog and is named Hound.

A522.1.2.r: Central Algonquian tribes: Thompson PMLA XXXVII 130ff.
A522.1.2.p: A rabbit serves as the culture hero.

A522.1.3.r: N. Am. Indian: Alexander N. Am. 141ff., 298 n. 48.
A522.1.3.p: A coyote serves as the culture hero.

A522.1.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 369, (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484.
A522.1.4.p: A fox serves as the culture hero.

A522.1.5.r: N. Am. Indian: Boas RBAE XXXI 585.
A522.1.5.p: A mink serves as the culture hero.

A522.2.p: A bird serves as the culture hero.

A522.2.1.r: N. A. Indian: Boas RBAE XXXI 646 and passim.
A522.2.1.p: A blue jay serves as the culture hero.

A522.2.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 3, BBAE CXLIII (1) 368.
A522.2.3.p: A hawk acts as the culture hero, the figure who brings useful arts, customs, or the world as people know it.

A522.2.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 3.
A522.2.4.p: An aquatic bird, such as a waterfowl, acts as the culture hero, the figure who brings useful arts, customs, or the world as people know it.

A522.3.p: An animal other than a bird acts as the culture hero, the figure who brings useful arts, customs, or the world as people know it.

A522.3.1.r: Dakota: Dorsey JAFL II 134.—African: Werner African 213.
A522.3.1.p: A spider acts as the culture hero, the figure who brings useful arts, customs, or the world as people know it.

A523.r: Irish myth: Cross; Persian: Carnoy 294; Chinese: Werner 305.
A523.p: A giant acts as the culture hero, the figure who brings useful arts, customs, or the world as people know it.

A523.1.p: The culture hero, who is a giant, carries a giant sword as his weapon.

A524.p: The culture hero owns remarkable or magical possessions, such as special animals or weapons.

A524.1.p: The culture hero owns remarkable or magical animals.

A524.1.1.p: The culture hero owns marvelous dogs with extraordinary abilities.

A524.1.2.p: The culture hero owns marvelous horses with extraordinary abilities.

A524.2.p: The culture hero owns remarkable or magical weapons.

A525.r: Walapai: Alexander N. Am. 180; S. Am. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93; Melanesia: Dixon 122ff.; Polynesia, Micronesia: ibid. 122 n. 1.
A525.p: Culture heroes are of two kinds: some are good and helpful, while others are bad or destructive.

A525.1.p: The culture hero quarrels and fights with his older brother.

A525.2.p: The culture hero, who is a god, kills his own grandfather.

A526.p: The culture hero has notable bodily traits or physical features that set him apart.

A526.1.p: The culture hero can be injured or wounded, so he is not invulnerable.

A526.2.p: The culture hero is a skilled and mighty hunter.

A526.3.p: The culture hero has a beauty spot of irresistible charm, known in the source as a ball seirc.

A526.4.p: The culture hero has three locks of hair, each a different color.

A526.5.p: A culture hero, a semi-divine figure who brings civilization, is described as having seven pupils in each eye and seven toes and seven fingers on each limb.

A526.5.1.p: A culture hero has eyes of two different colors, one brown and one green.

A526.6.p: A culture hero becomes physically twisted or contorted into strange shapes when he is angry.

A526.7.p: A culture hero performs extraordinary feats of strength and skill.

A526.8.p: A culture hero can bend his feet and knees backward.

A526.9.p: Lightning flashes out from under the arms of a hero.

A527.p: A culture hero has various special supernatural powers beyond ordinary human abilities.

A527.1.p: A culture hero shows unusually early mental or physical development as a child.

A527.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 143, 156, (Carib): ibid. 147.
A527.1.1.p: The divine twin heroes, while still very young, make themselves a bow and arrows.

A527.2.p: A culture hero has a body part, such as a thumb or tooth, that gives him knowledge.

A527.3.p: A culture hero works as a magician, using magic arts.

A527.3.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A527.3.1.p: A culture hero, acting as a magician, can change his own shape or form.

A527.3.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 168.
A527.3.1.1.p: A culture hero, using shapeshifting, takes on an ugly and deformed appearance.

A527.4.p: A culture hero is a poet or musician with artistic skill.

A528.p: A culture hero is aided by supernatural helpers.

A530.r: Norse: Boberg; Greek: Fox 103; Jewish: Neuman.
A530.p: A culture hero establishes laws, customs, and order in the world.

A530.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII (3) 724.
A530.1.p: A culture hero finishes the work that the creator began, completing the world.

A531.p: A culture hero defeats monsters, making the world safer for people.

A531.1.p: A culture hero chooses to spare certain evil spirits because they are useful to people.

A531.1.1.p: A culture hero drives out demons.

A531.2.p: A culture hero drives snakes away or banishes them.

A531.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 148, (Amuesha): ibid. 150, (Apapocuvu-Guarani): ibid. 138.
A531.3.p: A culture hero, a semi-divine figure who brings order to the world, wipes out an entire race of tigers.

A531.4.p: A culture hero defeats a sea monster.

A531.4.1.p: A demigod defeats a giant octopus.

A532.r: Western Mono: Gifford JAFL XXXVI 326ff. Nos. 9, 10.
A532.p: A culture hero subdues the winds and keeps them shut up in caves.

A533.p: A culture hero sets rivers in order, controlling or regulating their courses and flow.

A533.1.p: A culture hero makes himself the current of a river, staying in it to hold the water in place.

A535.p: A culture hero is swallowed by an animal and later comes back out alive.

A536.p: Demigods fight on the side of human beings against their enemies.

A536.1.p: A saint who is a culture hero defends Ireland against foreign invaders.

A537.p: Culture heroes clear open plains, making flat land fit for use.

A538.p: A culture hero builds raths, the ancient circular earthen forts or enclosures.

A541.2.p: A culture hero is worshipped as the god of farming and agriculture.

A547.p: A culture hero provides food and hospitality to people.

A560.r: Irish myth: Cross; Finnish: Kalevala rune 50; India: Thompson-Balys.
A560.p: The departure of a culture hero or demigod from the world, a general heading for stories of how such a figure leaves.

A562.r: S. A. Indian (Tehuelche, Patagonia): Alexander Lat. Am. 336.
A562.p: A divine being departs toward the east.

A564.p: A culture hero, the demigod who taught people their basic arts, is said to have lived an unusually long life.

A565.r: Irish myth: Cross; California Indians: *Thompson Tales 285 n. 52a.
A565.p: A culture hero teaches people how to die by dying himself, so that mortality begins with his death.

A566.r: S. Am. Indian (Apapocuvá-Guaraní): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 136ff., (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 148f., 157.
A566.p: A culture hero goes back up to the sky or heavenly world after finishing his work among people.

A566.1.p: A mortal who is the reincarnation of a heavenly being returns to the land of the gods once his earthly mission is complete.

A566.2.p: A culture hero climbs up to heaven led by a blind ancestral woman.

A567.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A567.p: A divine being withdraws to the far edge of the world and retires from contact with people.

A570.p: A culture hero is believed not to have died but to still be alive somewhere.

A571.2.p: A culture hero still lives on a mysterious, hidden island.

A572.r: S. Am. Indian (Apapocuvá-Guaraní): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 138.

A572.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Guaraní): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93.
A572.1.p: A culture hero is believed to still live at the highest point of the sky, directly overhead.

A575.p: A god who has departed from the world still grants the requests of people who come to visit.
