A581.p: A culture hero or divinity comes back as expected.

A581.1.p: A returning culture hero comes back to help humans.

A581.2.p: A returning culture hero comes back to fight alongside his followers in battle.

A581.3.p: A culture hero returns to show the power of a saint.

A590.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about demigods and culture heroes that do not fit the other categories.

A591.p: A semi-divine hero is allowed to freely visit or be with men's wives.

A592.p: Culture heroes and their descendants: a general heading for stories about semi-divine founders who gave people their arts and skills, and the lineages that follow from them.

A592.1.p: A demigod is born to a witch woman who lives in the upper world, so the culture hero's parentage is a divine being and a sorceress from the sky realm.

A592.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 168.
A592.2.p: The daughter of a culture hero is a virgin, a maiden who has not been married or had relations with a man.

A592.2.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 169.
A592.2.1.p: Although she is a virgin, the daughter of a culture hero gives birth to a boy, so the child is born without a human father.

A605.1.p: Before the world was made, everything was in primeval darkness, with no light.

A605.2.p: Before the world was made, the primeval state was one of cold, with no warmth.

A610.p: The universe is created by a creator who already existed before all things and made everything that exists.

A610.1.p: The creator makes all things in pairs, such as heaven and earth, with each thing having a counterpart.

A610.2.p: The creator makes heaven, earth, and hell as the three parts of the cosmos.

A611.r: Irish myth: Cross; Hebrew: Genesis ch. 1; Jewish: Neuman.—Pelew Group, Western Caroline Is., Central Caroline Is., Gilbert Group: Dixon 248; Mono-Alu (Fauru): Wheeler 66; Tahiti: Henry 338.
A611.p: The universe is created simply by the creator's command: the creator speaks or orders it into being and it comes to be.

A611.0.1.p: The creator uses a particular formula, made of letters or magic words, to bring the universe into being.

A611.1.p: The druids, the priests of the ancient Celts, are described as the creators of the universe.

A612.r: *Dh I 10f., 15, 17ff., 58, 113; Jewish: Neuman.—Zuñi: Cushing RBAE XIII 379ff.; Thompson Tales 280 n. 36.
A612.p: The creator produces the universe by thinking it into existence, so that the world takes form from the creator's thought.

A612.1.p: A world-soul: the universe is a manifestation of the creator, an expression of one divine spirit that animates everything.

A613.p: The creator makes the universe, or parts of it, out of tears that the creator sheds.

A614.p: The creator god makes the world out of parts of his own body, so that different parts of the universe come from different body parts. In the Norse version the giant Ymir's body becomes the world.

A615.p: The creator, often a sky father, begets the various parts of the universe as children, with different wives bearing different parts of the world.

A615.1.p: The creator makes the universe by masturbating into water, stone, and earth, which then yield the world's parts.

A615.2.p: Various objects copulate with one another and their offspring become the other parts of the universe.

A617.2.p: The universe is created from a calabash (gourd), as a variant of the clam-shell creation.

A618.p: The creator makes the universe through various actions, such as coughing, spitting, or other bodily activities.

A618.1.p: The universe comes into being when the creator coughs it out.

A618.2.p: The universe is created when the creator spits it out.

A620.r: Greek: *Grote I 4.—Maori: Dixon 6ff.; Marquesas Is.: ibid. 10 n. 13; Tahiti: Henry 343.
A620.p: The universe arises on its own, without any creator acting to make it.

A620.2.p: The heavens and the earth spontaneously begin to move toward or encroach upon each other, and a creator stops them.

A621.1.p: A primeval giant is produced from vapors of a half-frozen primeval river, and the universe is then created from the giant's body.

A622.p: The universe is created out of a primeval world of fire.

A623.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 324—26, 304, 329, Herrmann Saxo II 584.
A623.p: The universe is created out of ice and mist.

A625.2.p: The sky was originally close to the earth, usually because the sky-father and earth-mother lay together, and it was later lifted up to its present place.

A625.2.3.p: An old woman, whose hump struck the clouds as she swept, hit the sky with her broom and so pushed it up.

A641.1.r: Greek: Fox 5.—Indonesian: L. d. Backer L’Archipel indien 232.
A641.1.p: Heaven and earth come from an egg, forming its two halves; Eros escapes when they are separated.

A641.2.p: The universe is made from duck eggs: the upper and lower vaults come from the shell halves, moonlight from the whites, sunshine from the yolks, starlight from the mottled parts, and clouds from the dark parts.

A642.p: The universe is formed from the body of a slain giant.

A642.1.p: A primeval woman is cut in pieces, and houses and other things are made from her body.

A644.p: Rocks already exist at the start, and everything else is made from them.

A645.p: Creation happens through a chain of descent, where one being begets another, and so on, until the universe takes its present form.

A647.p: The universe is made from a cosmic fowl, a great bird.

A650.p: The whole universe considered as one complete structure. This is a general heading for stories and beliefs about how the cosmos is arranged as a whole.

A651.r: Irish myth: Cross; Egyptian: Müller 366 n. 7; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 307, 309f., 410; Hindu: Keith 15, 134, 228; India: *Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 287 n. 58, Alexander N. Am. 7, 60, 105, 136, 263, *275 n. 11 (Eskimo, Cherokee, Mandan, Kiowa, Thompson River, Bella Coola); Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 52f.; Maya: ibid. 140; Amazon: ibid. 307; Bororo: ibid. 296; S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Métraux MAFLS XL 24, Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Witoto): Métraux MAFLS XL 25; Chuckchee: Bogoras AA n. s. IV 590; Maori: Dixon 59.—Cf. Icel.: De la Saussaye 346 n. 4.
A651.p: The universe is pictured as a stack of worlds arranged one above the other. Each level sits above the next.

A651.0.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 974.
A651.0.1.p: The universe is said to contain nine worlds, one set above or below another in the stacked arrangement.

A651.0.2.p: The universe is said to consist of four world systems arranged in the stacked order.

A651.1.p: A series of upper worlds lies above the earth, arranged in layers one above another.

A651.1.0.1.p: The highest of the heavenly worlds is made up of twenty separate heavens.

A651.1.1.r: Icel.: Snorra Edda Gylf XVII, Boberg.—Hawaii: Thrum 15, Beckwith Myth 42, 74; Maori: Clark 163ff.; S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A651.1.1.p: There are three heavens stacked above the earth.

A651.1.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Witoto): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A651.1.1.1.p: The third sky above the earth keeps the sun from burning the earth, because it stands between them and blocks the heat.

A651.1.1.2.p: Beyond or above the three worlds there is another region that lies outside the three-part arrangement.

A651.1.2.r: Irish myth: Cross (A651.1.6.).—S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A651.1.2.p: There are four heavens stacked above the earth.

A651.1.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25, BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A651.1.3.p: There are five heavens stacked above the earth.

A651.1.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Hindu: Penzer VII 246; Mohammedan: Hartland Science 224; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 400f.—Sumatra: Dixon 160.
A651.1.4.p: There are seven heavens stacked above the earth, a series of seven upper worlds.

A651.1.5.p: There are eight heavens stacked above the earth.

A651.1.6.r: Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 400f.—Fiji: Beckwith Myth 150; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 77.
A651.1.6.p: There are nine heavens stacked above the earth.

A651.1.6.1.p: The nine heavens are divided into nine ranks or orders, like the grades of a hierarchy.

A651.1.7.r: Jewish: Neuman; Maori: Clark 186; Tonga: Gifford 18; Tahiti: Henry 164, 343.
A651.1.7.p: There are ten heavens stacked above the earth.

A651.1.8.p: A miscellaneous group of stories about series of upper worlds that do not fit the other numbered heavens.

A651.1.8.1.p: Heaven is pictured as a building of seventeen stories, one above another.

A651.2.p: A series of lower worlds lies beneath the earth, arranged in layers one below another.

A651.2.0.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Witoto): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A651.2.0.1.p: The creator lives in the lowest sky, which is the sky beneath us, rather than above.

A651.2.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25, BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A651.2.1.p: The lower world is pictured as a series of two underworlds stacked beneath the earth.

A651.2.2.r: Finno-Ugric: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 77.—S. Am. Indian (Witoto): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A651.2.2.p: The lower world is pictured as a series of three underworlds stacked beneath the earth.

A651.2.3.r: Hindu: Penzer IV 21 n. 1, VIII 162 n. 1.
A651.2.3.p: The lower world is pictured as a series of seven underworlds stacked beneath the earth.

A651.3.p: The universe is pictured as having several worlds stacked above and below the earth.

A651.3.1.r: Under him in turn are: rock, bull, fish, vast sea, air, fire, and serpent.—*Chauvin VII 58 No. 77 n. 1.
A651.3.1.p: The universe is pictured as seven worlds above and below the earth, with an angel holding up the seven worlds on his shoulders.

A651.3.2.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 42; S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A651.3.2.p: Miscellaneous tales in which the universe is pictured as a set of worlds above and below the earth, not covered by the more specific motifs.

A652.r: (Cf. A878.)—**Holmberg Baum des Lebens.—Irish myth: Cross; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 331ff., De la Saussaye 346ff.; Hagen MPh I (1903—4) 57; **Olrik Danske Studier, 1917, 49ff.; Babylonian: Spence 138; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 286 n. 56a.
A652.p: A great tree stretches from the lowest world up to the highest world, linking all levels of the universe.

A652.1.r: Lithuanian and Lettish: Gray 325; Finnish: Kalevala rune 2; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Alexander N. Am. 294f. n. 42; Maya: Alexander Lat. Am. 140; S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Métraux MAFLS XL 24f.
A652.1.p: A tree grows up from the earth all the way to heaven.

A652.1.1.p: A goddess hangs her necklace on a branch, and the necklace becomes a tree that reaches up to heaven.

A652.2.p: A tree hangs upside down from the sky, and people climb its branches to travel between the earth and the upper world.

A652.3.p: A tree stands in the upper world, the realm of the sky or heaven.

A652.4.p: The sky is pictured as a tree that spreads over and shades the earth like a canopy.

A653.p: The earth is pictured as covered or held up by an umbrella-like object.

A654.r: (Earth, air, fire, water, etc.).—Jewish: *Neuman; Chinese: Werner 84. Cf. the early Greek philosophers.
A654.p: Myth explaining the basic materials or elements from which the universe was formed.

A655.r: Hindu: Penzer I 10 n. 3; Greek: Fox 5.
A655.p: The world is pictured as an egg, whose two halves form heaven and earth.

A657.r: Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 304, 313; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian.
A657.p: A river flows between the earth and the upper and lower worlds, connecting them.

A657.1.p: A bridge spans from the earth up to heaven, connecting the two.

A657.2.p: Heaven and earth are pictured as meeting or touching at the east, west, and south.

A658.p: Myths describing how large the universe is and how far apart its parts are.

A658.1.p: Falling from heaven to earth takes nine days, and falling from earth to hell takes the same nine days.

A658.1.1.p: A journey from heaven to earth, or from earth to hell, is said to take nine nights of riding.

A658.2.p: Travel across the universe is said to take five hundred years.

A659.p: A general heading for miscellaneous beliefs about the universe as a whole.

A659.1.r: Jewish: Neuman. (The general philosophical theory of the music of the spheres is not treated here).
A659.1.p: The heavenly bodies are believed to make music as they move.

A659.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25.
A659.2.p: A large lake is believed to lie beneath the earth.

A659.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 24.
A659.3.p: A river is believed to rise at the place where sky and earth meet.

A659.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A659.4.p: Each of the worlds is believed to have its own color.

A660.p: A general heading for beliefs about what the upper world, the realm above the earth, is like.

A661.r: Kohler Heaven and Hell in Comparative Religion (New York 1923); Jeremias Hölle und Paradies bei den Babyloniern (Leipzig 1903); Gaster Thespis 286; Irish myth: Cross, Beal XXI 330; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 312; German: Grimm Nos. 3, 35, 81, 82, 112, 167, 175, 178; Egyptian: Müller 176; Persian: Carnoy 345; Hindu: Keith 99, 131, 201.—Japanese: Anesaki 237, 241.—Haida: Alexander N. Am. 263; Eskimo: ibid. 7; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 81; Maya: ibid. 138, 140; Isthmian tribes (Panama): ibid. 193.
A661.p: Heaven is pictured as a blissful upper world, a place of happiness.

A661.0.1.p: Heaven is said to have gates, which are the entrances to it.

A661.0.1.1.p: The gate of heaven is guarded by a clap of thunder and a mysterious sword.

A661.0.1.1.1.p: The doors of heaven are guarded by rivers of fire.

A661.0.1.1.2.p: In front of the main door of heaven are veils made of fire and ice.

A661.0.1.2.r: *Types 800, 801, 804; *Köhler Aufsätze 48; *Fb. “Sankt Peder”.—Irish: Beal XXI 329; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s. v. “Antoine” (St. Anthony); French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 25; U.S.A.: *Baughman.
A661.0.1.2.p: Saint Peter acts as the doorkeeper of heaven.

A661.0.1.3.p: The archangels Michael and Ariel guard two of the doors of heaven.

A661.0.1.4.p: Abersetus guards the river of fire at one of the doors of heaven.

A661.0.1.5.p: Virgins carrying iron rods guard two of the doors of heaven.

A661.0.2.p: Heaven is believed to be filled with music.

A661.0.2.1.p: The heavenly music is made by four columns standing under the Lord's chair.

A661.0.2.2.p: The music of heaven is produced by precious stones.

A661.0.3.p: Heaven contains chairs for those who dwell there.

A661.0.4.p: Heaven has a fountain of cleansing water.

A661.0.5.p: A bridge leads up to heaven.

A661.0.5.1.p: The bridge to the afterlife is easy for good people to cross but hard for wicked people.

A661.0.6.p: Heaven's firmament has sixty-six (or seventy-two) windows.

A661.0.7.p: Precious stones in heaven give off their own light.

A661.0.8.p: Heaven is filled with a sweet smell.

A661.0.9.p: Heaven is enclosed by seven walls.

A661.0.10.p: The land of the saints is encircled by a ring of fire.

A661.1.r: **Neckel Walhall (Dortmund, 1913); M. Olsen Acta Philol. Scand. VI 151f.; MacCulloch Eddic 312; Irish myth: Cross.
A661.1.p: Valhalla is the great hall in Norse myth where slain warriors go to be with Odin; they die and are brought back to life every day.

A661.1.0.1.p: Valhalla has five hundred and forty doors.

A661.1.0.2.p: In Valhalla a goat named Heidrún gives mead to drink.

A661.1.0.3.p: In Valhalla a boar named Soehrímnir provides meat to eat.

A661.1.0.4.p: In Valhalla a deer named Eikthyrnir keeps the spring Hvergelmir full by dripping water into it.

A661.1.0.5.p: A rooster in Valhalla wakes the gods.

A661.1.1.p: The people of heaven are sorted into separate groups.

A661.1.2.p: A saint has a vision of heaven containing three cities: one of gold, one of silver, and one of glass.

A661.2.p: There are eight paradises in the afterlife.

A662.p: The heavens are imagined as a mountain, with the sky being the hollowed-out underside of that mountain.

A663.p: Heaven is pictured as having broad open plains.

A665.p: A general motif about what holds up the sky, with the specific supports listed under it.

A665.0.1.p: A god keeps the sky steady and in place.

A665.1.p: A god of open space or the air holds up the sky.

A665.2.r: *Holmberg Baum des Lebens 12ff.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 333ff.; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 334ff.
A665.2.p: The sky rests on one or more pillars set into the earth.

A665.2.0.1.r: Tahiti: Henry 342; Eskimo (Ungava): Turner RBAE XII (266), (Cape York): Rasmussen III 169, (Greenland): Rink 440.
A665.2.0.1.p: Several pillars together hold up the sky.

A665.2.1.r: Cook Zeus II 140ff.; Frobenius Erdteile VI 165ff.—Egyptian: Müller 35.
A665.2.1.p: Four columns hold up the sky, one at each corner of the world.

A665.2.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—Aztec: Krickeberg Märchen der Azteken 208, 316.
A665.2.1.1.p: Four gods, each standing at one of the four quarters of the world, hold up the sky.

A665.2.1.2.p: Four dwarfs hold up the sky.

A665.2.1.3.p: The sky is made larger or reached farther by means of pillars.

A665.3.p: A mountain holds up the sky.

A665.3.1.p: Four mountains hold up the sky, one at each corner of the world.

A665.4.p: A tree holds up the sky.

A665.5.p: A giant octopus holds the sky against the earth.

A665.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A665.6.p: A serpent holds up the sky.

A666.p: A ladder reaches from earth up to heaven, and in some tales a saint climbs it.

A666.1.p: The ladder to heaven has eight steps, which carry symbolic meaning.

A666.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Brazil): Oberg Mato Grosso 109.
A666.2.p: A rodent gnaws through the ladder to the other world, so the ghosts cannot climb up and stay behind on earth.

A667.p: Heaven has its own language, different from the languages spoken on earth.

A669.p: Miscellaneous beliefs about the nature of the upper world, the realm above the earth, that do not fit a more specific heading.

A669.1.p: The upper world has judges who decide matters there.

A669.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 164.
A669.2.p: The sky is imagined as a solid substance, like a hard dome or firm material rather than open air.

A670.p: Beliefs about the nature of the lower world, the realm beneath the earth.

A671.r: Jeremias Hölle und Paradies bei den Babyloniern (Leipzig 1903); Kohler Heaven and Hell in Comparative Religion (New York 1923); *Landau Hölle und Fegfeuer in Volksglaube, Dichtung, und Kirchenlehre (Heidelberg, 1909); *Jataka Index s.v. “hell”.—Norse: De la Saussaye 256, 291, MacCulloch Eddic 303, Herrmann Saxo Gr. II 588, *Boberg; Greek: Fox 143; Egyptian: Müller 179; Babylonian: Spence 128; Persian: Carnoy 345; Hindu: Penzer X 169 s. v. “Hades”, Keith 100, 160; India: Thompson-Balys.—Japanese: Anesaki 237.—Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 80; Maya: ibid. 138; Chaco: ibid. 324; Chibcha: ibid. 198; Eskimo: Alexander N. Am. 7.
A671.p: Hell, the lower world of torment where the wicked are punished after death.

A671.0.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319.
A671.0.1.p: Hell is placed in the north.

A671.0.1.1.p: Hell is said to be located in places other than the north.

A671.0.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 2, 5, 7; Jewish: Neuman.
A671.0.2.p: An account of how hell was created or came into being.

A671.0.2.1.p: The origin of the fire in hell: Christ created it from his blood, since hell was formerly cold.

A671.0.3.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman. (Cf. A671.5.).
A671.0.3.p: The entrance to a cave serves as the gateway to hell.

A671.0.4.p: Hell is mistaken for or confused with the land of the fairies.

A671.0.5.r: Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 786.
A671.0.5.p: Descriptions of how large hell is and how it is laid out.

A671.1.p: Hell has a doorkeeper who guards its entrance.

A671.2.p: Frightening sights that are seen in hell.

A671.2.1.r: Wimberly Folklore in Ballads 424; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319, 321, 332, Boberg; Irish myth: Cross.
A671.2.1.p: Hell is full of serpents and snakes.

A671.2.1.1.p: Hell is full of adders, a kind of venomous snake.

A671.2.2.p: Hell has rivers of blood flowing through it.

A671.2.2.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319f.; Jewish: Neuman.
A671.2.2.1.p: Hell has rivers of poison flowing through it.

A671.2.2.2.p: A river in hell is filled with weapons.

A671.2.2.3.p: Hell has rivers of fire flowing through it.

A671.2.2.4.p: Hell has rivers of black water flowing through it.

A671.2.2.5.p: Hell contains four (or three) rivers that flow with blood.

A671.2.2.6.p: Hell contains rivers other than the blood rivers, which are listed as further horrible features of the underworld.

A671.2.3.p: In hell there is a tree whose fruit or branches are living heads of the dead.

A671.2.4.p: Hell is full of fires, a general heading for the various burning features of the underworld.

A671.2.4.1.p: Hell contains a sea of fire.

A671.2.4.2.p: Hell has islands rising out of its sea of fire.

A671.2.4.3.p: Hell has showers of fire falling from above.

A671.2.4.4.p: Hell has plains that are burning.

A671.2.4.5.p: Hell has fiery valleys or glens.

A671.2.4.6.p: Hell has wheels of fire that turn as a form of torment.

A671.2.4.7.p: Hell has chains made of fire used to bind the damned.

A671.2.4.8.p: Hell has fiery sticks or rods, used as instruments of punishment.

A671.2.4.9.p: Hell has stones made of fire.

A671.2.4.10.p: Hell has fiery nails, likely used to fix or pierce the damned.

A671.2.5.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319, 332 (Nidhogg).

A671.2.7.p: Hell is infested with gnats or biting insects.

A671.2.8.p: Toads are among the horrible creatures seen tormenting the damned in hell.

A671.2.9.p: Scorpions are among the horrible creatures seen tormenting the damned in hell.

A671.2.10.p: Griffins, fabulous winged beasts, are among the horrible creatures seen in hell.

A671.2.11.p: Birds made of iron are among the horrible sights seen in hell.

A671.2.12.p: Lions are among the horrible creatures seen in hell.

A671.2.13.p: Scratching cats are among the horrible creatures seen in hell, clawing at the damned.

A671.2.14.p: Tigers are among the horrible creatures seen in hell.

A671.3.r: Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 786.
A671.3.p: Hell is extremely cold, a frozen place rather than only a place of fire.

A671.3.2.p: Hell has rugged mountains covered in ice and snow.

A671.3.3.p: Hell alternates between intense heat and intense cold.

A671.4.p: A well in hell, named Hvergelmir in Norse tradition, from which waters or streams flow.

A671.5.p: A gate or barrier encircles hell, enclosing it.

A671.6.p: Beings born in hell have long bodies and grip the walls with long nails.

A672.r: Gaster Oldest Stories 50; Greek: Fox 143; Norse: De la Saussaye 350, MacCulloch Eddic 330, Boberg.—Chibcha: Alexander Lat. Am. 198; India: Thompson-Balys.
A672.p: A river in the lower world, which the dead must cross. In Greek myth there are five such rivers in Hades.

A672.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 142; Egyptian: Müller 176; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 45; Babylonian: Jensen Gilgamesch-Epos X, XI, 46ff., cf. 136ff.
A672.1.p: A ferryman rows the dead across the river in the lower world; in Greek myth this is Charon.

A672.1.1.p: The ferryman of the lower world demands payment to carry souls across the river Styx.

A672.2.p: A maiden stands guard at the bridge leading to hell.

A673.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics I 493a; *Fb “hund” III 678b.—Gaster Thespis 214; Greek: Fox 88; Frazer Apollodorus I 232 n. 1; Norse: Herrmann Nordische Mythologie 599ff., MacCulloch Eddic 303f.; Persian and Hindu: Keith 69.—Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 326, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 165.
A673.p: A monstrous dog, Cerberus in Greek myth, guards the bridge to the lower world.

A673.1.p: Dogs are found in hell, often as guardians or tormentors.

A673.2.p: A rooster (cock) that crows in hell and belongs to the hound-guarded lower world. It is a cock of the underworld.

A675.r: Greek: Fox 143.—Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 206 No. 155; Japanese: Anesaki 238.
A675.p: The beings who sit in judgment over the dead in the lower world, deciding the fate of souls.

A676.p: A ship that belongs to hell or the lower world, used to carry or ferry the dead.

A677.p: Craftsmen and tradesmen who work in the lower world, such as smiths and millers.

A677.1.p: A blacksmith who works at a forge in hell.

A677.2.p: A miller who grinds grain in hell.

A678.p: The otherworld is divided into three rooms: one holds the dead, one holds the souls of unborn children waiting to enter women's wombs, and one holds all the evil spirits.

A681.r: S. Am. Indian (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 550.
A681.p: The sun is found in the underworld, where it shines or resides when it is not in the sky.

A682.r: S. Am. Indian (Terino): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A682.p: A hole or opening in the ground through which people come up from the lower world into this world.

A689.p: Miscellaneous other traits of the lower world that do not fit under the more specific headings.

A689.1.p: Hell contains dark, dirty pools or puddles.

A689.2.p: Hell has a foul, bad smell.

A689.3.p: Hell is a place of hunger, where the damned are always starving.

A689.3.1.p: Dogs are set on the souls in hell to devour them.

A690.p: A miscellaneous motif about the nature of the universe, with several different worlds or world-structures.

A692.r: Irish myth: Cross.—Greek: Fox 147, Grote I 62, Güntert Kalypso 81; Gaster Oldest Stories 50.—Oceanic: Kruyt Het Animisme 368ff.; Landman Kiwai Papuans 12; Lévy-Bruhl L’âme primitive 382ff.
A692.p: Islands of the blessed, happy otherworld islands where good people go after death.

A692.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; S. Am. Indian (Guarayú): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147.
A692.1.p: A happy otherworld lying overseas to the west, reached by sea.

A693.p: An intermediate world in the afterlife where people go whose good and evil deeds exactly balance out.

A694.p: The Christian paradise, the heavenly place of the blessed in the afterlife.

A694.1.p: The Christian paradise, called the Land of Promise, is identified with the older pagan Celtic otherworld of Ireland.

A695.p: The moon serves as the next world, the place where the dead go after death.

A696.p: The universe is pictured as a world made of serpents, a mythical realm in which snakes make up the whole of existence.

A697.p: Assorted otherworlds from Buddhist belief, the various heavenly or spiritual realms that exist beyond the earth.

A697.1.p: The Brahma world is a Buddhist heavenly realm, the abode of the god Brahma.

A697.2.p: The Tusita world is a Buddhist heavenly realm where the Buddha-to-be dwells before his final rebirth on earth.

A697.2.1.p: Time runs differently in the Tusita world, so that a year there passes as a single day.

A697.3.p: The deva world is a Buddhist heavenly realm inhabited by the devas, divine beings.

A700.r: Irish myth: Cross; Pawnee: Alexander N. Am. 108; Navaho: ibid. 163; Persian: Carnoy 276; Babylonian: Spence 115.
A700.p: The sun, moon, stars, and other heavenly bodies are brought into being by some act of creation.

A700.1.p: The sun, moon, and stars are made from objects thrown up into the sky.

A700.2.p: The creator brings forth the heavenly bodies by vomiting them up.

A700.3.p: A woman gives birth to four children, who become the sun, the moon, fire, and water.

A700.4.p: The heavenly bodies are created only after the plants have already been made.

A700.5.p: A smith forges the sun, moon, and stars as if they were metal objects.

A700.6.p: The sun and moon are bought, rather than made or given freely.

A700.7.p: The sun, moon, and stars are fed or sustained by fire.

A700.8.p: The sun, the moon, and darkness are regarded as three children of God.

A701.r: Babylonian: Spence 79; Hebrew: Genesis, ch. 1; Jewish: Neuman; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 384; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
A701.p: The sky itself is created, brought into being by some act of creation.

A701.0.1.p: The firmament, the solid vault of the sky, is created.

A701.1.p: The sky comes from an egg that was brought up out of the primeval waters.

A701.2.p: The sky is made from the skull of the giant Ymir.

A702.p: Describes what the sky is like, its nature and substance.

A702.1.p: The sky is imagined as being made of water. It is a belief about what the heavens are composed of.

A702.2.r: Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 336; Hatt Asiatic Influences 63; Eskimo (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 153.—African: Werner African 130.—Cf. Isaiah, ch 40.
A702.2.p: The sky is pictured as a solid dome or tent stretched over the earth, rather than open air.

A702.3.r: (Cf. A665, A774.)—Gaster Thespis 170; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 335; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 386.—Finno-Ugric: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 221.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 337.
A702.3.p: The sky is held up by the north star, which is seen as a nail or peg that the whole heavens turn around.

A702.3.1.p: The stars, sun, and moon are fixed to a wheel in the heavens, and they travel around as it turns.

A702.4.p: A tale explaining the reason the sky has its blue color.

A702.5.p: The earth and the sky are imagined as a married couple, whose union is the origin of the world or of things.

A702.6.p: The height or extent of the sky is measured by means of a bird, such as by how far it flies.

A702.7.p: Clouds are thought of as supports or pillars holding up the sky.

A702.8.p: The sky is black because it was once lifted up using a dirty stick, which left it stained.

A702.9.r: S. Am. Indian (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 348.
A702.9.p: The sky is immortal and renews itself by shedding its skin periodically, as a snake does.

A703.p: Angels are responsible for setting and regulating the movements of the sun, moon, stars, and other heavenly bodies.

A705.p: Explanations of where clouds come from and what they are made of.

A705.1.p: Stories telling how clouds came into existence.

A705.1.1.p: A creator god makes the clouds out of his own body or internal organs.

A705.1.2.p: Clouds are imagined as bark cloth (tapa) beaten out by a woman who lives in the moon.

A705.2.p: Clouds are described as having a covering or skin over them.

A710.r: *Rühle Sonne und Mond im primitiven Mythus (Tübingen, 1925).—Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.—Indonesian: Dixon 177; Australian: ibid. 275; Navaho: Alexander N. Am. 166ff.; Hopi: ibid. 205; Quileute: Farrand JAFL XXXII 254f.; Sinkyone: Kroeber JAFL XXXII 346f.; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 205.—Inca: Alexander Lat. Am. 240; Africa (Luba): Donohugh Africa V 180.
A710.p: Stories about how the sun was created or came to exist.

A711.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Bushman: Bleek and Lloyd 45; Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 97 No. 18; Ekoi: Talbot 357, 359; British New Guinea: Dixon 113; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-g 3/191); S. Am. Indian (Eastern Brazil): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 434, (Guarayú): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147, (Kaigua): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 138ff., (Manasi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 393, (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 122, 158—165, (Guaporé River): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 379.
A711.p: A man, often born by supernatural means, goes up into the sky and becomes the sun.

A711.1.p: The sun and the moon are said to be an uncle and his nephew who rose up into the sky.

A711.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Crow: Lowie PaAM XV 157.
A711.2.p: The sun is depicted as a man-eating monster that devours human beings.

A711.3.p: Originally the sun did not exist; what is now the sun was first a moon, and the moon was the only light in the sky. Some tales explain the origin of the sun this way.

A711.4.p: In this origin tale there was no sun at all at first, and the world was lit some other way until the sun came into being.

A712.p: The sun is a fire that is rekindled or renewed each morning, so that it rises fresh every day.

A712.1.p: The moon is made from light and the sun from fire, so the two heavenly lights have different origins.

A713.p: The sun and moon come out of a cave, where they were kept or from which they emerged to light the world.

A713.1.p: The sun and moon were brought out of the belly of a fish, which had swallowed them and then released them into the sky.

A714.r: Bushman: Bleek and Lloyd 54; Pelew Is. (Micronesia): Dixon 253; Cook Group: ibid. 37; Admiralty Is., Woodlark Is.: ibid 112; Australian: ibid 275.
A714.p: The sun is created from an object that is thrown up into the sky and becomes the sun.

A714.1.r: Maori, Society Is., Samoa, Cook Group: Dixon 37.
A714.1.p: The sun and moon are placed in the sky to serve as the eyes of the heavens.

A714.2.r: A652), but they give no light at first.—Finnish: Kalevala rune 49, cf. FFC LXXII 108.
A714.2.p: A hero makes the sun and moon and fastens them to the top of the World Tree, the cosmic tree that holds up the heavens.

A714.3.p: The sun is made from fire that is flung up into the sky, where it becomes the sun.

A714.4.p: The sun and moon are metal mirrors set in the sky.

A714.5.p: The sun is a grindstone full of fire, set in the sky.

A714.6.p: The sun and moon are spangles that fall from the creator's forehead into his own urine.

A714.7.p: The sun and moon are the eyes of Rama, which he tore out after his brother died and threw into the sky.

A714.8.p: The sun and moon were originally wooden circles that came to life after being given human blood in sacrifice.

A715.r: Gilbert Is.: Dixon 254; Samoa: Beckwith Myth 254; S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba, Tembé, Apapocuva): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 123, (Jivaro): Stewart-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 627, (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, (Paressi): Métraux ibid. 359, (Viracocha): Stewart-Métraux ibid. 550.
A715.p: The sun is born of the first couple, the original man and woman, as one of their children.

A715.1.p: The sun and moon are born from a woman, who gives birth to them as her children.

A715.2.p: The sun and moon are born from a goddess who became pregnant by the wind.

A715.3.p: The sun and moon are born from an ogre, a monstrous giant-like being.

A715.4.p: The sun and moon come from the breasts of Mother Earth, who nurses them into being.

A715.5.p: The sun is said to have been born as a child of the moon, making the moon the sun's parent in the origin story.

A715.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Amuesha): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 149.
A715.6.p: In this origin story the sun and moon are born from a lizard.

A716.r: Dh I 128ff.; cf. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 498.
A716.p: A dispute arises between God and the devil over how the sun should be made: God plans two suns, but the devil persuades him to make only one.

A716.1.p: At first there are four suns, and a culture hero shoots three of them down, leaving only one in the sky.

A717.p: A hero makes the sun and moon out of a tree and sends them up into the sky to take turns.

A717.1.p: A hero makes the sun and moon from a tree and brings them to life with the blood of the creator's son.

A718.p: The sun comes into being through a transformation of some earlier being or object.

A718.1.p: The sun is formed from the head of a youth who was offered in sacrifice.

A718.2.p: The sun and moon are the visible bodies of gods.

A718.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 683.
A718.3.p: The sun grows from fruit kernels that are thrown into floodwater.

A718.4.p: The sun is formed from maggots that have been transformed.

A719.p: Miscellaneous other stories about how the sun was created that do not fit the more specific categories.

A719.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Amyra): Tschopik BBAE CXLIII (2) 571.
A719.1.p: The sun rises up out of a lake.

A719.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 154ff.
A719.2.p: After a world catastrophe, a new sun appears and begins a new age.

A719.3.p: The sun is created on the fourth day of creation.

A720.p: Stories about what the sun is like and what state it was once in.

A720.1.p: Long ago there were seven suns in the sky.

A720.2.p: Formerly the sun's great heat caused suffering to people.

A721.p: The sun is kept shut away inside a box.

A721.0.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Bakairi, Amazon): Alexander Lat. Am. 313, (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 683. Cf. N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 282 n. 45 (light kept in box or basket).
A721.0.1.p: The sun and moon are kept in pots when they are not shining.

A721.0.2.p: The sun is imprisoned in a pit and kept from shining on the world.

A721.0.3.p: The sun is kept shut up inside a case or box, so the world is dark.

A721.1.r: BP III 288; Dh I 136ff., III 113ff.—Cf. Kaffir: Kidd 238 No. 7; Finnish: Kalevala runes 47, 49.—Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 483; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 60; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 683.
A721.1.p: Someone steals the sun from the monster that keeps it and brings it down to earth.

A721.2.p: A bird (or the devil) swallows the sun and then spits it out, which lets the thief succeed.

A721.2.1.p: When a crow-like bird called an awk swallows the sun, the world falls into great darkness.

A721.3.r: Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 83; India: Thompson-Balys.
A721.3.p: The stolen sun is put back into the sky where it belongs.

A721.4.p: A pale or dim sun is made bright again by using an egg, yellow grass, or similar things.

A721.5.r: S. Am. Indian: (Mocovi): Métraux MAFLS XXXX 34.
A721.5.p: The sun falls from the sky, but it is lifted back up and tied fast to the sky.

A722.r: Armenian: Ananikian 50; S. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 281.
A722.p: The sun travels at night around or under the earth to return to its starting point in the east.

A722.1.p: At night the sun's chariot is carried back east in a golden cup or bed.

A722.2.p: The sun returns from west to east along the same path, but turns its bright side toward the sky so the earth stays dark.

A722.3.r: Gaster Thespis 195; Egyptian: Müller 27, 84; Armenian: Ananikian 50; India: Thompson-Balys.
A722.3.p: The sun passes through the land of the dead during its night journey.

A722.4.p: In the evening the sun goes home and shuts its doors and windows for the night.

A722.5.p: The sun is pictured as a man lying down with his arm raised; his light comes from his armpits, and when he lowers the arm the light goes out.

A722.5.1.p: At night the sun bathes in a stream of fire.

A722.5.2.p: The sun is led through a stream at night to cool its heat, since otherwise it might burn up the earth.

A722.6.p: The sun hides at night because it is afraid to wander in the dark.

A722.7.p: A mountain is the place through which the sun passes on its way.

A722.7.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A722.7.1.p: At night the sun slips into a crack or gap between the sky and the earth.

A722.8.p: The sun sits on the back of a male buffalo.

A722.9.p: At dawn the sun comes out to play with the moon. Dawn is pictured as a time when the sun and moon meet and amuse themselves together.

A722.10.p: The sun and the moon each spend half of their time in the underworld, below the earth. This explains their periods of absence from the sky.

A722.11.p: By night the sun worships God. While out of sight, the sun is shown praying or paying honor to a deity.

A722.12.r: S. Am. Indian (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 348.
A722.12.p: The sun we see is a kind of pet or favorite of the real sun. The visible sun is treated as a companion or plaything of the true sun.

A722.13.p: During the day the sun takes the form of a man. The sun is pictured as a human being while it shines.

A723.r: Egyptian: Müller 26; Icel.: cf. Du Chaillu The Viking Age 100ff., 107; Almgren Hällristningar och Kultbruk (Stockholm, 1926—27) passim.
A723.p: The sun travels across the sky in a boat. The sun is imagined as sailing on a vessel.

A724.r: *Helm Altgermanische Religionsgeschichte I 178, 256; Cook Zeus I 205ff.—Greek: Fox 243, cf. A722.1., Grote I 313; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 198; Babylonian: Spence 236; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A724.p: The sun travels across the sky in a chariot. The sun is imagined as riding in a vehicle pulled by horses or other animals.

A724.1.r: Howey Horse in Magic and Myth 114ff.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 196; Greek: Fox 243; Hindu: Penzer I 143 n. 2, II 150ff.
A724.1.p: The sun drives his horses and chariot across the sky. The sun is the one who steers the chariot that carries him.

A724.1.0.1.p: The coyote rides along with the sun in its chariot. A coyote is shown as a passenger in the sun's journey.

A724.1.1.r: Krappe “Phaëthon”, The Review of Religion (1944) 115—129.—Greek: *Roscher s.v. “Phaëthon”, *Frazer Pausanias II 59.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 291 n. 66.
A724.1.1.p: The sun gives his chariot to another, usually his son, and the horses run wild. The earth nearly burns up as a result.

A724.1.2.p: The sun's chariot is attended by angels. Angels accompany the chariot as it crosses the sky.

A724.2.p: The sun is pictured as a golden bowl with a peacock sitting on its rim. Bowl and peacock are enclosed in a crystal box that rides on a flying chariot.

A725.p: A man has power to control when the sun rises and sets.

A725.1.p: Through the power of a saint, the sun does not set for a whole year.

A726.p: The sun's daily path across the sky from dawn to dusk.

A726.1.p: The sun and moon make their daily trips across the sky by direct command of God.

A726.2.p: The sun has wings with which it flies across the sky.

A727.r: Cherokee: Alexander N. Am. 60; Navaho: ibid. 167ff.
A727.p: The sun was originally low in the sky and was raised up little by little by magicians or conjurors.

A727.1.p: The sun was originally so hot that it threatened all life on earth.

A728.r: Luomala Oceanic, American Indian, and African Myths of Snaring the Sun (BMB No. 168 [Honolulu, 1940]); *Dh III 120ff.—India: Thompson-Balys; African: Frobenius Atlantis V 38, 70f., XII 160, 185f.
A728.p: The sun is caught in a snare or trap, and is held until released.

A728.1.r: American Indian: *Thompson Tales 290 n. 65. Cf. Luomala.
A728.1.p: A boy's burnt mantle makes him angry at the sun, so he snares the sun, which causes everything to scorch until a mouse gnaws the snare apart.

A728.2.r: Polynesian: *Dixon 44ff. n. 26; Society Is., Samoan: ibid. 46; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 10, 227, 230; Marquesas: Handy 103. Cf. Luomala.
A728.2.p: The sun moves so fast that clothes cannot dry, so the hero roped the sun's legs as it climbed out of the underworld and freed it only after it promised to slow down.

A728.3.p: The sun visits the earth as a black bull, is caught by a man, and this causes night.

A728.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 348.
A728.4.p: The sun and moon are carried across the sky by animals, and how fast they move depends on the time of day and season.

A731.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman; Africa: Bouveignes 14.
A731.p: The sun is considered the ruler of both the sky and the earth.

A731.1.p: The sun is pictured sitting on a throne.

A732.1.r: 350 of each (= days and nights of the lunar year).—Greek: Fox 242.
A732.1.p: The sun owns cattle and sheep.

A732.2.1.p: A slave shoots an arrow into the leg of the sun's horse.

A733.p: Tales and beliefs about the sun's heat and light.

A733.1.p: Explains why sunlight is much stronger than moonlight.

A733.2.p: No mortal can look at the sun because God's name is engraved on it.

A733.3.p: The sun has two faces: a fiery one turned toward the earth and a hail-producing one turned toward heaven.

A733.4.p: Sunbeams are snares by which the sun is tied to the earth.

A733.5.p: The sun dries out the earth with its heat.

A734.1.p: The sun hides inside a cave.

A735.r: Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 89; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 274 n. 9.—Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 189; African: Frobenius Atlantis XII 181, (Fang): Einstein 34, Trilles 173, (Dahomé): Einstein 30.
A735.p: The moon chases the sun across the sky.

A735.1.p: The moon is tied to the sun so that when the sun sinks, the moon is dragged up and brings the sun back into view to light the earth.

A735.2.p: The sun and moon are chased across the sky by a dark planet riding in a black chariot.

A736.p: The sun is imagined as a human being.

A736.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Macobi: Alexander Lat. Am 319; Africa: Meinhof 200.
A736.1.p: The sun and moon are imagined as a man and a woman.

A736.1.1.r: She is sun and he the moon.—*Rank Das Inzestmotiv 446ff.; Frazer Ovid III 31.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 196; Lappish: Friis Lappisk Mythologi 79; German: Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens I 642, II 1511; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 10 No. 3.—Eskimo: *Thompson Tales 273 note 6; S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Manasi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 393, (Witoto, Shipaya, Canelo, Warrau, Arawak): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (3) 54; African (Baluga): Einstein 176.
A736.1.1.p: The sun is a sister and the moon a brother. The brother visits his sister at night, she marks him so she can recognize him, he flees, and she follows him with a flaming torch.

A736.1.2.r: Icel.: De la Saussaye 344; India: *Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian (Montagnais and Menominee): Alexander N. Am. 25.
A736.1.2.p: The sun is a brother and the moon a sister.

A736.1.3.r: (Cf. A736.1.1.).—India: Thompson-Balys.—S. Am. Indian (Amazon): Alexander Lat. Am. 306, (Caviña, Tumupasa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 448; African (Ekoi): Talbot 359.
A736.1.3.p: The sun and moon are lovers.

A736.1.4.r: *Fb. “sol” III 457b.—Lettish: Gray 321; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 133, Eberhard FFC CXX 113.—African: Werner African 232, (Fang): Trilles 171f.; Hatt Asiatic Influences 74f.—Tlingit: Alexander N. Am. 257; S. Am. Indian (Fuegian): Alexander Lat. Am. 342, (Jivaro): Stewart-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 627, Métraux RMLP XXXIII 129, (Aymara): Tschopik BBAE CXLIII (2) 571, (Chibcha): Kroeber ibid. 908.
A736.1.4.p: The sun and moon are married to each other.

A736.1.4.1.p: The sun and moon quarrel because the sun eats all their children except two.

A736.1.4.1.1.p: The moon kills the sun's children.

A736.1.4.2.p: The moon and sun are brother and sister, and also wife and husband.

A736.1.4.3.p: The creator separates the sun and moon so that they cannot produce more stars.

A736.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Mocoví): Métraux MAFLS XXXX 20.
A736.2.p: The sun is imagined as a woman.

A736.3.r: N. Am. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs Northwest Sahaptin Texts 16; S. Am. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, (Chiriguano): Métraux ibid. 484; (Guaporé River): Lévi-Strauss ibid. 379.
A736.3.p: The sun and moon are imagined as brothers.

A736.3.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Mataco, Chamacoco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Amuesa): *Métraux RMLP XXXIII 131.
A736.3.1.p: The sun and moon are twin brothers.

A736.3.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Mataco, Chamacoco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Timbira, Sherente, Caingang, Mashachali): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 397, 515.
A736.3.2.p: The sun and moon are brothers, with the sun being clever and the moon being stupid.

A736.3.3.p: The sun and his brother, the moon, take turns rising and setting.

A736.4.p: The sun and moon are sisters, daughters of the sky-god.

A736.5.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Caviña, Tumupasa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 448.
A736.5.1.p: The sun's son is so hot that no one can hold him.

A736.5.2.p: The children of the sun are human in form only at night; when exposed to daylight they turn into a drop of blood.

A736.6.p: The sun and the moon are depicted as friends who share a close companionship.

A736.7.p: The sun falls in love with a human girl, and the moon becomes jealous of this affection.

A736.7.1.p: As part of the sun's affection for a human girl, the sun takes her as a wife.

A736.8.p: The moon was originally the sun and the sun was originally the moon; their roles were swapped.

A736.9.p: The moon places a curse on the sun.

A736.10.p: A human being is the son of the sun.

A736.11.p: The sun and the moon compete against each other in a contest.

A737.r: *Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens II 1511; Penzer II 81f.—Estonian: Loortis Grundzüge I 153, 410ff.; Icel.: De la Saussaye 344; Jewish: Neuman; Korean: Zong in-Sob 11 No. 4; Hindu: Keith 137, 151, 192, 232f.; India: *Thompson-Balys.—Montagnais: Alexander N. Am. 25; Mataguaya (Pampean): Alexander Lat. Am. 319.
A737.p: Explanations of why the sun or moon is eclipsed.

A737.0.1.p: The explanation for how a lunar eclipse (eclipse of the moon) came about.

A737.1.r: *Fb “solulv”; *Encyc. Religion and Ethics I 492a.; Gaster Oldest Stories 234; Gaster Thespis 206.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 279; Finnish: Kalevala rune 47; Jewish: Neuman; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 424; Jugo-Slav: Máchal Slavic Myth 229; Armenian: Ananikian 48.—Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 736; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: Wilken Indische Gids (1885) I 240; Tahiti: Henry 227; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 123, 158, 165, (Mocoví): Métraux MAFLS XL 20, (Manao): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 712, (Guarani, Manasí, Guarayú, Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, 393, 483, (Guayaki): Métraux-Baldus BBAE CXLIII (1) 444; (Toba, Abipón, Mocovi, Mataco, Vilela): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Eastern Brazil): Lowie ibid. 434 (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII (3) 724.
A737.1.p: An eclipse happens because a monster is swallowing the sun or moon.

A737.2.p: An eclipse is caused by a mother's curse placed on her third son.

A737.3.p: A toad is the cause of solar eclipses.

A737.4.p: The ghosts of the sun's children return and bring about an eclipse.

A737.5.p: The moon is eclipsed because it steps in between an attacker and the person being attacked.

A737.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 348, (Lule): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A737.6.p: An animal hides the sun behind its body, causing an eclipse.

A737.7.r: S. Am. Indian (Botocudo): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 540.
A737.7.p: Eclipses result from quarrels between the sun and the moon.

A737.8.r: S. Am. Indian (Caviña, Tumupasa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 448.
A737.8.p: The sun smears his face with mud or ash as a sign of mourning, and this causes an eclipse.

A737.8.1.p: The sun hides his face in shame, and the result is an eclipse.

A737.9.p: An eclipse is a punishment sent by a god.

A737.10.p: An eclipse is explained as the sun hiding or turning away because it cannot bear to witness tragic events in history.

A737.11.r: S. Am. Indian (Mojo): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 424.
A737.11.p: A partial eclipse is explained as the result of the sun or moon being ill or ailing.

A738.p: A general heading for the sun's characteristics, including its physical form, its mind and feelings, its healing power, and its influence on plants.

A738.1.p: A subheading for the sun's physical form and appearance in folk belief.

A738.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 347f., (Paressi): Métraux ibid. 360.
A738.1.1.p: The sun and moon are described as balls of feathers.

A738.1.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A738.1.2.p: The sun is pictured as a fat woman walking across the sky.

A738.2.p: A subheading for the sun's mind, personality, and disposition in folk belief.

A738.2.1.p: The sun and moon are treated as religious or sacred beings.

A738.2.2.p: The sun is described as wise and as having strong passions or feelings.

A738.3.p: The sun has the power to heal illness.

A738.4.p: The sun has power over plants, affecting how they grow or thrive.

A739.p: A miscellaneous heading for other traits and situations of the sun that do not fit the groups above.

A739.1.p: The sun is located at the edge of the sky.

A739.2.p: The sun is involved in a war, fighting against someone or something.

A739.3.p: The sun has brothers who take turns: each works one month and plays for the other eleven, because if all worked together the heat would burn up the world.

A739.4.p: An explanation for why the sun's heat changes with the seasons.

A739.5.p: An explanation for why the sun appears red.

A739.6.p: The sun sets and refuses to rise again, so it must be coaxed back up from the underworld.

A739.7.p: The sun has an eye that sees everything.

A739.8.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 165.
A739.8.p: The sun looks after and cares for the poor.

A739.9.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A739.9.p: The sun is said to carry iron weapons with which it drives away enemies.

A740.p: A myth explaining how the moon was created.

A741.p: The moon is made from a person or object that is thrown up into the sky.

A741.1.p: The moon is made from water that has been flung up into the sky.

A741.2.p: The chest of a young person who was sacrificed becomes the moon.

A741.3.p: The moon is a grinder that draws fire out of the sun.

A742.p: The moon is made from shining fragments that fall from an opened cap and are gathered into a box until the moon is full.

A743.p: The moon is created when some object is changed into it.

A743.1.p: The moon originates from a shell.

A744.p: A heavenly smith is hammering on the moon, shaping or working it.

A745.p: A myth describing the family relationships of the moon.

A745.1.p: The moon is born from the first couple.

A745.2.p: The moon's mother is the most distant star in the sky.

A745.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158, 165.
A745.3.p: The moon is the younger brother of the sun.

A747.p: A person is transformed into the moon.

A750.r: Many motifs in A720 to A739 refer to the moon and are not here repeated.
A750.p: Beliefs about the nature and condition of the moon, such as what it is made of or how it changes.

A751.p: A figure, often a man, is said to be seen in the face of the moon; various stories explain how he got there.

A751.1.r: *Dh I 254ff.; *ibid. II 242 (Judas); Köhler-Bolte I 114 (Judas), III 597; *Fb “måne” II 659b.; Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 275ff., (1928) 171; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3907; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII 84 No. 4; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 37f. A751.1.p: The man in the moon is a person who was thrown or sent there as a punishment.

A751.1.1.r: **Hench The Man in the Moon and his Sticks (SFQ XIV 169).—North Carolina: Brown Collection I 631.
A751.1.1.p: The man in the moon was put there for punishment for burning brush on Sunday.

A751.1.2.p: The man in the moon was put there as punishment for cursing God.

A751.1.3.r: Emerson “Medieval Legends of Cain” PMLA XXI 840ff.
A751.1.3.p: The man in the moon is a person who was sent up there as punishment for showing disrespect in a sacrifice.

A751.1.4.p: The man in the moon was banished there for stealing a bundle of thorns.

A751.2.r: *Werhan Die Sage 65; Fb “måne” II 659b.—Hindu- Keith 137, Penzer I 109 n. 1, II 82, V 101 n. 2, IX 143, Jataka Index s. v. “moon”, Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 675, 1079; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 339.—Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 57, 89; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503 (jaguar).
A751.2.p: The figure seen in the moon is a rabbit, hare, or some other animal rather than a man.

A751.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Warrau): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 123.
A751.3.p: The dark shape on the moon is a frog.

A751.3.1.p: The man in the moon is a frog that jumped onto a person's face and stayed stuck there.

A751.4.r: Finnish: *Aarne FFC VIII 4 No. 8; XXXIII 51 No. 8; Livonian: *Loorits FFC LXVI 81 No. 7; Estonian: *Aarne FFC XXV 140 No. 6.
A751.4.p: A man tried to tar the moon and got stuck there with his tar bucket, and that is why he appears in it.

A751.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Caviña, Tumupasa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 448, (Chamacoco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, (Tembé): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 140, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 142f., (Peru): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 123.
A751.5.p: The markings on the moon's face are explained as scratches or paint marks left there.

A751.5.1.p: A hare scratched the moon's face to get revenge for an injury the moon had done to the hare.

A751.5.2.p: The sun smeared dung or ashes on the moon's face, and that is why the marks are there.

A751.5.2.1.p: The moon wanted to marry his sister, the sun, and she angrily threw hot ashes on his face in response.

A751.5.3.p: The marks on the moon's shoulder are the mark of his mother's hand.

A751.5.4.p: The markings on the moon are the paw print of a tiger.

A751.5.5.p: The spots on the moon are tattoo marks.

A751.6.p: The moon has a cotton tree and nettles growing on it.

A751.6.1.p: The dark spots on the moon are a banyan tree that the creator planted there to dim its light.

A751.7.p: Two children are seen in the moon, carrying a yoke and bucket.

A751.8.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 242, Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/1010).
A751.8.p: A woman, rather than a man, is the figure seen in the moon.

A751.8.1.p: The figure in the moon is an old woman busy spinning thread with her spindle.

A751.8.2.p: The figure in the moon is a woman threshing grain, with a dog beside her.

A751.8.3.p: The figure in the moon is a goddess with a calabash (gourd container) at her side.

A751.8.4.p: A woman is said to be visible on the moon, sitting in its oven, and can be seen on clear nights.

A751.8.5.p: A girl and a tree are carried up to the moon, where they can be seen as markings on its surface.

A751.8.6.p: A goddess living in the moon is seen beating tapa cloth beneath a tree.

A751.9.p: Various other figures or objects are said to be visible as images on the surface of the moon.

A751.9.1.p: The dark spots on the moon are said to be rows of palm trees.

A751.9.2.p: A bag is said to be visible in the moon.

A751.9.3.p: A giant is said to be visible in the moon.

A751.10.p: A particular named person is said to be the face or figure seen in the moon.

A751.10.1.p: The figure in the moon is identified as Joshua.

A751.10.2.p: The figure in the moon is identified as Jacob.

A751.11.p: Other markings on the moon are explained in various ways that do not fit the other listed images.

A753.p: The moon is treated as a character with human feelings and actions, able to love, marry and have children.

A753.1.r: Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 61 n. 2 (Endymion); Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 427.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 273 n. 6a.
A753.1.p: The moon falls in love with a mortal and pursues or courts them.

A753.1.1.r: Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 29, (Cape York): Rasmussen III 50.
A753.1.1.p: The moon carries off a woman to be with it.

A753.1.2.r: Maori: Beckwith Myth 74; Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 47; S. Am. Indian (Cubeo): Goldman BBAE CXLIII (3) 798.
A753.1.2.p: The moon, in the form of a man, lives with a woman as her husband.

A753.1.3.p: The moon, in the form of a goddess, lives with a mortal man as his lover or wife.

A753.1.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys (A753.2); Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 29ff., (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 198, (Greenland): Rasmussen III 50, 52, Rink 441, Holm 47.
A753.1.4.p: The moon marries a mortal woman.

A753.1.4.1.p: The moon marries the son of the sky-god.

A753.1.4.2.p: The moon is the wife of all twelve brothers, the sun's sons, and each has her for one month at a time, because she devoured her sisters.

A753.1.5.r: Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 199, (Greenland): Holm 47.
A753.1.5.p: The moon and a mortal have a child together.

A753.2.r: Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 30, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 598, (Greenland): Rasmussen I 81, 83, II 25, 33, III 51, 170, Rink 442, Holm 73, 75, 80.
A753.2.p: The moon is said to have a house, so it is imagined as a dwelling-place with a home of its own.

A753.3.p: A general heading for miscellaneous stories in which the moon behaves like a person with human traits and actions.

A753.3.1.p: The moon tricks or fools the sun in some way.

A753.3.2.p: The moon sneaks in and steals something from a garden.

A753.3.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Ipurina): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A753.3.3.p: During the day the moon stays hidden under the earth with its mother, returning to the sky only at night.

A753.3.4.p: The moon is given both wisdom and strong emotions, like a human being.

A754.r: (Cf. A755.1).—French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 11.—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 282 n. 45; German New Guinea: Dixon 112.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 421; Chinese: Graham.
A754.p: The moon is imagined as being shut up in a box or container.

A754.1.p: The moon is put into a pit and buried there.

A754.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Guayaki): Métraux-Baldus BBAE CXLIII (1) 444.
A754.1.1.p: The moon falls into a pit, and a man rescues it from there.

A755.r: Irish: Beal XXI 323; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 183; Baltic: (Lithuanian and Lettish): Gray 320; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 422f.; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 34 No 4; Hindu: Oldenberg Religion des Veda 171; Yakuts: Holmberg Siberian 424; India: *Thompson-Balys.—Maori: Dixon 88.—African: Werner African 227f. (Ekoi): Talbot 349, (Fang): Trilles 172.
A755.p: A general heading for stories explaining why the moon changes shape through its phases.

A755.1.r: (Cf.A754). When it is closed up in the box, it is dark; when taken out of the box, light.—Ekoi: Talbot 344.
A755.1.p: The moon's changing phases are explained as the result of the moon having been put into a box.

A755.2.p: The moon's phases are explained by the death of men who tend it: the moon hangs in a tree, four men care for it, and it loses a quarter as each one dies. Later it is joined together again in the lower world.

A755.3.r: Belden MLN XX 205; Penzer VI 119 n. 1.—Maori: Clark 182; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A755.3.p: The moon's waning is explained as being caused by the moon being ill.

A755.3.1.p: A sacrifice is offered to cure the moon's illness so that it can grow bright again.

A755.4.p: The sun cuts the moon in two, and this is why the moon waxes and wanes.

A755.4.1.p: The moon is cut in half.

A755.4.2.p: The moon is stolen and cut into quarters, which explains its phases.

A755.4.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 360.
A755.4.3.p: Animals gnaw at the edge of the moon, and this causes its phases.

A755.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19, (Ipurina): Métraux ibid. 20.
A755.5.p: The moon grows or shrinks depending on whether it is fed or kept hungry.

A755.6.p: The moon's phases are a punishment for something the moon did wrong.

A755.7.p: The moon wanes (grows smaller) because of a woman's menstrual period, explaining the moon's phases.

A756.p: The moon serves as the sun's stand-in, shining at night while the sun is away.

A757.p: The moon is imagined as a boat that travels across the sky.

A757.1.p: The moon is imagined as a chariot that carries it across the sky, a variant of the moon-boat.

A758.r: *BP III 288f. Cf. Thompson Tales 281 n. 42; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 483.—Finnish: Kalevala runes 47, 49.
A758.p: The moon is kept by a monster, and someone steals it and brings it down to earth.

A759.r: For eclipse of the moon see A737, where both eclipses of the sun and moon are handled.
A759.p: Miscellaneous tales about the nature and condition of the moon that do not fit a more specific heading.

A759.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A759.1.p: The moon is said to have wooden weapons, which is why it is vulnerable.

A759.2.p: The sun and moon are given as wedding presents to a divine hero.

A759.3.p: An explanation for why the moon is pale in color.

A759.4.p: The moon is a silver-covered hare living in a crystal house with fifteen windows; it rides a chariot around Mount Meru.

A759.5.p: There were once seven moons instead of one.

A759.6.p: The moon is directly controlled by a deity.

A759.7.p: The planet Mars lies on the moon to warm it, so the moon does not freeze the earth.

A760.p: Tales explaining how the stars were created and what condition they are in.

A760.1.p: A creator god makes the stars.

A760.2.p: A star is formed from the union of a girl and a peacock.

A761.p: People or animals rise up into the sky and become stars.

A761.1.p: A river is carried up to the sky and becomes a star.

A761.2.p: A chariot from heaven carries a couple up to live with the sages in the Great Bear constellation.

A761.4.p: Stars are the fires burning in the hearths of the dead, seen as lights shining from the sky.

A761.5.p: Stars are people looking down through holes in the sky.

A761.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Warrau): Kirchoff BBAE CXLIII (3) 879.
A761.6.p: Stars are regarded as living beings with their own life.

A762.r: Persian: Carnoy 269; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 56.
A762.p: A star comes down to earth and takes on the form of a human being.

A762.1.r: **Thompson “The Star-husband Tale,” Studia Septentrionalia IV (Oslo 1953) 93—163; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 330 n. 193, Alexander N. Am. 94, Hatt Asiatic Influences. Cf. Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 538f.
A762.1.p: A star comes to earth and takes a mortal woman as his wife.

A762.2.r: Chinese: Graham; African (Lamba): Doke Lamba Folk-Lore 14 No. 11; S. Am. A762.2.p: A mortal man marries a girl who is a star.

A763.p: Stars are created from objects that people throw up into the sky.

A763.1.p: Stars are created from arrows shot up into the sky.

A763.2.p: A god hangs stars in the sky to decorate the heavens.

A764.p: Stars are pieces that have broken off from the moon.

A764.1.r: Cook Zeus I 523 n. 6.—Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: Kruyt Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land-, en Volkenkunde van Nederlandsch-Indië LXXIX 470; Philippines: Beckwith Myth 537; S. Am. Indian (Amyara): Tschopik BBAE CXLIII (2) 571.
A764.1.p: Stars are the children of the moon.

A764.1.1.r: Frazer Ovid III 205; Hatt Asiatic Influences 74f.—India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Fang): Trilles 172.
A764.1.1.p: The sun eats his children, who are stars, so that there are no stars in the daytime.

A764.1.2.p: The sun eats all of his own children except the morning star, while the moon hides all of hers away.

A764.1.3.p: Stars are children of both the sun and the moon.

A764.2.p: Stars are drops of blood that fall from the moon.

A764.3.p: The brightest stars are children of the sun, and the other stars are children of the moon.

A764.4.p: Stars are the spittle of the moon that has been transformed into light.

A765.p: Someone gives names to the stars; in one version the Great Star does the naming.

A766.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 176.—Quileute: Farrand JAFL XXXII 266; Ojibwa: Carson JAFL XXX 493; S. Am. Indian (Amazon): Alexander Lat. A767.r: Hebrew: Job 38:7; Jewish: Neuman; Pawnee: Alexander N. Am. 110.
A767.p: The stars make singing sounds together.

A769.p: A general heading for miscellaneous tales about how the stars came to be created.

A769.1.p: The stars are said to be trees that grow on the clouds.

A769.3.p: The stars are watched over and supervised by angels.

A769.4.p: The stars are able to speak.

A769.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 550.
A769.5.p: The sun gives its light to the stars, which otherwise would have none of their own.

A773.p: A general heading for tales explaining how the Pleiades star cluster came to be.

A773.1.p: The Pleiades are a princess and her six suitors, and she could not choose among them, so she was placed in the sky.

A773.2.p: The Pleiades are six wives who were cast out by their husbands because they seemed unfaithful.

A773.3.p: The Pleiades are girls who died of grief.

A773.4.p: The Pleiades are seven children born out of wedlock.

A773.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25, BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A773.5.p: The Pleiades are hunters who were left stranded in the sky after they cut down the world-tree.

A773.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 483.
A773.6.p: The Pleiades are a swarm of bees.

A773.7.p: Two stars were moved from the Great Bear constellation over to the Pleiades.

A774.p: A tale explaining how the North Star (Polaris) came to be.

A775.r: Greek: Fox 46, 248ff., Frazer Apollodorus I 321 n. 5; African: Werner African 229; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 365, MAFLS XL 21.
A775.p: A tale explaining how the Hyades star cluster came to be.

A776.1.r: Maori: Beckwith Myth 101; Korean: Zong in-Sob No. 6.
A776.1.p: Explains how the bright star Vega, in the constellation Lyra, came to be.

A777.p: Explains how the constellation Scorpio came to be in the sky, through a tale about its origin.
