A778.p: Explains how the Milky Way, the band of light across the night sky, came to be.

A778.0.1.r: Tonga: Gifford 105, 109; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 21f., 47, (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 483.
A778.0.1.p: Explains how the Magellanic Clouds, two faint cloud-like patches near the Milky Way, came to be.

A778.1.r: Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 436.—Tehuelche (Pategonia): Alexander Lat. Am. 336.
A778.1.p: The Milky Way is seen as a hunting party moving across the sky.

A778.1.1.r: German: Brunk Zs. f. Vksk. XIII 184; Russian: Ralston Songs of the Russian People 109; Hungarian: Spolyi Zs. f. deutsche Myth. II 161; Finno-Ugric: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 82; Greek-Latin: Cook Zeus II 37.
A778.1.1.p: The Milky Way is identified with the Wild Hunt, a ghostly company of hunters riding through the sky.

A778.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 20, Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 365.
A778.2.p: The Milky Way is seen as a road or path across the sky.

A778.2.1.r: Finno-Ugric: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 82.—Mandan, Pawnee: Alexander N. Am. 96, 117; S. Am. Indian (Amazon): Alexander Lat. Am. 307, (Chaco, Pampean): ibid. 323.
A778.2.1.p: The Milky Way is the path along which souls or demons travel.

A778.3.r: Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 435; Japanese: Ikeda.—Blackfoot: De Josselyn de Jong Blackfoot Texts 29ff.
A778.3.p: The Milky Way is seen as a river flowing across the sky.

A778.4.p: The Milky Way is seen as a seam in the sky where the heavens were stitched together.

A778.5.p: The Milky Way is said to be milk flowing from a woman's breast.

A778.6.p: The Milky Way is said to be the semen of the gods.

A778.7.r: Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 434; S. Am. Indian (Pañ’): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, (Chiriguano): Métraux ibid. 483.
A778.7.p: The Milky Way is seen as the route followed by a migrating bird.

A778.8.r: African: Werner African 231; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 21, (Mocovi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 365.
A778.8.p: The Milky Way is said to be smoke or ashes in the sky.

A778.9.p: The Milky Way is seen as a race track across the sky.

A778.10.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 20f.
A778.10.p: At the far end of the Milky Way there is a bottomless abyss.

A779.r: Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 22; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 21f.
A779.p: A group of miscellaneous tales explaining how particular stars came to be.

A779.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 22, 47.
A779.1.p: Explains how the Coal Sack, a dark patch in the southern Milky Way, came to be.

A779.2.p: Explains how the constellation Aquila, the eagle, came to be in the sky.

A779.3.p: Explains how the constellation Argo came to be in the sky. It is an origin story for one particular star group.

A780.p: A general heading for myths about the planets and other bright bodies such as comets. It covers stories about where these objects came from and what they do.

A780.1.p: The planets are watched over or guided by angels. Each planet has a heavenly guardian assigned to it.

A781.r: *RTP XVII 227 and references to earlier volumes.—Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 434f., 535—540; India: Thompson-Balys; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 432.—Eskimo: Alexander N. Am. 9; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 365, (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 550; Africa (Fang): Trilles 136.
A781.p: Explains how the planet Venus came to exist or to be in the sky.

A781.1.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 466; Chinese: Graham.—Maori: Clark 50; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 23, (Warrau): Kirchoff BBAE CXLIII (3) 880.
A781.1.p: Explains how the Morning Star, the bright planet seen before sunrise, came to be.

A781.2.r: Greek: Fox 247; Maori: Clark 50; Tonga: Gifford 110.
A781.2.p: Explains how the Evening Star, the bright planet seen after sunset, came to be.

A782.r: Africa: Werner African 229; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 19.
A782.p: Explains how the planet Jupiter came to exist or to be in the sky.

A786.r: Frazer Ovid III 198 n. 4.—Tahiti: Henry 227; S. Am. Indian (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 551.

A787.p: Describes how the planets affect people's lives and fates.

A788.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 24, (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 551.
A788.p: A general heading for stories explaining where meteors, or shooting stars, come from.

A788.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Guayaki): Métraux-Baldus BBAE CXLIII (1) 444.
A788.1.p: Shooting stars are believed to be pieces that broke off the moon and fell to earth.

A788.2.p: A shooting star is a heavenly body that has come down close to earth and only grazed it before going back up.

A788.3.p: Shooting stars are spirits that descend to earth and cause a woman to become pregnant.

A788.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 624.
A788.4.p: Shooting stars are said to be dung dropped from the stars.

A788.5.p: Shooting stars are said to be unfaithful wives who have been punished and cast down from the sky.

A790.p: A general heading for stories about the heavenly lights, the sun, moon, and stars.

A790.1.p: The heavenly lights come out of the firmament, the solid dome believed to hold up the sky.

A791.r: *Wünsche “Der Regenbogen in den Mythen und Sagen der Völker” Nord und Süd LXXXII (1898) 70—82; *RTP XXIII 221 and references to earlier volumes.—Irish myth: Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 30; India: Thompson-Balys.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 234; S. Am. Indian (Amuesha): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 149, (Botocudo): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 540, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 38; Zulu: Callaway 293, 295.
A791.p: Explains how the rainbow came to be.

A791.1.r: Gaster Thespis 261 n. 21; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 443f.
A791.1.p: The rainbow is the bow of a deity, a god's bow set in the sky.

A791.2.r: African: Werner African 234; S. Am. Indian (Moré): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 406, (Ashluslay): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 38, (Vilela): ibid. 40.
A791.2.p: The rainbow is a snake, often a giant serpent arching across the sky.

A791.3.p: The rainbow is explained as a bridge built across the sky by the gods.

A791.4.p: The rainbow is said to have three colors.

A791.5.p: The rainbow is a king who has been transformed, and the smaller, fainter rainbow is his wife.

A791.6.p: The rainbow comes from the gods emptying their drinking cups, the spilled drink forming the colors.

A791.7.p: The rainbow is the horse of the rain-god.

A791.8.p: The rainbow comes out of an anthill.

A791.8.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 38.
A791.8.1.p: The rainbow lives in a hole in the ground, as a variant of the anthill origin.

A791.9.p: The rainbow arose from transformed butterflies, which are the souls of lovers.

A791.10.p: The rainbow is a sign of a covenant or promise between the creator and humankind.

A795.r: Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 140 No. 8; Finnish: Aarne VIII 4 No. 9; Finno-Ugric: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 81, 287.—Eskimo (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 153, (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 266.
A795.p: A tale explaining how the northern lights (aurora borealis) came to be.

A796.p: A tale explaining how the signs of the zodiac came to be.

A797.p: A tale explaining why the sky takes on its colors at sunrise and sunset.

A800.r: *H. F. Feilberg Skabelses og Syndflodssagn (1915); A. Kühn Berichte über den Weltanfang bei den Indochinesen und ihren Nachbarvölker (1935); Irish myth: Cross; Persian: Carnoy 280; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.—N. A. Indian (general): Thompson Tales 272 n. 1, (Ojibwa) Skinner JAFL XXXII 287, (Kaska) Teit JAFL XXX 441ff.—See also all references in this section (A800-839).
A800.p: A general heading for stories about how the earth was created.

A801.p: The earth comes out of chaos, a formless primeval state.

A802.p: China is said to be the first land to appear in our world.

A810.r: **Dh I 1—89 passim; Gaster Oldest Stories 69.—Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 325—26; Finnish: Kalevala rune 1; Egyptian: Müller 48; Babylonian: Spence 71; Jewish: Neuman; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 313ff.; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 786; India: *Thompson-Balys.—Batak: Voorhoeve Oversicht 63ff.; Marquesas: Handy 122; Marshall Is.: Davenport 221; Oceanic: Dixon 8 n. 7 (Maori), 18f. (Samoa), 20 (Society Is., Tonga), 105 (Admiralty Is., Polynesia, Indonesia, Micronesia), 157 (Minahassa), 158f. (Borneo), 248f. (Marshall Is., Yap), 270 (Arunta); Bushongo: Werner African 144, African: Stanley 5; S. Am. Indian (Guarayu): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 437.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 279 n. 29, Alexander N. Am 260 (Haida), (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 53; Mixtec: Alexander Lat. Am. 86; Quiché: ibid. 160.
A810.p: In the beginning everything is covered by water.

A810.1.p: God and the Devil fly together over the primeval water.

A810.2.p: The primeval water subsides after a set period of time.

A810.2.1.p: The waters of heaven would flood and engulf the earth if the firmament did not hold them back.

A811.r: (Cf. A812.)—India: Thompson-Balys.—New Britain, New Hebrides: Dixon 105.
A811.p: The earth is brought up from the bottom of the primeval water.

A811.1.r: Oceanic (Maori, Hawaiian, Central Polynesian, Tonga, Samoan, New Hebrides, Union Group, Gilbert Is., New Britain): Dixon 43f.
A811.1.p: The earth comes up out of the sea bottom: a fish brought up from the depths is cut apart, and its pieces become the mountains.

A811.2.p: Three gods bring the earth up from the bottom of the primeval water.

A812.r: **E. W. Count The Earth Diver and the Rival Twins (Proceedings 29th International Congress of Americanists [Chicago, 1952] 55—62); Walk “Die Verbreitung des Tauchmotivs in den Urmeerschöpfungs- (und Sintflut-) Sagen” Mitteil. d. anthrop. Gesellschaft Wien LXIII (1933) 60—76.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 318, *322ff.; Hatt Asiatic Influences 12—36, India: *Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 279 n. 30, (Calif. Indian): Gayton and Newman 53.
A812.p: A creator on a raft in the primeval sea sends down animals to fetch earth; after others fail, one (often the muskrat) brings up a bit of mud from which the earth is made.

A812.1.r: *Dh I 2—89 passim, *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 277ff.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 3 No. 1; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 455f., Aarne FFC XXV 139 No. 1; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 80 No. 1; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3005; Legends Nos. 7—10, 12f.; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 313ff.
A812.1.p: The Devil dives for earth at God's command; he succeeds only on the third try, hides the earth under his tongue, and his tongue swells until God rescues him.

A812.2.p: A bird recovers earth from an egg lying at the bottom of the sea.

A812.3.p: After creating a crow, the creator sends it out to search for the nucleus of the earth.

A813.p: In the beginning the creator floats on a raft in the primeval sea and creates the earth from there.

A813.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A813.1.p: The earth is shaped like a raft and held up by spirits.

A813.2.p: The raft on the primeval sea is a lotus leaf.

A813.3.p: The creator rests on a tree or a stake while floating in the primeval waters.

A814.p: The earth is made from something thrown or spread onto the primeval water.

A814.1.r: Oceanic: Dixon 18 (Samoa), 158 (Borneo), 163 n. 29—32. (Philippines, Samoa, Tonga, Micronesia).
A814.1.p: A stone thrown onto the primeval water becomes the earth.

A814.2.p: Sand scattered on the primeval water becomes the earth.

A814.3.r: Mongolian, Japanese, Tungus: Holmberg Siberian 328f.; Japanese: Anesaki 223.—Hawaii: Dixon 15.
A814.3.p: Decayed matter thrown onto the primeval water becomes the earth.

A814.4.p: The earth grows from a tree that sprouts in the primeval water.

A814.5.p: Steam produced by a fire thrown into the primeval water becomes the earth.

A814.6.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 55.
A814.6.p: Earth is scattered in a circle over the primeval water, spread out in all four directions.

A814.7.p: Earth is made from primeval water mixed with tobacco seeds.

A814.8.p: Earth grows from a lotus seed placed on the water.

A814.9.p: Earth is formed when an egg breaks on the primeval water.

A814.10.p: The earth is created when the creator's spittle, or a similar object thrown onto the primeval water, builds up into land.

A814.10.1.p: A primeval potter spits, and the spittle spreads out over the surface of the water to form the earth.

A815.p: The earth is held up on the back of a turtle that floats in the primeval water.

A815.1.p: The earth is raised up on the head of a serpent floating in the primeval water.

A816.r: *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 279.—Icel: *Olrik Ragnarök 23, MacCulloch Eddic 325.—Mixtec: Alexander Lat. Am. 86.
A816.p: Land rises up out of the sea to form the earth.

A816.1.p: A stone rises out of the primeval water, and it becomes a mountain after a devil sits on it.

A816.2.p: There is an ocean lying beneath the world.

A816.3.p: God makes the primeval sea roll back, leaving the hills bare and dry.

A817.p: The earth is lowered down from the sky onto the primeval ocean.

A820.p: A heading for other ways the earth was created that are not based on primeval water.

A821.p: The earth is made of lac, a resinous substance secreted by insects.

A822.p: The earth is formed from mud shaken off the back of a primeval boar.

A822.1.p: The world is transformed from a mud parrot kept in a golden cage.

A823.p: The earth is made by setting cups of earth on a spider's web.

A824.p: The earth is made when broken ground is transformed into the world.

A825.p: The earth is made when the first couple dance on a piece of cloth laid on the water.

A826.p: The earth sets and solidifies like curds forming from milk.

A827.p: The earth is made when the primeval water dries up.

A828.p: The earth is made from a worm that the creator scratches with his nails.

A828.1.p: The earth is excreted by a worm.

A830.r: Genesis ch. I.—Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Tahiti: Henry 341; Marquesas: Handy 122; Pawnee: Alexander N. Am. 109.
A830.p: A creator god makes the earth. This is the basic motif of the earth being brought into existence by a maker deity.

A831.p: The earth is made out of the body of a person or animal, such as a primeval being that is killed or dismembered and whose body becomes the land.

A831.1.p: The earth is formed from the body of a son of a god.

A831.2.r: (Cf. A614.1.). *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 282.—Icel: MacCulloch Eddic 325; India: Thompson-Balys.
A831.2.p: The earth is formed from the body of a giant, in the Norse version named Ymir.

A831.3.p: The earth is created when the first man and woman are sacrificed, and their son and daughter are killed to make the earth from their bodies.

A831.4.p: The earth is made when the first brother and sister are murdered, and their bodies become the land.

A831.5.p: The earth is made from the body of a child who has been murdered.

A831.6.p: The earth is made from the body of an animal that has been slain.

A831.7.p: The earth is made from the body of a god who has killed himself.

A831.8.p: Gods make the earth from the blood and bones of a victim they have killed.

A831.9.p: The earth is made from the body of Adam, the first man.

A832.p: God creates the earth because he is lonely and dissatisfied at being alone in the middle of the primeval waters.

A833.r: (Cf. A1211.5.). India: Thompson-Balys; San Carlos Apache: Goddard PaAM XXIV 7.
A833.p: The earth is formed from the creator's cuticle, meaning the thin outer skin or layer shed from his body.

A835.p: God throws a nut over his shoulder, the devil catches it in his mouth, and it grows large and is spat out, forming the earth.

A835.1.p: The earth is created from snow lying under the divine throne.

A836.p: The creator shapes the core or nucleus of the earth the way a cook would prepare a rice cake.

A837.p: The creator makes the earth bit by bit, one piece at a time, rather than all at once.

A840.p: Explanations of what holds the earth up and keeps it from falling.

A841.r: Irish myth: Cross; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 385, 400; Jewish: Neuman; Greek: *Grote I 70; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX III No. 66.—Sumatra: Dixon 163; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 286 n. 56; Maya: Alexander Lat. Am. 154.—See also references to A665.2.1.
A841.p: Pillars or supports, usually four (or two and similar numbers), hold up the earth.

A841.0.1.p: Two gods fix the four world-columns firmly in place using their mother's hair, so they cannot move.

A841.1.p: The earth is hung from the sky by cords fastened at its four corners.

A841.2.p: Four maidens stand at the cardinal points and hold up the earth, one at each direction.

A841.3.p: Twelve iron pillars hold the earth steady and keep it from moving.

A841.4.p: Four great nails fix the earth in place at its corners.

A842.r: Greek: Fox 88, *Grote I 70; Gaster Oldest Stories 129.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 286 n. 56b; Chibcha: Alexander Lat. Am. 203.
A842.p: A man carries the whole earth on his shoulders, holding it up from below.

A842.1.p: A goddess stands on her head and so supports the earth with her body.

A842.2.p: An old woman carries the earth balanced on her head.

A843.r: Finno-Ugric: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 222.—N. A. Indian (Tlingit, Hare): Boas RBAE XXXI 732.
A843.p: A post holds up the earth, and an old woman guards it; when she gets hungry the post shakes and causes earthquakes.

A843.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93, (Apapocuvá): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 136.
A843.1.p: The earth is held up by a wooden cross instead of a single post.

A844.p: The earth rests on the back of some animal that carries it.

A844.1.r: (Cf. A815.).—Siberian: *Holmberg Siberian 327; India: *Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 279 n. 31.
A844.1.p: The earth rests on the back of a giant turtle or tortoise.

A844.3.r: *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 281.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian.

A844.5.p: The earth rests on the horns of a bull, and that bull stands on a fish.

A844.6.p: The earth rests on a tortoise, which rests on a serpent, which rests on an elephant.

A844.7.p: The earth rests on the back of an elephant.

A844.8.p: The earth rests on the head of a cobra.

A844.9.p: The earth is supported on the tusk of a great boar.

A844.10.p: The earth is supported on the legs of a vast number of birds.

A844.11.p: The earth is said to rest on a huge sea monster called a leviathan.

A844.12.r: (Cf. A844.6.). Hindu: Keith 120, 155, Penzer VI 71 n. 1 (thousand-headed serpent); India: *Thompson-Balys.
A844.12.p: A serpent is said to hold up the earth, keeping it from falling.

A849.p: Miscellaneous other beliefs about what holds up the earth, not covered by the more specific categories.

A849.1.p: The earth is said to be set firmly on a foundation of stone.

A849.2.p: The earth is said to rest on the arm of God.

A849.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Apapocuvá-Guaraní): Métraux MAFLS XL 36.
A849.3.p: The earth is held up by some kind of prop or support, in a miscellaneous version of this creation idea.

A850.p: Stories about how the earth changed or came to be in its present state.

A851.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 3 No. 2; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 139 No. 3.
A851.p: The earth is said to have become oblong (elongated), with God the Father on one end and the Son on the other.

A852.p: The earth is made smaller; God learns from the devil, through trickery, how to shrink it because it was made too large.

A853.r: See references to A812 in which this idea is always involved.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 317.—Oceanic: Dixon 29; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 279 n. 30.
A853.p: The earth is made larger, growing gradually during the creation.

A853.1.p: The earth's size is doubled because a growing population makes the change necessary.

A855.r: courses of rivers, height of mountains, human reproduction, etc.—are at first the reverse of the present condition.—N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 225.
A855.p: Everything on the earth is the opposite of how it is now.

A856.p: The earth is at first soft and is later hardened by the sun's rays.

A856.1.p: The original soft earth is hardened by the wind.

A856.2.p: Ground that was once entirely wet dries out after the first woman cuts her little finger and her blood drips onto it.

A857.p: Stories about how the earth is kept steady or stabilized.

A857.1.p: The earth is warm and wet because two huge copper vessels steaming over a fire lie beneath it.

A857.2.p: A giant servant of the creator makes a valley where the earth's crust is heavy and a mountain where it is light, so the earth stays balanced.

A857.3.p: A giant servant of the creator plants trees to hold the earth together where it has slipped.

A857.3.1.p: Roots are created to hold the land firm.

A870.p: Stories and beliefs about the nature and condition of the earth itself.

A871.r: Irish myth: Cross; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 308.
A871.p: The earth is pictured as a square divided into four quarters, each corner or quarter marking a region of the world.

A871.0.1.p: Taprobane, an island, is placed at the eastern end of the world.

A871.0.2.r: S. A. Indian (Mbayá, Mataco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A871.0.2.p: A fire that never goes out is located at the far end of the earth.

A871.1.p: Four streams flow out from the four corners of the earth.

A871.2.p: Four rivers rise in paradise and flow out to water the primitive world below.

A872.r: Greek: *Grote I 220, 232, 310 (River Ocean); Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A872.p: A great river is imagined as flowing around the whole world, encircling it.

A872.1.p: Seven seas are imagined as surrounding and encircling the world.

A873.p: Great clouds are imagined as lying both above and below the earth.

A875.r: Greek: Grote I 4, 310; Hindu: Keith 16; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 308.
A875.p: The earth is pictured as a flat, round disc shaped like a wheel.

A875.1.r: *Holmberg Baum des Lebens 150 s.v. “Mittelpunkt”; *Frazer Pausanias V 314f.; *Pease Cicero De Divinatione 353 (Bk. II 115); *Roscher Abh. kgl. Sächs. Ges. d. Wiss. (Phil. hist. Kl.) XXIX (1913) 9, XXXI (1915) 1, Berichte d. kgl Sächs. Ges. d. Wiss. (Phil. hist. Kl.) LXX (1918) 2; Warren Paradise Found (1885) 225ff.; Gaster Thespis 170f.; Jewish: Neuman; Norse: Boberg.
A875.1.p: The earth has a navel, a central point at its middle, which is the center of the earth disc.

A875.1.1.p: A mountain stands at the center of the earth.

A875.2.p: A well in the middle of the earth is the source of eleven rivers.

A876.r: Icel.: De la Saussaye 346, MacCulloch Eddic 279, 328, Boberg; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 345; Western Asia (general): Frobenius Erdteile VI 196; India: Thompson-Balys.—Arapaho: cf. Dorsey FM IV 13; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 57.
A876.p: A giant serpent is imagined as encircling the entire earth.

A876.1.p: A sea monster called a leviathan is said to wrap around the whole globe.

A878.r: *Wünsche “Das Wasser des Lebens in den Märchen der Völker” Zs. f. vgl. Litteraturgeschichte XIII 166ff.; **Holmberg Baum; Dh I 6 (five eastern branches given to man, others forbidden); *Albright Am. Jour. Semitic Langs. XXXIX 161.—*Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 150ff., 200.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 331ff. (Yggdrasil); Irish Myth: Cross; Egyptian: Müller 36.
A878.p: A great tree stands in the world, understood as the tree of life or of fate.

A878.1.p: A stream of paradise flows from the roots of the world-tree, a mythic picture of the cosmos.

A878.1.1.p: Other streams flow out from the roots of the earth-tree.

A878.1.2.p: Three wells lie beneath the three roots of the earth-tree.

A878.2.p: A lake of milk lies beside the tree of life.

A878.3.p: various animals live at or gather around the earth-tree.

A878.3.1.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319, 332; Boberg; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 357.
A878.3.1.p: A snake lies at the roots of the earth-tree.

A878.3.2.p: A hart or deer is said to eat the leaves or fruit of the cosmic earth-tree that holds up the world.

A878.3.3.r: Holmberg Baum 67ff. Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 332ff., Boberg.
A878.3.3.p: A chattering squirrel lives in the earth-tree that stands at the center of the world.

A878.3.4.p: A wise eagle perches in the earth-tree that supports the world.

A878.3.5.p: A hawk lives in the earth-tree that supports the world.

A878.3.6.p: A golden cock or rooster is found in the earth-tree.

A878.4.p: The earth-tree produces sap that heals sickness and removes hunger when eaten or drunk.

A881.p: The division of the earth into zones is linked with the twelve signs of the zodiac.

A900.p: A general heading for stories explaining the origin of the earth's landforms and features.

A901.r: *Dh II 8, 68, 199; *Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens III 240 s.v. “Fussspur”; *Wehrhan Die Sage 65; *Basset and others RTP XXIV 299 and references to earlier volumes.—Irish myth: Cross; Breton: MacCulloch Celtic 135; Icel.: De la Saussaye 280; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 303 Nos. 22, 23; Finnish: Kalevala rune 1; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3008, Legends Nos. 12ff.; Greek: Fox 250.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 331; Japanese: Anesaki 248f.; Indo-Chinese: Scott Indo-Chinese 291; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 31, 768, 957, 1211.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 18; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 70; Africa (Fang): Trilles 153.—Cf. A911, A920.1.2, A920.1.5, A924, A931, A932, A933, A941.1, A941.2, A951, A955, A964, A972, A982.1, A984.
A901.p: Landforms and landmarks are explained as results of the deeds of a powerful hero, demigod, or deity, such as footprints or paths they made.

A901.1.p: Hills, valleys, or other landmarks are said to have been formed by a battle between gods.

A901.2.p: Natural rock formations are explained as the result of huge rock pillars fighting or colliding with one another.

A902.r: (Cf. A0.)—Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.—African: Werner African 143.—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 30.
A902.p: The creator deliberately arranged the earth's landforms and features in their present places.

A902.1.p: Two creators travel by different routes, each establishing features of the earth along the way.

A903.p: Landforms or landmarks are explained as having been caused by animals.

A910.p: A general heading for stories explaining how bodies of water such as seas, lakes, and rivers came to exist.

A910.1.p: Waters are said to have been created on the first day of creation.

A910.2.p: Waters are created as a punishment.

A910.3.p: Bodies of water that were in the primeval abyss sink down, leaving the earth dry.

A910.4.r: S. A. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 133.
A910.4.p: Some bodies of water are remnants left behind by a great flood.

A910.5.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 167.
A910.5.p: Waters are created by a pair of divine twins.

A911.r: (Cf. A901, A920.1.5, A941.2, A1012.)—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 135; Nebraska: Pound WF VI 305—316; Finnish: Kalevala rune 4; African (Upoto): Einstein 127.
A911.p: Bodies of water are said to have come into being from someone's tears.

A913.r: *Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens II 513 s. v. “Ebbe und Flut”.—Persian: Carnoy 278.—Shetland Is.: Teit JAFL XXXI 198.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 293 n. 76a, and add (Malecite) Speck JAFL XXVIII 60, (Tahltan) Teit JAFL XXXII 201.
A913.p: An explanation for why the sea rises and falls in tides.

A913.1.p: A tidal wave or surge appears at the spot where a person died.

A913.2.p: The tide is caused by a sea-monster breathing in and out.

A913.3.p: The ebbing tide flows out into a great whirlpool.

A913.4.p: A tub drips when the tide is high but holds water when the tide is low.

A914.p: Mountains are said to push the water westward.

A915.p: An explanation for why the waters do not flood and cover the whole earth.

A917.p: A myth telling of a dispute or fight between the earth and the waters.

A918.p: Waters are described as having sexes, some male and some female.

A920.r: Jewish: Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 270, 277f.—Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 87; Buin: Wheeler 28.—Hatt: Asiatic Influences 17.
A920.p: A general heading for explanations of how the seas came to be.

A920.1.r: Fb “sø” III 731a.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 135 (cf. A911), Cross; Indo-Chinese: Scott Indo-Chinese 291 (cf. A901).—Tahltan: *Teit JAFL XXXII, 219f.; Malecite: Speck JAFL XXX 481.
A920.1.p: A general heading for explanations of how lakes came to be.

A920.1.0.1.p: An explanation for the origin of one specific named lake.

A920.1.1.p: Lakes come from endlessly refilling buckets that never run out.

A920.1.2.p: Lakes are formed from the holes dug by a primeval ox.

A920.1.3.p: A lake suddenly bursts forth and drowns a thief.

A920.1.4.p: Lakes burst forth to mark the birth, death, or battle of a primitive hero.

A920.1.5.p: Lakes are said to come from tears.

A920.1.5.1.p: Lakes are said to come from belches.

A920.1.6.p: A lake is said to come from a horse's urine.

A920.1.7.p: A lake is created when fairies make it, as part of their doings.

A920.1.7.1.p: Fairies are at war, and a lake suddenly bursts forth from the ground to stop the fighting.

A920.1.8.r: Kristensen Danske Sagn III (1895) 241ff., (1931) 162ff.; Fb “sø” III 731a; G. Schütte in Danske Studier (1925) 117ff.
A920.1.8.p: A lake bursts forth from the earth to drown wicked or godless people.

A920.1.8.1.p: A lake arises because someone breaks a taboo, a forbidden act that brings the flood that forms the lake.

A920.1.9.p: A lake bursts forth in the place where an island is plowed out of the ground.

A920.1.10.p: Lakes are said to have been made by a giant or a devil.

A920.1.11.p: A woman is changed into a pool of water.

A920.1.12.p: A lake bursts forth in the place where a blind king pulls up rushes.

A920.1.13.p: A lake of milk comes into being through the holiness of a saint.

A920.1.14.p: Lakes are described as daughters of the gods.

A920.1.15.p: An explanation of how the Dead Sea came to be.

A920.1.16.p: A lake was originally full of palm wine instead of water.

A920.2.p: An explanation of how channels of the sea came to be.

A921.p: The ocean is said to be the son of Earth and Heaven.

A922.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 325f.; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 51 No. 7**; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 86 No. 45.—Oceanic: Dixon 37 n. 107, 108 (Polynesia, Samoa, Marquesas).
A922.p: The ocean is said to have been made from blood.

A923.r: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 64.—Polynesian: Dixon 37 n. 106.
A923.p: The ocean is said to have come from the creator's sweat.

A923.1.r: (Cf. A933.)—Buin: Wheeler Mono-Alu 28, Aurora (New Hebrides): Codrington II 372.
A923.1.p: The ocean is said to have come from urine.

A924.p: Various other explanations of how the ocean came to be.

A924.1.p: The sea is said to have formed when a calabash (gourd) was overturned and its contents spilled out.

A924.2.p: The sea is said to have formed from rotting snakes.

A924.3.p: The sea comes into being when water is released from a tree-top, as part of a myth explaining where the ocean came from.

A924.4.p: The sea is formed from water that fills a hole dug into the earth, a myth explaining the origin of the ocean.

A925.p: A general heading for myths explaining why the sea has its various characteristics, such as waves, color, smell, sound and surf.

A925.1.p: A myth explaining why the sea has high waves.

A925.2.p: A myth explaining why the sea has the color it does.

A925.3.p: A myth explaining why the sea has a foul or bad smell.

A925.4.p: A myth explaining why fresh water wells up in the sea, so that the salt sea has patches of fresh water.

A925.5.p: A myth explaining why the sea makes a mournful or sad sound.

A925.6.p: A myth explaining the origin of surf, the waves breaking on the shore.

A925.7.p: A myth explaining why there are shining patches beneath the surface of the sea.

A928.r: Hindu: Keith 146.—Cf. Icel.: Meyer Mythologie der Germanen (1903) 244 (Thor lowers level of ocean).
A928.p: A giant drinks up the whole ocean, a motif in myths about giants and the sea.

A930.p: A general heading for myths explaining how streams and rivers came to exist.

A930.1.p: A being who creates rivers, in a myth explaining their origin.

A930.1.1.p: A snake is the creator of rivers and lakes, in a myth explaining where they came from.

A931.r: (Cf. A901.)—A fugitive’s doublings cause a river’s windings.—N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 224, (Micmac): Speck JAFL XXVIII 60, (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 62.
A931.p: A river follows a winding course because it is pursuing someone or something, as explained in a myth.

A933.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: Herrmann Nordische Mythologie 368, Boberg; French: Sébillot France II 327ff.; Sudanese: Frobenius Atlantis VI 219; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 15 No. 7.
A933.p: A river comes from the urine of a goddess or giantess, in a myth explaining its origin.

A933.1.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 328; cf. India: Thompson-Balys.
A933.1.p: A river comes from the slaver, or drool, of the Fenris-wolf, a mythological wolf.

A933.2.r: S. A. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359.
A933.2.p: A river comes from the vagina of the first woman, in a myth explaining the river's origin.

A934.p: A general heading for various different myths explaining where rivers came from.

A934.1.p: Rivers are formed when a primeval ox digs out the earth, in a myth explaining their origin.

A934.2.p: Rivers come into being because seven children each walk off in a different direction, leaving a stone every mile, and the lines of stones become rivers.

A934.3.p: Rivers gush out at the places where a primitive hero was born, died, or fought a battle, marking those events.

A934.4.p: A river appears where a god drags his staff along the ground.

A934.5.p: Rivers begin when a saint prays during a drought and water flows in answer.

A934.6.p: A hailstorm is said to have left twelve main rivers in Ireland.

A934.7.p: A river bursts out of a well while someone is being chased.

A934.8.p: Rivers flow out of a mythical well.

A934.9.p: A stream suddenly gushes out from the side of a mountain without warning.

A934.10.p: A river comes into being from a girl who drowned in a well.

A934.11.p: A river is created when someone or something is transformed into water.

A934.11.1.p: A girl is reborn as a river so that the god Vishnu can rest in its bed in the form of a stone.

A934.11.2.p: A person changes themselves into a river.

A934.11.3.p: A goddess, in anger, breaks herself into five pieces, and that is why a river has five branches.

A934.11.4.p: A river arises when flowing honey is transformed into water.

A934.12.p: A peacock guides the rivers to the large valley so they do not wander in circles.

A935.r: Irish myth: Cross.—Malecite: Speck JAFL XXX 480; S. A. Indian (Chibcha): Kroeber BBAE CXLIII (2) 908; African (Upoto): Einstein 135.
A935.p: Explains how waterfalls (cataracts) came to be.

A937.p: Explains why a certain river has no mist, because eagle's wings were used to fan the mist away.

A938.p: Rivers and streams are the children of the marriage between Ocean and his sister.

A939.1.p: A river bursts out of a well while someone is being chased.

A940.p: Explains how other bodies of water, such as lakes and seas, came to be.

A941.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.—Japanese: Ikeda; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 114 No. 69; S. A. Indian (Amuesa): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 131.
A941.p: Explains how springs of water came to exist. Tales give a cause for the origin of springs in general.

A941.0.1.p: Explains the origin of one specific spring, as told in a particular tale rather than as a general rule.

A941.1.r: (Cf. A901.)—Malten Jahrb. d. kaiserlichen deutschen archäologischen Inst. XXIX 185.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 134, 328, Herrmann Saxo II 216; Greek: Fox 40, 213; Hungarian: Ipolyi Zs. f. deutsche Mythologie u. Sittenkunde II 273; German: Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens s.v. “Brunnen”; India: Thompson-Balys.
A941.1.p: A spring comes into being where a horse's hoof has left a print in the ground.

A941.1.1.p: A spring arises from the urine of a horse.

A941.1.2.p: A spring bursts out at the spot where a fairy horse lies down.

A941.2.p: Springs are said to come from weeping, so that water flowing from the earth is the result of tears.

A941.3.r: Sébillot France II 181ff.; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 114 No. 69.
A941.3.p: A spring appears when someone strikes the earth with a sword.

A941.3.1.p: A spring breaks forth at the place where a magic spear strikes the ground.

A941.3.2.p: A god throws his staff or spear, and a spring appears where it lands.

A941.4.p: A spring bursts forth to mark or commemorate something that happened to a hero or deity there.

A941.4.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 188.
A941.4.1.p: A spring arises to commemorate the place where a hero died or was buried.

A941.4.2.p: A spring bursts out in response to a primitive hero's need for water.

A941.4.2.1.r: Icel.: Herrmann Saxo II 216, MacCulloch Eddic 134, Boberg.
A941.4.2.1.p: A spring bursts out to meet the need of a demigod's warriors for water.

A941.5.p: A spring bursts forth through the power of a saint.

A941.5.0.1.p: A fountain bursts forth through the power of the Virgin Mary.

A941.5.0.2.p: Wells break forth at the moment of Christ's birth.

A941.5.1.p: A spring breaks forth where a saint strikes a rock.

A941.5.2.p: A many-colored fountain bursts forth where a saint strikes the earth with his foot.

A941.5.3.p: Through a saint's power, a spring breaks forth at the place where a leper pulls up a clump of rushes.

A941.5.4.p: A spring breaks forth where an animal brings back a book the saint had left behind.

A941.5.5.p: A spring bursts forth from the ground at the spot where a saint's stolen cow is found.

A941.5.6.p: A holy man spreads a magic cloth from a goddess over a place, and water springs up out of the earth there.

A941.5.7.p: A spring comes into being at the place where a god dug into the earth.

A941.5.8.p: A spring rises from the blood of an innocent king.

A941.6.p: The bursting forth of springs is one of the causes of a great flood.

A941.7.p: A spring flows out from under a magic or holy object.

A941.7.1.p: A spring rises from beneath the world-tree.

A941.7.2.p: A spring gushes from the roots of a sacred tree after an arrow is shot into it.

A941.7.3.p: A stream flows out from under the holy of holies in a temple.

A942.p: The origin of hot springs, also called geysers, is explained.

A942.1.p: Hot springs well up at the place where Christ bathed his feet.

A942.2.p: The origin of salt springs is explained.

A950.r: Chinese: Graham; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 47.
A950.p: The origin of the land itself is explained.

A951.r: (Cf. A901.)—*Olrik in Danske Studier (1910) 1ff.; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 181; Danish: De la Saussaye 280.
A951.p: The hills and hollows of the land are formed by a goddess plowing the earth.

A951.1.p: A river valley is scooped out by a giant beast licking the ground.

A951.2.p: Hills and hollows of the land are formed when swine root up the ground.

A951.3.p: Hills and furrows in the land are formed by a magical hero driving a harrow across it.

A952.p: Land rises up out of the sea.

A953.p: Land is thrown down from heaven to earth.

A954.p: Land is born from a goddess.

A955.p: Myths explaining how islands came to exist.

A955.0.1.p: A god or deity orders islands into being.

A955.1.p: Islands are the stepping-stones a deity uses to cross water.

A955.2.r: (Cf. D936, D1092.)—Greek: Pauly-Wissowa s.v. “Anaphe” 2060, Apollonius Rhodius IV 1709ff.
A955.2.p: An island is formed where an arrow shot by someone lands and becomes land.

A955.3.p: Explanations for why an island has the particular shape it has and where it lies.

A955.3.1.p: An explanation for why an island has the particular shape it has.

A955.3.2.p: An explanation for why an island lies where it does.

A955.3.2.1.r: *Frazer Pausanias II 48.—Japanese: Anesaki 248ff., Ikeda; Marshall Is.: Davenport 222.
A955.3.2.1.p: A primeval hero moves islands into their current places.

A955.4.p: A goddess plows an island up out of the earth or water.

A955.5.p: Islands arise from a cow and her calf after a one-eyed god's evil eye transforms them.

A955.6.p: A giantess casts stones that become islands.

A955.7.p: Islands are formed from webs woven by primeval spiders.

A955.8.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 61, 227, 308; Tonga: Beckwith Myth 369, Gifford 15, 20; Maori: Clark 48ff.; Marquesas: Handy 103; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (x-G. 13/52).
A955.8.p: A demigod or hero fishes an island up out of the water.

A955.9.p: A goddess gives birth to islands.

A955.10.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 347; Tahiti: Henry 129, 346; Marshall Is.: Davenport 222; Tonga: Gifford 24, 68, 179; Marquesas: Handy 44.
A955.10.p: An island is formed when some object or person is transformed into land.

A955.11.r: Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 468; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 216f., 230, 328; Marquesas: Handy 112; Tonga: Gifford 81; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 389.
A955.11.p: Islands were once part of a continent and later broke away from it.

A955.12.p: An old woman guards the floating islands belonging to the gods.

A956.p: Myths explaining how peninsulas came to exist.

A957.p: Myths explaining how deserts came to exist.

A960.r: Norwegian: Solheim Register 22; Persian: Carnoy; Chinese: Graham; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 47.
A960.p: Myths explaining how mountains and hills came to exist.

A961.p: Mountains are created from the body of a primeval animal, which is the origin of the landscape.

A961.1.p: Hills and valleys form when a giant primeval bird flaps its wings while the earth is still soft.

A961.2.p: The earth comes from a fish pulled out of primeval water, and when it is chopped up its pieces become mountains.

A961.3.p: A primeval lizard is broken while passing through a mountain, and its front and back halves turn into mountains.

A961.4.p: Mountains arise from the scattered pieces of a giant serpent that has been slain.

A961.5.p: Mountains or cliffs are formed from the bones of a giant who has been killed.

A962.p: Hills and mountains are explained as the leftover results of things a god or hero did long ago.

A962.1.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 170 (bones), 188f.; Maori: Beckwith Myth 379 (navel); Tahiti: Henry 339 (ribs, spine).
A962.1.p: A mountain is formed from a part of a god's or hero's body.

A962.2.p: God shaped the mountains with his own hand.

A962.3.p: Mountains came into being from the long journeys a god made in primeval times.

A962.4.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 4 No. 4, XXXIII 51 No. 4.
A962.4.p: God pressed mountains together, forming them.

A962.5.p: Mountains were made by hand, by a god or hero shaping them.

A962.6.p: Mountains arose from the journeys the first man made in the beginning.

A962.7.p: A hero strikes the earth with his sword, and the blow raises hills.

A962.8.p: Hills and ridges are the pieces of a god's head that was shattered.

A962.9.p: Some mountains and hills are said to be former sons and daughters of gods who were turned into landforms.

A962.10.p: Hills are the burdens that a culture hero carried on his shoulders and then set down.

A963.p: Mountains are formed from stones, soil, or sand that were dropped or thrown down somewhere.

A963.1.r: German: Grimm Deutsche Mythologie I 443; Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 1043; French: Sébillot France IV 7ff.; Swedish: Wessman 68 Nos. 581—3.—Indonesian: L. de Backer L’archipel indien 232ff.
A963.1.p: A giant carries stones in his clothes, and as he walks he loses them, and they become mountains.

A963.2.r: (Cf. A971.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 4 No. 5; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 34 No. 1.
A963.2.p: A god is sifting stones when the bottom of his sieve breaks, and huge stones and mountains fall through.

A963.3.p: A mountain or hill is formed when soil is dropped or thrown down in one place, so the pile becomes a rise in the land.

A963.4.r: Germanic: Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens s. v. “Findlingssteine”; Celtic: Thurneysen Irische Helden- und Königssage 431; Danish: Schmidt Danmarks Kaempesten (1932) (DF XXXIX) 66ff.; Kristensen Danske Sagn III (1895) 19ff., (1931) 11ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 493—96; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 68 Nos. 586—591.
A963.4.p: A giant throws stones at a church, and the stones that land become mountains and hills.

A963.5.p: Giants cast stones, and the stones they throw form hills.

A963.6.p: A hill is formed from an anvil that a supernatural smith has cast or thrown down.

A963.7.p: A hill is formed from sand that passersby have left behind, piling up over time.

A963.8.p: A hill is said to be an unfinished tower, built in the likeness of the Tower of Babel (Nimrod's tower).

A963.9.p: Clay soil falls from the sky and piles up to form a hill.

A964.p: Mountains or hills are explained as the result of an ancient contest or fight.

A964.1.p: Holes in hills are explained as the result of a fight between gods.

A964.2.p: Mountains are said to have fought each other, and that fight is why they have their present shape.

A964.2.1.p: Mountains fight one another for the honor of being the place where a divine revelation is given.

A964.3.p: A battle between demons tears up the hills, leaving them torn and broken.

A965.p: A mountain chain is explained as having an origin in a particular tale or event.

A965.1.p: One mountain loves another and stretches out a leg to reach her, and the stretched shape becomes a mountain chain.

A966.p: Volcanoes are explained by a tale of how they came to be.

A967.p: Mounds, which are raised heaps of earth, are explained by a tale of how they came to be.

A967.1.p: Mounds are formed from horns that cattle have cast or thrown off.

A968.p: Cliffs are explained by a tale of how they came to be.

A968.1.r: (Cf. A975.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 3 No. 3; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 139 No. 2.
A968.1.p: Cliffs were formerly soft but became hard, by God's command.

A968.2.r: *Crane Vitry 220f. No. 214; Ward Cat. Romances III 17; U.S.: Baughman.—Common among the North American Indians.
A968.2.p: A cliff is formed from a lovers' leap: desperate lovers throw themselves from a high place, and the place becomes a cliff.

A969.p: A miscellaneous group of myths explaining how mountains and hills came to be.

A969.1.p: A mountain is said to have arisen from the body of a buried giant.

A969.2.p: A cloud settles on a tall male mountain because a beautiful female mountain persuades it to bow at her feet, and this is why the mountains have their present shapes.

A969.3.p: Mountains and valleys are said to have been formed by a great fire.

A969.4.p: Hills are said to have formed because the sky asked the earth to wrinkle up its feet.

A969.5.p: Water freezes and so forms mountains.

A969.6.p: A hill is brought into a country as an adopted child.

A969.7.p: Mountains came into being as a punishment.

A969.8.p: A crevasse or deep crack in the ground is explained as having a mythical origin.

A969.9.p: A mountain or hill is created by the devil's actions.

A970.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 325f.; Jewish: Neuman.—Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 47.
A970.p: Myths explaining how rocks and stones came to exist.

A971.p: Rocks are said to have come from the breaking of God's sieve.

A972.r: (Cf. A901.)—*Fb “sten” III 552b; *Andree Ethnographische Parallelen (1878) 96; Dh II 8.—Irish: Thurneysen Irische Helden-u. Königssagen 189, Cross; Icel.: Boberg; Danish: Schmidt DF XXXIX 13ff.; French: Sébillot France I 369ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: Krickeberg Indianermärchen aus Nordamerika 245, Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 59; Aztec: Krickeberg Märchen der Azteken 60, 204, and passim; S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 132.
A972.p: Hollows or marks in rocks are explained as the prints left by a man or beast.

A972.1.r: *Toldo Studien zur vgl. Literaturgeschichte V 337ff.; Andree Ethnographische Parallelen (1878) 95.—Irish myth: *Cross; Eng., Scot., Ire., Wales, U.S.: *Baughman; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 977; Greek: *Grote I 180.—Hawaii Beckwith Myth 65, 142, 212f.; S. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 281.
A972.1.p: Marks in rocks are explained as the imprints left by gods or saints.

A972.1.1.r: Dh II 199.—Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: Kirialaxsaga 66.
A972.1.1.p: Marks in rocks are explained as footprints left by Christ.

A972.1.2.p: A priest stamps on a stone to prove the pope's truth, and his footprint remains visible in the stone.

A972.1.3.p: A holy man's footprints are still seen in a stone where he stood to preach.

A972.2.r: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 303 Nos. 22, 23.—Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 500ff.
A972.2.p: Marks in rocks are explained as footprints of fairies, angels, or devils.

A972.2.1.p: A mark in a rock is explained as the footprint of an angel.

A972.2.2.p: A mark in a rock is explained as the footprint of the devil.

A972.3.r: Irish: Plummer Vitae Sanctorum Hiberniae clvi.
A972.3.p: Holes in stones are explained as having been pierced by a saint's finger.

A972.3.1.p: Holes in a rock are said to have been pierced by a saint's finger, as a mark of his holy power.

A972.3.1.1.p: Dents or hollows in a rock are said to have been made by the weapons or limbs of robbers, struck down by a saint's power.

A972.3.1.2.p: Hollows in rocks are said to be the footprints of a saint's cow.

A972.4.r: French: Sébillot France I 383ff.; Danish: Thiele Danmarks Folkesagn I 209, II 47, Schmidt DF XXXIX 22—23; German: Þiðriks saga I 157, 220.—India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
A972.4.p: The mark of a horse's hoof is said to be imprinted in rock.

A972.5.p: Dents or hollows in rocks are said to have been left by the marks of various people.

A972.5.1.p: Hollows in a rock are said to have been made by the head of an infant hero or saint.

A972.5.2.p: Gaps or chasms between rocks are said to mark the leaps of giants or heroes.

A972.5.3.p: Dents in a rock are said to have been made by the paws of King Arthur's dog.

A972.5.4.p: Dents in rocks are said to have been made by the weapons, knees, and elbows of people slain by a hero.

A972.5.5.p: Rocks or hilltops are flat because gods or people slept or cooked on them.

A972.5.6.p: A hole in a stone is said to have been made by a warrior's weapon.

A972.6.p: Dents or hollows in rocks are said to have been caused by giants.

A972.7.p: A great fish was killed by a hero and cut into sixteen pieces, and the large stones left behind are still visible.

A973.r: *Dh II 95.—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 140 No. 4; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 80 No. 2, England: Baughman.
A973.p: Stones came into being as a punishment for rudeness: Jesus turned a man's sown crop into stones after the man mocked him.

A974.r: Greek: Fox 175; Icel.: Boberg.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 175; Marshall Is.: Davenport 229; Tonga: Gifford 99, 130; Marquesas: Handy 106; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo: Boas RBAE VI 639; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 97.
A974.p: Some rocks are people who were transformed into stone.

A974.1.p: Certain stones are druids who were turned to stone by a saint's power.

A974.2.p: Certain stones are giants who were transformed into stone.

A975.r: By God’s order. (Cf. A968.1.)—Schmidt DF XXXIX 36; von Sydow Folkeminder och Folktankar VI 73; Fb “Adam” IV 3a.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 3 No. 3; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 139 Nr. 2; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 80 Nos. 3, 4.—Oceanic: Beckwith Myth 88.
A975.p: An explanation for why stones became hard.

A975.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3015, Legends Nos. 16f.
A975.1.p: Stones no longer grow because God sent cold to stop the Devil's sown stones from growing.

A975.1.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3015. Legends Nos. 19, 25.
A975.1.1.p: Stones no longer grow as punishment for someone injuring the foot of a holy person.

A975.2.p: Explains why a certain rock gives off sparks of fire when struck with steel.

A975.2.1.p: The fire-producing rock comes from a contest between the god of fire and the god of rain.

A976.r: Jamaica Negro: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 259 No. 49.
A976.p: Explains why the rocks at a river's edge are covered with moss.

A977.p: Gives an origin story for a particular stone or group of stones.

A977.1.r: (Cf. A963.1.)—Canada, England, U.S., Wales: *Baughman; Icel.: Boberg.
A977.1.p: A giant is said to be responsible for the existence of certain stones.

A977.2.p: The devil is said to have thrown stones, which became the stones seen today.

A977.2.1.p: The devil and a man take part in a contest of throwing stones.

A977.2.2.p: The devil throws stones at a church or at churchmen.

A977.2.3.p: The devil throws quoits, which remain as stones to this day, after he is told that playing games on Sunday is wrong.

A977.3.p: The devil drops stones, which then lie where they fell.

A977.3.1.p: The devil drops stones out of his apron.

A977.4.p: The devil turns some object or animal to stone, and the stone can still be seen.

A977.5.p: Gives an origin story for one particular rock.

A977.5.1.p: Certain stones are cheeses that a saint turned into stone.

A977.5.2.p: A pile of stones in a certain chapel is made of pieces of a salmon that a saint transformed into stone.

A977.5.3.p: A stone column is the phallus of an ancient hero, turned to stone.

A977.5.4.p: Two rocks are said to have been split from, and formed out of, a transformed lapdog.

A978.p: Gives an origin story for minerals.

A978.1.p: Minerals are said to have come from the body of a dead culture hero.

A978.2.p: Iron was created to punish the pride of the cedar tree.

A978.3.p: Emeralds are said to come from a wonderful vase that broke into pieces, scattering the gems across the land.

A979.r: Tahiti: Henry 341; Marquesas: Handy 132; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 18, 22.
A979.p: A miscellaneous group of other stories explaining how particular stones or rocks came to be.

A979.1.p: A stone is said to have split open or been torn apart at the moment of Jesus's crucifixion.

A980.p: A general heading for tales explaining how particular named places or sites came to exist.

A983.p: A tale explaining how a valley or hollow in the land was formed.

A984.p: Hercules is said to have set up the Pillars of Hercules at Gibraltar.

A986.p: A quarrel among the gods breaks a natural bridge of the gods, which causes rapids in a river; in one version this explains the rapids of the Columbia River at The Dalles, Oregon.

A988.p: A pile of stones heaped up marks where someone was buried.

A989.p: A miscellaneous group of other tales explaining how particular places came to be.

A989.1.p: Dark brown patches on the soil are said to mark the spot where a marvelous cow named Glas and her calf lay down.

A989.2.p: Roads are said to have been marked out by supernatural cows.

A989.3.p: Certain stones are said to be the seats or chairs of druids or saints.

A989.4.p: A pile of stones, called a cairn, is said to mark the site of a battle.

A990.p: A miscellaneous group of other tales explaining land features not covered elsewhere.

A991.p: A tale explaining how a village came into being.

A992.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3725; India: Thompson-Balys.
A992.p: A general heading for tales explaining how a sacred place came to be holy.

A992.1.p: A sacred post is said to have been set in place by an ancestral culture hero.

A992.2.r: Blinkenberg The Thunderweapon (Cambridge 1911); Handwb. d. Abergl. II 325 “Donnerkeil”.
A992.2.p: A place where lightning struck the ground is regarded as sacred.

A992.3.p: The ground bursts open and a temple rises up out of it.

A994.p: Five great roads of Ireland are said to have been discovered on the night the king was born.

A995.p: Explains how cities came to exist, as a traditional origin story about the beginning of urban settlements.

A996.p: Explains the origin of places that were not yet inhabited but would later be settled by people.

A997.p: Explains how boundaries or borders between lands came into being.

A998.p: Explains how clay, the soft earth used for pottery and building, came into being.

A1000.r: **Olrik Ragnarök; Fb “verden” III 1039ab; *G. Neckel Studien zu den germanischen Dichtungen vom Weltuntergang (Stzb. d. Heidelberger Akad. d. Wissenschaften 1918); **H. Fischer Weltwenden (1928); **Henne-am Rhyn Das Jenseits: kulturgeschichtliche Darstellung der Ansichten über .... Weltuntergang (1881); **Reitzenstein Weltuntergangsvorstellungen (Kyrkohistoriska Årsskrift [Uppsala 1924]).—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 336ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Egyptian: Smith Dragon 111; Hindu: Keith 105.—S. Am. Indian (Guarani): *Métraux RMLP XXXIII 124.
A1000.p: The world is destroyed by some great catastrophe, either finally or in a way that is later followed by renewal of the earth.

A1001.r: **Olrik Ragnarök; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 336ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3012, Legends No. 15.—Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 95.
A1001.p: The world suffers a sequence of several catastrophes, one after another.

A1002.r: *Olrik Ragnarök.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 336ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 461ff.; Jewish: Moreno Esdras (M307), *Neuman; Hindu: Keith 105; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 279.—pawnee: Alexander N. Am. 116ff.—Cf. Revelations passim.
A1002.p: The end of the world at the Day of Judgment, when disasters come before the final reckoning.

A1002.1.p: A widespread calamity will strike when the feast of John the Baptist falls on a certain day of the week.

A1002.2.r: **Heist Fifteen Signs Before Doomsday (East Lansing, Michigan, 1952).—Irish myth: Cross.
A1002.2.p: Various omens or signs that will appear before the Day of Judgment to warn that the end is near.

A1002.2.1.p: For the fifteen years before the Day of Judgment, no rainbow will appear in the sky.

A1002.2.2.p: Wood bleeds, so that blood flows from it, as a sign that Doomsday is coming.

A1002.2.3.p: A stone speaks, and this speech is a sign that Doomsday is near.

A1002.2.4.p: Birds migrate in an unusual way, and this unusual movement is a sign that Doomsday is approaching.

A1003.r: Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Maori: Beckwith Myth 317; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158.
A1003.p: A world calamity is sent as a punishment for human sin and wickedness.

A1005.r: (Cf. A1020, A1038, A1045.)—Persian: Carnoy 308; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484.
A1005.p: Some people or creatures survive a world-wide calamity, kept alive by some means while others perish.

A1005.1.p: Certain people in Ireland are spared and kept alive during the great Flood.

A1005.2.p: During a world calamity, people and animals are saved by being shut inside an enclosure, and only the best kinds of animals and people are kept alive.

A1005.3.p: The Holy Land is spared and not flooded or ravaged by the great deluge.

A1006.r: Icel.: De la Saussaye 352, Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.—S. Am. Indian (Bakairi): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 347, (Namicuara): Lévi-Strauss ibid. 369.
A1006.p: After a world calamity, the world is renewed and made new again.

A1006.1.r: (Cf. A1038, A1045.)—*Olrik Ragnarök 479 s.v. “Erneuerung”.—Greek: *Grote I 93; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.—Marquesas: Handy 110; Ellice Is.: Beckwith Myth 270; Hawaii: ibid. 315; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 91; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 144, (Chiriguano): ibid. 157, 163, 170f., (Guaporé River): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 379; African (Lamomi): Bouveignes 29.
A1006.1.p: After a world calamity, a new race of people arises from a single pair or from a few survivors.

A1006.2.r: Hindu: Keith 92; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
A1006.2.p: After a world-wrecking disaster, a new human race comes into being from an incestuous union.

A1006.3.p: After a world calamity, a new race of people is made out of red earth.

A1006.4.p: A new race of people arises from the union of a girl and a rat.

A1006.5.p: Ireland is repopulated after a flood by people who survived the flood.

A1006.6.p: After a flood leaves Ireland empty and barren for centuries, it is repopulated by immigrants.

A1006.7.p: An entire tribe descends from a single woman who survives the destruction of a doomed city.

A1006.8.p: A single bear-child survives a death that threatens all, and becomes the ancestor of all bears.

A1006.9.p: After a world destroyed by fire, life is brought back and recreated from a tree.

A1007.p: A world catastrophe is said to begin in Palestine.

A1009.p: A miscellaneous account of the destruction of the world in a catastrophe.

A1009.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Aymara): Tschopik BBAE CXLIII (2) 571, (Chibaya): La Barre ibid. 585.
A1009.1.p: The first race of men dies off when the sun first rises.

A1009.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158.
A1009.2.p: Both living things and objects, animate and inanimate, try to destroy humanity.

A1009.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Moré): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 406.
A1009.3.p: A large stone falls from the sky, killing everyone except one couple.

A1010.p: A great flood covers the whole world or a large part of it.

A1010.1.p: During the great flood, the sun and moon give no light.

A1010.2.p: The great flood lasts for eight months.

A1011.r: **Schmarsel Die Sage von der untergegangenen Stadt; *RTP XXVIII 27 and references to earlier volumes.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 81 n. 2; Jewish: Neuman.
A1011.p: Floods that cover only a limited area, not the whole world.

A1011.1.p: A local flood is caused partly by springs bursting forth from the ground.

A1011.2.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 170.
A1011.2.p: A local flood is caused by a river rising over its banks.

A1011.3.p: God's promise never to destroy the world by water does not cover small local floods.

A1012.p: A flood is caused by fluids from the body, such as blood or other bodily liquids.

A1012.1.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 287 n. 57b; polynesian: Dixon 38 n. 117.
A1012.1.p: A flood is said to have been caused by tears, so the great waters of the world come from weeping.

A1012.1.1.p: The great flood comes from tears that Adam shed in repentance after his sin.

A1012.1.2.r: N. Am. Indian (N’tlaka’panaq): British Association for the Advancement of Science LXIX 574f.; S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Nordenskiöld Indianerleben 253f.
A1012.1.2.p: A flood is caused by the tears of a lover who is grieving.

A1012.2.p: A flood is said to have been caused by urine, so the great waters come from someone urinating.

A1012.2.1.p: A flood is caused when a magical fairy horse is loosed and allowed to urinate, releasing a deluge of water.

A1012.3.p: A flood is said to have been caused by blood, so the great waters come from spilled blood.

A1012.3.1.p: The flood comes from the blood of a slain giant.

A1013.r: Indonesian: Dixon 196 n. 33; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 287 n. 57c.; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 127.
A1013.p: A flood is said to flow out of the belly of a monster that has been pierced.

A1013.1.p: A flood is caused when a whale vomits up water.

A1015.r: (Cf. A1018.)—Babylonian: Jensen Gilgamesch Epos XI 53ff., 69ff.; Marquesas: Handy 109f.; S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 133, (Yuracare): ibid. 503.
A1015.p: A flood is caused by gods or other superior beings acting deliberately.

A1015.1.r: Cook Group: Dixon 39 n. 121, 122; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Campana Archivio per l’Antropologia et la Etnologia XXXII 22.
A1015.1.p: A flood is caused by a quarrel between gods, here the sea god and the rain god.

A1015.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Araucanian): Cooper BBAE CXLIII (2) 753, (Aymara): Tschopik ibid. (2) 571, (Chiriguano): Métraux ibid. (3) 484.
A1015.1.1.p: A flood is caused by a fight between monsters, which are giant animals.

A1015.2.r: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 299 No. 10.—S. Am. Indian (Eastern Brazil): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 434, (Guaporé River): Lévi-Strauss ibid. (3) 379.

A1015.3.p: A flood is caused when a deity stamps on the floor of the heavens, breaking it open so water pours through.

A1016.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684; Tuamotu: Beckwith Myth 267.
A1016.p: Explanations of the flood that attempt a natural or scientific cause rather than a supernatural one.

A1016.1.p: A flood is caused when animals such as turtles or crawfishes bore holes into the ground, letting water out.

A1016.2.r: American Indian (Salinan): Mason JAFL XXVII 163f., (Krawak): Ehrenreich Mythen und Legenden 49.
A1016.2.p: A flood is caused by a hot liquid that burns as it spreads over the land.

A1016.3.r: N. Am. Indian (Déné): Petitot Traditions 373—378; S. Am. Indian (Gusinde): Métraux MAFLS XL 37.
A1016.3.p: A flood is caused when ice melts after a long spell of severe cold.

A1016.4.r: American Indian (Puerto Rico): Fewkes RBAE XXV 73f., (Carajá): Baldus Ensaios de Etnologia Brasileira 174, Lowie Encyc. Rel. Ethics s.v. “flood”.
A1016.4.p: A flood is caused when broken calabashes, gourd containers of water, release their contents.

A1016.5.r: N. Am. Indian (Apache): Goddard PaAM XXIV 28f.
A1016.5.p: A flood is caused when mountains are made out of what was flat earth, displacing the water.

A1016.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Fueginos): Coazzi Rev. Chil. Hist. Geogr. X 31.
A1016.6.p: The moon falls into the sea and its overflowing water causes a flood. This is a pseudo-scientific explanation for why a deluge happened.

A1016.7.p: A piece of stone or shard at the center of the earth shifts, and each time it moves a flood results. This is a pseudo-scientific explanation of floods.

A1017.p: A flood is brought about to satisfy someone's emotional wish or need, such as longing or desire.

A1017.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Métraux BBAE CXXXIV 26.
A1017.1.p: A man's longing or desire for the sun causes a flood to come.

A1017.2.p: A flood is caused when someone prays for it to happen.

A1017.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484.
A1017.3.p: A flood is caused by someone's curse.

A1018.p: A flood is sent as a punishment for wrongdoing.

A1018.1.r: Fiji, Tahiti, Maori, Andaman: Beckwith Myth 316—319; S. Am. Indian (Toba, Mataco, Lengua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A1018.1.p: A flood is sent as punishment for breaking a taboo, that is, violating a sacred prohibition.

A1018.2.p: A flood is sent as punishment for incest, sexual relations within a forbidden family relationship.

A1018.3.r: Tuamotu: Beckwith Myth 318; N. Am. Indian (Carrier): Jennes JAFL XLVII 141ff., (Ts’etsaut): Boas JAFL IX 262, (North Pacific Tribes): Boas Indianische Sagen 79, (Haida): Swanton BBAE XXIX 142, (Kwakiutl): Boas and Hunt JE III 100, (Mono): Gifford JAFL XXVI 326, (Shasta): Dixon JAFL XXIII 36, (Pima): Lloyd Aw-Aw-Tam 36ff., (Ojibwa): Jones-Michelson PAES VII 151, 271, (Menomini): Skinner and Satterlee PaAM XIII 255—260, Hoffman RBAE XIV 133; Central and S. Am. Indian (Cahita): Beals BBAE CXLII 216f., (Bororo): Baldus Ensaios de Etnologia Brasileira 176ff., (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 133.
A1018.3.p: A flood is brought as revenge for an injury someone has suffered.

A1019.p: Miscellaneous flood stories that do not fit the other flood categories.

A1019.1.p: The earth beneath a flood sinks down, so that the water rises over the land.

A1019.2.p: A serpent king causes a flood by damming up rivers.

A1019.3.p: A flood comes because the earth has become too crowded with people.

A1019.4.r: (Cf. A1030.)—S. Am. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 133, (Tucuna): Nimuendajá ibid. 724, (Cubeo): Goldman JAFL LIII 244.
A1019.4.p: A flood puts out a fire that has spread over the whole world.

A1020.p: A person or group escapes from a great flood that destroys the world.
