A1021.p: People escape a flood by sailing or floating in a boat, usually called an ark.

A1021.0.1.p: People who are left out of Noah's ark build another ark of their own and sail to Ireland.

A1021.0.2.r: Chinese: Graham; S. A. Indian (Guaporé): Lévi-Strauss BBAE CXLIII (3) 379.
A1021.0.2.p: A person escapes a flood by floating in a wooden cask or drum.

A1021.0.3.p: A person escapes a flood by floating in a gourd.

A1021.0.4.p: During a great flood, people escape by floating away on a tree that has been carried off by the water.

A1021.0.5.r: American Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 636ff., (Mexican): Bancroft Native Races of the Pacific States of America (New York 1874—76) III 66ff.
A1021.0.5.p: During a great flood, people escape by riding inside a hollowed-out tree trunk that floats on the water.

A1021.0.6.r: American Indian (Tlingit): Bancroft Native Races V 14, (Cahita): Beals BBAE CXLII 216f.
A1021.0.6.p: During a great flood, people escape by floating away on a building that the water has lifted off its foundations.

A1021.1.r: See references to “Sintflutsage” in A1010; also Dh I 267ff.—Irish myth: Cross; Hebrew: Genesis 6:19; Babylonian: Spence 175; Hindu: Keith 147.—Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 85f.
A1021.1.p: Before a great flood destroys the world, a pair of every kind of animal is placed in a boat so that life can continue afterward.

A1021.2.r: *Dh I 283.—Irish myth: Cross; Hebrew: Genesis 8:7ff., Neuman; Babylonian: Spence 176.
A1021.2.p: During a flood, birds are sent out from the boat to look for dry land and report back on whether the waters have receded.

A1022.r: Greek: Grote I 93; Hebrew: Genesis 8:4, Neuman; Hindu: Keith 99; India: Thompson-Balys.—Philippine: Dixon 179; Borneo: ibid. 180; West Caroline Is.: ibid. 257; Australian: ibid. 280; Polynesian: ibid 38 n. 118; Cook Group: ibid. 39 n. 121; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 215.—N. Am. Indian (Bella-Bella): Boas MAFLS XXV 1f., (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 232ff., (Luiseño): Du Bois UCal VIII 157, (Shasta): Dixon JAFL XXIII 36, (Blackfoot): Wissler paAM II 19, (Chiricahua Apache): Opler MAFLS XXXVII 1f., (Zuñi): Benedict CU XXI 10ff.; S. Am. Indian (Araucanian): Alexander Lat. Am. 330, (Inca): ibid. 230, (Yunca, Peru): ibid. 230, (Caingang, Amazon): ibid. 312. (Only a selection of references for North and South America.).
A1022.p: People survive a great flood by climbing up and staying on a mountain until the waters go down.

A1023.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—American Indian (Paiute): Steward UCal XXXIV 372, (Plains Cree): Skinner JAFL XXIX 350, (Fox): Jones JAFL XIV 233ff., (Catawba): Speck CU XXIV 23, (Ackawoi): Alexander Lat. Am. 270, (Caingang): ibid. 312, (Guayaki): Métraux-Baldus BBAE CXLIII (1) 444, (Maina): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 649.
A1023.p: People survive a great flood by climbing into a tree and staying there until the waters recede.

A1024.r: Andaman Is.: Beckwith Myth 319; American Indian (Cheyenne): Dorsey FM IX 36, (Arawak, Antis, Yuracare): Spence The Problem of Atlantis 95.
A1024.p: People survive a great flood by sheltering inside a cave.

A1025.p: People survive a great flood by reaching an island that stays above the water.

A1026.p: People survive a great flood by walking or running away on foot to higher ground.

A1027.p: A fish rescues people from a great flood, for example by carrying them to safety.

A1028.p: A character brings a great flood to an end.

A1028.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 369.
A1028.1.p: A trickster plants a spear in the ground and channels the floodwater out to the sea, so the flood drains away.

A1028.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A1028.2.p: Birds carry dirt and drop it into the sea until the water is filled in and the flood is overcome.

A1029.p: A miscellaneous flood-escape story that does not fit the other categories under escaping a deluge.

A1029.1.p: A wondrous tree remains standing and survives a great flood.

A1029.2.p: Four people, one from each quarter of the world, survive the flood and thereby preserve the old traditions.

A1029.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 170, (Guarayu): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 438.
A1029.3.p: People escape a great flood by getting inside a pot or jar that floats on the water.

A1029.4.p: People escape a great flood by taking refuge in huge gourds, each with seven rooms inside.

A1029.5.r: American Indian (Thompson River): Teit JE VIII 230, (Apache): Gould JAFL XXXIV 319, Russell JAFL XI 253ff., (Guarayu): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 438, (Cubeo): Goldman ibid. (3) 798, (Chaco): Nordenskiöld Indianerleben 253f.
A1029.5.p: People escape a great flood by getting inside a box or basket that floats on the water.

A1029.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 170f.
A1029.6.p: After a great flood, the few people who survive go on to build new homes and settle the land again.

A1030.r: *Olrik Ragnarök 483 s. v. “Weltbrand”, *Danske Studier (1913) 204ff.; *Eisler Weltenmantel und Himmelszelt 452.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 336ff., Boberg; Greek: Grote I 94; Lithuanian: Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI 133f.; Jewish: Neuman; Babylonian: Meissner Babylonien und Assyrien II 118; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 368ff.; Hindu: Keith 105; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 84.—Maori: Dixon 47 n. 33; N. Am. Indian: *Thompson Tales 287 n. 57d.; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare, W. Brazil): Alexander Lat. Am. 313, (Araucanian): ibid. 330, (Chaco, Tupinamba, Apapocuva-Guarani, Tembé, Shipaya, Carajá, Mura, Cashinawa, Witoto, Arawak, Yuracare): Métraux MAFLS XL 36 (Mataco): ibid. 35, (Toba): ibid. 33, (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII (3) 724, (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss ibid. (3) 347.
A1030.p: A great fire burns up the earth, either as a destruction of the whole world or, in some tales, only a local catastrophe, and sometimes it marks the end of the world.

A1031.p: Stories giving the reasons why the world is set on fire and destroyed.

A1031.1.p: The world is burned by a fiery flame, faster than the wind, as punishment for the sins of the Irish.

A1031.2.p: The world is set on fire as a consequence of someone stealing fire.

A1031.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare, Tupinamba, Arawak): Métraux MAFLS XL 36.
A1031.3.p: Evil demons set the world on fire.

A1031.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba, Mataco, Lengua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367, (Mocovi): Métraux MAFLS XL 34.
A1031.4.p: The sun falls to earth and its fall sets the world on fire.

A1031.4.1.p: The sun's wife pours fire from a small bowl, and every country is burned as a result.

A1031.5.p: The world is burned because people have become arrogant and proud.

A1031.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Witoto, Apapocuva-Guarani): Métraux MAFLS XL 36, (Toba): ibid. 19, (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 316.
A1031.6.p: Various other reasons, not covered by the more specific categories, for why the world is set on fire.

A1035.p: Ways in which the world-fire is put out or stopped.

A1035.1.p: Rain is called down to put out the world-fire and destroy it.

A1035.2.r: S. A. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 316.
A1035.2.p: The creator puts out the world-fire by striking it with his staff.

A1036.r: S. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 282.
A1036.p: After the world has burned, the earth is made new again and recreated.

A1038.r: (Cf. A1006.1., A1045.)—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 311 No. 47; India: Thompson-Balys.—S. Am. Indian (Toba, Arawak, Mura, Yuracare, Tupinamba): Métraux MAFLS XL 34—36, (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158; African (Fang): Trilles 133f.
A1038.p: Some men hide from the world-fire and survive, and from them the human race is renewed.

A1039.p: Miscellaneous other tales about world-fire that do not fit the more specific categories.

A1039.1.p: A vulture is sent out as a scout to find out whether the earth has cooled down after the world-fire.

A1040.r: Spoken of as “Fimbulwinter”. It ushers in the end of the world.—*Olrik Ragnarök 479; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 336ff.; Persian: Carnoy 309.—S. Am. Indian (Toba, Pilagá, Tierra del Fuego): Métraux MAFLS XL 30, 37, (Chaco): Métraux BBAE CLXIII (1) 367.
A1040.p: A continuous winter that never ends kills off the human race.

A1045.p: A single pair of people survives the endless winter and from them the human race is renewed.

A1046.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—S. Am. Indian (Toba, Mocovi, Mataco, Choroti): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367, (Tupinamba): Métraux ibid. (3) 131, (Guarani): Métraux MAFLS XL 33.
A1046.p: The world is continually darkened by an eclipse that never ends.

A1046.1.p: The world goes dark for a long stretch, and a bat is said to end the eclipse by making the sun smile again.

A1050.p: The sky itself breaks apart when the world comes to an end.

A1051.p: The stars behave in unusual ways when the world ends.

A1051.1.r: *Olrik Ragnarök 482 s. v. “Sterne”; Irish myth: Cross.
A1051.1.p: At the end of the world the stars drop out of the sky and fall to earth.

A1051.2.p: The world ends when the stars of one constellation catch up with and pass those of another.

A1052.p: The sun behaves in unusual ways when the world ends.

A1052.1.p: At the end of the world a monster swallows the sun.

A1052.2.p: The sun shines at night, and this is a sign that Doomsday is coming.

A1052.3.p: The world ends when four (or seven) suns appear in the sky at once.

A1053.p: The moon behaves in unusual ways when the world ends.

A1053.1.p: The moon shines during the day, and this is a sign that Doomsday is coming.

A1057.p: For seven days at the end of the world, the whole universe falls silent.

A1058.r: S. Am. Indian (Guaraní): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93.
A1058.p: The world ends when a culture hero pulls out one of the supports holding up the world.

A1060.p: The earth is thrown into violent disturbance when the world comes to an end.

A1061.p: At the end of the world the earth sinks down into the sea.

A1061.1.r: Jewish: Moreno Esdras (M307.12).—S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158.
A1061.1.p: Earthquakes shake the earth at the end of the world.

A1062.p: At the end of the world the mountains collapse and fall together.

A1063.p: The waters are thrown into violent disturbance when the world ends.

A1063.1.p: At the end of the world the sea roars loudly and casts fish up onto the land.

A1063.2.p: At the end of the world salt sea water mixes with fresh water.

A1065.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 736; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 171.
A1065.p: At the end of the world, the land suffers a drought that never lets up.

A1066.p: At the end of the world, the sun traps the moon in a deep pit beneath the earth and devours the stars.

A1067.p: At the end of the world, a wind of unusual violence blows across the earth.

A1068.p: At the end of the world, the sun is thrown into a fire, bringing a period of darkness followed by rain.

A1069.p: At the end of the world, rivers of molten metal flow over the land.

A1070.r: *Olrik Ragnarök 278, 478ff. s.v. “Erdbebenriese”, “Schlange”, “Raubtier”, “Ungeheuer”, Danske Studier (1913) 3ff.; Anholm Danske Studier (1904) 141; *Krohn Der gefangene Unhold; *Von der Leyen Der gefesselte Unhold.—Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: De la Saussaye 246; Lettish and Lithuanian: Gray 322; Persian: Carnoy 324; Babylonian: Spence 78.
A1070.p: At the end of the world, a giant or monster chained deep in the earth breaks free, ending the world. His movements cause earthquakes until then.

A1070.1.p: The birth of monsters is taken as a sign that the end of the world is near.

A1071.p: A monster living underground is bound in fetters so that he cannot move.

A1071.1.r: *Type 803; *Olrik Ragnarök 204ff., 248ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Lithuanian Legends of the Devil in Chains (Tautosakos Darbai III [1937] 321—331.)
A1071.1.p: The underground monster is chained after being tricked into trying on the fetters. Sometimes the same story is told of Satan.

A1071.2.p: Smiths forge chains for the monster, and the blows that miss the iron on the anvil go to making the chains for the devil.

A1072.p: The fettered monster takes on a particular shape or form.

A1072.1.p: The fettered monster appears in human form.

A1072.2.r: *Olrik Ragnarök 85, 481 s.v. “Erdbebenriese”.—S. Am. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93.
A1072.2.p: The fettered monster appears as a fierce wild animal.

A1072.3.p: The fettered monster appears as a snake.

A1072.4.p: The fettered monster appears as a dragon.

A1074.p: The monster remains held in captivity in his fetters.

A1074.1.p: The monster is chained with a sword placed just beyond his reach. If he reaches it, he will free himself.

A1074.2.p: The fettered monster tries in vain to reach a sword with a man's help. If he could reach it, he would escape.

A1074.3.p: The fettered monster asks a visitor whether lambs are still being born, meaning whether nature still follows its normal laws. He must stay bound until he hears that those laws have stopped.

A1074.4.p: A vulture preys on the fettered monster.

A1074.5.p: A bound monster is kept just beyond reach of water, so that it can never drink; a vulture always takes the water before he can.

A1074.6.p: A chained monster keeps trying to loosen the stake pinning him, but each time he loosens it, it is driven back into the ground.

A1074.7.p: A monster's chains are nearly gnawed through by a dog, but supernatural power then restores them so they are whole again.

A1074.8.p: A monster's weakened chains are made strong again by a smith's blow, restoring his captivity.

A1075.p: The end of the world is announced by the arrival of Antichrist, a huge, destructive monster with one eye.

A1075.1.p: Before Antichrist is born, various omens or warning signs appear.

A1080.r: Armageddon.—Revelations 16:16; Fb “krig” II 296b.; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman, Moreno Esdras (N307.13).
A1080.p: A great battle takes place at the end of the world.

A1080.1.p: At the final battle of Armageddon, horses wade in blood up to their chests.

A1081.p: The gods fight one another in a battle at the end of the world.

A1082.p: At the end of the world, the gods fight a monster in battle.

A1082.1.p: At the end of the world, the gods fight giants in battle.

A1082.2.p: At the end of the world, Odin fights the wolf Fenris.

A1082.2.1.p: At the end of the world, other gods fight the wolf Fenris.

A1082.2.2.p: At the end of the world, a god fights the hound of hell.

A1082.3.p: At the end of the world, Thor fights the Midgard serpent.

A1082.3.1.p: The end of the world will come when the serpent that encircles the world dies of disease.

A1082.4.p: At the end of the world, God fights the sea monster Leviathan.

A1082.5.p: At the end of the world, God defeats Satan.

A1082.6.r: *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 781ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI 133f.
A1082.6.p: At the end of the world, saints fight Lucifer in battle.

A1082.7.p: At the end of the world, angels fight the monsters Leviathan and Behemoth.

A1084.p: A prophecy that a battle will be lost is taken as a sign that the world is about to end.

A1085.p: The gods themselves perish, marking the end of the divine order.

A1087.p: At the end of the world, monsters fight and destroy one another until none remain.

A1090.p: A heading grouping miscellaneous myths about world calamities and the renewal of the world.

A1091.r: *Olrik Ragnarök 46ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Chinese: Graham.
A1091.p: At the end of the world, the normal laws of nature stop working.

A1091.1.p: On the last day of the world, three horses come out of a dove's egg.

A1093.p: The end of the world is announced by the sounding of a trumpet.

A1095.p: A coming golden era of peace and blessing, a messianic age in which the world is made right.

A1097.p: An exceptional man appears at the end of the world.

A1099.p: A heading for additional motifs about world calamities.

A1099.1.p: The world is destroyed by a shower of stones falling from the sky.

A1099.2.p: The world is devoured by an ogre.

A1099.3.p: The world is turned upside down and eaten by an earthworm.

A1100.p: A heading for myths explaining how the natural order of the world was established.

A1101.r: **Encyc. Religion and Ethics s.v. “Ages of the World”.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 17, Grote I 62; Hindu: Keith 105, Penzer IV 240 n. 1, VII 1 n. 5; Chinese: Ferguson 33.
A1101.p: The world develops through four successive ages or periods, such as golden, silver, bronze, and iron.

A1101.1.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 927ff.—Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: De la Saussaye 165, MacCulloch Eddic 327, 378 n. 49, Boberg; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 35 No. 8; Greek: Fox 105, Grote I 62; Jewish: Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 300, 305; Hindu: Keith 103; India: Thompson-Balys.—Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G 13/50); Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 66; Carib: ibid 262; Ackawoi: ibid. 269.
A1101.1.p: A former age of perfection that existed long ago in the world's history.

A1101.1.1.r: Icel.: Herrmann Saxo II 377; Irish myth: Cross; Persian: Carnoy 300, 305; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Ferguson 33.
A1101.1.1.p: In the golden age, peace and justice reign under a particular king.

A1101.1.2.p: In the golden age, even trees are able to speak.

A1101.1.3.p: In a former age, spirits and ogres lived among men, and gods appeared to people in human form.

A1101.2.p: In a former age, the normal workings of nature were reversed.

A1101.2.1.p: In a former age people plowed the fields while cattle were their masters, reversing the natural order.

A1101.2.2.p: In a former age people ate grass while cattle ate rice and pulse, the reverse of the present order.

A1101.2.3.p: In a former age people could not speak, while birds and animals could talk.

A1101.2.4.p: In a former age people could walk safely under the sea.

A1102.p: Explains why the powers of nature operate on the Sabbath (the day of rest).

A1103.p: God transforms nature once every seven years.

A1110.p: Explains how the present order of the waters was established.

A1111.r: *Chauvin VI 3 No. 181, VII 132 No. 399.—Hindu: Keith 33 (guarded by dragon); India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Ferguson 155; Japanese: Anesaki 276.—Australian: Dixon 279, 297; Papua: Ker 25; Baining of New Britain: ibid. III; Samoan, Melanesian: ibid 38 n. 109, 110.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 293 n. 76, (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 201, 203; S. Am. Indian (Bacairi, Amazon): Alexander Lat. Am. 313, (Botocudo): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 540, (Caingang): Lowie ibid. (1) 397, (Bolivia, Peru): Jijena Sanchez Perro Negro 134.—Africa: Stanley 8, (Basuto): Jacottet 148 No. 21, 154 No. 22 cf. 8 No. 1, (Hottentot): Bleek 27 No. 14, (Ekoi): Talbot 144, 197, (Ababua): Einstein 101.
A1111.p: Water is held back by a monster so people cannot use it; a hero defeats the monster and frees the water. Sometimes the monster is a giant frog.

A1113.p: God promises that He will never again destroy the world by water.

A1115.r: New Guinea: Ker 25; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 43.
A1115.p: Explains why the sea is salty.

A1115.1.p: The sea became salty because a ship carrying salt was wrecked and its cargo dissolved into the water.

A1115.2.r: *Type 565; *BP II 438ff.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 283; cf. Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 108.
A1115.2.p: A magic mill that ground out salt was stolen by a sea-captain and taken aboard his ship. It would grind only for its master, so when the ship sank the mill kept grinding, and the sea remains salty.

A1115.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Tupi): Ehrenreich 16, (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 133.
A1115.3.p: The sea is salty because heavy rain fell on the ashes of wood burnt by the first fire, and the salt of those ashes washed into the water.

A1116.p: Explains how sea waves came to be.

A1116.1.p: Sea waves are the manes (mane hair) of the sea-god's horses.

A1117.p: Explains how foam came to be on the waters.

A1118.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 283f.; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 4 No. 7, XXXIII 51 No. 7; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 140 No. 5; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 81 No. 6.
A1118.p: Explains why water swirls around in whirlpools or eddies; animals and birds are said to scratch in the water to make the swirling.

A1119.p: Miscellaneous explanations of other features of the waters and how they were established.

A1119.1.p: Explains why the sea is blue.

A1119.2.p: The sea is warm because the monster Leviathan keeps it heated.

A1119.3.p: Explains the origin of the sea's unpleasant smell.

A1120.r: Jewish: Neuman; India. Thompson-Balys.—Tonga: Gifford 16; Quileute: Farrand JAFL XXXII 269ff.; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 224.
A1120.p: Myth explaining how the winds came to be in their present form or order in the world.

A1121.r: Chinese: Werner 77; Maori: Clark 19; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 175, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 153, (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 267; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 28.
A1121.p: A god or spirit breathing out causes the winds to blow.

A1122.r: Roman: Virgil Aeneid I lines 52 ff.; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 457.—Maori: Dixon 55; Western Mono: Gifford JAFL XXXVI 328 No. 9.
A1122.p: The winds are originally kept shut up in a cave and released from it.

A1122.1.p: The winds are kept in a cave whose opening is plugged by a wooden stopper; when the stopper is destroyed, the winds escape and the land dries up.

A1122.2.p: The wind is a bird that lives in a hole in a mountain.

A1122.3.p: A lost wind is found inside a hollow tree, where it had been banished, and people need it.

A1122.4.p: The wind comes out through holes in the sky when a gut covering is cut.

A1123.p: The winds are the offspring of giants (titans).

A1125.r: Gaster Thespis 158; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 276; Babylonian: Spence 117; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 292 n. 74; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 39ff. No. 5.
A1125.p: A giant bird makes the wind by flapping its wings; a culture hero cuts the wings so it cannot flap so hard.

A1125.1.r: Peigan: Uhlenbeck Verhandelingen der Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenshappen XIII (1) 64.
A1125.1.p: A giant's flapping ears cause the wind.

A1126.p: The wind-god's movements cause the wind; when his son lies down, the wind blows.

A1127.r: Winnebago, Omaha: Alexander N. Am. 99; Quileute: Farrand-Meyer JAFL XXXII 271 No. 13.
A1127.p: Explanation that the winds come from the four directions and are fixed in that way.

A1127.1.r: Jewish: Neuman.—Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 224; Ojibwa: Jones JAFL XXIX 372.
A1127.1.p: The four winds affect the weather in different ways.

A1127.1.1.p: The north wind calms the fierce south wind.

A1127.1.2.p: The south wind brings heat and hurricanes.

A1127.2.p: The gentle west wind is said to be tired out from having fled from a god.

A1128.p: Winds are controlled or regulated so that they do not blow too hard.

A1128.1.p: Angels' wings shield the earth from the winds.

A1128.2.p: When the wind-spirit is awake there are storms; when it sleeps the weather is calm.

A1129.p: Miscellaneous other myths about how the winds were established in their present order.

A1129.1.p: Explains why the winds have different colors, as a set of established facts about the world's order.

A1129.1.1.p: A creator god makes twelve winds and gives each one a different color.

A1129.2.p: Explains the origin of the monsoon as coming from the chewed skin and spit of two divine friends who were eating guavas.

A1129.3.p: Explains why the wind is considered blind, so that it cannot see where it blows.

A1130.p: A general heading for stories explaining how weather phenomena were set in their present order.

A1130.1.p: Angels are appointed to be in charge of clouds, winds, and rains.

A1130.2.p: Explains that storms originate in the sixth heaven.

A1131.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Bushman: Bleek and Lloyd 113.
A1131.p: Explains how rain came to fall on the earth.

A1131.0.1.p: Explains how the rains are controlled or regulated so that they fall at certain times.

A1131.0.2.p: Explains why most rain falls in the hills rather than elsewhere.

A1131.1.r: Jewish: Neuman; Ekoi: Talbot 344; Kaska: Teit JAFL XXX 448; Maori: Clark 19.
A1131.1.p: Explains that rain comes from weeping, so that rain is the tears of someone.

A1131.1.1.r: Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 61, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 600, (East Greenland): Rasmussen I 100; Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 142.
A1131.1.1.p: A variant of rain from tears in which the rain is said to come from urine.

A1131.2.p: A saint sends rainy weather as a punishment.

A1131.3.r: Fb “hav” IV 203a.—Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (East Greenland): Rasmussen I 81; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 26, (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684.
A1131.3.p: Explains that rain comes from a sea in the upper world, above the sky.

A1131.4.r: Gaster Thespis 192; Eskimo (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 266, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 153, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 600, (East Greenland): Holm 95; S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco, Ashluslay): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A1131.4.p: Explains that rain is kept in a container in the sky and released from it.

A1131.4.1.p: Rain is kept in a waterskin that is dragged along the floor of the sky.

A1131.5.r: See all references to A287.—Greek: Fox 159 (Zeus); S. Am. Indian (Toba, Chamacoco, Mataco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, MAFLS XL 26f.
A1131.5.p: Explains that rain is sent by a rain god or rain spirit.

A1131.6.p: Explains that rain comes from stars, which shed it.

A1132.r: Knoop Zs. f. Vksk. XXII 89; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 331ff.; Jewish: Neuman.
A1132.p: Explains how dew came to be.

A1133.r: Jewish: Neuman; Maori: Clark 19; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 97; Eskimo (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 79; S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366.
A1133.p: Explains how clouds came to be.

A1133.1.p: Clouds come from the brain of the giant Ymir, in a Norse myth about how the sky was made.

A1133.2.p: A creator decorates the sky with clouds, and as a result clouds sometimes cast shadows on the mountains.

A1133.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 26f.
A1133.3.p: Clouds are explained as smoke that rises up into the sky.

A1133.4.p: Clouds are described as a shield held up by God.

A1134.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 176.
A1134.p: Explains how mist or fog came to exist.

A1135.p: Explains how wintry weather came to be.

A1135.1.p: Explains how winter's cold came into the world.

A1135.1.1.p: Winter's cold is caused by the sun turning its fiery face upward, away from the earth.

A1135.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Flemish: De Meyer FFC XXXVII 83 No. 9b; Jewish: Neuman.—Eskimo (West Greenland): Rasmussen II 33, Rink 44.
A1135.2.p: Explains how snow came to fall from the sky.

A1135.2.1.r: *Hoffmann-Krayer Zs. f. Vksk. XXV 119 n. 5; *Fb “sne” III 427b.
A1135.2.1.p: Snow is said to fall from the feathers or clothes of a witch, as in the tale of Frau Holle.

A1135.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 22; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1135.3.p: Explains how frost came to form.

A1135.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Aymara): Tschopik BBAE CXLIII (2) 571.
A1135.4.p: Explains how hail came to fall from the sky.

A1137.p: Hot weather is blamed on God boring a hole in hell, letting heat escape upward.

A1141.r: Jewish: Neuman.—Bushman: Bleek and Lloyd 113; Liberia: Bundy JAFL XXXII 422f.; Nootka: Sapir JAFL XXXII 354; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 61, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 175, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 600.
A1141.p: Explains how lightning came to exist.

A1141.1.p: Lightning is explained as a fiery snake.

A1141.2.p: Lightning is said to come from a flashing sword.

A1141.3.p: Lightning is caused by heavenly horses striking their hooves against the stars.

A1141.4.p: Lightning is described as the whip of a god.

A1141.5.p: Lightning is described as God's messenger.

A1141.6.r: Greek: Grote I 8; Jewish: Neuman; Maori: Clark 168.
A1141.6.p: Lightning is said to be produced by a deity.

A1141.7.r: S. Am. Indian (Chorotí, Lengua, Ashluslay): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 366, (Tupinamba): Métraux ibid. (3) 132.
A1141.7.p: Lightning is said to come from fire.

A1141.7.1.p: Lightning is explained as the torches carried by invisible dancers moving through the sky.

A1141.8.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba, Mataco, Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 27f., (Huamachuco): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 151.
A1141.8.p: A miscellaneous myth giving some other explanation for the origin of lightning, not covered by the more specific lightning motifs.

A1142.r: *Blinkenberg The Thunderweapon in Religion and Folklore (Cambridge 1911); *Saintyves Pierres magiques (Paris 1936); Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 82 No. 9a.; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman.—Cook Group: Dixon 88; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 175, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 153, (Cape York): Rasmussen III 62; Nootka: Sapir JAFL XXXII 354; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 683f.; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 97, (Bushman): Bleek and Lloyd 113, Liberian: Bundy JAFL XXXII 422f.
A1142.p: A general heading for myths explaining where thunder comes from.

A1142.0.1.p: Thunderbolt is explained as the origin of the thunderbolt, the bolt that falls with thunder.

A1142.1.p: Thunder is caused by the voice of a creator god or deity speaking or calling out.

A1142.2.p: Thunder is caused by a dragon flying through the sky.

A1142.3.r: Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 96; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 177.
A1142.3.p: People escape to the sky and turn into thunder.

A1142.4.p: Thunder clouds come from the wings of mountains that rise into the air.

A1142.5.p: Thunder is the sound of God firing a gun.

A1142.5.1.p: Thunder is caused by God beating a weapon.

A1142.5.1.1.p: Thunder comes from stones crashing together in the moon while a goddess beats tapa cloth.

A1142.5.1.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684.
A1142.5.1.2.p: Thunder is caused by a thunder spirit beating his children.

A1142.6.p: Thunder is caused by the sound of horses' hooves as gods play ball.

A1142.6.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 26.
A1142.6.1.p: Thunder comes from the clashing weapons of warring spirits fighting in the sky.

A1142.7.p: Thunder is caused by a deity separating winds that try to join together.

A1142.8.p: Thunder is the noise of a waterskin that the rain-god drags across the floor of the sky.

A1142.9.p: Thunder is made by giants moving about in the sky.

A1142.9.1.p: Thunder is the drums of the dead, beaten by spirits of the dead in the sky.

A1145.p: A general heading for myths explaining what causes earthquakes.

A1145.1.r: (Cf. A844).—*Encyc. Religion and Ethics I 491b; *Olrik Ragnarök 278; Icel.: De la Saussaye 264.—Greek: Fox 211 (Poseidon); Jewish: Neuman; Egyptian: Müller 104; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 311f.; Armenian: Ananikian 93; India: Thompson-Balys.—S. Am. Indian (Chibcha): Kroeber BBAE CXLIII (2) 908.
A1145.1.p: Earthquakes are caused by a monster moving beneath the ground.

A1145.2.p: An earthquake is caused by a sea monster moving or shifting its body beneath the earth or sea.

A1147.p: Explains how the sky came to be stormy, with dark clouds and tempests.

A1147.1.r: Kaska: Teit JAFL XXX 448; Tahiti: Henry 339.
A1147.1.p: Explains why the sky is red, saying the redness comes from blood.

A1148.p: Explains why certain strange sunsets appear before tornadoes, as an omen that a tornado is coming.

A1150.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 87 n. 3; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 288 n. 60, (Ojibwa): Jones JAFL XXIX 372, Carson JAFL XXX 493, (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 226, 246, (Naskapi): Speck JAFL XXVIII 76.
A1150.p: Explains how the seasons of the year came to be determined or fixed.

A1150.1.p: Explains how the proper times for planting crops and harvesting them were set.

A1151.p: A season is missing from the world, so a culture hero steals it from a monster and brings it back to his people.

A1152.r: N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 276 n. 16.
A1152.p: Seasons are produced by turning over a boneless man, whose movement brings the change of season.

A1153.p: Seasons come from the marriage of the North and the South, personified as a union between them.

A1154.p: Gives a family tree for summer and winter, saying where they came from and who their parents were.

A1155.p: Explains why days grow longer in spring.

A1156.p: Explains why days grow shorter in autumn: the real sun sets early because the red cockscomb plant, which was used to kill the sun's brother, reaches its full height at that time.

A1157.p: Explains the seasons as the work of gods who push the sun back and forth at the solstices.

A1160.p: Explains how the months of the year came to be determined or fixed.

A1161.r: *Köhler-Bolte I 380f.; Destriche RTP II 53; Gaidoz Mélusine VII No. 11 (with references to earlier numbers); Shaineanu Romania XVIII 107.
A1161.p: Explains why February has fewer days, saying January and March stole some of its days.

A1170.p: Explains how night and day came to be.

A1171.p: Explains how daylight first came into being.

A1171.1.p: Daylight is created when the creator opens his eyes.

A1171.2.p: Daylight comes through openings or windows in the sky that let light shine down.

A1171.3.p: Angels who belong to the day are responsible for bringing daylight, in a Jewish tradition named Neuman.

A1171.4.p: Day is explained as the child of Night and Dawn, a myth accounting for why day follows night.

A1172.r: Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Maori: Clark 43, 46; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 289 n. 62; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 683; African (Fang): Einstein 169.
A1172.p: After much debate, the relative lengths of day and night are settled, so that each gets its proper share of time.

A1172.1.p: The amount of sunshine is controlled or regulated, so the sun's light is set to a fixed portion.

A1172.2.p: Night and day are kept inside a wallet or bag, and are released or shared out from it.

A1172.3.p: Night and day are personified as riders on horses that chase each other across the sky.

A1174.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 205.
A1174.p: Night is explained as having a origin, telling how darkness first came to the world.

A1174.1.r: Released.—Munderucú: Alexander Lat. Am. 310; Arawak, Carib, Surinam: ibid. 274.
A1174.1.p: Darkness is kept in a package or bundle, and is released to bring night.

A1174.2.p: Some nights are dark and others light, and a tale explains why.

A1174.3.r: Originally no night. Culture hero goes to distant land and buys it. He introduces sleep, etc. Cock to crow for day. (Cf. B755, J2272.1.).—Banks Is.: Dixon 113.
A1174.3.p: Night is bought or acquired through a purchase, so that darkness is obtained from someone who sells it.

A1174.3.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 683.
A1174.3.1.p: Night is stolen and kept sealed in a jar, so that darkness is confined until released.

A1174.4.p: A god wraps himself in a dark cloak, and the night falls as a result.

A1177.r: *Dh II 30.—Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 83 No. 9c; Jewish: Neuman.
A1177.p: A tale explains why the sun shines on a particular day of the week, here Saturday or Friday.

A1178.p: The words "yesterday" and "today" are explained by a tale of their origin.

A1179.p: Miscellaneous tales explaining the origin of night and day that do not fit the other headings.

A1179.1.p: Twilight, the dim time between day and night, is explained by a tale of its origin.

A1179.1.1.p: The red glow of twilight is explained as the reflection of the fires of hell.

A1179.2.p: Dawn, the first light before sunrise, is explained by a tale of its origin.

A1179.2.1.p: The pink or red glow of dawn is explained as the reflection of the roses of paradise.

A1180.p: Miscellaneous tales explaining how the present order of the world was established, under the natural order heading.

A1181.r: N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 223.
A1181.p: A tale establishes where the center of the world is, found by reaching out to its ends.

A1182.p: The world is divided into its four quarters, the cardinal directions, which are fixed or determined in the beginning.

A1185.r: They are cut off by thunderbolt.—Hindu: Penzer VI 3 n. 1; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1185.p: In the beginning mountains have wings and fly about, until someone cuts their wings off so they stay in place.

A1186.p: A figure measures the world, establishing its size or extent as part of the ordering of creation.

A1187.p: The creator assigns a chief or overseer to each kind of created thing, such as a ruler of demons (Lucifer) and a ruler of mountains (Sion).

A1191.p: At creation, every thing is given its name.

A1195.p: A myth explaining how the echo, the repeated sound returned from a hollow or cliff, came to exist.

A1196.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A1196.p: A story explaining why salt is no longer found in forests, so it must be gathered elsewhere.

A1200.r: *Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 460 s.v. “Anthropogonie”; *DeCock Volkssage, 146ff.; *Basset RTP XVIII 542 and references to earlier volumes.—Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 34 No. 6; Jewish: *Neuman; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 371ff.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 283 n. 49, (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 94; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XI 338, (N. Alaska and Mackenzie River): Jenness 80, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 152, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 167; Quiché: Alexander Lat. Am. 163.
A1200.p: The general heading for myths about how humans were created.

A1201.p: Humans are created so that they will rule over the earth.

A1205.p: Gods that are unsuitable or unacceptable are the first beings to live on the earth, before humans appear.

A1210.r: *Dh I 89.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: *Grote I 71; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3030; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 81.—Maori: Dixon 23, 26; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 312; Hawaiian, Tahitan: Dixon 26; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 92; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684, (Tucuna): Nimuendajú ibid. 724; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 105, (Ibo of Nigeria): Basden 282, (Ekoi): Talbot 373.
A1210.p: A creator deliberately makes humans, as opposed to humans arising by some other means.

A1211.p: The first human is made from the body of the creator (a god or hero).

A1211.0.1.p: A human simply appears out of the deity's body as soon as the deity thinks of him.

A1211.1.r: Eitrem Opferritus und Voropfer der Griechen und Römer (Skrifter Akad. Oslo 1914 No. 1 426).—Gaster Oldest Stories 69; Babylonian: Spence 81.—New Britain: Dixon 107 (figures drawn on ground and sprinkled with creator’s blood).
A1211.1.p: Humans are made from dirt mixed with the creator's blood.

A1211.2.r: Dh I 113; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 33.—Persian: Carnoy 293.
A1211.2.p: Humans are made from the sweat of the creator.

A1211.3.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 32; Oceanic: Dixon 24.
A1211.3.p: Humans are made from the spittle, or saliva, of the creator.

A1211.3.1.p: A person is made from the spittle of the gods, a specific form of the spittle motif.

A1211.4.p: Humans are made from the eye of the creator.

A1211.5.p: Humans are made from dirt rubbed off the body of the creator or hero.

A1211.5.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A1211.5.1.p: A human is made from a toenail that the creator broke off, with the dirt from it forming the first person.

A1211.6.p: The first human pair comes into being from two drops of the creator's urine, with the woman made from one of the drops.

A1211.7.p: The first man arises when a maid licks semen-stained cloth belonging to the creator's teacher.

A1211.8.p: A primeval crab pulls the first five kinds of living creatures out of his own side.

A1212.p: Mankind is created in the likeness of the creator (god).

A1215.p: Man originates from a god who comes down to earth.

A1216.r: Greek: Fox 11.—India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: Dixon 156, 167, Voorhoeve Overzicht 64.
A1216.p: Human beings are regarded as the offspring of the creator.

A1216.1.p: Mankind comes into being when the creator masturbates over earth.

A1217.r: Dh I 90ff., 156ff.; *Fb “menneske” II 578a.—Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 4, 39, 41, 149; Jewish: *Neuman; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 61; Maidu: Dixon BAM XVII 39ff. No. 1.
A1217.p: The devil tries to bring to life his creatures as God did, but succeeds only in making an animal.

A1217.1.p: Rebellious angels oppose God's creation of man.

A1218.r: *BP III 54.—Icel.: De la Saussaye 263, MacCulloch Eddic 327; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 39; Jewish: Neuman; Greek: Fox 15.
A1218.p: Mankind is created through the joint work of several gods.

A1220.r: Hawaiian: Dixon 15f.; Samoan: ibid. 18, 28; Maori: ibid. 27.
A1220.p: Mankind comes into being gradually through a process of evolution rather than a single act of creation.

A1220.1.p: Human beings gradually degenerate over time into the present kind of people.

A1221.p: Mankind arises from an unusual primeval mating between beings.

A1221.1.p: A giant begets mankind by touching one of his feet with the other.

A1221.2.p: Mankind arises from the union of "Peace and Quiet" fertilized by "Light."

A1221.3.p: Mankind arises from the mating of pairs of reeds.

A1221.4.p: Mankind arises from the mating of a tree and a vine.

A1221.5.p: Mankind arises from the mating of a frog and a "daughter of fire."

A1221.6.p: Mankind arises from the mating of a human and an animal.

A1222.r: Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 89 No. 49; India: Thompson-Balys; Oceanic: Dixon 109 (Fiji, Torres Straits, Admiralty Is.), 109 n. 17 (Polynesia, Indonesia, Micronesia), 160 (Sumatra), 169f. (Indonesia), Handy 125 (Marquesas); S. Am. Indian (Jivaro): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 148, (Mbaya): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A1222.p: Mankind hatches or emerges from eggs.

A1224.r: *Lang Myth I 179, 184; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 465; *Frazer Old Testament I 33ff.—Australian: Van Gennep Mythes et légendes d’Australie 2f., 8f.; Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 374; Eskimo (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 168, (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 261, (Greenland): Rink 471, (Cape York): Rasmussen III 85, (W. Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 359, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 152, (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 482, (Mackenzie River): Jenness RCanAE XIII 81; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 104.
A1224.p: Humankind is descended from animals through a gradual process of evolution.

A1224.0.1.r: Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 482, cf. Thompson Tales n. 2; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A1224.0.1.p: Human beings come from a union between a human and an animal.

A1224.1.p: Humankind comes from tadpoles that changed into people.

A1224.2.r: Eastern Indonesian: Dixon 169; Tonga: Gifford 15f.; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684.
A1224.2.p: Humankind comes from worms or larvae that developed into people.

A1224.3.r: Eve.—*Dh I 114ff.; *Bolte Zs f. Vksk. XI 255 n. 3; Polívka ibid. XVI 212.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VII 5 No. 11, XXXIII 52 No. 11; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 140 No. 10; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 82 No. 17; Flemish: DeMeyer XXXVII 83 No. 11; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 36ff., 52, 65.
A1224.3.p: The first woman was formed from a dog's tail.

A1224.4.p: Humankind is born from a cow.

A1224.5.1.p: Men are monkeys that have lost their tails.

A1224.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII 93, 294.

A1224.7.p: A creator makes humans from ants, ordering the ants to become men.

A1225.r: Arunta: Dixon 272; Borneo: ibid. 159; Society Is.: ibid. 29, 164; Nias Is., Samoan: ibid. 164 n. 35, 36.
A1225.p: The first humans were undeveloped, shapeless beings that gradually took on their present form.

A1225.1.r: Like Siamese twins. (Cf. A1275.2.)—Jewish: Neuman.—S. Am. Indian (Chaco): Alexander Lat. Am. 322, (Lengua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 267.
A1225.1.p: The first couple were joined together as one body.

A1225.2.p: The first humans had no hands or feet; a boy stole them from Python, and people have had them ever since.

A1225.2.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 68.
A1225.2.1.p: A monkey gives humans hands, feet, a mouth and a nose.

A1226.r: Greek: *Grote I 62; Quiché: Alexander Lat. Am. 163ff.; Cakchiquel: ibid. 180; Banks Is.: Beckwith Myth 61.
A1226.p: The creator tries several failed attempts before finally succeeding in making humans.

A1226.1.p: The creator first makes a human from butter, which does not hold its shape and melts.

A1227.p: Various kinds of people all arose from one original type of human.

A1230.p: The first human comes down or emerges onto the earth from another place.

A1231.r: *Lang Myth I 75; India: *Thompson-Balys; German New Guinea: Dixon 111; Northern Australia: ibid. 274; Kei Is. (Indonesia): ibid. 156; Eastern Indonesian: ibid. 167.—N. A. Indian: Krickeberg Indianermärchen aus Nordamerika 10; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 517; Carib: Alexander Lat. Am. 38; S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 315, (Yagua): Steward-Métraux ibid. (3) 736, (Warrau): Kirchoff ibid. (3) 880, (Bacairi): Lévi-Strauss ibid. (3) 347, (Tiatinagua): Métraux ibid. (3) 448, (Toba, Mataco): Métraux ibid. (1) 367, Métraux MAFLS XL 21f., 101.—African: Werner African 152.
A1231.p: The first human descends from the sky to the earth.

A1231.1.p: Humankind comes from a featherless bird that is sent down from the sky.

A1232.r: (Cf. A1631.) Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.—S. Am. Indian (Chaco, Pampean): Alexander Lat. Am. 322, (Tereno, Caduveo, Mbaya): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367, (Inca): Rowe ibid. (2) 315, (Munderucú): Horton ibid. (3) 281, (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux ibid. (3) 550, (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 25; N. Am. Indian (Zuñi): *Benedict 337.
A1232.p: Mankind rises up out of the earth, so that the first people are imagined as coming up from underground.

A1232.1.p: Humankind is created from the bones of the dead, which are brought up from the underworld.

A1232.2.r: Chibcha (with reference to other South American tribes): Alexander Lat. Am. 199.
A1232.2.p: The first people come out of a lake; a woman and a boy emerge, marry, and populate the earth.

A1232.2.1.p: The first people emerge from water in general, not specifically from a lake.

A1232.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Haitian: Alexander Lat. Am. 30; S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 317, (Aymara): Tschopik ibid. (2) 571, (Araucanian): Cooper ibid. (2) 753, (Yuracare): Métraux ibid. (3) 503, (Mbaya): Métraux ibid. (1) 367, (Tiatinagua): Métraux ibid. (3) 449, (Caduveo): Métraux MAFLS XL 106; African: Werner African 147.
A1232.3.p: The first people come out of caves in the earth.

A1232.3.1.p: The first people come out of a pit in the ground.

A1234.r: Greek: *Grote I 177; Australian: Dixon Oc. Myth. 271; Papuan (British New Guinea): ibid. 110; Indonesian: ibid. 169 n. 79—81; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 312; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 47; African: Werner African 147.
A1234.p: Mankind comes forth from the ground itself, with the earth acting as the source of people.

A1234.1.p: The earth is regarded as a virgin mother who gives birth to Adam, the first man.

A1234.1.1.p: The first man and woman are born from the womb of Mother Earth.

A1234.3.p: A child spontaneously arises from the ground without parents; in the tale, scientists find a child on a deserted island and suggest he came out of the earth.

A1234.4.p: The earth gives birth to a woman.

A1236.r: (Cf. A1251.)—Indonesian: Dixon 168f.; Papuan (British New Guinea): ibid. 110; Sumatra: ibid 160.—S. Am. Indian (Warrau): Kirchoff BBAE CXLIII (3) 880, (Chamacoco): Métraux ibid. (1) 367; African: Werner African 145f.
A1236.p: Mankind comes out of a tree, so that the first people are imagined as born from trees.

A1236.1.p: Mankind emerges from buds that grow on trees.

A1236.2.p: Tribes emerge from inside a melon.

A1240.p: Mankind is made from a mineral substance, such as earth or clay, rather than from living beings.

A1241.r: *Dh I 89-III passim; Barton JAOS XXXIX 287; *Frazer Old Testament I 3—29.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 51 n. 5, Fox 10f., 13, 208; Jewish: *Neuman; Hindu: Penzer III 59; Babylonian: Spence 86; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 373; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 114ff.—Polynesian (Maori, Hawaii, Tahiti, Society Is., Marquesas): Dixon 24—26; Indonesian: ibid. 172ff. n. 96—100, 104—106; Australian: ibid. 273; Marquesas: Handy 122f.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 44ff.; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 315.—Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 454; N. A. Indian: Krickeberg Indianermärchen 267, 307, 321f., (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 56; S. Am. Indian (Lengua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367, (Apapocuva-Guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 136; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 85; Quiché: ibid. 163.
A1241.p: Man is made out of clay or earth, shaped into a human form.

A1241.1.p: Man is made from a piece of clay thrown onto the ground, which then takes human shape.

A1241.2.p: Man is made from sand that has been sprinkled with water so that it can be shaped.

A1241.3.r: (Cf. A1241.2, A1252.1.)—Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 4, 34f.; Jewish: *Neuman, Moreno Esdras; Indonesian: Dixon 172ff.; Banks Is., New Hebrides: ibid. 107; Hawaii: *Beckwith Myth 43—46; S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 315, (Yuracare): Métraux ibid. (3) 504; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 94.
A1241.3.p: Man is made from a clay image that is then brought to life.

A1241.4.p: In this creation story, the first man is shaped from earth that has been reddened with the blood of a human sacrifice.

A1241.4.1.p: Man is created from clay mixed with the blood of an animal.

A1241.5.p: The earth used to make the first man is gathered from four different places.

A1245.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 463.—Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 55 n. 2; Fox 11.—Nauru (Pleasant Is.): Dixon 252; Tongan, Samoan, Melanesian: ibid. 158; Indonesian: Kruyt Het Animisme 469.—Central American: Van Cappelle Mythen en Sagen uit West Indië 19; S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 315, (Paressi): Métraux ibid. (3) 359.
A1245.p: Humankind is created out of stones.

A1245.1.r: (Cf. A1254.1.).—Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 55 n. 2, Fox 19.
A1245.1.p: After a flood, a new race of people arises from stones thrown over the head.

A1245.2.p: Mankind comes from a stone image that is brought to life.

A1245.3.p: Mankind comes out of a split or cleft rock.

A1245.4.p: Mankind arises from a salty stone or block of ice licked by a cow.

A1245.5.p: A man is born from mountains.

A1250.p: The first human is made from plant material rather than earth or stone.

A1251.r: (Cf. A1236, A1275.6.)—Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 461, 955; Holmberg Baum 69; BP III 54.—Icel.: Herrmann Nordische Mythologie 579, MacCulloch Eddic 327f., Boberg; Greek: Fox 11; Hindu: Berguigne La religion védique I 100.—Australian: Dixon 274; Island of Nieue: ibid. 30; Melanesian: ibid. 106; Solomon Is.: ibid. 110; Ceram, Amboina, Formosa, Borneo, Nias: ibid. 168; Indonesian: Voorhoeve Overzicht 65, Kruyt Het Animisme 465.—Central American: Van Cappelle 18; S. Am. Indian (Tembé): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 140.
A1251.p: The first man is created from a tree.

A1252.r: Borneo: Dixon 174f.; S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 360.
A1252.p: The first man is created from wood.

A1252.1.r: (Cf. A1241.3, A1245.2)—Indonesian: Dixon 172ff.; Admiralty Is., Banks Is.: ibid. 106; India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Bacairi, Amazon): Alexander Lat. Am. 312.
A1252.1.p: A wooden carved image is brought to life and becomes the first human beings.

A1253.p: The first man is created from a fruit or nut.

A1253.1.p: The first man is created from some kind of fruit.

A1253.1.1.p: The first man is created from a fig.

A1253.1.2.p: The first man is born from an apple.

A1253.2.p: The first man is created from a nut.

A1253.2.1.p: The first man throws a coconut onto the ground, and from it the first woman is created.

A1253.2.2.p: Men come from long nuts and women come from short nuts, so the shape of a nut determines the sex of the person made from it.

A1254.r: Burmese: Scott Indo-Chin. 281; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 450; Isthmian tribes (Panama): Alexander Lat. Am. 193; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684.
A1254.p: Humankind is created from seeds rather than from clay or other material.

A1254.1.p: After a great flood, a new human race grows from seeds that are thrown over the head.

A1255.p: Humankind is created from a plant.

A1255.1.p: The first man is made from the stalks of sugar cane.

A1255.2.p: The first man is made from ears of corn.

A1256.p: Humankind is created from an herb or leafy green plant.

A1256.1.p: The first man is made from grass.

A1260.p: Humankind is created from a variety of miscellaneous materials, not one single substance.

A1260.1.r: Grimm Deutsche Mythologie I 468ff.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 371.
A1260.1.p: Man is formed by combining several different objects or substances into one body.

A1260.1.1.p: Man is made from the four elements, usually earth, water, air and fire.

A1260.1.2.p: Man is made from substances gathered from eight different sources.

A1260.1.3.r: or warmth, fire; cold, air; dryness, earth; instability, water.—*Dh I 111ff.; Köhler-Bolte II 1ff.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 326f.; Siberian: *Holmberg Siberian 376.
A1260.1.3.p: Adam's body is made from eight (or four) pairs of things: the body from earth, bones from stones, veins from roots, blood from water, hair from grass, thoughts from wind, and spirit from clouds.

A1260.1.4.p: Seven substances are used to make up the human body.

A1260.1.5.p: Man is made of clay, with bones of stone, blood of water, and vines for veins.

A1261.1.p: The first human is created from sea foam.

A1261.2.p: The first human is created from an egg that was formed from sea foam.

A1262.1.p: Mankind is shaped from sweat, body heat, and breath. It is a myth of how the first humans came into being from bodily fluids and vapors.

A1263.p: The first human is formed from a piece of some living being's body. This is a creation myth in which humans grow out of body parts.

A1263.1.p: The first human comes from blood. In this creation myth, blood is the material from which a man is made.

A1263.1.1.r: Chatham Is., Samoan, Melanesian: Dixon 30; Admiralty Is., Polynesian, Indonesian, Melanesian, New Britain: *ibid. 109 n. 17.
A1263.1.1.p: The first man is formed from a clot of blood. This is a creation myth in which a human develops from congealed blood.

A1263.1.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684.
A1263.1.2.p: Humans are made from the blood of a hunted game animal. In this creation myth, the blood of a wild animal becomes the source of people.

A1263.2.p: The first man is made from a fingernail. This is a creation myth in which a human grows from a paring of nail.

A1263.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Zuñi: Parsons JAFL XXIX 394 n. 1.
A1263.3.p: Man is made from rubbed-off bits of skin. In this creation myth, flakes or scrapings of skin form a human being.

A1263.4.p: A man is created from the spittle of a holy person. In this creation myth, saliva from a sacred figure becomes a human being.

A1263.5.p: A man is created from animal horns that bloom and bear him like fruit. In this creation myth, horns sprout and a human is born from them as if from a plant.

A1263.6.p: Mankind is made from the genitals of a culture hero. In this creation myth, the sexual organs of a culture hero become the source of humans.

A1263.7.r: Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 51.
A1263.7.p: The first man is formed from an animal's bone. This is a creation myth in which a human comes from bone.

A1265.r: Cadmus, Jason.—Grierson FL XXXIII (1922) 380.—Greek: Fox 10, 45, 112; Frazer Apollodorus I 315 n. 2.
A1265.p: Men spring up from dragon's teeth that have been sown in the ground. In this myth, planted dragon teeth grow into fully formed human warriors.

A1266.p: Mankind is created from food. In this creation myth, some kind of food is the material from which humans are made.

A1266.1.p: A man is made from a meatball. In this creation myth, a ball of meat becomes a human being.

A1268.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Gilbert Is. (Micronesia): Dixon 252; Aztec: Alexander Lat. Am. 85.
A1268.p: Mankind is created from ashes or cinders. In this creation myth, the remains of a fire become human beings.

A1268.1.p: A whole tribe is born from fire. In this origin myth, a people come into existence out of flames or the remains of a fire.

A1270.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Apapocuva-Guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 138, (Yuracare): Métraux ibid. 144, (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359.
A1270.p: The first human couple, the earliest man and woman, appear in the myth of origins.

A1270.1.p: The first human pair lives in innocence before any fall or trouble. It describes their untroubled early life.

A1271.p: This motif tells how the first parents of humanity came into being. It concerns the origin of the first man and woman.

A1271.1.p: The sun, moon, and stars give birth to the first parents. In this myth, the sun and moon have a son, and the morning and evening star have a daughter, who become the first humans. At first they lack understanding, which is later awakened by demigods.

A1271.2.p: The first human parents come into being from a stone and a bird that were created from the sun and moon, which are transformed into the first man and woman.

A1271.3.r: Persian: Carnoy 294; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 88.
A1271.3.p: The first human parents are described as children of a god.

A1271.4.p: The first human parents arise from gold that comes from the body of the first man; they are born fifteen years old.

A1273.p: The first human parents are twins.

A1273.1.p: The first human parents are twins who have sex with each other, so they are incestuous.

A1275.p: The creation of a mate for the first man (or first woman), told as a story of how the first partner came to be.

A1275.1.r: *Dh I 115ff.; *Frazer Old Testament I 9f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 34, 36ff., 52, 65; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 379; Hawaiian: Dixon 24; cf. Central Caroline Is.: ibid. 251, Beckwith Myth 43, 46.
A1275.1.p: The first woman is made from one of the first man's ribs.

A1275.1.1.p: A god creates a princess out of a prince's body and gives her to him as his wife.

A1275.2.p: The first man is split in two, and one half becomes his mate.

A1275.3.r: New Hebrides: Dixon 107; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 49.
A1275.3.p: Of the ten original men, one magically changes into a woman.

A1275.4.r: New Zealand: Dixon 24f.; Society Is.: ibid. 25; Marquesas: ibid. 26.
A1275.4.p: The creator first makes a woman and then fathers a man by her.

A1275.5.p: A man creates a woman from melted butter, sour milk, sour cream and curds that he offers on the waters.

A1275.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 144.
A1275.6.p: The first woman's mate is made from a tree that has been transformed.

A1275.7.p: The first man is created from nothing and wanders about until he finds a mate.

A1275.8.p: An explanation of why Eve was not made at the same time as Adam.

A1275.9.p: The first man comes down to earth, falls in love with a fairy, and marries her.

A1275.10.p: The first created man catches a woman in his snare.

A1276.p: In the beginning only women lived on earth. A god accidentally kills one of them and promises any reparation; the women choose a man as the gift.

A1277.p: Tales about the children of the first human parents.

A1277.1.p: The first parents eat their own children.

A1277.2.p: The first human couple is allowed to have as many children as they wish, with no limit on how many they bear.

A1277.3.p: The first couple's son is killed by a tiger sent by a god, and his body parts become cosmic and natural features: his head becomes the sun, his chest the moon, and his blood colors the earth red.

A1277.4.p: The first man and woman bring their children in and dress them in clothing.

A1279.p: A miscellaneous group of tales about the first human pair that do not fit under the more specific headings.

A1279.1.p: The first husband is so ugly that he has to be kept hidden away from others.

A1280.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 276, 280f.; Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 120; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 315.
A1280.p: Stories about who the first man, or first woman, was.

A1281.p: Stories describing what the first man, or first woman, was like physically or in condition.

A1281.1.r: (Cf. A1310.1.)—*Dh I 225; Jewish: Neuman.—Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 34; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 376.
A1281.1.p: The first man is covered with a hard, horn-like skin or shell.

A1281.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 34; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 383.
A1281.2.p: The first man is covered with hair all over his body.

A1281.2.1.p: In ancient times animals and humans exchanged or changed their skins, explaining how the hairy first condition changed.

A1281.3.p: The first man goes about without any clothing.

A1281.4.p: The first men give off their own light and glow.

A1281.5.p: The first man is created already circumcised.

A1281.6.p: The first man, Adam, has no name at the beginning.

A1281.6.1.p: Adam's name is formed from the first letters of four stars, one from each quarter of the sky.

A1282.p: Stories about the first mother of all human beings.

A1282.1.p: The mother of the world gives birth to three sons.

A1285.p: Stories about what the first man did or was responsible for.

A1285.1.p: The first man is made ruler over the entire world.

A1285.1.1.p: Adam prays, and in answer God sends him down to earth to become the father of all mankind.

A1290.p: A general heading for other tales about how humankind was first made, not covered by the more specific motifs.

A1291.p: Humans are made by a supernatural being other than God, such as a spirit or demon.

A1291.1.p: Humans are made by angels rather than by God himself.

A1293.p: With God absent, the Devil puts sickness into Adam's body when making him.

A1295.r: N. A Ind.: Kroeber JAFL XXI 223; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684.
A1295.p: Humans, or sometimes animals, are created inside a covered container such as a basket, bundle, or under a blanket.

A1296.r: S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 406.
A1296.p: The first human is multiplied by being cut or broken into pieces, each piece becoming a new person.

A1297.p: The first human being is killed by jealous brothers, who are reptiles and insects.

A1300.p: A general heading for tales explaining how the basic conditions and customs of human life came to be.

A1301.r: Dh I 242ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Greek: *Grote I 5; Jewish: Neuman.
A1301.p: In early times people were as large as giants.

A1310.p: A general heading for explanations of how the parts and features of the human body were arranged or came to be as they are.

A1310.1.r: (Cf. A1281.1.)—Dh I 225.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3035, Balys Legends Nos. 34, 45—49.
A1310.1.p: Adam's body changes shape when he falls from grace; it was formerly horn-like.

A1310.2.p: The body is put together piece by piece, with its parts assembled into a whole.

A1310.3.p: Explains why men are clothed in skin, meaning the origin of human skin covering.

A1310.4.p: Explains why women have marks on the belly.

A1311.p: A general heading for tales explaining where human hands and feet came from.

A1311.1.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 288 n. 59; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 56.
A1311.1.p: Man's hand is modeled on the hand of a lizard.

A1311.2.p: God changes a man's right hand into his left after the man uses that hand to slap the Devil on the ears, so he loses it.

A1311.3.p: Explains how fingernails came to be.

A1312.p: A general heading for tales explaining where the human skeleton's bones came from.

A1312.1.p: A stone that magically joins a man to a woman's body gives origin to the knee-caps.

A1312.2.r: Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 83 Nos. 21, 22.—Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 226 (floating ribs).
A1312.2.p: Explains why the human body has an odd number of ribs on one side or the total count is uneven, giving a mythic reason for the rib count.

A1313.p: A general heading for stories explaining how the male and female sex organs came to be.

A1313.0.1.p: Explains how eunuchs, men without testicles, came to exist.

A1313.0.2.p: Explains how the difference between the sexes came to be.

A1313.1.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 21, XXXIII 52 No. 21; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman.—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 141 No. 14; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3040, Balys Legends Nos. 50—57; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 83f. Nos. 28—30; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 84 No. 21.—Plains Ojibwa: Skinner JAFL XXXII 283; Plains Cree: Skinner JAFL XXIX 351.
A1313.1.p: Explains how the male sex organs came to be.

A1313.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 22, XXXIII 52 No. 22; India: *Thompson-Balys; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 141 No. 14; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3040, Balys Legends Nos. 50—57; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 83f. Nos. 27, 29, 30; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 84 No. 22.
A1313.2.p: Explains how the female sex organs came to be.

A1313.2.1.p: Explains how the clitoris came to be.

A1313.3.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 56f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 288 n. 59a.; Hatt Asiatic Influences 84f.
A1313.3.p: In these stories the sex organs were first placed wrongly on the body, and a culture hero later put them in their proper places.

A1313.3.1.r: (See practically all references to F547.1.1, Vagina Dentata.)—S. Am. Indian (Toba, Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 99, 105, Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A1313.3.1.p: Women originally had teeth in their vaginas, and a culture hero breaks them so women will not harm men during intercourse.

A1313.4.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 20; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 83 No. 27; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 53ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.—S. Am. Indian (Apapocuva-Guarani): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 137.
A1313.4.p: Explains how women came to have breasts.

A1313.4.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A1313.4.1.p: In this tale women first had breasts on their foreheads, which were later moved to their chests.

A1313.5.p: Explains how the placenta, the organ that nourishes a baby in the womb, came to be.

A1315.p: A general heading for stories explaining how human hair and beards came to be.

A1315.1.r: Dh I 314.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 18.
A1315.1.p: Explains why men's hair turns gray with age.

A1315.2.r: Christensen Molboerne 212 No. 70; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 17, XXXIII 52 No. 17; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 82 No. 20; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 84 No. 17; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1315.2.p: Explains why some people have bald heads.

A1315.3.r: *Dh I 228ff.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 5 Nos. 13, 14, XXXIII 52 No. 13; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 83 Nos. 23, 24; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 141 No. 11; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 58—62, 70.
A1315.3.p: Explains how the beard came to be.

A1315.4.r: Hair stands on guard at mouth and eyes to see that Stomach does not escape.—Ekoi: Talbot 394.
A1315.4.p: Explains how hair came to grow around the mouth and eyes. In the story, Hair and Stomach dispute, and Stomach is forced to stay inside the body.

A1315.5.p: Explains how pubic hair came to be.

A1315.6.p: Explains how eyelashes came to be.

A1316.p: A general heading for stories explaining how the human face and its features came to be.

A1316.0.1.p: Myth in which the first man had two faces, which were separated when the first woman was created.

A1316.1.p: Myth explaining why people have different sized noses: those who came into being earlier got big noses and later arrivals got small ones.

A1316.1.1.p: Myth in which the nose is shaped from clay taken from the back of the already-made man.

A1316.3.p: Myth explaining how eyes came to be.

A1316.3.1.p: Myth explaining how eyes were distributed among people, so that some have more or fewer than others.

A1316.3.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 104.
A1316.3.2.p: Myth explaining why some women have only one eye.

A1316.3.3.p: Story in which people were originally blind and their eyes were opened by accident.

A1316.4.p: Myth explaining how ears came to be.

A1316.5.p: Myth explaining how the tongue came to be.

A1316.6.p: Myth explaining how teeth came to be.

A1317.p: Myth explaining how urine and other bodily waste came to be.

A1319.p: Miscellaneous myths explaining the origin of other parts and features of the human body.

A1319.1.r: *Dh I 208ff.; *Fb “Adamsæble” IV 4.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 5 No. 16, XXXIII 52 No. 16; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 35 No. 10; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 34; U.S.: Baughman; Jewish: Neuman.
A1319.1.p: Myth explaining the Adam's apple as the forbidden fruit stuck in Adam's throat.

A1319.2.r: Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 117 No. 72; Piegan: Michelson JAFL XXIX 409.
A1319.2.p: Myth explaining why men have no tails.

A1319.3.r: Cameroons: Gantenbein 69ff., Lederbogen Mitt. d. Sem. f. orient. Spr. IV 175f. No. 11.
A1319.3.p: Myth explaining why ear-wax is found inside the ear.

A1319.4.p: Myth explaining why the human buttocks are large.

A1319.5.p: Myth explaining how the liver came to be.

A1319.6.p: Myth explaining how blood came to be.

A1319.7.p: Myth explaining why the pupil of the eye is black: spirits blackened it so they could make themselves invisible.

A1319.8.p: Explains how human sweat came to be. A myth gives the origin of perspiration.

A1319.9.p: Explains how the act of sneezing came to be. A myth gives the origin of sneezing.

A1319.10.p: Explains how the feeling of itching came to be. A myth gives the origin of itching.

A1319.11.p: Explains how the sensation of being tickled came to be. A myth gives the origin of ticklishness.

A1319.12.p: Originally people renewed their youth by shedding their skin, as snakes do. Later this ability was lost.

A1319.12.1.p: Explains why people no longer shed their skin: in a contest, a toad representing man lost to a lizard, so man lost the power to change skin.

A1319.13.p: Explains why the human neck is the size it is today.

A1319.14.p: Explains how human skin came to be. A myth gives the origin of man's skin.

A1320.p: Tales about how the length of human life was fixed, or how its span was decided.

A1321.r: Years 1—30 vigorous (man’s own); 30—48 burdens and blows (ass’s); 48—60 no teeth (dog’s); 60—70 foolish (monkey’s).—*BP III 290 (Gr. No. 176); *Fb “menneske” II 577b; Halm Aesop No. 173; Wesselski Bebel II 135 No. 103.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3060, Balys Legends Nos. 113f.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A1321.p: At first all animals and humans were given thirty years. Since that was too long for animals and too short for man, man was given part of the animals' lives.

A1321.1.p: Explains why children take longer to learn to walk than young animals do, tied to the myth of animals giving humans part of their lives.

A1322.p: Explains how the number of births relates to the number of deaths, so that population stays balanced.

A1323.r: Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 108.
A1323.p: The first human lived for a very long time.

A1325.p: The first humans had short lives.

A1326.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 103.
A1326.p: Explains why infants die so easily.

A1330.r: Shasta and Athapascan: Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 225; Africa (Congo): Weeks 205.
A1330.p: Tales of how trouble and suffering first came upon mankind.

A1331.p: Mankind's original happy state was lost because of a single sin.

A1331.1.r: (Cf. A1346).—*Dh I 208ff.; *Frazer Old Testament I 45ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 34.—Persian: Carnoy 297; India: Thompson-Balys; Burmese, Indo-Chinese: Scott 265, 289.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 45; Quiché: Alexander Lat. Am. 171; Yuracare: ibid. 315; Biloxi: Dorsey and Swanton BBAE XLVII 32; African (Baluba): Einstein 199.
A1331.1.p: Humans lost their original paradise by eating or drinking something forbidden.

A1331.1.1.p: Humans lost paradise by eating a forbidden food (a specific kind of food, not a fruit or drink).

A1331.2.p: Humans lost their original paradise because of incest between brother and sister.

A1331.2.1.p: Paradise is lost because the first woman is seduced, here specifically through incest between brother and sister.

A1333.r: *Frazer Old Testament I 384ff.; Jewish: Neuman; Irish myth: Cross.—India: Thompson-Balys; Chin (Indo-China): Scott 266f.; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 365.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 285 n. 53; Maya: Alexander Lat. Am. 132.
A1333.p: Humans originally all spoke one language, and because of a sin they came to speak many different languages.

A1333.1.p: People come to speak different languages partly because they confuse the words for "stick" and "stone."
