A1335.p: Explains how death came into the world, as part of the troubles that began for humankind.

A1335.1.r: *Dh III 22; *Wesselski Theorie 43; Gaster Oldest Stories 91.—African: Werner African 160ff., 167, (Hottentot): Bleek 69 No. 31, 71 No. 32, 72 No. 33, 74 No. 35, (Basuto): Jacottet 46 No. 6, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 129 No. 23, (Togo): Einstein 5, (Sandeh): Casati I 222; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684, (Tropical Forests): Lowie ibid. (3) 55.
A1335.1.p: Death comes into the world because a message that should have granted life is falsified or garbled, so people die instead.

A1335.1.1.p: Death comes because the wrong messenger is sent to God, and the message that carries the decision is mistaken.

A1335.2.r: Banks Is.: Dixon 106; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 61.
A1335.2.p: A bad creator tries and fails to give his creatures life as the good creator did, and his failure introduces death.

A1335.3.p: Death comes from an unwise choice: people pick a large bundle of tempting goods over a bundle containing everlasting life, and lose immortality.

A1335.4.p: Death begins when people start putting on new skins, because a child fails to recognize its mother after she has put on a new skin and she returns the old one to her body.

A1335.5.r: Renews his skin.—**Delarue Nouvelle Revue des Traditions Populaires (1950) 262—275; Wesselski Theorie 45; Gaster: Oldest Stories 81.
A1335.5.p: Death comes to humans because the serpent is given immortality instead of man.

A1335.6.p: Death is punishment for a person scorning a deity.

A1335.6.1.p: Death is punishment for giving a disrespectful answer to God.

A1335.7.p: After the Flood, the first son to die is one who dies before his father, which marks the start of death.

A1335.8.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 173; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 171.
A1335.8.p: Death comes into the world because the earth has become overpopulated.

A1335.9.p: Death comes because people grow weary of living and wish to end their lives.

A1335.9.1.p: A culture hero or god, tired of humankind, sends death into the world.

A1335.10.p: Death comes because a snake creeps in to prey on people while the creator is resting.

A1335.11.p: The god of the dead demands that people die so that he will have subjects to rule.

A1335.12.p: God sends a woman to sell poisoned curds to people, and eating them brings death into the world.

A1335.13.p: God sends a centipede down to bring death into the world with its poisoned sting.

A1335.14.p: Death enters the world through the gods' trickery: a stick a man used to scratch his back is turned into a cobra.

A1335.15.p: God punishes a man by killing his child, and this is how death came to humankind.

A1336.r: Hebrew: Genesis 4:8ff.; Jewish: Neuman; Greek: Grote I 7.—Congo: Weeks 207 No. 4; Ila of Rhodesia: Smith and Dale 350 No. 5.
A1336.p: An explanation of how murder first came into the world.

A1337.r: *Dh I 98ff.—Finnish Kalevala rune 45; Greek: Grote I 72 (Pandora’s Box); Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 461; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 187.—Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 278, 282; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 113, 502; Shasta: Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 227; S. Am. Indian (Cubeo): Goldman BBAE CXLIII (3) 798.
A1337.p: An explanation of how diseases first came to humankind.

A1337.0.1.p: Illness is sent to people by the gods.

A1337.0.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 318.
A1337.0.1.1.p: A plague is carried to people in a box by a messenger sent by the creator.

A1337.0.4.p: Illness is caused by menstrual blood.

A1337.0.5.p: Disease comes as a punishment for wrongdoing.

A1337.0.6.p: Disease is sent to keep people from enjoying themselves too much.

A1337.0.7.p: Sickness and misfortune come from monstrous children born of an incestuous union between brother and sister.

A1337.1.r: Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 142 No. 21; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 42.
A1337.1.p: An explanation of how ulcers came to be.

A1337.2.p: An explanation of how cholera came to be.

A1337.3.p: An explanation of how epilepsy came to be.

A1337.4.p: An explanation of how fever came to be.

A1337.5.p: An explanation of how itch came to be.

A1337.6.p: An explanation of how leprosy came to be.

A1337.7.p: An explanation of how smallpox came to be.

A1337.8.p: An explanation of how illness arose from fire and cold.

A1338.r: St. Peter misunderstands what God says and lets them fall.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC No. 758A.
A1338.p: Explains how people came to have bodily deformities or injuries: wicked people who try to climb into heaven by rope fall back to earth and are hurt.

A1338.1.p: Explains the origin of lame or crippled people, a type of physical defect that is said to have begun in an early myth.

A1339.1.r: Jewish: Neuman; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 145.
A1339.1.p: Explains how blindness first came into the world as one of the early troubles that befell humankind.

A1341.r: Irish myth: Cross; Kaska: Teit JAFL XXX 469; Africa (Konnoh): Willans 136.
A1341.p: Explains how war first came among human beings, as part of the early troubles that entered human life.

A1341.1.p: Explains how the custom of shouting battle cries in war began.

A1341.2.p: Explains how the practice of dueling, a formal fight between two people, began.

A1341.3.p: Explains how thefts and quarrels first arose among people.

A1342.r: Greek: Grote I 7; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
A1342.p: Explains how quarrelling first came into the world among people.

A1343.r: Greek: Grote I 7; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 113, 911; Jewish: Neuman.
A1343.p: Explains how lying first came into the world.

A1344.r: Wienert FFC LVI 37; Halm Aesop Nos. 138, 355; Greek: Grote I 7, 72; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1344.p: Explains how tears and sighs first came into human life as part of its troubles.

A1344.1.p: A tradition that the first three cries to reach God were the cry of Abel's blood and similar cries of suffering; it explains the origin of tears and sighs.

A1345.r: Greek: Grote I 7; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Liberian: Bundy JAFL XXXII 421f.; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 216, 221.
A1345.p: Explains how hunger first came into the world as one of the troubles of human life.

A1345.1.p: Explains how thirst first came into the world, as part of the origin of hunger and related troubles.

A1346.r: (Cf. A1331.1.)—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 158; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A1346.p: Explains why people must earn their bread through hard labor, sweating for their food.

A1346.1.p: Explains that people must work hard for a living as a punishment for humanity stealing fire.

A1346.2.r: Greek: Grote I 61; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Seneca: Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 462; S. Am. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 59f.
A1346.2.p: In the early world everything came easily: crops grew by themselves, and trees dropped sugar, so people had no need to labor.

A1346.2.1.p: In the beginning cotton was already spun into thread, so people did not have to spin it themselves.

A1346.2.2.p: The first people had everything they wished for, so they did not have to work at all.

A1346.2.3.p: Because people were too happy, pain and sickness were created to trouble them.

A1346.2.4.p: In early times canoes moved by themselves without paddling.

A1348.p: Tells how humankind escaped from its troubles, ending the early hardships of human life.

A1348.1.p: A wren helps humankind win back prosperity for the world after it has been lost. This is a myth about how people escaped their early troubles.

A1350.p: A myth explaining how the sexual functions of human beings came to be.

A1351.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.—Maori: Dixon 78; Polynesian, Melanesian, Micronesian: ibid. 79 n. 79—82; Maori, Hawaii, Cook Is., Fijis: Beckwith Myth 502—504; Hawaii: ibid. 284, Marquesas: Handy 58, 122, 128; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 288 n. 59a, (Tahltan): *Teit JAFL XXXII 207 n. 2.
A1351.p: A myth explaining how childbirth came to be part of human life.

A1351.1.p: A myth explaining why childbirth is painful for women.

A1351.2.p: A myth explaining how abortion came to be.

A1352.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 63—66; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Tonga: Gifford 18; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 684; Africa (Mkulwe): Einstein 18f., (Loango): Pechuël-Loesche 267.
A1352.p: A myth explaining how sexual intercourse came to be.

A1352.1.p: A myth explaining why husband and wife have sex without any restrictions or limits.

A1352.2.p: Ways used to persuade people to have sexual intercourse, as told in a myth or tale.

A1352.3.p: A former way of having sexual intercourse, through the navel.

A1355.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 25, XXXIII 53 No. 25; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A1355.p: A myth explaining how menstruation came to be.

A1355.1.p: A myth saying menstruation is a punishment because Eve had intercourse with the serpent.

A1355.1.1.p: A myth saying menstruation is a punishment because Eve ate forbidden fruit.

A1355.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 24; Jewish: Neuman.
A1355.2.p: A myth explaining menstruation through the Virgin Mary: she hides her garment and a maiden finds it.

A1355.3.p: A myth saying that in earlier times men had menstruation instead of women.

A1357.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 112f.
A1357.p: A culture hero teaches women how to raise their children.

A1358.p: A myth explaining why some women cannot have children.

A1360.p: A myth explaining how people grow and reach maturity.

A1361.r: Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 84 No. 36; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 43f.; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 83 No. 11c.
A1361.p: A myth explaining why human children stay helpless and dependent for such a long time.

A1365.p: A myth explaining why a boy at puberty is full of energy but becomes lazy later in life.

A1370.p: A myth explaining how people came to have their mental and moral traits, such as character and disposition.

A1371.p: An origin explanation for why women are considered morally or mentally inferior. Myths of this kind give a cause for women's bad qualities.

A1371.1.r: St. Peter cuts off their heads and exchanges them.—Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 83 No. 11b.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3047, Balys Legends Nos. 82—93.
A1371.1.p: Women have bad qualities because the devil (in serpent form) exchanged heads with a woman, or because the devil and a woman fought over her. The note says the devil appears as a serpent and fights with a woman.

A1371.2.p: Women are bad because they were made by combining the traits of nine different animals.

A1371.3.r: *Dh II 191ff.; Fb “sø” III 449b.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 411.
A1371.3.p: Women are bad because two daughters were created by transforming animals, a hog and a goose. In the tale, Peter promises his only daughter to three men, then asks the Lord for two more daughters, who are made when Peter greets a hog and a goose he meets on two mornings.

A1372.p: A general heading for other explanations of why women have particular traits or characteristics, each told as an origin story.

A1372.1.p: An origin explanation for why women talk too much and chatter.

A1372.2.p: An origin explanation for why women laugh a lot. The note says Eve laughed at how small her first child was.

A1372.3.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 73; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 114.
A1372.3.p: An origin explanation for why women wander around or are restless and unable to stay at home.

A1372.4.r: Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 141 No. 13; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 84 No. 34.
A1372.4.p: An origin explanation for why women have a high-pitched voice.

A1372.5.p: An origin explanation for why women are dishonest or deceptive.

A1372.6.p: An origin explanation for why some women are beautiful.

A1372.7.r: Contest arranged by Virgin Mary—laughter forbidden for some time.—Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 79.
A1372.7.p: An origin explanation for why some women are agreeable and others are disagreeable.

A1372.8.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3046, Balys Legends Nos 74—78.
A1372.8.p: Women never have free time because of a refusal made to God. The note says they refused to show God the way, saying they had no time.

A1372.9.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 70ff.; India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Munderucú): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 282.
A1372.9.p: An origin explanation for why women are under men's authority and submit to them.

A1372.10.r: St. Andrew, sent to get salt to keep people clean, gets drunk and forgets. There is only enough for men.—Venezuela: Dominguez Collection II No. 33 (Archive of Venezuelan Institute of Folklore).
A1372.10.p: An origin explanation for why women constantly wash themselves or are concerned with cleanliness.

A1373.p: An origin explanation for why women are attractive to men and draw them in.

A1373.1.r: Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 220; cf. Kaska: Teit JAFL XXX 456.
A1373.1.p: Women who are pretty but soft and useless still attract men. This explains why such women draw men's attention.

A1375.r: Irish myth: Cross; Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 112 No. 19.
A1375.p: An origin explanation for why people feel jealousy and act selfishly.

A1375.1.p: An origin explanation for why some married couples quarrel and accuse each other of cheating.

A1376.p: An origin explanation for why men are considered superior to women.

A1377.p: A myth explaining why people are lazy or unwilling to work.

A1381.p: A myth explaining how people came to be brave.

A1381.1.p: A myth explaining why people are not afraid of earthquakes.

A1382.p: A myth explaining how people came to feel fear.

A1382.1.p: A myth explaining why people feel afraid when they are in the jungle or forest.

A1383.p: A myth explaining where the feeling of shame about being naked came from.

A1383.1.r: (Leaves for clothes).—Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Baluba): Einstein 19.
A1383.1.p: The first woman is said to be the first to feel shame at being naked.

A1384.p: A myth explaining how people came to have evil inclinations or wicked tendencies.

A1384.1.p: A myth saying evil inclinations came as punishment for the fall of man.

A1384.2.p: A belief that the evil inclination enters the body at the moment of conception.

A1386.p: A myth explaining how drunkenness came into the world.

A1388.p: A myth explaining how hatred came into the world.

A1388.1.p: Hatred is said to have been let loose among mankind, spreading hate among people.

A1390.p: A miscellaneous group of myths about how human life was ordained or arranged.

A1391.p: A tale in which the body's parts argue, and the other limbs are made to serve the belly; the result of a debate between members of the body.

A1391.1.p: A myth explaining why all the limbs depend on the body for their life or support.

A1392.p: A myth about Adam taking his first walk.

A1394.p: A belief that people live by the breath of the gods.

A1399.p: A group of additional miscellaneous myths about how human life was ordained.

A1399.1.p: A myth explaining how laughter came into the world.

A1399.2.p: Explains how dreams came to exist, as a feature of the world's ordering of human life.

A1399.2.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII (3) 724.
A1399.2.1.p: Explains how sleep came to exist, as part of the origin of dreams.

A1399.3.p: Explains how spitting came to be a human custom or habit.

A1399.4.p: Explains how coughing came to be part of human life.

A1400.p: Tells how human culture, the arts and skills of civilized life, was first acquired by people.

A1401.r: N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 226 s.v. “Departed race.”
A1401.p: Says that human culture was first started by an earlier race of people who lived before the present one.

A1402.p: The gods themselves build houses and make tools for people, giving them the means of living.

A1403.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3057, Balys Legends Nos. 110f.
A1403.p: A god instructs people in how to work and earn their living.

A1404.r: Marquesas: Handy 123; S. Am. Indian (Cariri): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 559.
A1404.p: The gods teach people everything they know, giving them all their knowledge and skills.

A1405.r: Jewish: Neuman; S. Am. Indian (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII (3) 724.
A1405.p: Culture was first introduced by an ancestor of a tribe or people.

A1410.p: Explains how the world came to have an environment fit for human life, such as light, fire and other basics.

A1411.r: Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Keith 34.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 281 n. 42; Eskimo (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 205, S. Am. Indian (Tapirape): Wagley-Galvao BBAE CXLIII (3) 178. Cf. Finnish: Kalevala rune 47.
A1411.p: A culture hero steals light, which was originally kept from people and held by someone else.

A1411.1.p: The stolen light is kept in a box or basket, which the hero must open or carry off.

A1411.2.r: He is reborn. As a child in the house he steals light.—India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 282 n. 44.
A1411.2.p: The hero shrinks himself into a tiny particle and is swallowed by the guardian's daughter while she drinks water, then is reborn with the light.

A1412.p: Miscellaneous explanations of how light originally came into the world.

A1412.1.p: Light comes from the shield of an old cobra that supports the earth.

A1412.2.p: Light is said to come from the souls of the dead, who dwell in heaven.

A1412.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Tucuna): Nimuendajú BBAE CXLIII (3) 724.
A1412.3.p: A culture hero obtains daylight for people.

A1414.1.1.p: Fire is invented by rubbing sticks together to make a spark, as the first way people made fire.

A1414.2.p: Fire is said to come from inside a person's own body, so that the origin of fire lies within people themselves.

A1414.3.p: Fire is discovered by accident when children strike rocks together and a spark appears.

A1414.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—Maori: Clark 42; Isabel Is.: Beckwith Myth 504; Hawaii: ibid. 499; S. Am. Indian (Sherente): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 515, (Cashiba): Steward-Métraux ibid. A1414.5.p: Explains how flint (a hard stone that sparks) and tinder (dry material that catches fire) came into being.

A1414.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Apapocuvú-Guaraní): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 171.
A1414.6.p: A bird is the guardian or keeper of the original fire.

A1414.7.p: Fire is kept hidden in some place or object from which people must obtain it.

A1414.7.1.r: Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 61; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158.
A1414.7.1.p: A tree is the place where fire is stored and kept, so people obtain fire from it.

A1414.7.2.p: A rock is the place where fire is stored and kept, so people obtain fire from it.

A1414.7.3.p: A cave is the place where fire is stored and kept, so people obtain fire from it.

A1415.0.1.p: Fire is withheld from people as a punishment, so they must suffer without it.

A1415.0.2.p: The original fire belongs to a single person or animal who jealously guards it.

A1415.1.p: Fire is smuggled away hidden inside a hollow reed or stalk.

A1415.1.1.p: Fire is carried down from heaven hidden under the fingernails.

A1415.2.r: *Dh III 92ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3020, Balys Legends Nos. 27f.; Eng.: Baughman; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 632.—Massim of British New Guinea: Dixon 115; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 370, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 345, (Fang): Nassau No. 3; N. A1415.2.p: Animals steal fire from its owner and bring it to people.

A1415.2.1.r: Persian: Carnoy 264 (storm god in form of bird); India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 685, (Jivaro): Steward-Métraux ibid. (3) 627, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 6.

A1415.4.p: Attempts to prevent fire from being stolen are tried but fail.

A1416.p: A land is cleared of ogres (man-eating giants) and afterward becomes peaceful and safe to live in.

A1417.p: The tablets on which the destinies of the world are written are stolen, in one account by a bird named Zu who carries them off from heaven.

A1420.p: Myths explaining how humankind first got its food supply.

A1420.1.p: Food comes from the body of a food goddess who was killed, so her body parts become the edible plants or foods.

A1420.2.r: Marquesas: Handy 114; Africa (Luba): Donohugh Africa V 180.
A1420.2.p: The gods show people how to find and prepare their food.

A1420.3.p: A being who makes or creates the food items themselves.

A1420.4.r: Jewish: Neuman; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 59.
A1420.4.p: In the beginning food was obtained with no work needed; people did not have to labor for it.

A1420.5.p: After the Fall, the first man and woman are fed and clothed from a single palm tree.

A1420.6.p: At the beginning of the world, people first eat earth as their food.

A1421.r: Hindu: Keith 33f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Kodiak: Jochelson JE VI 143, 164, 187, 367; Tonga: Gifford 91; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 434f.; S. Am. Indian (Yunca, Peru): Alexander Lat. Am. 229 (fish); Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 515, (Greenland): Rink 442, Holm 75, (Cape York): Rasmussen III 51.
A1421.p: Game animals are held shut up by a evil creature so people cannot hunt them, until a culture hero sets them free.

A1421.0.1.p: A culture hero makes stored rice available again to people after it had been hoarded away from them.

A1421.1.p: Humans are given power and control over wild beasts.

A1421.1.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3110, Legends No. 215.
A1421.1.1.p: Humans rule over all animals. God gives the lion the greatest strength, but because of human wisdom the lion ends up under man's power.

A1422.r: Hebrew: Leviticus ch 11; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 78, 149, (Hottentot): Bleek 73 No. 34.
A1422.p: Explanations for which animals people are allowed to eat.

A1422.0.1.p: Certain animals became food for people because they were once unfaithful, disobedient wives of a visitor from the land of the gods.

A1422.0.2.p: Tells which animals humans are allowed to eat.

A1422.1.p: Explains why people may eat hares.

A1422.1.1.p: Explains why the Santal people eat the entrails of a hare.

A1422.2.p: Explains why the Birhor people eat the flesh of monkeys and baboons.

A1422.3.p: Explains why men hunt wild boar for food: a faithless wife was once killed by her husband and became the boar.

A1423.r: Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Samoa: Beckwith Myth 439; Isabel Island: ibid. 504; Hawaii: ibid. 61, 63; Tonga: Gifford 194; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 364; African (Angola): Chatelain 249, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 179 No. 35, (Ekoi): Talbot 240, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 348 No. 3; S. A1423.p: Myths explaining how people got vegetables and grains such as cereals.

A1423.0.1.r: Rarotonga, Cook Island: Beckwith Myth 236; Hawaii: ibid. 290, 432; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 685.
A1423.0.1.p: Plants that had been hoarded away are released, so that vegetables and grains become available to people.

A1423.1.r: Samoa, Maori, Tonga: Beckwith Myth 101; Kai of New Guinea: ibid. 104; Tonga: Gifford 163, 169; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 317.
A1423.1.p: Explains how yams, sweet potatoes or taro first came to people, usually through a culture hero or divine gift.

A1423.2.r: (Cf. A2685.)—India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 130f. No. 86.
A1423.2.p: Tells how people first obtained rice.

A1423.3.r: Maniliki, Cook Island: Beckwith Myth 256; Tonga: Gifford 182.
A1423.3.p: Explains how the coconut palm or coconut first came to humankind.

A1423.4.p: Tells how people first obtained manioc, the cassava root.

A1425.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484.
A1425.p: General heading for stories explaining how people first got seed grain or seed for planting.

A1425.0.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Moré): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 424.
A1425.0.1.p: Seeds are kept back and hoarded by someone instead of being shared with people.

A1425.1.p: A culture hero cuts down a bamboo and finds that it contains every kind of seed.

A1426.p: General heading for miscellaneous stories about how people obtained other foods or food-related products.

A1426.1.p: Tells how people first discovered oil, such as oil from plants or seeds.

A1426.2.p: Tells how people first obtained ale, a fermented drink.

A1426.2.1.p: Tells how the making of beer or ale by fermentation was first introduced to people.

A1426.2.2.p: Explains how rice beer, a fermented drink made from rice, first came about.

A1427.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 636: S. Am. Indian (Guarayu): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 147.
A1427.p: General heading for stories about how people first obtained strong alcoholic liquors.

A1427.0.1.p: Liquor is discovered after birds become drunk on fermented fruit or similar substance.

A1427.0.2.p: A rain-god is the one who discovers or provides liquor.

A1427.0.3.p: An intoxicating drink is first served and drunk at the wedding feast of the first human couple.

A1427.0.4.p: A creator gives liquor to his servant, a giant, to drink.

A1427.1.r: (Cf. A1456.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 7 No. 31, XXXIII 52 No. 31; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 87 No. 54; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3291; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1427.1.p: The devil teaches people how to burn brandy, that is, how to distill it.

A1427.2.p: Tells how whiskey first came into being.

A1428.r: Greek: Fox 47, 222; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.—Africa (Tshi): Ellis 337, (Fang): Einstein 44, Trilles 162.
A1428.p: Tells how people first obtained wine.

A1429.p: A general heading for myths explaining how humans got their food supply, covering various foods and necessities not listed separately.

A1429.1.p: A myth in which people discover that oil can be eaten or used as food.

A1429.2.p: A myth explaining where yeast came from: a wasp stole it from an old woman living underground.

A1429.3.p: A general heading for myths explaining how people got water to drink or use.

A1429.3.1.p: A myth in which the first wells are dug, explaining how people first obtained water from the ground.

A1429.3.2.p: A myth in which the gods provide water that is fit to drink.

A1429.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Jivaro): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 627.
A1429.4.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained salt.

A1430.p: A general heading for myths explaining how people obtained other essential things besides food and water.

A1431.r: Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 84 No. 29; Africa (Fang): Trilles 132.
A1431.p: A myth explaining the origin of coal.

A1432.p: A general heading for myths explaining how people first obtained metals.

A1432.1.r: Finnish: Kalevale rune 9; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Bushongo): Torday 235.
A1432.1.p: A myth explaining the origin of iron.

A1432.1.1.p: A myth in which iron was first used for making food and tools rather than weapons.

A1432.2.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained gold.

A1432.2.1.p: A myth in which gold comes from a gourd received from fishes.

A1432.3.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained brass.

A1432.4.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained copper.

A1433.p: A general heading for myths explaining how money came into being.

A1433.0.1.p: A myth in which the first money comes from a kettle that two dead men try in vain to carry from hell to heaven.

A1433.1.p: A myth explaining the origin of gold coins.

A1433.2.p: A myth explaining the origin of silver coins.

A1433.2.1.p: Silver coins are said to have come originally from a pumpkin that fishes gave to people. Explains how silver money came to exist.

A1433.3.p: A myth explaining how shell money came into use as currency.

A1435.p: A myth about how people first obtained their homes or dwellings.

A1435.0.1.p: A myth explaining how people first learned to dig out caves to live in.

A1435.1.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained houses for hosting and sheltering guests.

A1435.2.p: A myth explaining how the ancient stone forts or earthen enclosures called raths, duns, or stone forts came to be built.

A1435.2.1.p: The boundaries of raths were first marked out using a brooch, according to this myth.

A1435.3.p: A myth explaining how people moved from living in caves to living in huts made of grass.

A1436.p: A myth about how people first obtained vehicles for transport.

A1437.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 456.
A1437.p: A myth about how people first obtained clothing.

A1438.r: Greek: Fox 279ff.; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 70f.; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 202, 205f.; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Ferguson 14; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 116f., 119; N. A. Indian (Joshua): Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 230; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 3, 69; (Manasi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 393.
A1438.p: A myth explaining how medicine and the art of healing came to people.

A1438.1.p: A myth in which the Creator sends a shaman down to earth equipped with medicine to heal people.

A1439.p: Explains how people came to obtain other basic necessities of life, beyond the main culture-giving gifts.

A1439.1.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained marble.

A1439.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Easter Is.: Métraux Ethnology 317.
A1439.2.p: A myth explaining how dyes first came to be available for coloring.

A1439.3.p: A myth, told among South American Indians, explaining how rubber was first obtained.

A1439.4.p: A myth explaining how cauldrons, large cooking pots, first came into use.

A1440.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 137; Icel.: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1440.p: A myth about how the various crafts and trades were first acquired by people.

A1440.1.p: The Creator opens a shop and hands out the plough, pen, bottle, scales, fishing-net, and loom to different groups of people, giving each its trade.

A1440.2.p: A myth explaining how work came to be divided among different people and occupations.

A1440.3.p: Early patriarchs, who lived very long lives, are credited with making inventions.

A1441.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Greek: *Grote I 163; Jewish: Neuman; Marquesas: Handy 128; Kai of New Guinea: Beckwith Myth 104; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 177.—S. Am. (3) 178, (Cashinawa): Métraux ibid. (3) 685.
A1441.p: Explains how humans came to farm the land and grow crops. This motif covers stories about the origin of agriculture.

A1441.1.r: Greek: Fox 171, Alphabet of Tales No. 654; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 69; S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A1441.1.p: Explains how people first learned to plow the ground. A story tells how the plow came to be.

A1441.2.p: Explains why people yoke oxen together to pull a plow or cart. It gives the origin of this custom.

A1441.3.p: Explains how the water wheel and the growing of rice came to be. A tale traces both to a single origin.

A1441.4.r: Greek myth: Grote I 41; Kauai: Beckwith Myth 367; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 115.
A1441.4.p: Explains how people first learned to sow seeds and plant crops.

A1441.4.1.p: Explains why sowing is done at regular times of the year. It gives the origin of seasonal planting.

A1441.5.p: Explains how people first learned to grow onions.

A1442.r: (Cf. A1446.5.3.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
A1442.p: Explains how grinding grain into flour, or milling, came to be.

A1443.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3108; Greek: Aeschylus Prometheus Bound, lines 462—465, Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa: Stanley 43, 196, (Bushongo): Torday 242f., (Fang): Tessman 18f.
A1443.p: Explains how humans first tamed and kept animals as livestock.

A1443.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1443.1.p: Tells of the first person who herded and tended animals as a shepherd.

A1445.p: Explains how humans learned the skills of building, such as construction and related crafts.

A1445.1.r: Greek: Aeschylus Prometheus Bound, line 468; Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Benga): Nassau No. 3, (Fang): Trilles 159; Marquesas: Handy 128; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 15; Samoa: ibid. 271.
A1445.1.p: Explains how people first learned to build boats.

A1445.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Aeschylus Prometheus Bound line 447; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 70.
A1445.2.p: Explains how people first learned carpentry, the craft of working wood.

A1445.2.1.p: Explains why carpenters are found all over the world: after a great flood, carpenters were scattered across the earth on a raft.

A1445.2.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 685.
A1445.2.2.p: Tells that a man learned to build a house by watching a wasp build its nest.

A1446.p: Explains how humans acquired tools for their work.

A1446.0.1.r: S. Am. Indian. (Tapirape): Wagley-Galvao BBAE CXLIII (3) 178.
A1446.0.1.p: A culture hero steals tools and gives them to humans, who lacked them.

A1446.1.r: Invented by devil.—Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 85 No. 30b.
A1446.1.p: Explains how the saw was first invented or came to be used.

A1446.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Carib: Penard JAFL XXX 258.
A1446.2.p: Explains how the axe was first invented or came to be used.

A1446.3.p: Explains how the ox-goad, a pointed stick used to drive oxen, came to be.

A1446.4.p: Explains how the adze, a cutting and shaping tool, came into being or was first obtained by people.

A1446.5.p: Explains how people first got everyday household tools and utensils.

A1446.5.1.p: Explains how the broom, used for sweeping, was first obtained or invented.

A1446.5.2.p: Explains how the pestle, a club-like tool for pounding grain or food in a mortar, was first obtained.

A1446.5.3.p: Explains how the grindstone, a stone used for grinding grain or other materials, was first obtained.

A1446.5.4.p: Explains how the winnowing-fan, a flat basket used to separate grain from chaff by tossing it in the wind, was first obtained.

A1446.5.5.p: Explains how baskets were first made or obtained by people.

A1446.5.6.p: Explains how the oil-press, a device for squeezing oil from seeds or fruit, was first obtained.

A1447.r: Hebrew: Genesis 4:22; Greek: Fox 171; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A1447.p: Explains how people first learned to work metal.

A1447.1.p: Explains how the bellows, the device that blows air into a fire to make it hotter, was first obtained.

A1447.2.p: Explains how blacksmith work, shaping metal by heating and hammering it, was first learned or begun.

A1447.3.p: Explains how goldsmith work, making objects from gold, was first learned or begun.

A1447.4.p: Explains how smelting, extracting metal from ore by heating, was first discovered.

A1448.p: Explains how mining, digging minerals or metal out of the earth, was first started.

A1451.r: Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; African (Basuto): Jacottet 50 No. 7; S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359, (Yagua): Steward-Métraux ibid. (3) 736, (Jivaro): ibid. (3) 627, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 86.
A1451.p: Explains how pottery, making vessels from clay, was first discovered or taught.

A1452.p: Explains how charcoal making, burning wood to make charcoal, was first learned.

A1453.p: Explains how cloth-making, producing fabric from fibers, was first discovered or taught.

A1453.1.r: Greek: Fox 171, *Grote I 163; S. Am. Indian (Chibcha): Kroeber BBAE CXLIII (2) 909.
A1453.1.p: Explains how spinning, twisting fibers into thread, was first discovered.

A1453.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 171; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 7 No. 27; India: *Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 113, (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 685.
A1453.2.p: Explains how weaving, interlacing threads into cloth, was first discovered or taught.

A1453.3.p: Explains how dyeing, coloring cloth or thread, was first discovered.

A1453.4.p: A myth explaining how people first began making clothing from leaves.

A1453.5.p: A myth explaining how people first learned to make cloth from the inner bark of trees.

A1453.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 315.
A1453.6.p: A creator god shapes clay figures of men and paints on them the clothing they are to wear.

A1453.7.p: A myth explaining how people first learned to make cloth from raffia palm fibre.

A1454.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 7 No. 28; Jewish: Neuman.
A1454.p: A myth explaining how shoemaking, or the first making of shoes, came about.

A1455.r: Greek: Grote I 163; India: *Thompson-Balys; Marquesas: Handy 104, 128; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 108f.; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 373 (water for cooking.)
A1455.p: A myth explaining how people first learned to cook food.

A1455.1.p: A myth explaining how the domestic hearth, the household fireplace, was first established.

A1456.p: A myth explaining how people first learned distilling, the making of strong spirits, and the source of this knowledge is the devil.

A1457.r: Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Cubao): BBAE CXLIII (3) 798.
A1457.p: A myth explaining how people first learned to fish.

A1457.1.r: Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 317, 363; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 210.
A1457.1.p: A myth explaining how the fish hook was first invented or obtained.

A1457.2.p: A myth explaining why people fish at night as well as during the day.

A1457.3.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 146; Maori: Clark 27f.; Tonga: Gifford 16.
A1457.3.p: A myth explaining how the fishing net was first made or obtained.

A1457.4.p: A myth explaining how fishing spots or stations were first established.

A1457.5.p: A myth explaining how fish-traps were first invented.

A1457.6.p: A myth explaining how fish ponds were first made.

A1458.r: India: Thompson-Balys; New Hebrides: Codrington 368; S. Am. Indian (Yagua): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 736, (Toba): Métraux ibid. (1) 368, MAFLS XL 3. 84.
A1458.p: A myth explaining how people first learned to hunt.

A1458.1.p: A myth explaining how the pitfall trap for catching animals was first invented.

A1459.p: A general heading for myths explaining the origin of various crafts that do not fit the other categories.

A1459.1.p: A myth explaining how people first obtained weapons.

A1459.1.1.p: A myth explaining how bows and arrows were first made or obtained.

A1459.1.2.p: Explains how broad-headed spears were brought into the province of Leinster. The story gives a mythical origin for this kind of weapon.

A1459.1.2.1.p: Explains that spear points made of obsidian, a sharp volcanic glass, came from a particular source. It is a myth about where such spear tips originated.

A1459.1.3.p: Explains how sling-stones, the stones thrown from a sling as a weapon, came to exist. It is a mythical origin for this missile.

A1459.1.4.p: Tells how the gai bulga, a barbed spear in Irish legend, was invented. It gives a mythical origin for this weapon.

A1459.1.5.p: Explains how horse-whips came into being. It is a mythical origin for this riding tool.

A1459.2.p: Tells how people learned seamanship, meaning sailing and handling boats. It is a myth about the origin of sea navigation skills.

A1459.3.p: Tells how people acquired sorcery, the practice of magic. It is a myth about the origin of magical arts.

A1460.p: Tells how humans acquired the arts, meaning skilled creative and cultural practices. It is a general myth about where artistic skills came from.

A1460.1.p: Says that an angel taught people the arts. The story credits a heavenly messenger with passing on artistic skills.

A1461.r: Wallaschek Sagen und Märchen über den Ursprung der Musik (Leipzig 1903).—Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1461.p: Tells how music came into being or was first learned by people. It is a myth about the origin of music.

A1461.1.r: Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 84 No. 30a; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1461.1.p: Explains how the violin came into being. It is a mythical origin for this stringed instrument.

A1461.2.r: Greek: Fox 192, Frazer Apollodorus II 9 n. 2.—Finnish: Kalevala rune 40 (from bones of a pike); cf. rune 44.
A1461.2.p: Explains how the lyre, an ancient stringed instrument, came into being. In this motif Hermes makes it from a tortoise shell.

A1461.2.1.p: Explains how the harp came into being, as a development of the lyre. It is a mythical origin for this stringed instrument.

A1461.3.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 7 No. 30; Irish myth: Cross.
A1461.3.p: Explains how the organ, a large keyboard wind instrument, came into being. It is a mythical origin for this instrument.

A1461.4.p: Explains how people first began using the rattle, a noisemaking instrument. It is a mythical origin for this practice.

A1461.5.p: Explains how the whistle came into being. It is a mythical origin for this simple wind instrument.

A1461.6.p: Explains how the shepherd's pipe, a simple wind instrument played by herders, came into being. It is a mythical origin for it.

A1461.7.p: Explains how the nose-flute, a flute played by blowing through the nostril, came into being. It is a mythical origin for this instrument.

A1462.p: Explains how dancing came into being or was first learned by people. It is a myth about the origin of dance.

A1464.p: Explains how literary arts, meaning writing and the making of literature, came into being. It is a myth about the origin of literature.

A1464.1.p: Myths explaining how poetry first came into being. Poetry is the literary art whose origin the myth accounts for.

A1464.1.1.p: A myth in which the first poetry was made by copying the rhythmic ringing sounds of a hammer striking an anvil.

A1464.2.p: Myths explaining how the hymn, a song of praise to a god, first came to be sung.

A1464.2.1.p: Myths explaining how one particular song came to be composed or sung.

A1464.3.p: Myths explaining how satire, the mocking or ridiculing form of writing or speech, first arose.

A1465.5.p: Myths explaining how the craft of carving designs or figures in wood first began.

A1465.6.p: Myths explaining how masks, worn over the face, first came to be made.

A1471.2.p: Explains how weights and measures were first invented or introduced.

A1473.p: Explains how slavery began among people.

A1512.p: Explains the custom of not eating in the dark, by a story in which the devil eats from the plates.

A1514.1.p: Explains the origin of ceremonies that involve drinking.

A1528.p: Explains why a person gives a visitor the first fish they catch.

A1540.p: A general category of myths explaining how religious ceremonies came to be.

A1541.p: A general category of myths explaining how religious feasts and fasts came to be.

A1541.1.p: Explains how the feast for the dead began.

A1541.1.1.p: An Irish myth explaining the origin of digging graves, in which a cross is involved.

A1541.1.2.p: A communion feast is held to appease the dead, explaining the origin of a meal shared to placate departed spirits.

A1541.2.p: A feast is instituted in honor of a particular god or goddess, explaining how such a festival came to be held.

A1541.2.1.p: The origin of a feast held in honor of the goddess Zise.

A1541.3.p: The origin of Hallowe'en, the festival held on the night before All Saints' Day.

A1541.3.1.p: Hallowe'en is explained as a night of mystery when supernatural things happen.

A1541.4.p: The origin of the Sabbath, the weekly holy day of rest and worship.

A1541.4.0.1.p: A holy day is set apart and made sacred on the seventh day of the week.

A1541.4.1.p: The Sabbath is said to have originated from a feast held in honor of the goddess Venus.

A1541.4.2.p: The origin of a dragon festival, a holiday built around a dragon.

A1541.5.p: The origin of the Passover, the Jewish spring festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt.

A1541.6.p: The origin of Pentecost, the festival held fifty days after Easter.

A1541.7.p: The origin of religious fasting, explaining how the practice of abstaining from food for religious reasons began.

A1555.2.p: A myth explaining why men pay a price, such as goods or money, to buy their wives.

A1578.1.p: An explanation of how family crests came to be.

A1579.1.p: An explanation of why children must not be left alone in the house to sleep.

A1592.r: Icel.: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 239ff.
A1592.p: A story explaining how the custom of cremating the dead, burning them on a fire, began.

A1597.2.p: Explains how the custom of shaving the beard began. It is a myth giving a reason for why men shave.

A1599.9.p: Explains how the custom of suicide by strangling began.

A1599.10.p: Explains how witchcraft, the practice of magic harming others, came into being.

A1599.11.p: Explains how quarrels between people came to exist.

A1599.12.p: Explains how the custom of sworn or covenanted friendship between people came about.

A1599.13.p: Explains why a particular caste is kind to animals.

A1599.14.p: Explains why a household must have a lamp lit in it at least once every two weeks.

A1614.1.p: Explains the dark skin of Black people as a curse placed on Ham for laughing at his father Noah's nakedness.

A1614.1.1.p: Explains that luchrupain (leprechauns, dwarfs, and pygmies) arose from the curses of Ham.

A1614.1.2.p: Explains that goat-headed beings arose from the curse of Ham.

A1614.2.r: each becoming darker because of the condition of the water.—N. A. Indian (Biloxi): Swanton BBAE XLVII 32; Carib: Alexander Lat. Am. 271; American Negro: Harris Remus 163; Africa (Loango): Pechuël-Loesche 268, (Cameroon): Rosenhuber 57. Cf. Dh. I 247 (Danish).
A1614.2.p: Explains dark skin as the result of bathing after white men: all peoples bathe in a river in turn, with the white man first, so later bathers come out darker, the last being the Black person.

A1614.3.p: Explains that light-skinned and dark-skinned peoples were made from light and dark coconuts.

A1614.4.p: Explains that different tribes came into being from choices people made.

A1614.4.1.p: Different human peoples arose from the kinds of meat their ancestors chose to eat.

A1614.4.1.1.p: The skin colors of the races came from eating ox meat: those who ate the liver became black, and those who ate the lungs and blood became red.

A1614.4.2.p: Different peoples arose from the different chairs they chose to sit on.

A1614.4.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 360.
A1614.4.3.p: Different peoples arose from choosing either bows and arrows or guns, horses and cattle. In the telling, Indians chose the former and whites the latter.

A1614.5.p: Black people were made from leftover scraps of material remaining when the world was created.

A1614.6.p: A tale explaining why some people have light skin and others have dark skin.

A1614.7.p: Indians and white people came from different legs of the first man.

A1614.8.r: S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 175.
A1614.8.p: A black tribe came about because a woman was put on the fire.

A1614.9.r: Eskimo (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 261, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 168.
A1614.9.p: A tale explaining how the white man came into being.

A1616.r: Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 142 No. 25; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 9 Nos. 45—47; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 85 Nos. 38, 40; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 35 No. 11; Icel.: Snorra Edda Prologue V; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 123; Jewish: Neuman.
A1616.p: Tales explaining how particular languages came to be spoken.

A1616.1.p: Cold, which came before humans stole fire, makes certain languages hard to speak, explaining why some languages are difficult.

A1616.2.p: A tale explaining how the Irish language came to be.

A1617.r: India: Thompson-Balys. (No attempt is given here to collect references to place-name origins. Stories of this kind are world wide.)
A1617.p: A tale explaining how a particular place got its name.

A1618.p: Tales explaining why some people are richer, stronger, or higher in rank than others.

A1620.r: Hebrew: Genesis ch. 10; Indo-Chinese: Scott 292.—Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 149, (Fjort): Dennett 108 No. 31; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: (general) *Thompson Tales 285 n. 54, (Hopi): Alexander N. Am. 205, (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 213; Cakchiquel: Alexander Lat. Am. 181; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): ibid. 315.
A1620.p: Tales explaining how tribes came to be spread across different regions of the world.

A1621.p: Tales explaining why some areas have many more people than others.

A1630.r: Icel.: Snorra Edda Prologue IV-V, Hermann Saxo II 85ff.; Hebrew: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy; Jewish: Neuman; Armenian: Ananikian 65.—N. A. Indian (Thompson, Gros Ventre, Sarcee, Blackfoot, Cheyenne): *Teit MAFLS XI 48ff., (Creek): Alexander N. Am. 63, (Sia): ibid. 203f.; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503, (Mundurucú): Horton ibid. (3) 281, (Brazil): Oberg. 108.
A1630.p: Tales explaining why and how tribes wandered and moved from place to place.

A1631.r: Creek: Alexander N. Am. 62; Choctaw: ibid. 63; Mandan, Kiowa: ibid. 105; Arikara: ibid. 107; Navaho: ibid. 159; Pima: ibid. 177; Sia: ibid. 203; Hopi: ibid. 205; Warrau (Carib): Alexander Lat. Am. 273; Amazon tribes: ibid. 309.
A1631.p: A tribe emerged onto the surface of the earth from a world below it.

A1631.1.r: Warrau (Carib tribe): Alexander Lat. Am. 272 (references to Kiowa, Mandan, and Pueblo).
A1631.1.p: As a tribe climbed out of the lower world, a fat or pregnant woman got stuck in the exit hole and blocked the others.

A1631.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Tropical Forest): Lowie BBAE CLXIII (3) 55.
A1631.2.p: A tribe came down from the sky to live on the earth.

A1640.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 502.—Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 207; S. Am. Indian (Tropical Forest): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (3) 53.
A1640.p: Explains how the various tribes or subgroups of a people came to exist as separate divisions.

A1641.r: Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 216; Laguna and Zuñi: Parsons JAFL XXXI 263.
A1641.p: Describes the traits or habits that set one tribal subdivision apart from another.

A1650.p: Explains how the different social ranks and occupations among people came into being.

A1650.1.r: *BP III 308ff. (Gr. No. 180); *Dh I 247, II 98f.—Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 85 No. 41; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 87 No. 758.
A1650.1.p: Eve is ashamed of having so many children that she hides some; those hidden miss God's blessing, and this is said to explain why people differ in rank and nation.

A1650.2.p: Introduces the custom of marking social classes by the color of their clothing.

A1650.3.p: Explains how the different trades or crafts came into existence.

A1650.3.1.p: Explains why some men turn out to be skilled at making baskets.

A1650.3.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3056, Balys Legends No. 107.
A1650.3.2.p: God assigns each man a profession according to his physical appearance.

A1651.0.1.p: Describes the attitude people take toward those considered untouchable, outcast by caste.

A1651.1.p: Says the castes came about because someone received instructions about them in a dream.

A1651.2.p: Says a person's caste is decided by which kind of tree he catches hold of while crossing a river.

A1653.p: Explains how the institution of kingship or royal rank came about.

A1653.1.r: Icel.: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 241 (Rigsthula), Snorra Edda Prologue.
A1653.1.p: Says kings descend from gods or were created by gods.

A1653.2.p: Says a king's family descends from a prince who was a fairy.

A1654.p: Explains how the role of priests, shamans, and similar religious specialists came into being.

A1654.1.p: Explains how priests first came to exist.

A1654.2.p: Explains how diviners, people who foretell the future or read signs, came to exist.

A1655.r: Icel.: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 237 (Rigsthula); African (Senegambia): Bérenger-Feraud II 185ff. No. 2.
A1655.p: Explains how the class of farmers and peasants came into being.

A1655.1.p: Says the peasant is always busy because he works eagerly to grow food for all living creatures.

A1656.p: Explains how the class of noblemen came into being.

A1656.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3050, Balys Legends Nos 97, 104ff.
A1656.1.p: Origin of the Polish nobility: the nobles are said to have come from wheat dough that a bitch devoured.

A1657.r: Icel.: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 235 (Rigsthula); Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
A1657.p: Explains how slaves came to exist as a social class.

A1657.1.p: Explains the origin of subject tribes, called aithech-thuatha, who were dependent people under others.

A1657.2.p: Explains the origin of the Fir Bolg, whose name means Men of the Sacks, because as slaves they were forced to carry earth in sacks.

A1658.p: Explains how professional warriors came to exist as a class.

A1658.1.p: Explains the origin of the fiana, bands of professional warriors.

A1659.p: Miscellaneous explanations of how various other social or occupational classes came to be.

A1659.1.p: Explains the origin of the Fomorians, a race of giants.

A1659.1.1.p: The Fomorians are said to be descended from Ham (or Cain), the biblical figures cursed or marked as wicked.

A1660.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 153, Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 234 ff. Irish myth: Cross.
A1660.p: Explains why various peoples differ from one another in their looks and bodily traits.

A1661.p: Explains the hair and beard traits that different peoples have.

A1661.1.p: Explains how white men came to have beards.

A1661.2.p: Explains why white men have short hair.

A1661.3.p: Explains why the Canaanites have curly hair.

A1662.p: Explains that certain peoples have a distinctive bodily smell.

A1662.1.p: Explains why Jews are said to smell bad: they rubbed Christ's body with garlic.

A1663.p: Explains the shapes of heads that different peoples have.

A1663.1.p: Explains why the Babylonians have round heads.

A1664.p: Explains why certain peoples are considered more beautiful than others.

A1665.p: Explains the characteristic appearance of the feet of various peoples.

A1665.1.p: An origin explanation for why Africans have bad feet, told as a myth about how the peoples of the world came to have their bodily traits.

A1666.p: A category of origin myths explaining why different peoples have different eye features.

A1666.1.p: An origin explanation for why the Canaanites have red eyes.

A1666.2.p: An origin explanation for why the Palmyrenes have narrow eyes.

A1667.p: A category of origin myths explaining why different peoples differ in intelligence.

A1667.1.p: An origin explanation for why Europeans know more than native peoples.

A1670.p: A category of origin myths explaining why different peoples have particular skills in work and fighting.

A1671.p: A category of myths explaining why certain peoples are inclined to work hard or not.

A1671.1.r: S. Carolina Negro: Davis JAFL XXVII 244; N. Carolina Negro: Brown Collection I 633; Africa (Cameroon): Mansfield 225.
A1671.1.p: An origin explanation for why the Black African people work, told as a myth about their labor.

A1673.p: A category of myths explaining why certain peoples excel at particular crafts or industries.

A1673.1.p: An origin explanation for why the Haida people excel at certain crafts or industries.

A1674.p: A category of myths explaining why certain peoples are inclined to steal.

A1674.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1638, Balys Legends No. 102.
A1674.1.p: An origin explanation for why stealing is not a sin for the Gypsies, who were supposedly helpful at Christ's crucifixion.

A1674.2.p: An origin explanation for why Russians are inclined to thefts and robberies.

A1675.p: A category of myths explaining why certain peoples are inclined to make war.

A1676.p: A category of myths explaining why certain peoples are brave or cowardly.

A1676.1.p: An origin explanation for why the Chittagong people are no longer as brave as they once were.

A1680.p: A category of myths explaining why different peoples have particular customs and eating or other habits.

A1681.p: A category of myths explaining why certain peoples have particular eating habits or foods.

A1681.1.p: An origin explanation for why Indigenous people chew spruce gum.

A1681.2.r: Jaworskij Der Urquell II 196; Fb “svin” III 676b.—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 142 No. 23; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1867A; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 85 No. 42; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 85 No. 43c.
A1681.2.p: An explanation of why Jewish people do not eat pork.

A1681.3.p: An explanation of why the Muria people eat snakes.

A1681.4.p: An explanation of why the Agaria people eat rats.

A1683.p: A general heading for stories explaining why different peoples dress as they do.

A1683.1.p: An explanation of why Russians wear their shirts hanging outside their trousers.

A1683.1.1.p: An explanation of why Russians wear red shirts.

A1683.2.p: An explanation of why a certain tribe wears clothing like dogs, said to be descended from a female dog.

A1683.3.p: An explanation of how the custom of wearing a mantle or cloak began.

A1683.4.p: An explanation of why certain peoples go naked.

A1683.4.1.p: An explanation of why the Canaanites go naked.

A1683.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 94.
A1683.5.p: An explanation of why certain peoples wear only a loincloth.

A1687.p: A general heading for stories explaining why different peoples decorate themselves as they do.

A1687.1.p: An explanation of why Zuni girls rub flour on their faces while grinding corn.

A1689.p: A heading for other stories explaining the origins of peoples' customs and their originators.

A1689.1.p: An explanation of why the Bhuiya yoke a cow and a bullock together to the plough.

A1689.2.p: An explanation of why the Agaria are not afraid of fire.

A1689.3.p: An explanation of why the Gond and Baiga eat all kinds of food.

A1689.4.p: An explanation of why the Saora wave axes and swords and shout while dancing.

A1689.5.p: An explanation of why the Kamar offer liquor to gods and spirits.

A1689.6.p: An explanation of why Jews read and write from right to left, because of an unpleasant name of the king of the Jews.

A1689.7.p: Explains why the Russian calendar has the form it has, as an origin story.

A1689.8.p: Explains why the Chapperbands make a living by counterfeiting money.

A1689.9.p: Explains why Chenchu women are considered ugly.

A1689.10.p: Explains why the Agaria people work as farmers and cultivators.

A1689.11.p: Explains why one people has more power or strength than another.

A1689.11.1.p: Explains why the English are more powerful than the Hindus: when qualities were handed out, the Hindus arrived late, so they must wash after defecating while the Englishman uses paper.

A1689.12.p: Explains why Egyptians are fond of donkeys or asses.

A1689.13.p: Explains why Jews keep themselves separate from other peoples.

A1690.p: A miscellaneous group of tales about how peoples were distributed across the world and how they came to differ from one another.

A1691.p: Explains the origin of the distinction between free people (saer) and unfree people (daer).

A1700.r: (Cf. Chapter B, Animals.) Quiché: Alexander Lat. Am. 162; Ekoi: Talbot 149.
A1700.p: General heading for myths about how animals were created.

A1702.p: A creator being, not necessarily God, makes the animals.

A1703.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A1703.p: A culture hero makes the animals that are useful to people.

A1704.p: Every kind of animal is created in male and female pairs.

A1705.p: Animals are created to serve humans.

A1710.r: (Cf. A1811.1, A1833.2, A1861.1, A1861.2, A1863, A1887).—India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham, Eberhard FFC CXX 79, 96, 122f. No. 82; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 98.
A1710.p: General heading for animals coming into being through transformation of other things or beings.

A1711.r: S. Am. Indian (Amazon Tribes): Alexander Lat. Am. 311f., Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 367.
A1711.p: After a flood or other world catastrophe, animals arise by transformation.

A1713.p: The creator sends someone for water, and in the meantime the animals take on their present forms.

A1714.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 22, 465; Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL 20 171, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 167, 169, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI, 588, (East Greenland): Rasmussen I, 82, 96, (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 261, (Labrador): Hawks GSCan XIV 155, (Cape York): Rasmussen III 79; S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473, (Araucanian): Cooper ibid. (2) 753, (Inca): Rowe ibid. 315, (Cashinawa): Métraux ibid. (3) 684.
A1714.p: Animals come from various objects that are transformed into them.

A1714.1.p: Animals come into being from transformed pieces of cloth.

A1714.2.p: Animals come into being when pieces of bark are thrown onto the ground.

A1714.3.p: Animals are formed out of earth or soil.

A1714.3.1.p: Buffaloes come up out of the earth one after another, and the first man grabs hold of the tail of the last one to emerge.

A1715.r: (Cf. A2005, A2011.2.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3115, Balys Legends Nos. 216—219, 261f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Maori: Clark 15; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 422; Raratonga (Cook Island): ibid. 101; Tuomatu: Stimson MS (z-G 3/1100); S. Am. Indian (Tiatinagua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 449, (Munderucú): Horton ibid. 281, (Cashinawa): Métraux ibid. 685, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 31, 79, (Mataco): Métraux ibid. 64.
A1715.p: Animals come into being when a human being is transformed into them.

A1715.1.p: The various animals come from the army of Pharaoh that drowned when crossing the Red Sea.

A1715.2.r: (Cf. A1831, A1862, A1871.)—*Dh. II 99ff. India: Thompson-Balys.
A1715.2.p: Men who behave discourteously toward God (Jesus) are transformed into animals.

A1715.3.p: Seven whistling creatures are the souls of the Jews who crucified Christ.

A1715.4.r: (Cf. A1811, A1853.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXV 150 No. 71.
A1715.4.p: Men are changed into different animals according to the food they most desire: one who asks for flesh, one for blood, and so on become mice, cats, and bugs.

A1715.5.p: Survivors of a shipwreck are transformed into animals.

A1716.p: Animals come into being when an ogre or giant is transformed into them.

A1716.1.r: Giant person, cow, ox, etc.—Persian: Carnoy 288.—Borneo, Philippines: Dixon 177.
A1716.1.p: Different animals come from the different parts of the body of a slain giant.

A1724.p: Animals come into being from transformed parts of a body, whether animal or human.

A1724.1.p: Animals come from the body of a person who has been killed.

A1724.1.1.r: (Cf. A2102.)—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 272; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1724.1.1.p: Animals come from the severed fingers of a woman.

A1724.3.p: All living things come from the blood of Jesus that was spattered about.

A1725.p: Animals come into being from parts of the body of a god or saint.

A1725.1.p: Animals come from the spittle of a god or saint.

A1725.2.p: Animals come from the dirt rubbed off the body of a god or hero.

A1727.p: The first animal of its kind is cut up or maimed, and its body parts are rearranged or shaped to become the animals we see today.

A1730.p: Animals are created as a punishment inflicted on people or beings who did something wrong.

A1731.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 89 No. 16.
A1731.p: Animals are created as a punishment for someone who beat a drum that was forbidden to be beaten.

A1732.p: A being creates animals in order to get revenge on someone.

A1733.p: Animals are created as a punishment for incest.

A1734.p: Frogs are changed into other animals or sent as one of the plagues on Egypt.

A1750.p: Animals come into being because a devil and God work against each other, each making some creatures.

A1751.r: Dh. I 164 (with lists of the animals). Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3081, Legends Nos. 124—130; German: Grimm No. 148.
A1751.p: In the contest between God and the devil, each makes certain animals, so some creatures are the devil's and others God's.

A1751.1.p: The devil creates a mouse and God, through the archangel Michael, creates a cat to destroy it.

A1755.p: The devil tries to create something but fails, and the failed attempt results in certain animals.

A1756.r: Dh I 146ff. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3086; Legends Nos. 139—146, 152.
A1756.p: The devil can only succeed in making animals when he uses God's name; without it his attempts fail.

A1757.p: A Persian account of the origin of animals in which a good power and an evil power each create creatures, giving a dualist explanation.

A1758.p: Animals are created while the god Mahadeo quarrels with his wife.

A1770.r: S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359.
A1770.p: Animals come into existence from an unusual mating that took place in the earliest times.

A1771.r: S. Am. Indian (Jivaró): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 627.
A1771.p: Animals are born from the mating of the sun and the moon.

A1772.r: S. Am. Indian (Tapirapé): Wagley-Galvao BBAE CXLIII (3) 253.
A1772.p: Animals are born from the first mating between a snake and a person.

A1790.p: A miscellaneous group of other tales about how animals were created that do not fit the more specific categories.

A1791.p: A giant ox is the first ancestor from which all animals descend.

A1792.p: The creator brings forth animals by vomiting them up.

A1793.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 287; S. Am. Indian (Warrau): Kirchhoff BBAE CXLIII (3) 880.
A1793.p: Animals come out of a tree, which is the source from which they originated.

A1795.p: Animals fall or come down from the clouds into the world, as a way of explaining where animals came from.

A1800.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1800.p: A general myth about how mammals, the warm-blooded animals that nurse their young, were first created.

A1810.p: A myth explaining how the cat family (lions, tigers and similar big and small cats) came into being.

A1811.r: Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 150 No. 71 (cf. A1715.4); Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 11 No. 55, XXXIII 53 No. 55, Dh I 166, 273 (cf. A1751.); ibid. I 157 (cf. A1755.)—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3120, Legends No. 133, 195, 220f.; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A1811.p: A myth explaining how the domestic cat came into being.

A1811.1.p: The cat comes from an eagle that was changed: the eagle mistook a stick of wood for a fish and got its feet caught, then wind blew off its feathers and turned them into fur.

A1811.2.p: The cat is sneezed out of a lion's nose. The devil, disguised as a mouse, gnaws a hole in the ark, and Noah asks the lion for help; the cat that is sneezed out eats the mouse.

A1811.3.p: The cat is of divine origin, and when it purrs it is really praying.

A1815.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Apapocuvu-Guaraní): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 138.
A1815.p: A myth explaining how the tiger came into being.

A1817.r: S. Am. Indian (Mojo): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 424.
A1817.p: A myth explaining how the jaguar came into being.

A1820.p: A general myth about how the weasel family (such as otters, martens and weasels) was created.

A1821.p: A myth explaining how the otter came into being.

A1821.1.p: A myth explaining how the sea otter came into being.

A1824.p: A myth explaining how the marten came into being.

A1830.p: A general myth about how the dog family (canids) and other meat-eating mammals (carnivores) were created.

A1831.r: Dh I 164 (Cf. A1751); ibid. II 101 (Cf. A1715.2).—Irish: Beal XXI 330; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 72; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 436, 500; Maori: Clark 50; Eskimo (Cape York): Rasmussen III 47; Ojibwa: Jones JAFL XXIX 376.
A1831.p: A myth explaining how the dog came into being.

A1831.1.p: Jesus, left to watch over the herd, creates the dog to drive off a wolf.

A1831.2.p: The lapdog is said to have first come to Ireland, as an explanation of its origin there.

A1832.p: A myth explaining how the fox came into being.

A1833.r: (Cf. A1751.) Dh I 147ff., I 164.—Quileute: Farrand JAFL XXXII 259.
A1833.p: A myth explaining how the wolf came into being.

A1833.1.r: (Cf. A1755.)—Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 145 No. 39. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3086; Legends Nos. 139—146.
A1833.1.p: The devil makes a wolf, but God gives it life so it can live.

A1833.2.p: A magician changes a man into a wolf. This explains how wolves came to exist.

A1833.3.p: The wolf is described as God's dog, a myth explaining the wolf's place as a divine companion animal.

A1834.p: A myth explaining how the coyote and other wild dog-like animals (canids) came into being.

A1834.1.p: A myth explaining how the coyote came into being.

A1834.2.p: A myth explaining how the jackal came into being.

A1834.3.p: A myth explaining how the hyena came into being.

A1836.r: Dh II 99 (Cf. A1715.2.)—Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 146 No. 41; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3112; Legends Nos. 175, 216ff.; India: Thompson-Balys; Ojibwa: Jones JAFL XXIX 370, Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 171, (West Hudson Bay): Boas ibid. 307, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 172.
A1836.p: A myth explaining how the bear came into being.

A1837.p: A myth explaining how the seal came into being.

A1838.p: A myth explaining how the walrus came into being.

A1840.p: A myth explaining how the rodents (gnawing animals such as mice, rats, and squirrels) came into being.

A1853.r: Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 150 No. 71 (Cf. A1715.4); Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3120. Legends No. 220f.
A1853.p: A myth explaining how mice came into being.

A1853.1.r: (Cf. A1811.2.)—*Dh I 166, 273; *Fb “mus” II 632a.; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 11 No. 55, XXXIII 53 No. 55.
A1853.1.p: The devil creates mice while the animals are aboard Noah's ark.

A1853.1.1.p: After the flood, mice arise from rotting matter, so there were no mice on the ark. This explains why mice appear from decay.

A1854.p: A myth explaining how rats came into being.

A1854.1.p: Rats exist because one rat escaped when the other rats were killed.

A1856.r: Dh I 164; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Central): Boas RBAE VI 639, (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 263.
A1856.p: A myth explaining how the hare (rabbit) came into being.
