A2171.p: The origin of crustaceans (shellfish with jointed limbs) is explained as a creation story.

A2171.1.p: The origin of the crayfish is explained as a creation story.

A2171.1.1.p: A crayfish comes into being from the devil's fleas that are shaken off into the water.

A2171.2.p: The origin of the crab is explained as a creation story.

A2171.3.p: The origin of the lobster is explained as a creation story.

A2171.4.p: The origin of the shrimp is explained as a creation story.

A2181.p: Explains how the snail came to be; a myth giving the origin of snails as animals.

A2182.p: Explains how worms came into existence; a creation myth giving the origin of worms.

A2182.1.p: Explains how the silkworm came into being; a myth giving the origin of the silkworm.

A2182.2.p: Explains how the leech came into being; a myth giving the origin of leeches.

A2182.3.p: Explains how the earthworm came into being; a myth giving the origin of earthworms.

A2182.4.p: Explains how the cutworm came into being; a myth giving the origin of cutworms.

A2182.5.p: Explains how the multipede (a many-legged creature such as a millipede or centipede) came into being; a myth giving its origin.

A2200.r: See “Register” to Dähnhardt (III 537ff.); also articles scattered through RTP, e. g., V 244, VI, 314, 473, VII 479, VIII 557, IX 165, 491, 646, X 26, 176, 301, 363, XII 667, XIII 344, XIV 379, XV 425, XVI 445, XVII 150, 344, 578.—Jewish: Neuman; Australian: Dixon 290; Miwok: Powers CNAE III 359; Karok: ibid. 36; Alsea: Frachtenberg BBAE LXVII 47ff.; Southern Ute: Lowie JAFL XXXVII 14 No. 6.
A2200.p: A general heading for tales explaining why animals have the characteristics they do.

A2201.p: Holds that every quality an animal has was present from the moment it was created, rather than acquired later.

A2210.p: A heading for explanations of animal features that arose from some change in an animal long ago.

A2211.p: Explains an animal feature as the result of an accidental action by an ancient animal.

A2211.1.p: A lynx looks out over the land from a mountainside, and this is said to be why it squints.

A2211.2.r: (Cf. A2216.3, A2234.4, A2342.1.)—*Type 47A; *BP III 75 n. 1.—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXV 144 No. 35; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 89 No. 71; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2211.2.p: A rabbit laughs and this is said to be why the hare has a split lip.

A2211.3.p: A wolf falls out of its nest, and this is said to be why wolves have a straight back.

A2211.4.p: The first whale died by coming ashore, and this is said to be why some whales die on land.

A2211.5.p: A shrew blows its nose and the nose is pushed into a snout; said to explain the shrew's snout. In the tale, after a fire goes out he finds only a little, which he tries to revive by blowing hard.

A2211.6.r: (Cf. A2433.5.3.)—Gold coast: Barker and Sinclair 84 No. 13.
A2211.6.p: A spider carries a large stone on its head and drops it, and this is said to be why spiders live under stones.

A2211.7.p: Birds cling to the sky during a flood, and this is said to explain why birds have their tail colors.

A2211.8.p: A lizard dips its head in palm oil, and this is said to be why lizards have red heads.

A2211.9.p: A lizard swallows a fish bone, and this is said to be why its head bobs up and down.

A2211.10.r: (Cf. A2312.1.)——Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 115 No. 20.
A2211.10.p: A tortoise left out in the rain grows a hard shell; the story explains why tortoises have hard shells.

A2211.11.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 68.
A2211.11.p: An earthworm feeds a rattlesnake chili pepper, which makes the snake harmful; the story explains why rattlesnakes are venomous.

A2211.12.p: A buffalo helps a tiger put out a fire by ducking him in water, and the tiger's grip leaves a white mark on the buffalo's neck.

A2211.13.p: A snail defeats a stag, and the stag vomits up its gall-bladder; the story explains this trait of stags.

A2211.14.p: A rat defecates on an octopus's head, creating the bumps on its head; the story explains why the octopus has tubercles.

A2211.15.p: A goddess scatters her pubic hairs on a fish, and these become the many bones; the story explains why the fish has so many bones.

A2212.p: An animal acquires a particular characteristic because of a great fright it suffers in the ancient past.

A2212.1.p: A frightened rabbit pushes its head into a charred tree, and its ears become black; the story explains why rabbits have black ears.

A2212.2.p: Frightened animals run off in all directions, and the story explains why each kind lives where it does now.

A2213.p: An ancient animal is squeezed or stretched, and this changes its size or features; the story explains the animal's present form.

A2213.1.r: (Cf. A2302.)—Dh III 2—7 (hazel-grouse, squirrel, eagle, wolf, snake’s head.)
A2213.1.p: An ancient animal is squeezed, and as a result it becomes small; the story explains why the animal is small.

A2213.2.r: (Cf. A2412.4.)—Dh III 54, (cf. I 201f., 248, II 195); India: Thompson-Balys.
A2213.2.p: An animal is pressed on or against something, leaving marks on its face or body; the story explains these markings.

A2213.2.1.r: (Cf. A2230.1.)—Dh III 5, 6.—N. Am. Indian: *Thompson Tales 300 n. 99; Australian: Dixon 290 (wombat).
A2213.2.1.p: A wildcat or lynx has its face mashed in, which explains why its face is flat.

A2213.2.2.p: A tortoise is pressed into the earth, and this makes its back humped; the story explains the tortoise's humpy back.

A2213.2.3.r: (Cf. A2317.10.)—Africa (Hottentot): Bleek 39 No. 19; Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 74.
A2213.2.3.p: A baboon is pressed on a hot, flat rock, leaving a bald patch on its back; the story explains the bald spot.

A2213.2.4.p: Cattle insultingly step on a lobster, which makes the lobster shallow in form; the story explains why lobsters are flat.

A2213.3.r: (Cf. A2312.1, A2301.)—Dh III 2—5 (fish, bat, flying squirrel, monkey).
A2213.3.p: Animals become larger because they are stretched.

A2213.4.p: An animal's characteristics are changed by stretching its body; the story explains the resulting feature.

A2213.4.1.p: A coyote's muzzle is pulled out long, which explains why the coyote has a long snout.

A2213.4.2.p: A fox's tail is pulled out long, which explains why the fox has a long tail.

A2213.4.3.p: A mouse's nose is pulled out long, which explains why mice have long noses.

A2213.5.p: An animal gets its distinctive appearance from being struck or hit, as an origin explanation.

A2213.5.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 109.
A2213.5.1.p: A mole is struck on the head while trying to steal fire, and that blow is why its head is flat.

A2213.5.2.p: A fish is struck by a coconut, and that blow is why its tail is flat.

A2214.p: An ancient animal is dropped from the air, and the fall explains a feature it has today.

A2214.1.r: (Cf. A2378.5.1.)—Dh II 126, III 419.—Aarne FFC VII 16 No. 85; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 87 No. 85.
A2214.1.p: A swallow is thrown onto its tail, and this causes its tail to split.

A2214.2.r: (Cf. A2355.1.2.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VII 22 No. 124, XXXIII 55 No. 124; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 149 No. 66; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 89 No. 124; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3200, Legends Nos 291—94; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2214.2.p: An ant is thrown down from heaven, which is why it has a narrow waist. In the tale, God settles a dispute between the ant and the spider in the spider's favor.

A2214.3.p: A unicorn is thrown from the ark and drowns, which is why unicorns no longer exist.

A2214.4.p: A crab is thrown to the ground and breaks into small pieces. This is why crabs are small.

A2214.5.r: Therefore amphibious. African (Nigeria): Herskovits JAFL XLIV 448ff.
A2214.5.p: A tortoise is hurled onto a rock so that one half lands on land and the other half in water.

A2214.5.1.p: An eagle drops a tortoise, and this is why its shell is cracked.

A2214.6.p: A bat falls from a high perch because the sun's rays are extremely hot, breaking its bones and more. This is why bats have peculiar feet and nose.

A2215.p: An ancient animal gets a feature because body parts are thrown at it.

A2215.1.r: (Cf. A2378.3.3.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 14 No. 77 (wolf).—Banks Is.: Dixon 144 (rat).
A2215.1.p: A stick or leaf is thrown at an animal's rump, and this is why animals have tails.

A2215.2.r: (Cf. A2378.4.1.)—Dh III 185.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 13 No. 72; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 86 No. 72.
A2215.2.p: A hare runs away when the world is created and nearly loses its tail. God throws a tail at it from a pile of tails, because the hare is the most timid of all beasts.

A2215.3.p: A bowl is placed on a turtle's back, and this is why the turtle has a shell.

A2215.4.p: A red fruit is thrown at a rail bird's head, and this is why it has a red lump on its head.

A2215.5.r: (Cf. A2378.8.1.)—Cf. Type 3.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 15 No. 79; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 146 No. 43.
A2215.5.p: A fox is struck with a churn-dash, and this is why its tail is white.

A2215.6.r: (Cf. A2371.2.9.) Dh III 46.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 18 No. 103.
A2215.6.p: God throws a diver's feet after him, so his feet reach backward.

A2216.p: An animal's body parts are bitten off or cut off, which explains its present form.

A2216.1.r: (Cf. A2378.2.4.)—*Type 2; Dh III 49.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 14 No. 78; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 146 No. 42; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 86 No. 78; Japanese: Ikeda.
A2216.1.p: A bear fishing through ice loses its tail, which explains why bears have no tail.

A2216.2.p: The devil pulls the tails off goats, which explains why goats have no tails.

A2216.3.p: The moon splits a hare's lip with a hatchet, which explains why hares have split lips.

A2216.4.p: A bush-rat bites off a tortoise's tail, which explains why the tortoise has a short tail.

A2216.5.p: A hawk's tail is cut in two by a sword while it is being transformed, which explains why the hawk has a forked tail.

A2216.6.p: A god in the form of a falcon has its tail cut off, which explains why falcons have short tails.

A2216.7.p: Animals formerly had ears like an elephant's, but a hare bites them off, which explains why animals have small ears.

A2217.p: An animal gets its present appearance from being marked or painted.

A2217.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3158; N. Am. Indian: *Boas RBAE XXXI 664, (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 208 No. 1 (10), (Cherokee): Alexander N. Am. 66 (robin redbreast).
A2217.1.p: Birds receive their present colors by being painted.

A2217.2.r: (Cf. A2413.2.)—Seneca: Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 111 No. 13, 422 No. 78, Curtin Seneca 437, 505.
A2217.2.p: A bear scratches a chipmunk's back while the chipmunk tries to escape, leaving it with permanent stripes.

A2217.3.p: Certain fish have dark marks because they were touched by a fingerprint.

A2217.3.1.r: (Cf. A901, A2217.2, A2412.4).—Dh II 180 ff., III 55.—Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 89 No. 119b; Irish: Beal XXI 305; England: Baughman.
A2217.3.1.p: Certain fish have marks because St. Peter left his fingerprints on them.

A2217.3.2.p: Certain fish have marks because the devil left his fingerprints on them.

A2218.p: An animal gets its present characteristics from being burned or singed.

A2218.1.r: (Cf. A2411.2.1.5.)—Dh III 72, 77ff.—N. A. Indian: *Boas RBAE XXXI 652, (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 203 No. 1 (3).
A2218.1.p: A raven is caught in a smoke-hole and is blackened by soot, which explains why ravens are black.

A2218.1.1.p: An animal scorches itself while putting out a fire in the land of fire, woe and darkness, which explains its burnt appearance.

A2218.2.p: A jackal carries the sun in a bag on its back and burns its back black, which explains the jackal's dark back.

A2218.3.p: An animal that steals fire is scorched, and this scorching causes its color.

A2218.4.r: Salinan: Mason U. Cal. XIV 88, cf. 107.
A2218.4.p: A coyote is burned when a haystack is set on fire, which explains the yellow patch behind its ears.

A2218.5.p: A robin steals fire and has its breast scorched, which explains its reddish breast.

A2218.6.r: (Cf. A2442.2.1.)—Dh III 72.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 17 No. 91.
A2218.6.p: A raven scorches its feet on hot stones, and this is why its wings make a clapping sound when it flies.

A2218.7.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 109.
A2218.7.p: A rabbit burns itself under the chin while stealing a glowing ember, which explains the mark or condition under its chin.

A2218.8.p: An eel is burned by a torch, and this is the reason its eyes are red.

A2219.p: Various other accidents happening to an animal long ago, which explain how it came to be the way it is today.

A2219.1.p: Paint or color is accidentally spilled on an animal, and this is the cause of its color.

A2219.2.p: A cow swallows a book, and this explains the leaves or folds (maniplies) found in its stomach.

A2219.3.p: Only one serpent originally had a sting, and it passed poison on to the other snakes.

A2220.p: An animal receives a particular characteristic as a reward for some good deed.

A2220.1.p: A hedgehog receives its spiny skin as a reward for a good deed.

A2221.p: An animal is given a special characteristic as a reward for a pious or religious act.

A2221.1.r: (Cf. A2231.4, A2356.2.7, A2381.1.)—Dh II 15f., 195ff.; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 86 No. 58c (cross on back of ass).—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 13 No. 67 (hog has good flesh); French: Sébillot France III 256.
A2221.1.p: Animals are blessed for honoring the infant Jesus.

A2221.2.p: Animals are blessed for helpful services they performed at the crucifixion of Jesus.

A2221.2.1.r: They may eat at the king’s table. (Cf. A2545.1.) Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 150 No. 68 (cf. No. 69).
A2221.2.1.p: Flies that settled on Christ's body are rewarded because their markings look like nails, and they prevent more nails from being driven in.

A2221.2.2.r: (Cf. A2353.2.)—Fb “rodkjælk”.—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 54 No. 92**; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 90 No. 82; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 87 No. 92**; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3130, Legends Nos. 229ff.; England: Baughman.
A2221.2.2.p: Blood from the cross falls on a robin redbreast, which helped Jesus, and it is rewarded with a red breast.

A2221.2.3.p: Certain spiders receive markings from the blood of the scourged Christ.

A2221.2.4.p: Swallows lift the crown of thorns from Christ's brow, and this is why their nests are never destroyed.

A2221.2.4.1.p: Swallows put on mourning clothes at the crucifixion and have never taken them off.

A2221.2.4.2.p: A crossbill tries to pull a thorn out of the crown of thorns and twists its bill in the effort, which is why its bill is crossed.

A2221.3.p: Markings on animals are seen as reminders of events in Christ's life and sufferings.

A2221.4.r: (Cf. A2451.1, A2453.1.)—Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 93 No. 98.
A2221.4.p: An ant gathers incense and myrrh for Christ, and as a result its middle becomes thin.

A2221.5.r: (Cf. A2231.7.1.)—Dh II 53ff.—Irish: Beal XXI 306; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 93 No. 100.
A2221.5.p: An animal is rewarded with a special trait for helping a holy person who is fleeing danger. The trait explains some feature the animal has today.

A2221.5.1.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 118, 304, *Neuman.
A2221.5.1.p: An ox is blessed for helping a patriarch, who in his joy kisses the ox on the lips. This is why the ox has no hair on its lips.

A2221.6.p: An animal is rewarded with a special characteristic for being obedient to a god. The trait explains a feature the animal has today.

A2221.6.1.p: A bird receives its coloring as a reward for obeying a god.

A2221.7.p: A dove returns to the ark because it obeys Noah, and as a reward it receives the glossy sheen of a raven.

A2221.8.p: A squirrel is rewarded by a god with its markings and with immunity from falling.

A2221.9.p: Sheep walk with bowed heads because their ancestors bowed to God, and they have kept that posture ever since.

A2221.10.p: Sheep are given wool as a reward because they were helpful to the Lord, so their woolly coat is explained as a gift for pious service.

A2221.11.p: A god rewards an animal for bringing him water, and this reward is the cause of the animal's present characteristics.

A2222.p: An animal receives a special characteristic as a reward for being hospitable to a guest.

A2222.1.p: A thrush is hospitable to a peacock and is rewarded with a motley coat of feathers.

A2223.p: An animal receives a special characteristic as a reward for helping a person or other being.

A2223.1.p: A cat helps a man build a house and is rewarded with the right to sit in the chimney corner.

A2223.2.p: A bird carries a god's daughter home from the land of skulls, and as a reward it is given brilliant plumage.

A2223.3.p: A mouse gathers rice for a man and is rewarded with the right to eat a little of his rice each day.

A2223.4.p: A pike helps Christ cross a stream and is made king of the fishes as a reward.

A2223.5.p: A dog guards its master's life and property and is rewarded with the right to eat before other animals.

A2223.6.p: A tortoise ferries the rice-goddess across a stream and is given a hard shell as a reward.

A2223.7.p: Ravens show Adam how to bury the dead, and as a reward they are born with white feathers.

A2223.8.p: A chameleon saves a hero's life and is rewarded with the ability to change color.

A2229.p: A miscellaneous reward in which an animal receives a special characteristic that explains a feature it has today, not covered by the more specific categories.

A2229.1.r: (Cf. A2335.4.3.)—*Dh III 72ff., 500—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 10 No. 48, XXXIII 53 No. 48; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 143 No. 27.
A2229.1.p: A dog saves a cow's udders from a fire, and as a reward keeps a black muzzle.

A2229.2.p: A dog lets the devil into a church so the devil can steal, and as a reward the dog receives a dog-skin (a dog's coat).

A2229.3.p: An owl refuses to betray a curate, and as a reward it is allowed to live in the church steeple.

A2229.4.p: A fly steals fire from a spider, which had brought it from hell, and as a reward the fly may eat everywhere.

A2229.5.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3137; Legends Nos. 253ff.
A2229.5.p: A cuckoo frees the other birds from their cruel king, and in return they agree to hatch the cuckoo's young.

A2229.6.p: A bird gets a red spot on its tail as a reward for moving a woman's organ to its present position.

A2230.p: Animals acquire certain characteristics as a punishment.

A2231.r: (Cf. A2221, A2311.8, A2422.2, A2302.2, A2355.1.2, A2542.1.)—Dh II 252f. (fish).—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 17 No. 97, XXXIII 54 No. 97 (hazelcock).
A2231.p: An animal is given a distinctive characteristic as punishment for impiety (disrespect toward sacred things).

A2231.1.p: An animal is punished with a characteristic for a rude or disrespectful answer to God or a saint.

A2231.1.1.r: Curse: “May you always be eating!” (Cf. A2472.1, A2478.)—Dh II 93; *Fb “hest” IV 211b.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 11 No. 59 (horse); ibid. 12 No. 62 (cow); Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 143 No. 32 (horse); Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3094, Legends Nos. 163—175.
A2231.1.1.p: A cow or horse is always eating because it gave a rude answer to God or Saint Peter, who wanted to use it, and the excuse was that it was eating.

A2231.1.2.r: (Cf. A2341.1.)—Dh III 24f.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 21 No. 117; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 91 No. 92; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 89 No. 117; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3178, Legends Nos. 273—281.
A2231.1.2.p: A flounder has a crooked mouth because, when God asked where it was going, it did not answer politely but turned toward God, and its mouth became crooked.

A2231.1.3.r: (Cf. A2332.4.1.)—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 151 No. 74; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3178, Legends Nos. 273—281.
A2231.1.3.p: A crab has eyes set at the back as a punishment for a rude answer.

A2231.1.4.r: Tortoise is late. Why? “I like my house.” “May you bear your house always.” (Cf. A2312.1.)—Dh IV 275f.—Wienert FFC LVI 76 (ET 424), 139 (ST 443); Halm Aesop No. 154.
A2231.1.4.p: A tortoise has a shell as a punishment for a rude answer; in the story Zeus holds a wedding and invites the animals.

A2231.2.p: An animal is punished with a characteristic for hostility shown at the crucifixion of Christ.

A2231.2.1.p: A crane refuses to weep at the crucifixion, being the only bird that will not, and as punishment it must suffer thirst in August and has broken bills.

A2231.2.2.p: Swallows torment Christ on the cross and as punishment they lose their voice.

A2231.3.p: An animal is punished with a characteristic for working on a holy day.

A2231.3.1.p: A cuckoo builds a nest on the Annunciation Day, a holy day, and as punishment has no nest.

A2231.3.2.r: (Cf. A2435.5.1.)—*Dh III 306ff.—North Carolina: Brown Collection I 634.
A2231.3.2.p: Bees work on the Sabbath and as punishment may not get honey from red clover.

A2231.4.p: A frog fails to show honor to the infant Jesus and as punishment loses its tail.

A2231.5.p: A spider tries to outdo the Virgin Mary at spinning and is cursed for the presumption.

A2231.6.r: (Cf. A2356.2.8.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 22 No. 123; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 149 No. 65.
A2231.6.p: A spider steals thread from Christ and is punished by being made to carry the thread in the back of its body.

A2231.7.p: An animal that harms a holy person is cursed, and the curse leaves it with a lasting bad trait.

A2231.7.1.r: (Cf. A2221.5.)—Dh II 51ff.; Child V 491 s.v. “partridge”; Ireland: Baughman.
A2231.7.1.p: An animal is cursed for betraying a holy person who is fleeing from enemies.

A2231.7.1.1.p: A beetle betrays the Holy Family on their flight to Egypt and is cursed so that its eyes always stay on the ground.

A2231.7.2.p: An animal is cursed for refusing to carry a holy fugitive across a stream.

A2231.7.3.p: A tortoise dives under water while ferrying a rice goddess and is cursed so that people can kill it with iron spears.

A2231.8.r: Cursed by Virgin Mary. (Cf. A2234.4, A2468.2.)—Dh II 247f.
A2231.8.p: A toad refuses to weep over its dead children and is punished by drying up when it dies.

A2231.9.p: Fish caught in a great flood mock God for being unable to control them, and are struck down so that they are flattened.

A2231.10.p: A crab beats a deity's forbidden drum and is punished by having its eyes pushed out of its body.

A2231.11.r: (Cf. A2426.3.1.)—Dh. III 376.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 22 No. 121.
A2231.11.p: A beetle makes an arrogant demand that God return its gold and is cursed to hum ever afterward.

A2231.12.p: Buffaloes fail to come when a god bids farewell, and as punishment they are now killed by tigers.

A2231.13.p: Lorises refuse to look at the sun while dancing, and as a result they never look at the sun again.

A2232.p: An animal asks for something too greedily, and when its wish is granted it ends up worse off than before.

A2232.1.r: (Cf. A2325.4.)—Dh IV 265f.; *Köhler-Bolte I 579; *Crane Vitry 148f. No. 37; Jewish: Neuman; *Chauvin II 110 No. 76, 118 No. 102 (ass), Sébillot RTP II 492; Wienert FFC LVI 78 (ET 437); 109 (ST 215, 389); Halm Aesop No. 184.
A2232.1.p: A camel asks for horns, and as punishment it is given short ears.

A2232.2.r: (Cf. A2346.1.)—Dh IV 266; Wienert FFC LVI 77 (ET 434), 110 (ST 216); Halm Aesop No. 287.
A2232.2.p: Bees pray for a sting, and as punishment their first sting kills them.

A2232.3.r: Ant is modest. Beetle punished by being made to creep on ground. Ant is given own castle. (Cf. A2441.3.1.) Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 92 No. 97.
A2232.3.p: A beetle asks for too much while an ant asks moderately, and the creator rewards the beetle with something that turns out badly and the ant with something good.

A2232.4.p: A griffin disdains to go on Noah's ark and is drowned, which is why it is now extinct.

A2232.5.p: Animals ask a goddess for her perfume and are punished with a bad smell instead.

A2232.6.p: Birds that aspire to the blackbird's coat are punished for their presumption.

A2232.7.p: A peacock is given ugly feet as punishment for asking too much, so that it will not become too proud.

A2232.8.p: A dog sent as an envoy to Zeus is driven away, and dogs therefore sniff each other under the leg to find a messenger to replace it.

A2232.9.p: Ants ask God for wings, and the wind blows them away as punishment for the request.

A2232.10.p: A raven tries to imitate a dove's walk and is punished by being left with a clumsy, awkward gait.

A2232.11.p: Donkeys ask God for an immediate reward and are punished by being made to eat their own dung.

A2233.p: Animals are given a characteristic form or trait as punishment for being lazy.

A2233.1.p: Animals refuse to help dig a well or make a road, and they are punished for it.

A2233.1.1.r: (Cf. A2435.1.1.)—Type 55; Dh III 312ff.—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 148 No. 54; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 90 No. 83; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3096, Legends Nos. 176—182.
A2233.1.1.p: Animals that refuse to help dig a well are punished by being forbidden to drink from a river or spring.

A2233.1.2.p: A snake refuses to help make a road and is punished by dying on the road.

A2233.1.3.r: (Cf. A2468.1.)—Dh III 323f.; cf. Type 55.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 15 No. 80; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3098, Legends Nos. 183—191.
A2233.1.3.p: A shrew refuses to help make a road and is punished by dying on the road.

A2233.1.4.p: A sloth refuses to help make a road and is punished by being forbidden to look at the sun.

A2233.2.p: A dog refuses to help build a house and is punished by having to stay outdoors.

A2233.2.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 72*, Legends No. 214; Finnish: Aarne Index No. 72*; Russian: Andrejev No. 72**.
A2233.2.1.p: A hare, or dog in some versions, is left without a house because it is too cold to build one in winter and unnecessary in summer.

A2233.3.p: An owl, set as watchman over a wren imprisoned in a mousehole, falls asleep on duty, and as punishment cannot see by day.

A2233.4.p: A grasshopper builds no house for winter, and an ant strikes him blind, so he is born blind.

A2233.4.1.p: A bird neglects to build a nest and as a result goes without one.

A2234.p: Animals are given a characteristic form or trait as punishment for disobeying a command.

A2234.1.r: (Cf. A2231.2.1, A2411.2.1.5, A2435.4.3.)—Variant: he is cursed to be black or to eat carrion. *Köhler-Bolte I 3; Dh I 284; Irish myth: Cross.
A2234.1.p: A raven does not return to Noah as commanded, and is punished with thirst and a broken bill.

A2234.1.1.p: A raven disobeys Noah by not returning to the ark, and its black color is the resulting punishment.

A2234.2.p: Animals eat a deity's forbidden fruit and are punished for it.

A2234.3.p: A lemur looks where it was forbidden to look, and as punishment it is left with big eyes.

A2234.4.r: (Cf. A2211.2, A2231.8, A2342.1.)—Bushman: Bleek and Lloyd 59.
A2234.4.p: A hare weeps for its mother when it has been forbidden to do so; the moon strikes it and splits its lip.

A2235.r: (Cf. A2378.2.5.)—Dh III 182ff.—India: Thompson-Balys; Mpongwe: Nassau No. 11 (hog lacks horns); Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 145 No. 28 (leopard cannot catch game that passes him on right side); Congo: Weeks 213 No. 9 (water snake lacks poison): Zulu: Callaway 355 (hydrax lacks tail); Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 368 No. 19 (zebra lacks horns); Marshall Islands: Davenport 222.
A2235.p: An animal ends up with unusual characteristics because it was late when qualities were handed out to animals.

A2236.p: An animal is punished with lasting bodily traits for plotting to bring about man's downfall.

A2236.1.r: (Cf. A2344.2, A2426.3.2.)—Dh I 281, 332ff.; Circassian: Nicolaides and Carnoy RTP I 80; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 192.
A2236.1.p: The gnat is asked which creature has the sweetest blood, and it reveals that man does; to keep it from telling, the serpent or swallow tears out its tongue, leaving the gnat only able to buzz.

A2236.2.p: An animal is punished for carrying the devil into paradise.

A2236.2.1.p: The snake carries the devil into paradise and as punishment loses its feet.

A2236.2.2.p: The peacock persuades the snake to carry the devil into paradise, and as punishment the peacock gets an ugly voice and ugly feet.

A2236.3.p: An animal is punished for failing to warn man of the devil's temptation in Eden.

A2236.4.r: (Cf. A2344.2.6, A2378.3.1.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 16 No. 89.
A2236.4.p: The magpie tells man he will die the next day, and God pulls out its tongue and makes its tail long as punishment.

A2236.5.p: An animal is punished for failing to announce the dawn.

A2236.6.r: (Cf. A2433.5.1.)—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 151 No. 72; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 94 No. 106.
A2236.6.p: The nit tries to bore through man's head, and as punishment it must stay at the edge of the hair.

A2236.7.p: The jay carries sulphur to the devil in hell and as punishment must be quiet at noon.

A2236.8.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3121. Legends Nos. 222ff.
A2236.8.p: The cat is commanded to pray so that it will not kill man, and this is why cats purr.

A2237.p: An animal is punished with lasting characteristics for meddling in others' affairs.

A2237.1.r: (Cf. A2411.2.1.5, A2422.1.1.).—Greek: Fox 280 (raven becomes black).—Zuñi: Handy JAFL XXXI 464 No. 17 (dog loses power of speech).
A2237.1.p: An animal reveals its mistress's adultery and is punished by its master for doing so.

A2238.p: An animal is punished with lasting characteristics for greed.

A2238.1.r: (Cf. A2335.2.4.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 21 No. 119; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 290.
A2238.1.p: A rabbit (or frog) eats seed-grain from the fields, so its nose is closed during sowing season as punishment.

A2238.2.p: A ring-dove eats a man's grain, so the man is allowed to kill it. A similar punishment applies to the francolin and guinea fowl.

A2238.3.p: Fish eat other fish, and the guilty ones are punished by being required to swim deep.

A2238.4.p: A diver eats the nests of small birds, and as a result it must never nest away from water. This explains why divers nest only on water, as punishment for its greed.

A2239.p: A general heading for origin tales in which an animal gains a characteristic as punishment for some misdeed, where the specific punishment is not named here.

A2239.1.p: A hare is punished for lying under oath, and as a result its eyes are set deep in its head.

A2239.2.p: A fly is punished for failing to answer a question. As a result it cannot speak, buzzes, and keeps company with filth.

A2239.3.p: An ass gives away a god's secret, and as punishment its bray is ugly.

A2239.3.1.p: An owl reveals a god's secret, and as punishment it loses the power of speech.

A2239.4.p: A woodpecker is punished for stinginess, and this explains its characteristic in the tale.

A2239.5.p: Animals are punished for attacking women, and as a result they receive a lasting characteristic.

A2239.6.p: An ass has a cross-shaped marking on its shoulders because Balaam struck it.

A2239.7.p: A crocodile tries to attack a man it is carrying, and as punishment it has only half a tongue.

A2239.8.p: An animal is punished for stubbornness: the frog is left toothless and the mole loses its sight.

A2239.9.p: A mouse is crushed whenever she crosses a road, because of an elephant's curse.

A2239.10.p: An elephant hurts itself when running through grass, because of a mouse's curse.

A2240.p: A general heading for tales in which an animal acquires another animal's qualities, such as by borrowing them.

A2241.r: (Cf. A2242, A2313.3, A2345.1, A2351.3, A2375.2.1, A2421.4, A2435.4.1.)—*Dh III 130 ff.—Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 268ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2241.p: An animal borrows a body part or quality from another animal and refuses to give it back. This explains why certain animals have their characteristics.

A2241.1.p: A stag gets its horns by borrowing them from a dog and never returning them.

A2241.2.p: An owl gets its wings by borrowing them from a rat or another animal and never returning them.

A2241.3.p: A partridge gets its voice by borrowing it from a tortoise and never giving it back.

A2241.4.p: A cuckoo borrows food from other birds and does not repay them.

A2241.5.r: Each has one eye. Nightingale borrow’s blindworm’s and will not return it. (Cf. A2332.6.1.)—*Type 234; *Dh III 136ff.; *Köhler-Bolte I 72.—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 55 No. 110** (frog in place of nightingale).—Japanese: Ikeda; English: Shakespeare Romeo and Juliet III v. 31.
A2241.5.p: A nightingale borrows a blindworm's eye and does not return it.

A2241.6.p: A jay borrows a cuckoo's skin, and this explains why the jay has the plumage it has.

A2241.7.r: (Cf. A2378.1.5, A2433.3.5.)—Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 357 No. 10.
A2241.7.p: A squirrel borrows the coney's tail and never returns it, so the coney is left without one and goes to live among rocks in shame.

A2241.8.p: A boy borrows the hands and feet of a python and keeps them, which is why pythons have no hands or feet.

A2241.9.p: A hornbill borrows the bill of a tomtit and does not give it back, explaining the hornbill's bill.

A2241.10.r: Menomini: Skinner and Satterlee PaAM XIII 405.
A2241.10.p: A beaver borrows the tail of a muskrat and never returns it.

A2241.11.p: A monkey borrows a tail from a deer and refuses to give it back.

A2242.p: An animal obtains another animal's quality for a feast and then does not return it.

A2243.p: An animal lends a quality to another animal, which then refuses to give it back when asked.

A2243.1.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 66 No. 9.
A2243.1.p: A spider hands a box to an ant and refuses to take it back, which is why ants carry huge loads.

A2245.p: An animal gets a quality by stealing it from another animal.

A2245.1.r: (Cf. A2423.1.1, A2423.2.1.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 18 No. 98.
A2245.1.p: A thrush steals the song of a woodcock, explaining why the thrush sings.

A2247.p: Two animals trade qualities with each other.

A2247.1.p: A buffalo and a cow exchange hides, which is why their hides fit badly.

A2247.2.p: A snake and a turtle exchange heads for fangs, explaining the snake's fangs and the turtle's snake-like head.

A2247.3.r: (Cf. A2411.1.6.2., A2411.1.6.7.)—Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 372 No. 22.
A2247.3.p: A rhinoceros exchanges its red hide for the black hide of a hippopotamus.

A2247.4.p: A dove and a magpie exchange eggs, the dove giving seven and receiving two, which is why the dove has only two eggs.

A2247.5.p: A toad trades its tail for the eyes of a mole.

A2247.6.p: A beaver and a muskrat exchange tails.

A2250.r: *Dh III 141ff.—Arawak and Carib: Alexander Latin American 274; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
A2250.p: An animal's characteristic results from the outcome of a contest.

A2250.1.r: (Cf. A2433.1.1, A2433.4.2, A2433.4.3.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 54 No. 83*; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 147 No. 49.
A2250.1.p: A cock and a ptarmigan hold a contest, and the winner gets to live in town.

A2250.1.1.p: A man and a tiger hold a contest, and the winner gets to live in town.

A2250.2.p: A lizard wins a contest against a toad, and as a result snakes and lizards shed their skins. This explains why these animals change their skins.

A2251.p: Animals get their characteristics from the outcome of a contest in carrying loads. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2251.1.p: An ant wins a load-carrying contest by carrying a burden as heavy as itself. In the contest it defeats a bear and a raven or other bird.

A2252.p: Animals get their characteristics from the outcome of a race. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2252.1.p: Animals race to decide where each will live. The winners and losers of the race are given their homes.

A2252.2.p: An ox and a horse race, and the horse wins. As a result the ox must labor as a draft animal for people.

A2252.3.p: A culture hero races an ostrich, and the ostrich loses its beautiful feathers as a result.

A2252.4.p: During a race between fish, a flounder cries out in jealousy because the herring is winning. As punishment he is given a crooked mouth.

A2253.p: Animals get their characteristics from the outcome of a jumping contest. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2253.1.p: A dog is burned while jumping over a fire in a contest, and this creates lasting enmity between dog and hare.

A2254.p: Birds get their characteristics from the outcome of flying contests. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2255.p: Animals get their characteristics from the outcome of a lawsuit. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2255.1.p: A sheep wins a lawsuit over a tuft of wool on his forehead, and is allowed to keep it when the rest of his body is shorn.

A2255.2.r: (Cf. A2474.1.)—Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 48 No. 5.
A2255.2.p: A lizard is accused of stealing the king's crow along with an ant. The ant scalds the lizard's throat with boiling water, so at trial the lizard can only bob its head. It is found guilty and condemned to bob its head forever.

A2256.p: Animals get their characteristics from the outcome of a contest in watching. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2256.1.p: A hare and a man compete to see who can first watch a leaf fall from a tree. The winner may eat the loser.

A2257.p: Animals get their characteristics from the outcome of a duel. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2257.1.p: A tiger does not attack a wild boar until the boar is old, as a result of a duel between them.

A2258.p: Animals get their characteristics from a quarrel. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2260.p: Animals get their characteristics from a transformation, such as a person or creature changing form. This is the general heading for such origin explanations.

A2261.p: A general heading for animals whose traits come from being transformed from some other creature. The traits are explained as the result of the change.

A2261.1.r: (Cf. A1952, A1965.2, A2275.3, A2425, A2426.2.3, A2426.2.4.)—*Dh III 392—396; BP III 285 (Gr. No. 173).—Japanese: Ikeda; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 123 No. 83, 127.
A2261.1.p: A shepherd is changed into a bird and still calls out to sheep, which explains why the bird makes its cries. Often told of the hoopoe and the bittern.

A2261.2.r: (Cf. A2433.5.3.)—Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 69 No. 10.
A2261.2.p: A spider is transformed as punishment for greed, and so now lives in dark corners.

A2261.3.p: A catfish was once a woman and still has the tattoo marks of women.

A2261.3.1.p: Catfish that were once children still bear marks from a children's knife holder.

A2261.4.p: A stingy woman is turned into a woodpecker, which explains why woodpeckers are stingy.

A2261.5.p: A weeping man is turned into an owl and still bewails his sorrows, explaining the owl's mournful cry.

A2261.6.p: A snipe serves as a messenger for warriors because it was a messenger when it was a man.

A2262.p: A general heading for animal traits explained as coming from the transformation of a tool or other object into an animal.

A2262.1.r: (Cf. A2371.2.7.)—Dh III 45.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 12 No. 61.
A2262.1.p: A horse originally had eyes on its feet, which were put out and left eyelike marks on its legs.

A2262.2.p: Pegs driven into the backs of baboons turn into their tails.

A2262.3.p: A serpent steals a stick from God's coat and it becomes a stick on the serpent's back.

A2270.p: A general heading for animal traits explained by miscellaneous causes not covered by transformation.

A2271.p: An animal acquires a characteristic by learning it from another animal.

A2271.1.r: (Cf. A2431.3.1.)—*Type 236; Dh III 191ff.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 17 No. 93; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 88 No. 93.
A2271.1.p: A thrush teaches a dove how to build a nest.

A2271.2.p: A lark teaches a sparrow to sing, but teaches it only partly, which explains where the sparrow's voice came from.

A2272.p: A general heading for animal characteristics that come from imitating another animal or object.

A2272.1.p: An animal's cry or call comes from imitating a sound it heard.

A2272.1.1.p: A nightingale hears a boy calling oxen and learns that call as her song.

A2272.1.2.p: A cricket hears water hissing on hot iron and learns that sound as its song.

A2272.1.3.p: A garden warbler hears a smith beating iron and learns to imitate that clanging sound in its song.

A2272.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 20 No. 110, XXXIII 55 No. 110.
A2272.2.p: A lizard's tail is explained as having been copied from a snake's tail.

A2275.p: An animal's habit is explained as a leftover memory of something it experienced in an earlier form or life.

A2275.1.r: (Cf. A2260, A2425.)—Dh III 387.—Benga: Nassau 163 No. 21; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A2275.1.p: An animal's cries are a lament for a person who was lost when the animal was transformed.

A2275.2.p: An animal's cries are a lament over its own transformation into an animal.

A2275.3.p: An animal's cries recall its former life as a human being.

A2275.4.r: (Cf. A2426.1.1, A2426.4.1.)—India: Thompson-Balys; Ibo (Nigeria): Basden 139; Angola: Chatelain 217 No. 38.
A2275.4.p: An animal's cry repeats a cry from an ancient adventure, when an ancestor of the animal was in difficulty.

A2275.4.1.p: A green pigeon is cheated out of its chick and is therefore always mourning.

A2275.5.p: An ancient animal loses something, and its descendants keep searching for it forever, explaining how certain animals carry themselves.

A2275.5.1.p: A hog loses a pancake in the mud and still searches for it.

A2275.5.2.p: A hawk or vulture loses its grandmother and still hovers and searches for her.

A2275.5.3.r: All shipwrecked. Diver is looking for his leather. Bush looks for his clothers and holds fast to all passers-by. Bat is abroad only at night to escape creditors. (Cf. A2471.4, A2491.1.)—*Dh IV 273f; *BP I 137. (Gr. No. 18).—Wienert FFC LVI 35; Halm Aesop No. 306.
A2275.5.3.p: A bat, a diver, and a thornbush are shipwrecked; the bat brings money, the bush puts on clothes, and the diver brings leather.

A2275.5.4.p: Dolphins go up and down in the sea because they are searching for King Solomon's magic ring, which he lost in the sea and God sent them to retrieve.

A2275.5.5.p: A dog loses its patent right and keeps seeking it, which explains why dogs sniff at one another under the tail.

A2275.6.p: A son accidentally kills his father, and the father returns to life as a cuckoo and tells people when to sow grain. The bird's habit is explained as a memory of its former life.

A2281.r: (Cf. A2494.1.1, A2494.1.3, A2494.2.3.)—Dh III 331.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 11 Nos 56, 57; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 143 No. 31; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 88 No. 62; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 86 No. 56; Jewish: Neuman; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 36 No. 20; Benga: Nassau 99 No. 6.
A2281.p: Enmity between two animals is explained as coming from an original quarrel between them.

A2281.1.r: (Cf. A2275.5, A2494.1.2.) *Type 200.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 11 No. 53; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 143 No. 30; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 88 No. 61; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 85 No. 53.
A2281.1.p: A cat loses a dog's certificate of nobility through carelessness, which causes enmity between cats and dogs.

A2281.1.1.p: A cat garbles a message from a man to a tiger, causing enmity between man and tiger.

A2281.1.2.p: A dog and a cat quarrel about which of them is of higher caste.

A2281.2.p: A squirrel steals a dog's needle, causing enmity between them.

A2281.3.p: Cat and dog are enemies because the dog ate the cat's share of the master's reward.

A2282.r: (Cf. A2433.3.3, A2433.3.4, A2433.3.21, A2433.6.1.)—Benga: Nassau 202 No. 32; Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 372, 381.
A2282.p: The places where animals live today are explained as the result of an old quarrel among them.

A2283.p: Two animals are taught songs together; one learns its song successfully and the other fails.

A2284.p: An animal is tricked or talked into injuring itself, and that injury becomes a permanent feature of its kind.

A2284.1.p: An animal is persuaded to cut off a limb, and that is why it now lacks that limb.

A2284.2.p: A bustard is persuaded to kill all but two of its children, which is why it now has only two eggs.

A2284.3.p: A worm, believing the world is ending, blinds itself so it will not have to see the disaster.

A2284.4.p: An elephant is tricked into eating its own testicles; the testicles are kept inside the body.

A2284.5.p: A coyote is persuaded to break its leg, which is why its right leg is thin.

A2284.6.p: A jackal persuades a hyena to jump and break its foot, which leaves the hyena with a short left hind foot.

A2286.p: A god or deity fixes the characteristics of an animal.

A2286.0.1.r: (Cf. A2402.1, A2494.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 19 No. 109.

A2286.1.p: God stops creating an animal partway because he has to go attend a fire, so the animal is left unfinished.

A2286.1.0.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 474.
A2286.1.0.1.p: An animal has its features because the creator did not have enough time to finish making it.

A2286.1.1.r: (Cf. A2335.4.2.)—Dh III 24, 493.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 12 No. 65.
A2286.1.1.p: God is called away to a fire while making the hog, so the hog is left with a round snout.

A2286.2.p: Animal characteristics result from a contest between God and the devil, each trying to shape creatures.

A2286.2.1.r: (Cf. A1751.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 20 No. 115; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 149 No. 63.
A2286.2.1.p: The devil's animals eat God's animals: God makes a white fish and the devil makes a pike to eat it, God makes a worm and the devil makes a frog to eat it, and so on.

A2286.2.2.p: The devil gives a horse four eyes, and God reduces them to two.

A2286.2.3.p: The devil's cows have one horn, and God makes them two-horned.

A2286.2.4.r: (Cf. A2378.1.)—Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 146 No. 47; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3083, Legends Nos. 134—137.
A2286.2.4.p: God changes the colors, or tails, of the devil's cows; the devil had made all animals one color or all tailless, and once they differ he no longer recognizes them.

A2287.p: Jesus is said to be the cause of certain physical features of animals. This is a folk explanation for why animals look the way they do.

A2287.1.r: (Cf. A2335.4.1.)—Dh II 81.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 12 No. 66.
A2287.1.p: Jesus drives evil spirits into hogs, and this is why hogs have short snouts.

A2287.1.1.p: Jesus drives evil spirits into hogs, and this is why hogs have toe-like marks on the back of their foreleg.

A2291.r: Jewish: Neuman; Achawoi: Alexander Lat. Am. 270.
A2291.p: Animals acquire their characteristic features during the great flood. The flood is given as the moment when their traits were fixed.

A2292.p: Animals change their characteristics so that they can do something more conveniently. Their features are explained as adaptations made for practical reasons.

A2294.p: Wild animals lose their fierceness because they fear Behemoth, a great mythical creature. Their tameness is thus explained by this fear.

A2300.p: A general heading for explanations of how animals got their bodily characteristics, meaning their physical shapes and parts.

A2300.1.p: The shape of a bee's body is explained by a tale telling how it came to be that way.

A2301.p: An animal's body is made larger, and the tale explains how it became big.

A2301.1.p: A mouse's body is made larger, and the tale explains how it came to be bigger.

A2301.2.p: A spider's body is made larger, and the tale explains how it grew bigger.

A2301.3.p: A coyote's body is made larger, and the tale explains how it became bigger.

A2301.4.p: A bat's body is made larger, and the tale explains how it became bigger.

A2301.5.p: A flying squirrel's body is made larger, and the tale explains how it grew bigger.

A2302.p: An animal's body is made smaller, and the tale explains how it became small.

A2302.1.r: Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 260 No. 55; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 231.
A2302.1.p: A mouse's body is made smaller, and the tale explains how it became small.

A2302.2.r: (See A2231, A2213.1.) Dh III 2.—Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 38 No. 51.
A2302.2.p: A hazel-cock's body, a type of grouse, is made smaller, and the tale explains how it became small.

A2302.3.p: A squirrel's body is made smaller, and the tale explains how it became small.

A2302.4.p: An eagle's body is made smaller, and the tale explains how it became small.

A2302.5.p: A wolf's body is made smaller, and the tale explains how it became small.

A2302.6.p: Explains how lice came to be made smaller, as a mythological origin for the animal's small body.

A2305.p: A general origin story explaining why some animals have flat bodies.

A2305.1.p: Explains how fish came to have flat bodies.

A2305.1.1.p: Explains how the steelhead salmon came to have a flat body.
