A2412.1.5.p: Explains why the elephant has white marks on its body.

A2412.1.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Yagua): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 736.
A2412.1.6.p: Explains why the peccary has spots.

A2412.2.p: A general heading for explanations of how birds came to have their markings.

A2412.2.1.p: Explains the markings on the tail feathers of the ruffed grouse.

A2412.2.2.p: Explains the markings of the francolin, a game bird.

A2412.3.p: A general heading for explanations of how insects came to have their markings.

A2412.3.1.p: Explains why the louse has a mark on its back.

A2412.3.2.p: Explains the origin of the markings on butterflies.

A2412.4.p: A general heading for explanations of how fish came to have their markings.

A2412.4.1.p: Explains the markings on the sunfish.

A2412.4.2.r: Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 242 (red marks below ears).
A2412.4.2.p: Explains the markings on the king salmon.

A2412.4.2.1.p: Explains why the king salmon has a purple belly. The belly color is given a mythic origin story.

A2412.4.3.p: Explains the markings on the cod-fish. The spots or marks on the cod are given a mythic cause.

A2412.4.4.p: Explains how the crab came to have a cross on its back. The cross-shaped marking is given a mythic origin.

A2412.4.5.p: Explains the markings on the flying fish. The patterns on these fish are given a mythic cause.

A2412.5.p: A general heading for origin stories of markings on animals other than fish. It covers patterns and marks on creatures such as tortoises, toads, and frogs.

A2412.5.1.p: Explains the markings on the tortoise's back. The patterns on its shell are given a mythic origin.

A2412.5.2.p: Explains why toads have warts on their backs. The bumpy skin is given a mythic cause.

A2412.5.2.1.p: Explains why the frog is spotted all over. The frog's spots are given a mythic cause, in the same story pattern as the toad's warts.

A2413.p: A general heading for origin stories of why certain animals have stripes. It covers several animals with striped markings.

A2413.1.p: Explains the stripes of the zebra. The zebra's striped coat is given a mythic origin.

A2413.2.p: Explains the stripes of the chipmunk. The stripes along the chipmunk's back are given a mythic cause.

A2413.3.p: Explains the stripes of the squirrel. The markings on the squirrel are given a mythic origin.

A2413.4.p: Explains the stripes of the tiger. The tiger's striped coat is given a mythic origin.

A2413.5.p: Explains the stripes of the alligator. The markings on the alligator are given a mythic cause.

A2413.6.p: Explains the stripes of the cony, a rabbit-like animal. The striped markings are given a mythic origin.

A2413.7.p: Explains why trout have stripes on their bodies.

A2416.p: A general heading for origin stories of an animal's smell, including how a smell arose and what it is like. It covers animals known for strong odors.

A2416.1.r: (See A2232.5.)—Dh III 233; Fb “gjedebuk” IV 178b.—Ibo (Nigeria): Thomas 125; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 226, (Cameroon): Mansfield 227.
A2416.1.p: Explains why the goat has a bad smell. The goat's strong odor is given a mythic cause.

A2416.2.p: Explains the burnt smell of the mink. The mink's odor is described as a burnt smell and given a mythic cause.

A2416.3.r: Dh III 233.—Central America: Krickeberg Märchen der Azteken und Inkaperuaner 254.
A2416.3.p: Explains why the skunk has a bad smell. The skunk's stench is given a mythic origin.

A2416.4.p: Explains the burnt smell of the wolverine. The wolverine's odor is described as a burnt smell and given a mythic cause.

A2416.5.p: Explains why the ram has a bad smell. It is an origin tale for the animal's strong odor.

A2416.6.p: Explains why bugs have a bad smell. It is an origin tale for the insects' unpleasant odor.

A2416.7.p: Explains why herrings give off a bad odor. It is an origin tale for the fish's unpleasant smell.

A2420.p: A heading grouping tales that explain how animals came to have their particular voices and hearing abilities.

A2421.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3168, Legends Nos. 263—270; Japanese: Ikeda.
A2421.p: A general type of tale explaining how an animal acquired its voice or sound-making ability.

A2421.1.p: Explains how the night-swallow (a nightjar-like bird) got its voice.

A2421.2.p: Explains how the woodcock got its voice: it traded with the turkey.

A2421.3.p: Explains how the crow got its voice. In this tale the crow obtains its voice by trading with the thunder-bird.

A2421.4.p: Explains how the partridge got its voice. The partridge borrowed its voice from the tortoise.

A2421.4.1.p: Explains how the quail got its voice. This is a variant of the partridge-borrowing tale, in which the quail's voice comes from the same source.

A2421.5.p: Explains how the nkundak (an animal named in the index) got its voice.

A2421.6.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 35 No. *205; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2421.6.p: Explains why cocks crow. It is an origin tale for the rooster's crowing.

A2421.7.p: Explains the characteristic cry of the peewit (lapwing). It is an origin tale for the bird's call.

A2421.8.p: Explains why cats purr. It is an origin tale for the cat's purring sound.

A2422.p: A general type of tale explaining how an animal lost its voice or power of speech.

A2422.1.p: Explains how the dog lost its power of speech. It is an origin tale for why dogs no longer talk.

A2422.1.1.r: Dh III 232. (See A2237.1.)—Benga: Nassau 163 No. 22; Zuñi: Handy JAFL XXXI 467; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 243; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2422.1.1.p: Explains why dogs do not speak. It is a further specification of the dog losing its speech, giving the reason dogs are silent in human language.

A2422.2.r: Curse of Virgin Mary. (See A2231).—Sébillot RTP II 492.
A2422.2.p: Explains why sheep do not speak. It is an origin tale for the sheep's lack of speech.

A2422.3.p: Explains why the white crow is mute. It is an origin tale for the white crow being unable to speak.

A2422.4.p: Explains why the tortoise has no voice. It is an origin tale for the tortoise's silence.

A2422.5.p: Explains why the fly has no voice. It is an origin tale for the fly's silence.

A2422.6.p: Explains why the raven lost the ability to speak.

A2422.8.p: Explains why the cormorant is unable to speak.

A2422.9.p: Explains why swallows lost their voices.

A2422.10.p: Explains why the rooster does not talk.

A2423.p: Stories explaining why an animal's voice sounds the way it does in general.

A2423.1.p: An animal is given an unpleasant voice, and a story explains why.

A2423.1.1.p: The woodcock is given an ugly voice; the note says it was exchanged with the thrush.

A2423.1.2.p: Explains why the peacock has a harsh, unpleasant voice.

A2423.1.3.p: Explains why the loon has an unpleasant cry.

A2423.1.5.p: Explains why the hornbill talks through its nose.

A2423.1.6.p: Explains the origin of the snail's dull, unvarying voice.

A2423.2.p: An animal is given a sweet, pleasant voice, and a story explains why.

A2423.2.1.p: Explains why the thrush has a beautiful song; the note says it was exchanged with the woodcock.

A2423.2.2.p: Explains why the cuckoo has a sweet call.

A2425.r: (See A2261.1, A2272.1, A2275.1, A2275.2.)—*Millier (A.) Petits Contes du Nivernais (Nevers, 1894); Dh III 355ff.; BP II 535; Wienert FFC LVI 40; Chauvin VIII 49 No. 17; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2425.p: Stories explaining how animals came to make their characteristic cries.

A2425.1.p: Explains how dogs first came to bark.

A2425.2.p: Traces birds' morning songs to singing angels.

A2426.p: Tales about what animal cries mean or signify.

A2426.1.p: General entry for the sounds that mammals make, with tales explaining why each animal cries as it does.

A2426.1.1.p: A tale explaining why the bush-cat (a wild cat) makes the cry it does.

A2426.1.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC IX 3 No. 3.—Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 220.
A2426.1.2.p: A tale explaining the cry of the squirrel.

A2426.1.2.1.p: The squirrel's call asks whether the viper, who ate up its children, is its friend.

A2426.1.3.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC IX 4 No. 13.—Jamaica Negro: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 259 No. 51; Angola: Chatelain 215.
A2426.1.3.p: A tale explaining why the hog grunts as it does.

A2426.1.4.p: A tale explaining the hedgehog's cry.

A2426.1.5.p: A tale explaining why the dog barks at a thief.

A2426.1.6.p: A tale explaining why bats cry out as they fly.

A2426.2.p: General entry for the songs and calls of birds, with tales explaining why each bird sings or calls as it does.

A2426.2.1.r: (See A2272.1.1.)—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3151, Balys Legends No. 260; Japanese: Ikeda.
A2426.2.1.p: A tale explaining why the nightingale sings as it does.

A2426.2.2.p: A tale explaining the song of the garden warbler.

A2426.2.3.p: A tale explaining the bittern's booming song.

A2426.2.4.p: A tale explaining the song of the hoopoe.

A2426.2.5.p: A tale explaining why the cuckoo calls as it does.

A2426.2.6.r: Dh III 126, 257, 357, 369, 371, 372.—Finnish: Aarne FFC IX 7 No. 39; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 223; Australian: Dixon 292.
A2426.2.6.p: A tale explaining why the crow caws as it does.

A2426.2.7.r: Dh III 364, 373, 392.—Finnish: Aarne FFC IX 9 No. 46.—Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 223; Eskimo (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 261.
A2426.2.7.p: A tale explaining why the raven croaks as it does.

A2426.2.8.r: *Dh III 554 s.v. “Taube”.—Finnish: Aarne FFC IX 12 No. 57; Angola: Chatelain 153 No. 16; Jamaica negro: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 259 No. 50; India: *Thompson-Balys.
A2426.2.8.p: A tale explaining why the dove coos.

A2426.2.9.p: A tale explaining why the goose quacks, or honks, as it does.

A2426.2.10.p: A tale explaining why the duck quacks.

A2426.2.11.p: A tale explaining what the parrot says, that is, why it repeats human words.

A2426.2.12.p: Explains what the swallow's song means or signifies. Tales give the swallow's twitter a meaning or message of its own.

A2426.2.13.p: Explains why the guinea hen makes its cackling sound. It is an origin tale for the guinea fowl's call.

A2426.2.15.p: Explains why a certain kind of eagle cries like a human baby: the spirit of a tortured baby turned into the eagle.

A2426.2.16.p: Explains how the brain-fever bird's cry came to be. It tells the origin of this bird's distinctive call.

A2426.2.17.r: (Cf. A2427.3.)—S. Am. Indian (Matoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 48.
A2426.2.17.p: Explains where the cries of owls come from. It is an origin tale for the owl's hooting or screeching.

A2426.2.18.p: Explains how the rooster's crow "cock-a-doodle-do" originated and what it means.

A2426.2.18.1.p: Explains why the cock crows while standing on a roof with its neck stretched out.

A2426.3.p: A general heading for tales that explain why insects make the sounds they do.

A2426.3.1.p: Explains why the beetle hums. It gives the origin of the beetle's buzzing sound.

A2426.3.2.p: Explains why the gnat buzzes. It is an origin tale for the gnat's high-pitched whine.

A2426.3.3.p: Explains why the fly buzzes. It gives the origin of the fly's buzzing sound.

A2426.3.4.p: Explains why the cricket chirps. It gives the origin of the cricket's chirping sound.

A2426.3.5.p: Explains why the mosquito buzzes. It gives the origin of the mosquito's whining sound.

A2426.3.6.p: Tells how fireflies speak or what their speech is. It gives a tale-based explanation of firefly communication.

A2426.4.p: A general heading for tales that explain the origins of other animal cries not covered by birds or insects.

A2426.4.1.r: (See A2275.4.)—Jewish: Neuman; Japanese: Ikeda; Angola: Chatelain 217 No. 38; Liberia: Bundy JAFL XXXII 420.
A2426.4.1.p: Explains why the frog croaks. It is a general heading for frog-croak origin tales.

A2426.4.1.1.p: Explains that frogs were once ducks stolen from Eden by Cain. God changed them into frogs, which is why frogs sound like ducks in spring.

A2426.4.1.2.p: Explains why the frog croaks when the weather is wet. It gives a tale reason for frogs calling before rain.

A2426.4.2.p: Explains why the toad croaks. It gives the origin of the toad's call.

A2427.p: Explains why certain animals howl or cry out at night. It gives a tale reason for nighttime animal cries.

A2427.1.p: Explains why the jackal cries out in the night. A myth origin for the jackal's nighttime howling.

A2427.2.p: Explains why the dog howls at night. A myth origin for the dog's nighttime howling.

A2427.2.1.p: Explains that dogs howl because a person is about to die, so the dog's howl is a sign of approaching death.

A2427.3.p: Explains why the owl hoots at night. A myth origin for the owl's nighttime call.

A2428.p: Explains the hearing of animals, a general heading for stories about how animals came to hear as they do.

A2428.1.p: Tells how an animal came to lose its hearing, so it can no longer hear as others do.

A2430.p: A heading for explanations of how animals came to have their homes and feeding habits.

A2431.p: A heading for stories explaining how birds' nests came to be as they are.

A2431.1.p: Tells how a bird first learned to build its nest.

A2431.2.p: Explains why a certain bird has no nest of its own.

A2431.2.1.r: (See A2231.3.1.)—Dh III 177, 195, 200; India: Thompson-Balys; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 198f., 250, 270.
A2431.2.1.p: Explains why the cuckoo has no nest of its own.

A2431.2.1.1.p: The crow hatches the cuckoo's egg, so the cuckoo is raised by another bird rather than building its own nest.

A2431.2.2.p: Explains why the heron has no nest of its own.

A2431.3.p: A heading for explanations of what birds' nests are made of or how they are shaped.

A2431.3.1.p: Explains the nature or form of the dove's nest.

A2431.3.2.p: Explains the nature or form of the diver's nest.

A2431.3.3.p: Explains the nature of the ring-dove's nest; in the tale, the ring-dove and the gull exchange nests.

A2431.3.4.p: Explains the nature of the gull's nest; in the tale, the gull and the ringdove exchange nests.

A2431.3.5.r: (See A2221.2.4.)—Dh III 5, 200, 415ff.; Sébillot RTP III 156; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 16 No. 87.
A2431.3.5.p: Explains the nature or form of the swallow's nest.

A2431.3.5.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3145, Legends No. 272.
A2431.3.5.1.p: Explains why the swallow avoids building its nest in green trees.

A2431.3.6.p: Explains the nature or structure of the crow's nest. It is an origin tale for why crows build their nests the way they do.

A2431.3.6.1.p: Explains why a crow is unable to enter a sparrow's nest. It is a story about the two birds' nests being different in a way that keeps the crow out.

A2431.3.6.2.p: Explains why the crow's nest is loosely made rather than tightly woven. It is an origin tale for the crow's careless nest-building.

A2431.3.6.3.p: Explains why crows must build their nests far away from human dwellings. It is an origin tale for crows keeping their distance from people.

A2431.3.7.p: Explains the nature or structure of the sparrow's nest. It is an origin tale for how sparrows build their nests.

A2431.3.7.1.p: Explains why the sparrow often builds its nest near human houses, and says it was rewarded for being hospitable. It is an origin tale in which the sparrow's nesting near people is a reward.

A2431.3.8.p: Explains the nature or structure of the turkey's nest. It is an origin tale for how turkeys build their nests.

A2431.3.8.1.p: Explains why the brush turkey builds its nest on the ground rather than in a tree. It is an origin tale for the brush turkey's ground nest.

A2432.p: Covers origin tales for the dwellings of animals other than birds, such as insects and mammals. It is a general heading for how such animals came to live where they do.

A2432.1.p: Explains why the ant lives in an ant-hill. It is an origin tale for the ant's underground or mound home.

A2432.2.p: Explains why the wasp builds a nest. It is an origin tale for the wasp's home.

A2432.3.p: Explains the beaver's dwelling. It is an origin tale for how beavers come to live in the homes they build.

A2432.4.p: Explains the porcupine's dwelling. It is an origin tale for where and how the porcupine lives.

A2432.5.p: Explains the muskrat's dwelling. It is an origin tale for how the muskrat comes to live in the home it has.

A2432.6.p: Explains the bear's den. It is an origin tale for where the bear sleeps and shelters.

A2432.7.p: Explains the wart-hog's burrow. It is an origin tale for the underground hole the wart-hog lives in.

A2432.8.p: Explains the bee's hive. It is an origin tale for why bees live in hives and how they make them.

A2432.9.p: An origin explanation for why the housefly lives on dung heaps. The motif concerns an insect other than a bird.

A2432.10.p: Explains why the elephant has no hut or house of its own. It is an origin tale for the elephant living without a dwelling.

A2433.p: Covers origin tales for an animal's characteristic haunt, the place it habitually frequents. It is a general heading for why animals return to certain places.

A2433.1.p: Explains how an animal came to establish its particular haunt or home territory. It is an origin tale for why the animal settled where it does.

A2433.1.1.p: An animal's home territory is set by a race or contest between animals, so the winner or result decides where that animal lives.

A2433.1.2.p: Animals change the kind of place they live in, moving from one type of dwelling to another.

A2433.1.3.p: A dog is given a place to live as a patent right, meaning a special legal grant of a home.

A2433.2.p: A general heading for the different places animals live, such as woods, water, being alone, or living with people.

A2433.2.1.p: Animals that live in the woods or forest rather than in villages or open country.

A2433.2.1.1.p: Explains why small ants make their nests in houses while driver ants stay in the bush.

A2433.2.1.2.p: Explains why gorillas and chimpanzees live in forests, as a punishment for neglecting their possessions.

A2433.2.2.p: Animals that live in or on water.

A2433.2.3.p: Animals that live alone instead of in groups.

A2433.2.3.1.p: Explains why the leopard goes about alone: after he treacherously killed those who had saved him, all the other animals abandoned him.

A2433.2.4.p: Animals that live with people rather than apart from them.

A2433.2.4.1.p: Explains why the chimpanzee lives among people.

A2433.3.p: A heading for the homes of various mammals, such as cats, dogs, hares, hyenas, hogs and coneys.

A2433.3.1.p: The place where cats characteristically stay or like to be.

A2433.3.1.1.p: Explains why the cat keeps to the chimney corner, staying by the warm hearth.

A2433.3.2.r: (See A2233.2.)—Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 214; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 213 No. 35 (by the fire), (Wute): Sieber 205.
A2433.3.2.p: The place where dogs characteristically live or stay.

A2433.3.3.p: Explains why the hare lives in the bush.

A2433.3.4.p: Explains why the hyena stays in a burrow.

A2433.3.5.p: Explains why the coney (a rock hyrax or similar small animal) lives among rocks.

A2433.3.6.p: Explains why the hog lives in a sty, a pen for pigs.

A2433.3.7.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 143 No. 27; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2433.3.7.p: Explains why rams live at home, as a origin tale for the animal's habitat. The ram's dwelling place is given a mythical cause.

A2433.3.8.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 153 No. 29; Benga: Nassau 100 No. 7.
A2433.3.8.p: Explains why the goat lives with people, giving a mythical cause for the goat's habit of staying among humans.

A2433.3.9.p: Explains why the squirrel lives in trees, giving a mythical cause for its tree-dwelling habit.

A2433.3.9.1.p: Explains why the squirrel keeps itself hidden in the jungle, a mythical cause for its secretive habit within its tree-dwelling haunt.

A2433.3.10.p: Explains why muskrats live in water, giving a mythical cause for their aquatic home.

A2433.3.11.p: Explains why the porcupine lives in high places in the mountains, giving a mythical cause for its habitat.

A2433.3.12.p: Explains why the beaver lives along rivers, giving a mythical cause for its riverside home.

A2433.3.13.p: Explains why the elk lives in the woods, giving a mythical cause for its forest home.

A2433.3.14.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 153 No. 29.
A2433.3.14.p: Explains why the wolf lives in the woods, giving a mythical cause for its forest dwelling.

A2433.3.15.p: Explains why the elephant does not live in towns, giving a mythical cause for its avoidance of human settlements.

A2433.3.16.p: Explains why the lion stays away from human settlements, giving a mythical cause for its avoidance of villages.

A2433.3.17.r: Australian: Dixon 298 (trees); Kaska: Teit JAFL XXX 444 (mountains).
A2433.3.17.p: Explains why the bear lives where it does, giving a mythical cause for its particular habitat.

A2433.3.18.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 143 (woods), ibid. 153 (desert). India: Thompson-Balys.
A2433.3.18.p: Explains why the leopard lives where it does, giving a mythical cause for its particular habitat.

A2433.3.19.p: Explains why the monkey lives in trees, giving a mythical cause for its tree-dwelling habit.

A2433.3.19.1.p: Explains why the monkey takes the first fruits of the harvest in every field, a mythical cause for its raiding of crops within its tree-dwelling habit.

A2433.3.20.p: Explains why the mole lives underground, giving a mythical cause for its burrowing habit.

A2433.3.21.p: Explains why the tiger lives in the jungle, giving a mythical cause for its forest habitat.

A2433.4.p: Groups tales explaining why particular birds live where they do, the mythical causes of birds' habitats.

A2433.4.1.r: (See A2229.3. steeple.)—Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 196 (away from other birds).
A2433.4.1.p: Explains why the owl lives where it does, giving a mythical cause for its particular habitat.

A2433.4.2.p: Explains why the rooster lives in town, giving a mythical cause for its habit of staying among human settlements.

A2433.4.3.p: Explains why the ptarmigan lives in a particular type of country, such as open or rocky terrain. It is a origin tale about the bird's habitat.

A2433.4.4.p: Explains why the parrot lives in trees. It is a origin tale about the bird's habitat.

A2433.4.5.p: Explains why the kingfisher lives over water in the air.

A2433.4.6.p: Explains why chickens and other fowls never close their doors at night, so they are always open to coming and going.

A2433.5.p: A heading grouping origin tales that explain where particular insects live and why they live there.

A2433.5.1.p: Explains why the nit, the egg of a louse, lives at the edge of the hair.

A2433.5.2.p: Explains why the common housefly lives among filth, dirt, and garbage.

A2433.5.3.r: (See A2211.6, large stones, A2261.2, dusty corners.) India: Thompson-Balys.
A2433.5.3.p: A heading grouping origin tales about where spiders live.

A2433.5.3.1.p: Explains why the spider lives under stones.

A2433.5.4.p: Explains why beetles live in manure or dung.

A2433.5.5.p: Explains why ants are masters of the bush or forest, with the idea that they hold dominion over it.

A2433.5.6.p: Explains why butterflies gather in places soaked with urine.

A2433.5.7.p: Explains why cockroaches live inside houses.

A2433.6.p: A heading grouping origin tales about where reptiles and similar creatures live and why.

A2433.6.1.p: A heading grouping origin tales about where tortoises and turtles live and lay eggs.

A2433.6.1.1.p: Explains why the tortoise lives in logs floating in a stream.

A2433.6.1.2.p: Explains why the turtle lays its eggs on the beach.

A2433.6.2.p: Explains why the oyster lives in salt water.

A2433.6.3.p: A heading grouping origin tales about where crabs live and why.

A2433.6.3.1.p: Explains why crabs live in water.

A2433.6.3.2.p: Explains why crabs dig burrows in sand.

A2433.6.3.3.p: Explains why the common crab lives underground, as an origin story for the animal's habit of burrowing.

A2433.6.4.p: Explains why the iguana lives in or near streams.

A2433.6.5.p: Explains why leeches live in water.

A2433.6.6.p: Explains where the frog makes its home.

A2433.6.7.p: Explains why the toad lives in a cold place.

A2433.6.9.p: Explains why the thousand-legged worm (millipede or centipede) avoids sunlight.

A2434.p: Explains why an animal lives in the particular country or locality where it is found.

A2434.1.p: Explains why certain animals are found in every place rather than only in one area.

A2434.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 209.
A2434.1.1.p: Explains why birds are found in every part of the world, as an origin story for their wide spread.

A2434.1.2.p: Explains why bluebirds are found everywhere.

A2434.1.3.p: Explains why snowbirds are found everywhere.

A2434.1.4.p: Explains why black ants are found everywhere.

A2434.1.5.p: Explains why the jackal may roam everywhere.

A2434.2.p: Explains why certain animals are missing from some countries or places.

A2434.2.1.p: Explains why porcupines and skunks are not found on Cape Breton Island.

A2434.2.2.p: Explains why foxes are absent from a certain island, because a god drove them out.

A2434.2.3.p: Explains why there are no snakes in Ireland.

A2434.3.p: Explains why particular animals live in particular countries.

A2434.3.1.p: Explains why locusts live in certain Pueblo towns.

A2434.3.2.p: Explains why wild turkeys are found in a certain Pueblo town.

A2434.3.3.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 153 No. 29.
A2434.3.3.p: An origin explanation for why elephants live in Nigeria, the country where they are found.

A2435.p: An explanation of what a given animal eats and why its diet is what it is.

A2435.1.r: Circassian: Nicolaides and Carnoy RTP I 80.
A2435.1.p: A story explaining how food was given or assigned to a particular animal.

A2435.1.1.p: An explanation for why certain birds avoid drinking from rivers.

A2435.1.2.p: An explanation of how the tiger once cooked its food and why it stopped doing so.

A2435.2.p: An explanation of the kind of food an animal eats, such as whether it eats plants or meat.

A2435.2.1.p: An explanation for why animals eat everything without salt.

A2435.2.2.p: An explanation for why certain animals are meat-eaters.

A2435.3.p: A group of explanations for the food of various mammal animals.

A2435.3.1.r: (See A2247, exchanged with cat.)—Dh III 124, IV 112ff., 121ff.
A2435.3.1.p: An explanation for what the dog eats.

A2435.3.2.r: (See A2247, exchanged with dog.)—Dh III 124, IV 121ff., 128 (to eat before dog).
A2435.3.2.p: An explanation for what the cat eats.

A2435.3.3.p: An explanation for what the bear eats.

A2435.3.4.r: Man.—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 53. No. 75*; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 144 No. 37.
A2435.3.4.p: An explanation for what the wolf eats.

A2435.3.5.p: An explanation for what the wolverine eats.

A2435.3.6.p: An explanation for why the moose eats willow.

A2435.3.7.p: An explanation for what the mouse eats.

A2435.3.7.1.p: An explanation for why mice eat grease and salmon.

A2435.3.8.p: An explanation for why the ant-bear (anteater) eats insects.

A2435.3.9.p: An explanation for what the tiger eats.

A2435.3.9.1.p: An explanation for why tigers eat dogs.

A2435.3.9.2.p: Explains why tigers eat their meat raw rather than cooked. A tale gives the reason tigers do not cook their food.

A2435.3.9.3.p: Explains why tigers hunt and eat people. A tale gives the cause of tigers becoming man-eaters.

A2435.3.9.4.p: Explains why tigers prey on water buffalo. A tale gives the reason tigers hunt buffalo.

A2435.3.10.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what rats eat. This is the general heading for tales about the food of rats.

A2435.3.10.1.p: Explains why rats eat rice. In the tale a rat brings the original rice plant from a pond, which is why rats are fond of rice.

A2435.3.11.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what reindeer eat. This is the general heading for tales about reindeer food.

A2435.3.12.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what hares eat. This is the general heading for tales about the food of hares.

A2435.3.12.1.p: Explains why hares never drink from rivers or streams. A tale gives the reason hares avoid running water.

A2435.3.13.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what squirrels eat. This is the general heading for tales about squirrel food.

A2435.3.14.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what pigs eat. This is the general heading for tales about pig food.

A2435.3.14.1.p: Explains why pigs eat excrement. A tale gives the reason pigs feed on dung and waste.

A2435.3.15.p: Explains why wildcats come to eat chickens. A tale gives the reason wildcats raid poultry.

A2435.3.16.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what jaguars eat. This is the general heading for tales about jaguar food.

A2435.3.16.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 83.
A2435.3.16.1.p: Explains why jaguars eat men. A tale gives the reason jaguars hunt and kill people.

A2435.3.17.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what leopards eat. This is the general heading for tales about leopard food.

A2435.3.17.1.p: Explains why leopards eat men. A tale gives the reason leopards hunt and kill people.

A2435.4.r: Joshua: Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 232 (corpses).—India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
A2435.4.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what birds eat. This is the general heading for tales about the food of birds.

A2435.4.1.p: Gives the traditional explanation of what cuckoos eat. This is a tale about the food of the cuckoo bird.

A2435.4.2.p: Explains why cranes suffer from thirst. A tale gives the reason cranes are always thirsty.

A2435.4.3.p: Explains why ravens suffer from thirst. A tale gives the reason ravens are always thirsty.

A2435.4.4.r: Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 242 (fish).—Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 372 No. 21.
A2435.4.4.p: Explains why the eagle eats the food it does. A mythological explanation for an animal's diet.

A2435.4.5.p: Explains why the buzzard eats the food it does.

A2435.4.5.1.p: Explains that vultures eat carrion (dead flesh) as their food, as the buzzard's diet.

A2435.4.6.p: Explains why hawks eat the food they do.

A2435.4.7.p: Explains why crows peck at the flesh of men, that is, of dead people.

A2435.4.7.1.p: Explains why the crow eats excrement (dung).

A2435.4.8.p: Explains why the cock (rooster) eats the food it does.

A2435.4.8.1.p: Explains why the rooster scratches the ground in search of food.

A2435.4.9.p: Explains why the owl eats the food it does.

A2435.4.9.1.p: Explains why the owl does not eat grain.

A2435.4.9.2.p: Explains why the owl does not drink water.

A2435.4.10.p: Explains why the jackdaw eats the food it does.

A2435.4.11.p: Explains why the wren eats the food it does.

A2435.4.11.1.p: Explains why the wren does not eat berries.

A2435.5.p: Explains why certain insects eat the food they do.

A2435.5.1.p: Explains why bees may not get honey from red clover flowers.

A2435.5.1.1.p: Explains why bees eat their own young (children, meaning larvae or offspring).

A2435.5.2.p: Explains why an insect fries human blood and eats it, as a mythological explanation of its feeding.

A2435.6.p: Explains why fish, reptiles and similar animals eat the food they do.

A2435.6.1.r: Jewish: Neuman; Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale 370 No. 21.
A2435.6.1.p: Explains why the tortoise eats the food it does.

A2435.6.2.r: Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 386; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2435.6.2.p: Explains what a snake eats. This is an origin story giving the reason snakes feed on what they do.

A2435.6.2.1.p: A snake sucks milk from a woman's breast. The tale explains why snakes feed in this way.

A2435.6.3.p: Explains why leeches feed on human blood.

A2436.p: Explains why animals do not have fire. They were sent to steal it for people but were lazy and failed.

A2440.p: A heading for explanations of how animals carry or hold their bodies, such as their posture and bearing.

A2441.p: A heading for explanations of how an animal moves on foot, meaning its gait or manner of walking.

A2441.1.p: A heading for explanations of how mammals walk or move their legs.

A2441.1.0.1.p: Explains why animals and people hop: the ground is so dry it cracks, so they must jump over the cracks.

A2441.1.1.p: Explains why monkeys walk the way they do.

A2441.1.2.p: Explains why baboons walk on all fours.

A2441.1.3.p: Explains why dogs walk the way they do.

A2441.1.4.p: Explains why hyenas walk the way they do.

A2441.1.5.p: Explains why wolverines walk the way they do.

A2441.1.6.p: Explains why skunks walk the way they do.

A2441.1.7.p: Explains why elephants walk the way they do.

A2441.1.8.p: Explains why oxen walk the way they do.

A2441.1.9.p: Explains why leopards walk the way they do.

A2441.1.10.p: Explains why cats walk the way they do.

A2441.1.11.p: Explains why hares move by hopping.

A2441.1.12.p: Explains why sheep walk the way they do, as an origin story for the animal's gait.

A2441.2.p: A general heading for stories explaining why birds walk the way they do, in the manner of their gait.

A2441.2.1.p: Explains why the raven hops rather than walks smoothly.

A2441.2.2.p: Explains why the dove walks with a graceful, dignified step.

A2441.3.p: A general heading for stories explaining why insects move the way they do.

A2441.3.1.p: Explains why the beetle crawls close to the ground.

A2441.3.2.p: Explains why the flea moves the way it does, by jumping or hopping.

A2441.3.3.p: Explains why the fly moves the way it does.

A2441.4.p: A general heading for stories explaining how reptiles and similar creatures move.

A2441.4.1.p: Explains why the snake keeps off the road or path.

A2441.4.2.p: Explains why the crab walks sideways.

A2441.4.4.p: Explains why the chameleon moves the way it does, slowly and deliberately.

A2442.p: A general heading for stories explaining how birds fly and the height at which they fly.

A2442.1.p: Explains why some birds fly high and others fly low.

A2442.1.1.p: Explains why certain birds are unable to fly high.

A2442.2.p: A general heading for stories explaining the particular way various birds fly.

A2442.2.1.p: Explains why the raven claps or flaps its wings while flying.

A2442.2.2.p: Explains why the cuckoo flies with difficulty and sings with its wings spread.

A2442.2.3.p: Explains why the lapwing (a bird) flies in a zigzag or curving path rather than in a straight line.

A2442.2.4.p: Explains the way the bluejay flies, giving a traditional reason for its characteristic flight.

A2442.2.5.p: Explains the manner of the hawk's flight, telling why it flies as it does.

A2442.2.6.p: Explains why water birds fly the way they do and why they dive as they do.

A2442.2.7.p: Explains the way the wild goose flies, such as its flight formation or path.

A2442.2.8.p: Explains the manner of the eagle's flight, telling why it flies as it does.

A2442.3.p: Tells how birds first came to take to the air and begin flying.

A2444.p: Explains the way an animal swims, telling why it moves through water as it does.

A2444.1.p: Explains why some fish swim in deep water while others stay near the surface.

A2444.2.p: Explains why dolphins swim by rising and sinking repeatedly through the water.

A2444.3.p: Explains the way the salmon swims through the water.

A2450.p: Explains why an animal has a particular daily job or occupation it performs.

A2451.p: Explains why an animal has the job of carrying things.

A2451.1.p: Explains why ants carry large loads or bundles many times their size.

A2452.r: *Dh III 272ff. (For animal’s favorite prey, see A2494, Why certain animals are enemies.)
A2452.p: Explains why an animal has the job of hunting for food.

A2452.1.p: Explains why dogs hunt, giving a traditional reason for their hunting behavior.

A2452.2.p: Explains why the stork must hunt and search for its own living rather than being fed.

A2452.3.p: Explains why hawks place the heads of mice and similar small animals on a heap of stones.

A2453.p: Explains why an animal has the job of gathering and storing things.

A2453.1.p: Explains why the ant gathers resin, a sticky tree sap.

A2455.p: Explains that a particular animal's way of life is stealing. It is a general heading for tales giving animals a thieving occupation.

A2455.1.p: Explains why the wolf is a thief, giving a tale of how the wolf came to steal for a living.

A2455.2.p: Explains why the swallow is a thief, giving a tale of how the swallow came to steal for a living.

A2455.3.p: Explains why the raven is a thief, because the raven lacks the Ten Commandments and bears a black mark on its breast.

A2455.4.p: Explains why the hen is unable to steal, giving a tale of why the hen cannot manage theft like other thieving animals.

A2455.5.p: Explains why the wolverine is a thief, giving a tale of how the wolverine came to steal for a living.

A2456.p: Explains that a particular animal's way of life is boring holes into things. It is a general heading for tales giving animals a boring occupation.

A2456.1.r: Am. Negro (North Carolina): Brown Collection I 633; Jamaica Negro: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 259 No. 53.
A2456.1.p: Explains why the woodpecker bores into wood, giving a tale of how the woodpecker came to drill holes in trees.

A2456.2.p: Explains why the wood-worm bores into wood, giving a tale of how the wood-worm came to eat its way through timber.

A2457.p: Explains that a particular animal's way of life is rolling something along. It is a general heading for tales giving animals a rolling occupation.

A2457.1.r: Jamaica Negro: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 258 No. 46.
A2457.1.p: Explains why the tumble-bug rolls balls of dung, giving a tale of how the beetle came to roll dung.

A2460.p: A general heading for explanations of animal behaviour in attacking and defending themselves.

A2461.p: A general heading for explanations of the means by which animals defend themselves.

A2461.1.p: Explains why the hare sleeps with its eyes open, which serves it as a defense against enemies.

A2461.2.p: Explains that the toad stays perfectly still when it hears footsteps, as a way of defending itself.

A2461.3.p: Explains that the killer whale uses its dorsal fin as a weapon.

A2461.4.p: Explains why the deer runs, stops, and then runs on again, as a way of defending itself.

A2462.p: A general heading for explanations of how particular animals behave when they are attacked.

A2462.1.p: Explains why the squirrel barks when it is attacked.

A2462.2.p: Explains why the beaver slaps its tail on the water and dives when it is attacked.

A2462.3.p: Explains why a mouse does not fight back when a cat attacks it. The mouse's passive behavior toward the cat is given a cause.

A2463.p: Explains how an animal attacks or fights, meaning the weapon or method it uses to harm others.

A2463.1.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 146 No. 28.
A2463.1.p: Explains why a leopard cannot catch an animal that passes it on the right side. The leopard's attack fails when its prey goes by on that side.

A2464.p: Explains why some animal refrains from attacking, so that a potential predator or enemy stays peaceful.

A2464.1.p: Explains why a lion does not attack a dog.

A2465.p: Explains how an animal is captured or caught by hunters or other creatures.

A2465.1.r: (Cf. Type 253.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 21 No. 118, XXXIII 55 No. 118.
A2465.1.p: Explains why fish are caught in nets, as an origin for the way fish are captured.

A2466.p: Explains how an animal behaves when it has been caught or seized.

A2466.1.r: Dh III 236f.—Am. Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 11 No. 3.
A2466.1.p: Explains why an opossum pretends to be dead when it is caught.

A2466.2.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 87 No. 15.
A2466.2.p: Explains why a turtle beats its forelegs against the ground or hands when it is caught.

A2468.p: Explains how an animal behaves at the moment of its death.

A2468.1.p: Explains why a shrew dies on the road.

A2468.2.p: Explains why a toad dries up after it dies.

A2468.3.p: Explains why a dragon is killed by fire.

A2470.p: Explains the habitual physical movements or actions that animals repeat regularly.

A2471.p: Explains why animals keep looking for or searching for something, so that their repeated seeking behavior has a cause.

A2471.1.r: (See A2275.5.5, A2232.8; also *Dh IV 129ff.)—Sébillot RTP ii 433; England, U.S.: Baughman.
A2471.1.p: Explains why dogs look at one another under the tail.

A2471.1.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *202; Prussian: Plenzat 10.
A2471.1.1.p: Explains why dogs sniff at one another. This is a more specific form of dogs inspecting each other under the tail.

A2471.2.p: Explains why hogs (pigs) keep inspecting one another while searching for a pancake.

A2471.3.p: Explains why a hawk or vulture hovers over a campfire, because it is looking for the speaker's grandmother.

A2471.4.p: Explains why a diver (loon-like waterbird) always looks at the sea.

A2471.5.p: Explains why the lynx keeps squinting as if gazing into the distance.

A2471.6.r: Jamaica negro: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 259 No. 48.
A2471.6.p: Explains why the dog is always looking around or staring about.

A2471.6.1.p: Explains why a dog glances back over its shoulder at the person who has beaten it.

A2471.6.2.p: Explains why dogs howl while gazing up at the sky.

A2471.7.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 128 No. 22.
A2471.7.p: Explains what hawks are constantly searching for while they look about.

A2471.8.p: Explains why the mason-wasp keeps looking for a fireplace.

A2471.9.p: Explains why all animals keep their eyes turned downward.

A2472.p: Explains why some animals chew the cud, regurgitating and rechewing food.

A2472.1.p: Explains why cows chew the cud.

A2473.p: Explains why some animals raise a leg, as in urinating.

A2473.1.r: Dh III 261.—Sébillot RTP II 436; Japanese: Ikeda.
A2473.1.p: Explains why dogs raise a hind leg when they urinate.

A2473.1.1.p: Explains why dogs leave their droppings or urine at crossroads.

A2473.2.p: Explains why pigs lift a leg when wallowing in mud.

A2474.p: Explains why some animals keep shaking their heads.

A2474.1.p: Explains why the lizard bobs its head up and down.

A2474.2.p: Explains why the hare shakes its head.

A2474.3.p: Explains why the owl shakes its head.

A2475.p: Explains why animals can smell things from far away.

A2475.1.p: Explains why deer can detect people by scent from a long distance.

A2476.p: Explains why animals constantly move their mouths, noses, or similar body parts.

A2476.1.p: Explains why the rabbit is always moving its mouth. The tale gives a mythical cause for this constant twitching or chewing motion.

A2477.p: A general explanation for why certain animals dig or push their snouts into the ground. It gives a mythical reason for this habit of rooting.

A2477.1.p: Explains why pigs root in the ground with their snouts. The tale gives a mythical cause for this digging habit.

A2477.2.p: Explains why hens scratch at the ground with their feet. The tale gives a mythical cause for this scratching habit.

A2478.p: Explains why some animals are always eating or chewing. The tale gives a mythical cause for this constant feeding.

A2478.1.p: Explains why the zebra is always eating or grazing. The tale gives a mythical cause for this constant feeding.

A2479.p: A general heading for other habitual body movements of animals, such as tail wagging, leaping, or snapping. The motifs under it give mythical causes for these habits.

A2479.1.p: Explains why the wagtail bobs its tail up and down. The tale gives a mythical cause for this habit.

A2479.2.p: Explains why the hare hops about in a light, skipping way like a leaf. The tale gives a mythical cause for this jumpy movement.

A2479.3.p: Explains why jackals make howling or yelping noises at night while searching for food. The tale gives a mythical cause for this nighttime calling.

A2479.4.p: Explains why the hedgehog curls up or draws itself up, out of shame at the sight of a good man. The tale gives this moral cause for the hedgehog's behavior.

A2479.6.p: Explains why caterpillars climb up trees. The tale gives a mythical cause for this climbing habit.

A2479.7.p: Explains why ants swarm over and attack every person. The tale gives a mythical cause for this habit of ants falling upon people.

A2479.8.p: Explains why the dog snaps at every fly. In the tale, a fly laughed at the dog while the dog was pretending to be dead, and this is the cause of the dog's fly-snapping.

A2479.9.p: Explains why flies buzz around the eyes of oxen. The tale gives a mythical cause for this habit.

A2480.p: A general heading for animal habits that happen at set times or seasons. The motifs under it explain why such regular patterns occur.

A2481.p: A general explanation for why some animals go into a long winter sleep or dormancy. The tale gives a mythical cause for hibernation.

A2481.1.r: Dh III 257.—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 53 No. 78**.
A2481.1.p: Explains why bears sleep through the winter in hibernation. The tale gives a mythical cause for this long winter sleep.

A2482.p: A general explanation for why some animals travel long distances seasonally from one region to another. The tale gives a mythical cause for migration.

A2482.1.r: Dh III 258.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 16 No. 86; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 87 No. 86.
A2482.1.p: Explains why swallows travel away and return each year in seasonal migration. The tale gives a mythical cause for this journey.

A2482.2.p: Explains why caribou make seasonal long-distance migrations from one region to another.

A2482.3.p: Explains why the wren does not migrate away for the winter like other birds.

A2483.p: Explains why certain animals shed their hair, skin, feathers or shell at regular intervals.

A2483.1.r: Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 88 No. 110a; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2483.1.p: Explains why a snake sheds its skin.

A2484.p: Explains why certain animals gather in large groups at particular times of the year.

A2484.1.p: Explains why fish arrive in large numbers at certain seasons.

A2486.p: Explains why animals lay their eggs in the particular way or at the particular time they do.

A2486.1.p: Explains why the raven lays its eggs in March.

A2486.2.p: Explains why the bustard hatches only two eggs.

A2486.3.p: Explains why the dove lays only two eggs.

A2486.4.p: Explains how birds came to start laying eggs.

A2489.p: Miscellaneous explanations of regular or periodic habits of animals that do not fit the more specific categories.

A2489.1.p: Explains why the rooster wakes people in the morning by crowing.

A2489.1.1.p: Explains why the rooster crows to greet the rising sun.

A2490.p: Explains other habits of animals that are not covered by the more specific categories.

A2491.p: Explains why certain animals avoid daylight or light.

A2491.1.r: (See A2275.5.3.)—Dh III 267.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3170; Legends No. 271; Japanese: Ikeda.
A2491.1.p: Explains why the bat flies only at night.

A2491.1.1.p: Explains why the bat sleeps during the day.

A2491.2.p: Explains why the owl avoids daylight.

A2491.3.p: Explains why the mole lives and burrows underground.

A2491.4.p: Explains why the tiger can see poorly in daylight but well at night. The tiger is said to have been cursed with this weak daytime sight.

A2491.5.p: Explains why grasshoppers and locusts keep out of sight during the day.

A2492.p: Explains why some animals live and travel in groups or herds while others do not.

A2492.1.p: Explains why jackals do not gather in herds or packs like some other animals.

A2492.2.p: Explains why birds do not form social groups or live together in communities.

A2493.r: Dh III 324ff.—Bödker Exempler 290 No. 45—46.—Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 86.
A2493.p: A general heading for tales explaining how various animals came to be friends, or why they are or are not friends.

A2493.0.1.p: Explains that domestic animals and wild animals were once friends, before their friendship ended.

A2493.1.p: Explains the friendship between the prairie-dog and the owl.

A2493.2.p: Explains the friendship between the bat and the owl.

A2493.3.p: Explains the friendship between the tiger and the buffalo.

A2493.4.p: Explains the friendship between a man and a dog.

A2493.5.p: Explains the friendship between the deer and the fish.

A2493.6.p: Explains the friendship between the squirrel and the quail.

A2493.7.p: Explains the friendship between the leopard-cat and the squirrel.

A2493.7.1.p: Explains the friendship between the leopard-cat and the night-jar, a variant within the leopard-cat and squirrel friendship tales.

A2493.8.p: Explains the friendship between the leopard and the goat.

A2493.9.p: Explains the friendship between the cat and the mouse.

A2493.9.1.p: Tells of a sworn oath of friendship between the cat and the rat, within the cat and mouse friendship tales.

A2493.10.p: Explains the friendship between the fox and the titmouse.

A2493.11.p: Explains the friendship between the jackal and the crocodile.

A2493.11.1.p: A friendship between a jackal and a crocodile, one of the animal friendships that explain animal habits.

A2493.11.2.p: A friendship between a jackal and an elephant, one of the animal friendships that explain animal habits.

A2493.11.3.p: A friendship between a jackal and a tiger, one of the animal friendships that explain animal habits.

A2493.11.3.1.p: A jackal and a tiger become partners in a business venture together.

A2493.11.4.p: A friendship between a jackal and a partridge, one of the animal friendships that explain animal habits.

A2493.12.p: A friendship between a turtle and a heron, one of the animal friendships that explain animal habits.

A2493.12.1.p: A friendship between a turtle and a wallaby, one of the animal friendships that explain animal habits.

A2602.p: A story in which the earth is planted, explaining how plants were first set on it.

A2610.p: A story in which plants arise by transformation, changing from some other being or thing into plants.

A2611.r: Dh I 79.—India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 23, 129; S. Am. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 128, (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A2611.p: A plant grows from the body of a person or animal that has been killed, so the plant is said to come from the slain body.

A2611.0.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Mono-Alu: Wheeler 67; S. Am. Indian (Brazil): Oberg 109, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 38, (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359f., (Cashinawa): Métraux ibid. 686.
A2611.0.1.p: A plant grows from the grave of a dead person or animal.

A2611.0.2.p: A plant grows from a fetus or from the body of a stillborn child.

A2611.0.3.p: A human afterbirth (placenta) turns into a plant.

A2611.0.4.p: Parts of a god's body turn into plants.

A2611.0.4.1.p: Women are changed into flowers, as part of the story of a god's body turning into plants.

A2611.0.5.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 130f. Nos. 85, 89; S. Am. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 128.
A2611.0.5.p: Parts of a human or animal body, such as a limb or organ, turn into plants.

A2611.1.r: (Cf. A2685.1.)—Babylonian: Spence 140; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 293 n. 77; S. Am. Indian (Amazon): Alexander Lat. Am. 292; Yunca (Peru): ibid. 225, (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 360, (Brazil): Oberg 108; (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A2611.1.p: Corn (maize or grain) grows from the body of a person who was killed.

A2611.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 23 No. 128. XXXIII 56 No. 128; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 152 No. 76; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 96 No. 125; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3240, Legends Nos. 326—337; S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 62.
A2611.2.p: Tobacco grows from the grave of a woman regarded as wicked.

A2611.2.1.p: Tobacco grows from the grave of a virgin.

A2611.3.r: Oceanic (Samoa, Union Group, Mangaia, Tahiti): Dixon 55; (Cook Is.): Beckwith Myth 104, (Solomon Is.): ibid. 104, (Papua): Ker 92, (Tuamotu): Beckwith Myth 103.
A2611.3.p: A coconut palm grows from the head of a monster that was slain.

A2611.4.p: A pepper plant grows from the body of a person who was killed.

A2611.5.r: (Cf. A2664.)—**Starck Der Alraun; *Taylor JAFL XXXI 561f.; Penzer III 153.; *Fb “alrunerod” IV 10a.
A2611.5.p: The mandrake plant grows from the blood of a person hanged on a gallows.

A2611.6.1.p: Grass grows from the hair of a person who was killed.

A2611.7.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3218, Legends No. 304.
A2611.7.p: Rue (a herb) is said to have arisen from drops of Christ's blood.

A2612.p: A plant grows from tears that someone or something has shed.

A2612.1.p: The tears of Adam and Eve, shed when they were expelled from paradise, become trees.

A2612.2.p: The tears of Mary at the Annunciation become daisies.

A2613.p: A plant comes into being from the spittle of a supernatural being.

A2613.1.r: (Cf. A2686.1.)—Dh II 107; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3230, Legends No. 325.
A2613.1.p: A mushroom grows from the spittle of a god.

A2615.p: An ordinary object is changed into a plant.

A2615.1.p: The Virgin Mary hides in the ground a nail meant for the cross, and thistles grow from it, explaining the origin of thistles.

A2615.2.p: A plant grows from milk that came from a mother, so the plant originates from transformed milk.

A2615.3.p: A canoe is transformed into a coconut palm tree.

A2616.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Labrador): Hawks GSCan XIV 152.
A2616.p: One kind of plant is changed into another kind of plant.

A2617.p: A person or animal is transformed into plants.

A2617.1.p: Living boys or girls are changed into plants.

A2617.2.p: Living animals are changed into plants.

A2620.p: Plants come into being because of an experience of a holy person.

A2621.p: Plants spring up where a holy person has walked or stepped.

A2621.1.p: Flowers grow from the ground under the feet of the Virgin Mary.

A2621.2.p: Plants grow where a goddess has trodden.

A2622.p: Saint Peter drops the key of heaven to earth in his excitement on learning a copy has been made; an angel returns it, and the primrose called Heaven Key grows where it fell.

A2623.p: A saint creates a plant as a cure for snakebite.

A2624.p: A plant grows from the staff of a holy person.

A2624.1.p: The thorn tree grows from the staff of Joseph of Arimathea.

A2625.p: Plants grow from the clothing of a god or deity.

A2630.p: Miscellaneous other ways that plants came into being.

A2631.p: A plant comes into being as a punishment imposed on someone for a wrong they committed.

A2631.1.p: After the first murder, thistles and other harmful plants began to grow; before that, only useful plants grew on earth.

A2631.1.1.p: Thistles and similar weeds are said to have appeared as punishment for the Fall of Man, the sin of the first humans.

A2632.p: A plant comes into being as a reward given to someone for a good deed or kindness.

A2632.1.p: A willow tree sheltered the Holy Family and was rewarded by becoming the weeping willow.

A2632.2.p: A tree grows from a plant set on the grave of the first father by Adam's son, and its wood is later used for Christ's crucifixion.

A2634.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Viracocha): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 550, (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 41.
A2634.p: Plants are created directly by the action of a god, without any other cause or story of transformation.

A2650.p: Stories explaining how particular flowers came to be.

A2651.p: A story explaining how the daisy came to exist.

A2653.p: A story explaining how the primrose came to exist.

A2654.r: Flemish: De Meyer FFC XXXVII 91 No. 251*.
A2654.p: A story explaining how the plant called "Mary's bed straw" (a wild thyme) came to be.

A2655.p: A story explaining how the bindweed, a climbing wild flower, came to be.

A2656.p: A story explaining how the rose came to exist.

A2656.1.p: A story explaining how the moss rose came to exist.

A2656.2.r: a variety of rose unknown before that time. England: Baughman.
A2656.2.p: The York and Lancaster rose grew from the dust and blood of those slain in the Wars of the Roses.

A2657.p: A story explaining how the forget-me-not flower came to exist.

A2658.p: A story explaining how the lady-slipper (a calceolaria hybrid) came to exist.

A2661.p: A story explaining how the snowdrop came to exist.

A2662.p: A story explaining how the hellebore plant came to exist.

A2663.p: A story explaining how the clove plant came to exist.

A2664.p: An origin tale explaining how the mandrake plant came to be.

A2665.p: An origin tale explaining how the wild morning glory came to be.

A2665.1.p: An origin tale explaining how the narcissus flower came to be.

A2666.p: An origin tale explaining how the rue plant came to be.

A2680.p: A general heading for origin tales about plant forms other than flowers and the trees listed beneath it.

A2681.r: (See A2612.1.)—Finnish: Kalevala rune 2; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 325—26; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2681.p: A general heading for origin tales explaining how particular kinds of trees came to be.

A2681.1.p: An origin tale explaining how the weeping willow came to be, often with its drooping branches tied to a sad event.

A2681.2.p: An origin tale explaining how the oak tree came to be.

A2681.3.p: Poplar trees arise when a god changes weeping maidens into them.

A2681.4.p: An origin tale explaining how birch trees came to be.

A2681.4.1.p: A tale telling how the first birch trees appeared in Ireland.

A2681.5.p: A general origin tale for palm trees.

A2681.5.1.r: (See A2611.3.)—Oceanic (Cove Is.): Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 104, (Tahiti): ibid. 101, (New Guinea): ibid. 102, (Marshall Is.): Davenport 223, (Marquesas): Handy 30.
A2681.5.1.p: An origin tale explaining how the coconut tree came to be.

A2681.6.p: An origin tale explaining how bamboo came to be.

A2681.7.p: An origin tale explaining how the sandalwood tree came to be.

A2681.8.p: An origin tale explaining how the dammar tree, a resin-producing tree, came to be.

A2681.9.p: An origin tale explaining how the mulberry tree came to be.

A2681.10.p: An origin tale explaining how the banyan tree came to be.

A2681.11.p: An origin tale explaining how the breadfruit tree came to be.

A2681.12.p: An origin tale explaining how the palm-wine tree, a palm yielding sap for drink, came to be.

A2681.13.p: Explains how the cedar tree came to exist. A myth origin for this particular tree.

A2682.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 128.
A2682.p: Explains how creeping or climbing vines (creepers) came into being.

A2683.p: Explains how grass came into being.

A2684.r: (Cf. A2685, A2691.2.)—Jibaro: Karsten, cf. JAFL XXXII 446; Tonga: Gifford 17f.; Japanese: Beckwith Myth 102.
A2684.p: Explains how cultivated, farmed plants came to be grown by people.

A2684.1.p: Explains how the flax plant came to be.

A2684.2.p: Explains how the hemp plant came to be.

A2684.2.1.p: Explains how the sorghum plant came to be, within the account of hemp's origin.

A2684.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 359.
A2684.3.p: Explains how the cotton plant came to be.

A2685.p: Explains how grain crops (cereals) came to be grown.

A2685.1.p: Explains how corn came to be.

A2685.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 172, (Tembé): Métraux ibid. 140, (Kaigua, Apapocuva-Guarani): Métraux ibid. 136, (Tenetehara): Wagley-Galvao BBAE CXLIII (3) 148.
A2685.1.1.p: Explains how maize came to be, as a form of corn.

A2685.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 10. No. 49, XXXIII 53 No. 49; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 143 No. 28; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2685.2.p: Explains why grain plants have straw. In one version the whole stalk once became grain, and the straw was left over to feed a dog.

A2685.3.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 23 No. 129; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2685.3.p: Explains how rye came to be.

A2685.4.p: Explains how barley came to be.

A2685.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Paressi): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 360, (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 128.
A2685.5.p: Explains how the manioc (cassava) plant came to be.

A2686.p: Explains how garden vegetables came to be grown.

A2686.1.p: Explains how mushrooms came into being.

A2686.2.p: Explains how peas came to be.

A2686.3.p: Explains how the pepper plant came into being, as an origin story for this vegetable.

A2686.3.1.p: Explains how the kava plant came to be, within the account of the pepper plant's origin.

A2686.4.p: Explains how edible roots, such as tubers, came to be.

A2686.4.1.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 242; S. Am. Indian (Brazil): Oberg 109.
A2686.4.1.p: A myth explaining how the sweet potato came to exist or to be grown.

A2686.4.2.p: A myth explaining how the taro plant, a starchy edible root, came to exist.

A2686.4.3.p: A myth explaining how the yam, an edible tuber, came to exist.

A2686.5.p: A myth explaining how the turmeric plant, a yellow spice root, came to exist.

A2686.6.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A2686.6.p: A myth explaining how beans, the edible pod-bearing plants, came to exist.

A2686.7.r: S. Am. Indian (Caingang): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 473.
A2686.7.p: A myth explaining how gourds, the hard-shelled squash-like fruits, came to exist.

A2686.8.p: A myth explaining how the cinnamon tree and its bark spice came to exist.

A2687.p: A general heading for myths explaining how various fruits came to exist.

A2687.1.p: A myth explaining how blood oranges, the red-fleshed citrus fruit, came to exist.

A2687.2.p: A myth explaining how melons came to exist.

A2687.3.p: A myth explaining how berries, small fleshy fruits, came to exist.

A2687.4.r: S. Am. Indian (Jivaro): Steward-Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 627.
A2687.4.p: A myth explaining how the pumpkin came to exist.

A2687.5.p: A myth explaining how the banana plant and its fruit came to exist.

A2688.p: A general heading for myths explaining how weeds, unwanted wild plants, came to exist.

A2688.1.r: (See A2615.1, A2631.1.)—Irish myth: Cross; Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 23 No. 130; Jewish: Neuman.
A2688.1.p: A myth explaining how thistles, prickly wild plants, came to exist.

A2688.1.1.r: Fb “torn” III 827a; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
A2688.1.1.p: A myth explaining how the thorn-bush, a prickly shrub, came to exist.

A2691.p: A general heading for myths explaining how narcotic, mind-altering plants came to exist.

A2691.1.p: A myth explaining how the coffee plant and its drink came to exist.

A2691.2.r: (See A2611.2, A2611.2.1.)—Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 131 No. 88; India: *Thompson-Balys; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 58; S. Am. Indian (Cariri): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 559.
A2691.2.p: A myth explaining how the tobacco plant came to exist.

A2691.3.p: A myth explaining how the ganja plant, cannabis, came to exist.

A2691.4.p: Explains how the opium plant came to exist, through a story about its origin.

A2691.5.p: Explains how the betel plant, whose leaf is chewed as a stimulant, came to exist, through a story about its origin.

A2692.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 686; Africa (Tonga): Gifford 27.
A2692.p: Explains how poisonous plants came into existence, through a story about their origin.

A2700.p: Explains why a plant has a particular trait or feature, giving a story as the reason.

A2710.p: A plant receives a distinctive trait as a reward for something good that it or its kind did.

A2711.p: A plant is given a special quality because it did something holy, kind, or good.

A2711.1.p: A plant is blessed for helping at the birth of Jesus.

A2711.2.p: Trees that were used to make the cross are given a special blessing.

A2711.2.1.p: The elder tree is never struck by lightning because its wood was used to make the cross.

A2711.3.r: Dh II 58ff.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 197f., 202ff.; Irish: Beal XXI 306.
A2711.3.p: A plant is blessed for helping a holy person who is fleeing danger.

A2711.4.r: (Cf. A2765.1.)—Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 152 No. 80 (fig); Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 94 No. 113 (pine).
A2711.4.p: A tree shelters Jesus from rain and as a reward stays green all year.

A2711.4.1.r: Blessed. *BP III 477; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 198f., 204.
A2711.4.1.p: The hazel tree gives the Virgin Mary shelter.

A2711.4.2.p: A thistle serves as a milk cup for the Virgin Mary, and so its leaves have white spots.

A2711.4.3.p: A plant receives its name because it served the Virgin Mary.

A2711.5.p: The rowan tree helps the god Thor get out of a river.

A2711.6.p: Ram blesses the plum tree, which is why the plum tree is so hardy.

A2711.7.p: The fig tree stays with the angels and is rewarded with the sap of all other trees.

A2720.p: A plant receives a lasting bad trait as punishment for a wrong deed.

A2721.p: A plant is cursed for a wicked or disrespectful act and so acquires a lasting flaw.

A2721.1.p: A plant is cursed for failing to help, or for harming, the child Jesus.

A2721.2.r: (Cf. A2711.2.)—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3222, Legends No. 323.
A2721.2.p: A plant is cursed by a holy figure as punishment for its part in the crucifixion of Jesus.

A2721.2.1.r: (Cf. A2751.3.1, A2751.3.2, A2755.2, A2762.1, A2775.)—Dh II 207ff.—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 23 No. 131, XXXIII 56 No. 131; Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 152 No. 77; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 94 No. 108; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 636.
A2721.2.1.p: A tree is cursed for being used as the cross on which Jesus was crucified.

A2721.2.1.1.p: The aspen tree is cursed for having been used as the cross at the crucifixion, which is said to explain why its leaves tremble.

A2721.2.1.2.p: The poplar tree is cursed for having been used as the cross at the crucifixion.

A2721.2.1.3.p: The cottonwood tree is cursed for having been used as the cross at the crucifixion.

A2721.2.1.4.p: The elder tree is cursed for having been used as the cross at the crucifixion.

A2721.2.2.p: Plants have marks or notches because Christ bit them during the crucifixion.

A2721.3.p: A plant is punished because it gave an ungracious or rude answer to a holy person.

A2721.3.1.r: Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 152 No. 78; cf. Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 96 No. 124; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3016.
A2721.3.1.p: A man tells Jesus he is sowing stones, and as punishment he is given stones, which is why peas do not soften when boiled.

A2721.3.2.p: A farmer tells a begging monk that his potatoes are as hard as stones, and as a result potatoes became hard, which is why they are hard.

A2721.4.p: A plant is cursed because it betrayed a holy person who was fleeing from enemies.

A2721.5.r: Dh II 236ff.; **Taylor “The Gallows of Judas Iscariot” Washington University Studies (Humanistic series) IX (1922) 135ff.
A2721.5.p: A tree on which Judas hanged himself is cursed.

A2721.6.p: The mogli flower and the lime tree are cursed by gods, which explains why they have their characteristics.

A2721.7.p: Trees failed to come to a god when he was leaving, and as punishment they now bear bitter fruit.

A2721.8.p: The earth is punished for disobedience at the fall of man by having its trees become barren.

A2722.p: A plant is punished for disobeying.

A2722.1.p: The plantain disobeys its mother and so bears only one stalk.

A2723.p: A plant is punished for being discontented.

A2723.1.r: Always discontented. Finally has needles again. (Cf. A2767.1.)—*Dh III 337.—Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 94 No. 114.
A2723.1.p: A discontented pine tree is the reason pine trees have needles; in some versions it was given silk or glass leaves instead.

A2723.2.p: God changes a plant's nature to punish a man for wasting it, so the plant's yield is reduced.

A2725.p: A plant is punished for being late, and its characteristics are given as the penalty. This is a myth explaining why a plant has a certain trait.

A2725.1.p: The ash tree arrived late when qualities were handed out at creation, so its buds last only a short time or come out late. This explains why its buds are slow to open.

A2726.p: A plant is punished for telling tales or gossiping, and its characteristics are given as the penalty.

A2726.1.p: A banana that tells tales is cursed, and the curse spreads to all other bananas. This explains a trait shared by bananas.

A2730.p: A group of miscellaneous myths giving various other reasons why plants have their characteristics.

A2731.p: A plant gets its characteristics because of a transformation, where a person or creature changes into the plant or its parts.

A2731.1.r: N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 304 n. 1091.
A2731.1.p: A trickster's burnt flesh turns into the gum that oozes from trees. This explains why tree gum exists.

A2731.2.r: (Cf. A2755.3.1, A2755.3.2.)—Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 82 n. 2, 86 n. 2.
A2731.2.p: A plant gets its characteristics from tears that fall and become the plant or its traits.

A2731.2.1.p: A plant gets its characteristics from tears shed by the Virgin Mary.

A2731.2.1.1.p: A plant gets its characteristics from milk of the Virgin Mary.

A2731.3.p: Blood from a wizard who tried to kill the sun turns into the red grain of the cedar. The wizard's bleeding head was placed on top of a tree.

A2731.4.p: Agar-tree has magic properties because it came from a transformed magician.

A2733.p: The poppy gets its characteristics through a series of reincarnations, with opium producing each of the appropriate qualities.

A2734.p: A plant gets its characteristics from an object thrown by the devil.

A2734.1.p: The devil angrily throws sand at an aspen, which is why its bark is rough. The devil was angered because aspens never stop quivering.

A2734.2.r: (Cf. A2755.3.)—Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 4 No. 10. Cf. Type 153.
A2734.2.p: The devil throws tar at a tree, which is why there is tar in the tree's heartwood.

A2736.p: An evil spirit out of spite puts bark and thorns on a tree.

A2738.p: Christ puts knots in wood. Peter, angry at carpenters, wants Christ to put iron knots in wood, but Christ makes hard knots that are not iron.

A2741.p: A plant gets its characteristics by accident, from something that happened to the original plant.

A2741.1.r: (Cf. A2793.1, F1025.1.)—Type 295.—Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 90 No. 126a; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 95 No. 121.
A2741.1.p: A bean laughs so hard that it splits, and this causes the black stripe on it.

A2741.2.p: Yams were dropped by a bird and split open, which explains why some yams are good to eat and others are bad.

A2741.3.p: The sky once rested on the tops of trees, which flattened their leaves; this explains why leaves are flat.

A2741.4.p: A bush lost its clothes in a shipwreck, and as a result it now catches passersby who are looking for clothes.

A2741.5.p: The khijur tree has long, narrow leaves because it was split with an arrow.

A2742.p: Plants get their characteristics because they exchanged qualities with one another.

A2743.p: A plant has a particular characteristic because it belongs to the devil.

A2743.1.p: The fuchsia belongs to the devil, which is why its flowers are shaped like balls and have red petals.

A2750.p: Explanations for why the inside and the bark of plants are the way they are.

A2751.p: Explanations for why the bark of plants has the features it has.

A2751.1.p: An explanation for how bark came to be on plants at all.

A2751.2.p: Explanations for how the bark of a plant feels or is textured.

A2751.2.1.p: Explains why the bark of the aspen tree is rough.

A2751.2.2.p: Explains why the bark of the red willow is thin.

A2751.2.3.p: Explains why the tinsa tree has no bark at the bottom of its trunk.

A2751.3.p: Explanations for markings that appear on the bark of plants.

A2751.3.1.r: (See A2721.2.1, A2721.2.2, A2732.)—Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 90 No. 130b.
A2751.3.1.p: Explains the notches or dents in the stalk of a reed.

A2751.3.2.p: Explains the cross-shaped marks found on certain trees.

A2751.4.p: Explanations for why the bark of a plant has the color it has.

A2751.4.1.r: Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 94 No. 110; Flemish: DeMeyer FFC XXXVII 91 No. 132f.
A2751.4.1.p: Explains why the birch tree has white bark.

A2751.4.2.p: Explains why the ebony tree is black.

A2751.4.3.p: Explains why the tamarind tree has black bark.

A2751.4.4.p: Explains why the bark of the saja and tinsa trees is white.

A2751.4.5.p: Explains why broom-corn has blood-red spots on it.

A2751.4.6.p: Explains why the kava plant is grey in color.

A2752.p: Explains the origin of thorns growing on plants.

A2752.1.p: Explains why the bombax (silk-cotton) tree has thorns.

A2755.p: Explains the origin of the inner parts of plants, such as their wood, pith, and sap.

A2755.1.p: Explains why the grain or heartwood of the cedar is red.

A2755.2.p: Explains why the sap of some trees is blood-colored.

A2755.2.1.p: Explains why the saja tree produces no sap.

A2755.3.p: Explains the origin of tar found in the heart of trees.

A2755.3.1.p: Explains how amber came to be found in poplar trees.

A2755.3.2.p: Explains the origin of the gum found in the myrrh tree.

A2755.4.p: Explains the origin of knots in wood.

A2755.4.1.p: Explains why the saja tree has knots.

A2756.p: Explains why bamboo has joints or nodes along its stem.

A2757.p: Explains why some reeds have hollow stems.

A2760.p: Explains the origin of plant leaves in general.

A2760.1.p: Explains why all trees have leaves.

A2761.p: Explains the origin of the shape of plant leaves.

A2761.1.p: Explains why the edges of oak leaves are cut into notches or lobes rather than smooth.

A2761.2.p: Explains why vine leaves are shaped like a hand with spread fingers.

A2761.3.p: Explains why plant leaves are flat and broad rather than some other form.

A2782.p: Explains why wood burns. The tale gives a mythic reason for wood's ability to catch fire.
